layers.text: After days without water, Israel came to Marah and found water at last, but it was too bitter to drink. The verse adds that this is how the place got its name.

layers.evidence: Wesley and the Companion Bible give Marah the meaning bitterness or bitter. Clarke and Gill say the place was named from its bitter water, as the verse itself says. Hebrew marah and marim, bitter, share the same root.
layers.text: Marah means bitter. The water there was marim, bitter, so the place was named Marah. In Hebrew the name and the reason for it sound almost the same, so the name itself remembers the bitter water.

passages.saying: It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: In the desert, the hungry Israelites find thin flakes on the ground after the dew lifts, like nothing they have seen before. Moses tells them it is bread from the LORD. They will eat it for forty years, until they reach Canaan.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: man, what? (H4478B), in 16:15, found only here, and man, manna (H4478A), in 16:31. The same verse then uses the ordinary Hebrew word for what, mah, in "they did not know what it was." The naming story is the Bible's own explanation.
layers.text: When they first see it they ask, man hu (said mahn hoo), "What is it?" And the food keeps the question as its name: they "called the bread manna," man in Hebrew. For forty years Israel's daily bread was called What-is-it.

passages.saying: He named the place Massah and Meribah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and the story of Exodus 17:1-6.
layers.text: Moses named the place where God gave water from the rock after the people's sin there. They had quarreled with Moses and tested the LORD by doubting whether He was with them at all.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Matthew Henry, Wesley and the Companion Bible all explain Massah as temptation or testing and Meribah as strife or contention, matching the two reasons the verse gives.
layers.text: Each name matches one of the two reasons in the verse. Massah means testing, because the people tested (nasah) the LORD. Meribah means quarreling, because they quarreled (riv) with Moses. The place kept the memory of their sin.

passages.saying: Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse after the victory over Amalek in Exodus 17:8-13.
layers.text: After Israel defeated Amalek, Moses built an altar to thank God for the victory and gave it a name that gave the credit to the LORD.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Gill, F. C. Cook (Barnes' Notes), Wesley, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all give the name as Jehovah my banner. Gill, Clarke and Matthew Henry link the banner to Moses' hands and rod held up during the battle.
layers.text: The altar's name, YHWH Nissi, means the LORD is my banner. A nes was a pole or flag raised high for soldiers to rally around. Moses had held up his hands with God's staff through the battle like a raised banner, and the name says the LORD Himself is Israel's banner who gave the victory.

passages.saying: I have been a foreigner in a foreign land
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Exodus 18:2-3, read with Gill's note on the sons Jethro brought.
layers.text: Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought Moses' wife Zipporah and her two sons to him in the wilderness. The first son was Gershom, a name Moses gave him while living as an outsider in Midian.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley and the Companion Bible all give the sense of Gershom as a stranger; Gill renders it there I was a stranger, the very reason the verse gives, and says the name taught the boy that Midian was not his proper country. The name was first given at his birth in Exodus 2:22.
layers.text: Gershom sounds like ger sham, a foreigner there. Moses chose the name in Midian to mark his years as an outsider, and it is explained again as the boy rejoins him. Moses also meant it as a lesson for his son: he too was a stranger, even in Midian where he was born.

passages.saying: The other son was named Eliezer
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and Moses' escape from Pharaoh in Exodus 2:15.
layers.text: Moses' second son was named to remember how God had rescued Moses when Pharaoh sought to kill him. The name was a lasting thank you for God's help.

layers.evidence: Gill and Wesley both explain Eliezer as my God is help and connect it to Moses' rescue from Pharaoh, as the verse itself does.
layers.text: Eliezer means my God is help. Eli means my God, and ezer means help. Moses explains the name with the same word: the God of his father was his helper (ezer) and saved him from the sword of Pharaoh.

passages.saying: Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the fourth commandment, Exodus 20:8-11.
layers.text: This verse gives the reason for the Sabbath command. The LORD made the heavens, the earth, the sea and everything in them in six days and rested on the seventh, so He blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.

layers.evidence: Gill says the command draws on what was recorded in the creation account. Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley both point to Genesis 2:3, where God rested on the seventh day and blessed and sanctified it. Both verses use the words for seventh, blessed and made holy.
layers.text: The reason given for the Sabbath points back to the first week. In Genesis 2:3 God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it He rested from His work. Exodus names the same rest, blessing and holiness, so the Sabbath Israel kept was rooted in the day God set apart at creation.

passages.saying: place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse with Leviticus 24:5-9, which describes the loaves.
layers.text: God told Moses to keep special bread on the golden table in the tabernacle at all times. The loaves were set before the LORD and replaced with fresh ones each Sabbath, so the table was never empty.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech name the play panim lephanai a paronomasia. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch say the bread was called bread of the face because it lay before God's face, and Gill says the same.
layers.text: In Hebrew the bread is lechem panim, literally bread of the face, and it is to lie lephanai, before My face. The same word for face is used twice, so the bread's name tells where it belonged: always in the LORD's presence.

passages.saying: See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint and the Mishnah named as ancient witnesses.

layers.text: God tells Moses to build a sanctuary "so that I may dwell among them," and to make it "according to the pattern I show you." The tent and its furniture follow a pattern Moses was shown on the mountain.

Hebrews quotes this verse and draws the conclusion: the earthly sanctuary "is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven." So Christ "did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself."

layers.evidence: TBESH: tavnit, pattern, plan, form. Abbott-Smith (in TBESG) lists typos for tavnit in the Septuagint of Exodus 25:40 (in 25:9 the Septuagint has paradeigma). TAGNT: typos in Hebrews 8:5 and Romans 5:14
layers.text: "Pattern" is tavnit, a plan or form. The Greek Old Testament renders it typos here, and Hebrews keeps that word when it quotes the verse. Paul uses the same typos when he calls Adam "a pattern of the One to come."

layers.evidence: Strong's: kapporet, from kaphar, a lid, used only of the cover of the sacred ark; the Septuagint has hilasterion, as does Hebrews 9:5 (Abbott-Smith, in TBESG). On Romans 3:25 Ellicott and Gill note the Septuagint word for the mercy seat; Richard Mayo (Poole's Annotations) and Bengel hear the mercy seat, while Barnes and Ellicott lean to an atoning sacrifice.
layers.text: The ark's lid, the "mercy seat," is kapporet, from kipper, "to atone," and was sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement. In Greek it is hilasterion, Paul's word for Christ: God "presented Him as the atoning sacrifice." Whether he means the lid is debated.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (in TBESG): katapetasma is chiefly the veil of the Most Holy Place in the Septuagint, and His flesh in Hebrews 10:20. JFB on Hebrews 10:20: the temple veil, a type of His flesh, was torn as He died
layers.text: Behind the veil only the high priest could go, "once a year, and never without blood." When Jesus died, "the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom," and Hebrews speaks of "the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body."

Hebrews says the floor plan itself carried a message: "the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing." Christ "entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood."

layers.evidence: Mishnah Yoma 5:1, paraphrased. Adam Clarke on Hebrews 9:28 hears an allusion to the high priest's return from the inner tabernacle to bless the people waiting for him in the court.
layers.text: On the Day of Atonement the people waited for the high priest to come out; by Jewish tradition he kept his prayer short so as not to alarm them. One commentator hears this in Hebrews: Christ "will appear a second time" to "those who eagerly await Him."

passages.saying: Then I will make you into a great nation.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the setting: God speaks after Israel's worship of the golden calf, and Moses then pleads for them (Exodus 32:11-14).
layers.text: After Israel worshiped the golden calf, God told Moses to leave Him alone so that His anger could destroy the people, and He offered to make Moses into a great nation instead. The words showed how great His anger was and put Moses to the test as the one who prays for the people.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say that even if the nation were destroyed, God would keep His promise in Moses and make of him a great nation, as He had promised Abraham in Genesis 12:2. The Hebrew wording of the two promises is almost the same.
layers.text: Some hear in God's offer the words of His first promise to Abraham: I will make you into a great nation (Genesis 12:2). On this reading, even if Israel were wiped out, God could keep that promise through Moses, a descendant of Abraham. Moses passed the test and pleaded for the people instead.

passages.saying: the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the command itself, given as God renews the covenant after the golden calf.
layers.text: Israel must not bow down to any other god, because the LORD is a jealous God. In God, jealousy is not petty rage but holy, just displeasure when the worship that belongs to Him alone is given to another.

layers.evidence: Gill says God's name and nature answer to one another and compares His jealousy to a husband's over his marriage. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the LORD's being called Jealous means He had revealed Himself as jealous.
layers.text: Here Jealous (qanna) is given as the LORD's very name, and then His nature is described with the same word: He is a jealous God. His name and His nature match. Like a husband who guards his marriage, He will not let His people give their worship to any other god.

passages.saying: a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the burnt offering law of Leviticus 1:3-9, where the whole animal is burned on the altar.
layers.text: After the inner parts and legs were washed, the priest burned the whole animal on the altar. It went up in smoke as a gift to God, and He accepted it with pleasure, like a pleasing aroma.

layers.evidence: Clarke renders the phrase an odour of rest. Keil and Delitzsch explain it as God's gracious acceptance of the sacrifice and point to Genesis 8:21. The Companion Bible notes that Genesis 8:21 is the first place the word nihoah occurs, that it is found only in this connection, and that it means rest.
layers.text: Pleasing aroma is reiach nichoach in Hebrew, a smell of rest. The phrase first appears after the flood, when Noah offered burnt offerings and the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma (Genesis 8:21). Israel's burnt offerings use the same words for God gladly accepting a sacrifice.

passages.saying: fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Leviticus 10:1, where Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire, and 10:5, where they are carried out still in their tunics.
layers.text: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu brought an offering of fire that the LORD had not commanded. Fire from the LORD struck them, and they died there before Him. It killed them without burning up their bodies or their clothes.

layers.evidence: Samuel Clark (Barnes' Notes) and Keil and Delitzsch both say the fire that had just shown God's pleasure in Aaron's service now destroyed his sons. The Companion Bible sets the fire of true worship (9:24) beside the fire of judgment (10:2), and Clarke makes the same point. The Hebrew of the two verses opens with the same words.
layers.text: This verse repeats the words of Leviticus 9:24. On the priests' first day, fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the offering, and the people rejoiced. Now, in the same words, fire consumes Nadab and Abihu. The fire that accepted true worship judged false worship.

passages.saying: The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the writers named under each note, and the cross-references from OpenBible.info, with the Mishnah and the Talmud named as ancient witnesses.

layers.text: On the Day of Atonement two goats make one sin offering. One is sacrificed; over the other the high priest confesses "all the iniquities" of Israel, puts them on its head, and sends it away alive into the wilderness.

layers.evidence: The Hebrew is la-azazel. TBESH: Azazel, meaning uncertain. Strong's: goat of departure, which Tyndale (1530) rendered scapegoat. Samuel Clark (Barnes' Notes) derives it from a root meaning to remove or separate; Ellicott, Clark and Keil and Delitzsch take it as the name of an evil spirit. The solitary place (gezerah) is a land cut off: Ellicott, Clark, Keil and Delitzsch; TBESH: a separation
layers.text: The goat is "for Azazel," a word of uncertain meaning. It has been read as "goat of departure," which gave English "scapegoat," or "entire removal"; many commentators take it as the name of an evil spirit. In any case, it goes to a land "cut off," with no way back.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: nasa (H5375) and avonot (H5771) in Leviticus 16:22, avonot in Isaiah 53:11, nasa in 53:12. Ellicott and JFB on Hebrews 9:28: taken from Isaiah 53:12. Pulpit and Gill on Leviticus 16:22 link the goat with Isaiah 53
layers.text: The goat "will carry" (nasa) Israel's "iniquities" (avonot). Isaiah's suffering Servant "will bear their iniquities" (avonot) and "bore the sin of many" (nasa). Hebrews applies that last line to Jesus: "Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many."

layers.evidence: Pulpit and Gill on Hebrews 13:11: the allusion is to the sin offerings of the Day of Atonement
layers.text: On that day the bodies of the sin offerings whose blood went into the Most Holy Place were burned "outside the camp." Hebrews draws the line to the cross: "Jesus also suffered outside the city gate," so "let us go to Him outside the camp."

layers.evidence: Rabbi Yishmael in Mishnah Yoma 6:8; Talmud Yoma 39b. Both paraphrased. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Isaiah 1:18 report the tradition, and JFB that it stopped forty years before Jerusalem fell.
layers.text: An early rabbi taught that a crimson strip turned white when the goat reached the wilderness, citing "Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow." Later tradition says it stopped turning white in the forty years before the temple fell.

layers.evidence: Epistle of Barnabas 7; Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 40
layers.text: Early Christian writers saw Christ in both goats. One reads the cursed goat, sent away with scarlet wool on its head, as a picture of Jesus; another says the two goats point to Christ's two appearances. Leviticus does not say this itself.

passages.saying: the life of the flesh is in the blood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the ban on eating blood in Leviticus 17:10-14, for which this verse gives the reason.
layers.text: Israel must not eat blood, because a creature's life is in its blood. God gave the blood for one use only: on the altar, where it makes atonement for His people.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that soul here is the Hebrew nephesh, because the soul is the life, so that one life is put in place of another. Keil and Delitzsch say the soul of the animal was offered on the altar as a substitute for the human soul.
layers.text: One Hebrew word, nefesh, runs through this verse. It is translated life, souls and soul. The animal's nefesh, its life in the blood, is given on the altar to make atonement for the people's nefesh. One life is given in place of another.

passages.saying: you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint, the Mishnah, the Talmud and Philo named as ancient witnesses.

layers.text: When harvest began, the first sheaf was waved before the LORD "on the day after the Sabbath." From that day Israel counted seven weeks, "fifty days," to the Feast of Weeks.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Leviticus 23:10: aparche (G536); Abbott-Smith (in TBESG) cites it of Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:20 and 23. Ellicott and Pulpit on 1 Corinthians 15:20: the firstfruits stood for the whole harvest
layers.text: Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep": "Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him." His word, aparche, is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for this sheaf, the pledge of the whole harvest.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry's Concise on Leviticus 23:10, and JFB, Bengel and Gill on 1 Corinthians 15:20, note that Christ rose on the day the sheaf was offered. Mishnah Menachot 10:3 records the dispute over the date with the Boethusians
layers.text: The sheaf was waved "on the day after the Sabbath," and Jesus' tomb was found empty "very early on the first day of the week," the day after the Passover Sabbath. Some commentators note the match, though Jewish groups disputed which Sabbath Leviticus meant.

layers.evidence: TBESG (Abbott-Smith): pentekostos, fiftieth, the fiftieth day after Passover. TAHOT: chamishim, fifty, in Leviticus 23:16. Barnes on Acts 2:1 calls it a harvest festival, the Feast of Harvest and the Feast of Weeks
layers.text: Pentecost is Greek for "fiftieth": the Feast of Weeks at the end of the fifty-day count, the feast of "the firstfruits of the wheat harvest." On that day the Spirit came, and "about three thousand were added to the believers."

layers.evidence: Talmud Pesachim 68b (Rabbi Elazar), paraphrased. Barnes on Acts 2:1: later Jews kept Pentecost for the giving of the law, but there is no trace of this in the Old Testament
layers.text: Israel reached Sinai "in the third month," the season of this feast, and later Jewish tradition remembered it as the day the law was given, though the Old Testament itself never says so. The law came at Sinai; the Spirit came at Pentecost.

layers.evidence: Philo, On the Decalogue 46 (Yonge translation), paraphrased. Ellicott on Acts 2:2 hears Sinai's trumpet in the sound from heaven; Matthew Henry and Clarke on Acts 2:1 set the fire and thunder of Sinai beside Pentecost's wind and tongues of fire; Barnes on Acts 2:3 names Sinai's fire among signs of God's presence.
layers.text: Sinai came with fire and a ram's-horn blast; Pentecost brings "tongues like flames of fire," and each hears "his own language." A Jewish writer of Jesus' own day pictured the voice at Sinai as a flame that spoke in a language its hearers knew.

passages.saying: I made the Israelites dwell in booths
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the command of Leviticus 23:42 to live in booths for seven days, which this verse explains.
layers.text: Each year, for a week, Israel was to live in booths, so that every generation would remember how God sheltered His people in booths on the journey out of Egypt.

layers.evidence: Gill (on this verse) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (on Exodus 12:37) link the feast with Succoth, Israel's first camp, whose name means booths. Clarke, F. C. Cook (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible also give booths as the meaning of Succoth, though Cook notes a similar Egyptian name for the district.
layers.text: Israel's first camp after leaving Egypt was Succoth, a name that means booths (Exodus 12:37). Some think the place was named for the shelters Israel put up there, and that this feast also looks back to that first camp.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the Feast of Tabernacles was kept in thankful memory of Israel dwelling in booths in the wilderness. Keil and Delitzsch say living in booths was the main point of the feast and explain sukkah as a booth or hut, not a tent.
layers.text: The Feast of Tabernacles is in Hebrew the feast of Sukkot, which means booths (Leviticus 23:34). It is named for the huts of branches the people lived in for seven days, and this verse explains them: they recall how God gave Israel booths to live in on the way out of Egypt.

passages.saying: proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants. It shall be your Jubilee
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Dead Sea Scroll 11QMelchizedek named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Every fiftieth year Israel was to "proclaim liberty in the land": land went back to the family that held it, and Israelites who had sold themselves were "released in the Year of Jubilee." The land was God's: "it is Mine."

layers.evidence: TBESH: yovel, ram's horn, and the jubilee year marked by its blowing. Ellicott on Leviticus 25:10: yobel signifies both ram's horn and the sound emitted from it. Poole and Benson give the ram's horn as one of two derivations of the name (the other is Jubal). Keil and Delitzsch on Leviticus 25:9: liberty could begin only with the full forgiveness of sins.
layers.text: Jubilee is yovel, "ram's horn": the year is named for the horn that announced it. The horn sounded "on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement," so liberty began on the day Israel's sins were atoned for.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qara (H7121) with deror (H1865) in both Leviticus 25:10 and Isaiah 61:1. JFB and Ellicott on Luke 4:19 see the Jubilee here
layers.text: Isaiah's anointed one is sent "to proclaim liberty to the captives" and "the year of the LORD’s favor." "Proclaim liberty" is the Jubilee's own phrase, qara deror. The prophet takes the Jubilee as a picture of the great release God will bring.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Luke 4:19: the primary reference is to the year of Jubilee, which was to our Lord, as to Isaiah, the type of the year of the divine kingdom. JFB and Barnes on Luke 4:19 also hear the jubilee
layers.text: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads this passage, rolls up the scroll, and says, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing." Commentators hear the Jubilee in "the year of the Lord’s favor": Jesus announces Himself as its fulfillment.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (in TBESG): aphesis stands for yovel and deror in the Septuagint; release in Luke 4:18, and pardon of sins. TAGNT: 17 uses in the New Testament, two in Luke 4:18 and 15 of sins, as in Luke 24:47
layers.text: Luke's word for "liberty" is aphesis, which the Greek Old Testament uses for the Jubilee and its liberty. In the New Testament it usually means "forgiveness," as in "repentance and forgiveness of sins." Release and forgiveness are one word.

layers.evidence: JFB on Luke 4:19: the day of vengeance was only to come on the rejecters of His message. JFB on Isaiah 61:2: the acceptable year runs from His first to His second coming. Barnes on Isaiah 61:2 also notes where He stopped
layers.text: Jesus rolls up the scroll mid-sentence, after "the year of the Lord’s favor," before Isaiah's "and the day of our God’s vengeance." Commentators note the stop: the time of favor runs from His first coming to His second, and vengeance falls only on those who reject His message.

layers.evidence: 11QMelchizedek (11Q13), first century BC, cites Leviticus 25:13 and Isaiah 61 and names Melchizedek as the heavenly deliverer, as F. F. Bruce describes it ("The Background to the Son of Man Sayings", 1982). The scroll sets the release on a Day of Atonement at the end of the tenth jubilee.
layers.text: A Dead Sea Scroll read Leviticus 25 and Isaiah 61 together about the last days: Melchizedek, a heavenly deliverer, proclaims liberty and release to the captives in the tenth and last jubilee.

passages.saying: the crown of consecration to his God is upon his head
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the BSB wording of the verse and Wesley's note on it.
layers.text: Even if his father, mother, brother or sister dies, a Nazirite must not make himself unclean by going near the body, because his uncut hair marks him as set apart to God for the time of his vow.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch derive Nazir from nazar, to separate, and say the uncut hair is called in this verse the diadem of his God, like the golden diadem on the high priest's turban in Exodus 29:6. The Pulpit Commentary makes the same comparison and says the diadem is called nezer, from the same root as nazir.
layers.text: The word for consecration here is nezer, from the same root as Nazirite, one who is separated. Nezer is also the word for the holy diadem on the high priest's turban (Exodus 29:6). So the Nazirite's uncut hair is his separation to God, worn like a crown on his head.

passages.saying: So that place was called Taberah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the BSB wording of the verse and Wesley's note on it.
layers.text: After the people complained and the LORD's fire broke out at the edge of the camp, the place was named Taberah, so that it would be remembered that the fire of the LORD had burned among them.

layers.evidence: Gill, T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes), Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all explain Taberah as burning. The name and the verb burned in this verse share the Hebrew root ba'ar.
layers.text: Taberah means burning. The place was named for what happened there, because the fire of the LORD had burned among them. The name and the verb burned (ba'ar) come from the same Hebrew root.

passages.saying: So they called that place Kibroth-hattaavah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the BSB wording of the verse and Wesley's note on it.
layers.text: After the LORD struck the people with a plague while they ate the quail, the place was named Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had craved meat instead of the manna.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and the Companion Bible render the name graves of lust, and Keil and Delitzsch graves of greediness, because there the people found their graves while giving vent to their greedy desires.
layers.text: Kibroth-hattaavah means graves of craving. Both parts of the name echo the verse: kivrot (graves) matches qavru (they buried), and hattaavah (the craving) matches the people who craved (mit'avvim).

passages.saying: Moses gave to Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the writers named under each note, and the cross-references from OpenBible.info, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Joshua son of Nun was Moses' "young assistant." Moses gave him his new name (Numbers records it with the spies, though Exodus already calls him Joshua), and after Moses died God told him to "cross over the Jordan into the land."

layers.evidence: TBESH: Hoshea, salvation; Joshua, Jehovah is salvation. Strong's: from the LORD's name and yasha, to save. Ellicott on Numbers 13:16: Hoshea means help, or salvation; Joshua, Jehovah is help, or salvation
layers.text: Hoshea means "salvation." Moses adds Yeho-, a short form of God's name, and makes Yehoshua, which means that the LORD is salvation. The new name says who saves.

layers.evidence: TBESG (Abbott-Smith): Iesous is Jesus in Matthew 1:21 and Joshua in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8. NET Bible note on Matthew 1:21: the name is the Hebrew Yeshua (Joshua), meaning Yahweh saves
layers.text: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are one name, Iesous; the BSB writes "Joshua" for it in Acts 7:45. So the angel's words rest on its Hebrew meaning, "Yahweh saves": "you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins."

layers.evidence: Gill on Hebrews 4:8: Hoshea, Joshua and Jesus are one and the same name; Barnes: Jesus is the Greek way of writing Joshua. The continuation of Poole's Annotations calls Joshua a type of Jesus bringing believers into the true rest of the heavenly Canaan
layers.text: Joshua led Israel in, and "the LORD gave them rest on every side." Yet Hebrews says that if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day: "There remains, then, a Sabbath rest." Commentators call Joshua's rest a shadow of Christ's.

layers.evidence: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 113 (second century)
layers.text: Moses saw the land but heard, "you will not cross into it"; Joshua led the people over. An early Christian writer saw Christ here: Joshua, not Moses, brought the people in, as Jesus will gather His scattered people. The New Testament does not say this.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Zechariah 6:11: Iesous. NET Bible note on Zechariah 6:12: Branch (tsemach) comes from the verb for branch out; Zerubbabel in the immediate context, Jesus as the ultimate referent. TBESH: mofet, sign, a token of something to come. Justin Martyr, Dialogue 115, reads Zechariah 3 of Christ
layers.text: After the exile the high priest Joshua is crowned and told, "Here is a man whose name is the Branch." He and his companions are "a sign" of "My servant, the Branch," and in Greek his name is Iesous. Christian commentators read the Branch as the Messiah.

passages.saying: that place was called the Valley of Eshcol
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the BSB wording of the verse and Gill's note on it.
layers.text: The valley where the spies cut down a branch with a single huge cluster of grapes was named the Valley of Eshcol because of that cluster.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley, Keil and Delitzsch, T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all give Eshcol as cluster. Espin and Thrupp, and Keil and Delitzsch, add that the valley may first have been named after Abraham's ally Eshcol, but Israel took the name up in this new sense.
layers.text: Eshcol means cluster. The valley was named for the cluster (eshkol) of grapes the spies cut there. Some think the place already bore the name of Abraham's ally Eshcol (Genesis 14:13), but from then on Israel heard it as the Valley of the Cluster.

passages.saying: We even saw the Nephilim there
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the BSB wording of the verse and Gill's note on it.
layers.text: The spies who gave the bad report say they saw the Nephilim, the descendants of Anak, and felt as small as grasshoppers beside them. They overstate the danger to turn Israel back from the land.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible gives the Hebrew as nephilim and points to Genesis 6:4. Clarke gives nephilim and sends the reader to his note on Genesis 6:4, and Keil and Delitzsch call them primeval tyrants (see at Gen 6:4). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also refers to Genesis 6:4.
layers.text: The spies say they saw the Nephilim, the name Genesis 6:4 uses for those on the earth in the days before the flood. The word appears only in these two places, so the report links the sons of Anak with the Nephilim of old and makes Canaan seem impossible to take.

passages.saying: It is you sons of Levi who have taken too much upon yourselves
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the BSB wording of the verse and Gill's note on it.
layers.text: Moses tells Korah and his company to put fire and incense in their censers before the LORD the next day, so that the LORD Himself will show which man He has chosen to be holy.

layers.evidence: Gill says Moses retorts their own language upon them, and Keil and Delitzsch say that with the expression rav lakhem in this verse Moses gives the rebels back their own words from verse 3.
layers.text: Korah's men told Moses and Aaron, "You have taken too much upon yourselves!" In Hebrew that is rav lakhem, literally enough for you. Moses throws the same words back at them: "It is you sons of Levi who have taken too much upon yourselves!"

passages.saying: brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the reply of Dathan and Abiram when they refuse Moses' summons (verses 12-14).
layers.text: Dathan and Abiram refuse to come when Moses calls them. They accuse him of bringing them out of Egypt only to let them die in the wilderness, and of making himself a ruler over them.

layers.evidence: Gill says the phrase belongs to Canaan and is turned here against the Lord's own description of that land. T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes) say the rebels give Egypt the terms used elsewhere for Canaan, with perverse contempt for the promises. Keil and Delitzsch call it bitter irony applied to Egypt.
layers.text: When God called Moses, He promised to bring Israel out of Egypt to "a land flowing with milk and honey." Dathan and Abiram take God's own description of the promised land and give it to Egypt, the land of their slavery, mocking the promise.

passages.saying: that they may join you and assist you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's charge to Aaron about the Levites' share in the tabernacle work (verses 1-7).
layers.text: God tells Aaron to bring his fellow Levites alongside him. They are to help Aaron and his sons in the service of the tabernacle, while the priestly duties stay with Aaron's family.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it a fine paronomasia: Levi comes from lavah, to join, and the Levites shall be joined (yillavu) to the priests. Gill says the name Levites means persons joined, pointing to Genesis 29:34. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under Paronomasia.
layers.text: The name Levi is linked to the Hebrew verb lavah, to join. At Levi's birth Leah hoped her husband would now become attached to her. Here God says the Levites will join (yillavu) Aaron, so the tribe lives out its name by serving beside the priests.

passages.saying: These were the waters of Meribah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the closing summary of the account of water from the rock at Kadesh (verses 1-13).
layers.text: The account of the water from the rock ends here. The place is remembered for Israel's quarrel with the LORD, and there God showed His holiness by giving the people water and by disciplining Moses and Aaron.

layers.evidence: T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes) call the words he was sanctified in them an allusion to the name Kadesh (holy), which gained new significance when God vindicated His own holiness there.
layers.text: Israel was camped at Kadesh (verse 1), a name meaning holy. Here the LORD showed Himself holy (vayyiqqadesh), a verb from the same root. Some see the old place name taking on fresh meaning from what God did there.

layers.evidence: Gill: Meribah, or strife, because the children of Israel strove with the Lord. T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes): Meribah means strife; elsewhere this one is called Meribah-Kadesh to set it apart from the Meribah of Exodus 17. Wesley: Meribah, that is, strife. Keil and Delitzsch: the water of strife, about which Israel strove with Jehovah.
layers.text: Meribah means strife or quarreling. It comes from the Hebrew verb riv, and the verse uses that very verb: the Israelites quarreled (ravu) with the LORD there. An earlier place in Exodus 17 was given the same name for the same reason.

passages.saying: so they named the place Hormah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's answer to the vow Israel made in verse 2.
layers.text: The LORD answered Israel's vow and gave them victory over the Canaanites of Arad. Israel devoted those people and their cities to destruction, and the place was named Hormah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: Israel put the cities under the ban, and Hormah means banning, ban-place. T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes): Hormah means ban. Wesley: that is, utter destruction. Gill also says it took its name from cherem, the destruction it was devoted to.
layers.text: Hormah means devoted to destruction, a banned place. It comes from the verb charam, used for handing something over wholly to God by destroying it. Israel vowed to do this in verse 2 and did it here, and the name records it.

passages.saying: So Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's command in verse 8 and Moses' obedience here.
layers.text: As God commanded, Moses made a bronze snake and set it on a pole. Anyone bitten by the snakes who looked at it lived. The healing came from God's power and grace, not from the metal itself.

layers.evidence: Gill calls the lifting up of the serpent a figure of the lifting up of Christ. Clarke says our Lord refers to it in John 3:14-15, though he will not make the serpent itself a type. T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes) say the Christian fathers rightly see in it a figure of Christ. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Henry also link it to John 3, and Wesley calls the pole a picture of the cross.
layers.text: Jesus pointed back to this scene when He told Nicodemus, "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up." As the bitten Israelites looked and lived, all who believe in Him have eternal life.

layers.evidence: Clarke gives the Hebrew nechash nechosheth and says the word for brass or copper comes from the same root as nachash, probably because of the colour, though he adds that the root's true meaning is uncertain. The Companion Bible glosses nachash as a shining thing of brass.
layers.text: In Hebrew a bronze snake is a nechash nechoshet. The words for snake (nachash) and bronze (nechoshet) sound almost alike and may share a root, perhaps because a snake's skin can gleam like polished bronze.

passages.saying: From there they went on to Beer
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's promise of water to the gathered people, celebrated in the song of verses 17-18.
layers.text: Israel moved on to a place called Beer. There the LORD told Moses to gather the people, promising to give them water, and the people answered with a song about the well.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: Beer (a well), named because God gave the people water there. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Beer, that is, a well. Gill: a place so called from a well that sprang up there. T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes): probably the Well later known as Beer-elim.
layers.text: Beer is simply the Hebrew word for a well. The verse explains the name at once: it was the well where God gave His people water, and they celebrated it with a song (verses 17-18).

passages.saying: Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Israel's victories over Sihon and Og in Numbers 21, which Gill says left Balak sure that Moab could not stand either.
layers.text: Balak, the king of Moab, saw how Israel had defeated the Amorite kings Sihon and Og. If those strong kings could not stand against Israel, he reasoned, his own people had even less hope.

layers.evidence: T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes) give Zippor as 'Bird' and say it recalls the names of other Midianites, Oreb ('Crow') and Zeeb ('Wolf'). The Pulpit Commentary also says Zippor is a small bird.
layers.text: Balak's father's name, Zippor, is the Hebrew word for bird. It recalls the names of the Midianite princes Oreb (raven) and Zeeb (wolf), who were also named after creatures.

passages.saying: Who can count the dust of Jacob
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of Balaam's first oracle: Israel's countless numbers and the blessed end of the upright.
layers.text: Balaam marvels that Israel is as countless as dust; even one of its four camps is too many to number. Then he wishes that he might die as the righteous die and that his end might be like theirs.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say these words point back to the promise in Genesis 13:16; T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Genesis 13:16 and 28:14, and Gill and Wesley also tie the dust to God's promise. Genesis 13:16 uses the same Hebrew words for count (manah) and dust (aphar).
layers.text: When Balaam asks who can count the dust of Jacob, he echoes God's promise to Abraham and Jacob that their offspring would be like the dust of the earth, too many to count. The prophet hired to curse Israel ends up witnessing that the promise was coming true.

layers.evidence: Gill says the word is pretty near in sound and meaning to Jeshurun, Israel's name in Deuteronomy 32:15. Keil and Delitzsch link the same word to God making Israel a Jeshurun, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes it to mean the Israelites. Hebrew yesharim (upright ones) beside Yeshurun.
layers.text: The word for the righteous here is yesharim, the upright ones. It is close in sound and meaning to Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel, so Balaam's wish to die as the upright die is in effect a wish to die like Israel.

passages.saying: He crouches, he lies down like a lion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the lion picture and the closing blessing and curse in Balaam's third oracle.
layers.text: Balaam pictures Israel as a lion lying at rest that no one dares to disturb. He closes by declaring that those who bless Israel will be blessed and those who curse Israel will be cursed.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the lion image here is in words taken from Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49:9; the Companion Bible also points to Genesis 49:9. Both verses share crouch (kara), lioness (lavi) and rouse (qum).
layers.text: The lion that crouches and lies down, which no one dares to rouse, repeats Jacob's blessing on Judah in Genesis 49:9 almost word for word. What Jacob said of one tribe, Balaam now says of the whole nation of Israel.

layers.evidence: Gill calls these the very words in which Isaac blessed Jacob in Genesis 27:29; Keil and Delitzsch add that Isaac was passing on the blessing of Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and that Balaam used it to warn Balak. Both verses pair bless (barakh) and curse (arar).
layers.text: The closing words repeat Isaac's blessing on Jacob in Genesis 27:29, which carried on God's promise to Abraham. Balak had hired Balaam to curse Israel, but Balaam ends by warning that whoever curses Israel will himself be cursed.

passages.saying: A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the star and scepter as royal images; the commentaries read the ruler as David in part and Christ in full.
layers.text: Balaam sees a ruler far in the future, pictured as a star coming from Jacob and a scepter rising from Israel, who will crush Moab and Israel's enemies. This points first to King David and above all to the Messiah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the scepter of Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49:10 is used here for the future ruler; Wesley calls it that sceptre mentioned in Genesis 49:10, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown sends the reader to Genesis 49:10. Gill on Genesis 49:10 points back here too. Both verses use shevet (scepter).
layers.text: The scepter rising from Israel takes up the promise "The scepter will not depart from Judah" that Jacob spoke in Genesis 49:10. Balaam uses the same royal symbol for the same promised King who would come from Jacob's line.

passages.saying: your nest is set in a cliff
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of a nest in the rock, which Gill explains as the Kenites' rocky and secure dwelling places.
layers.text: Balaam turns to the Kenites and says their home is strong and lasting, like a bird's nest built high in a rocky cliff where enemies cannot easily reach it.

layers.evidence: Gill says Balaam calls their home Ken, a nest, in allusion to their name; Clarke, and T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes), call it a play on words, Wesley says nest alludes to their name, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse as a paronomasia. Hebrew qeni (Kenite) and qen (nest), with qayin (Kain) in verse 22.
layers.text: Balaam plays on the tribe's name. The Kenites are Qeni in Hebrew, and nest is qen, so their name itself becomes a picture of a nest set high in the rock. The next verse uses the name Kain, which carries the same sound.

passages.saying: captured their villages and called them Havvoth-jair
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and on Keil and Delitzsch's account of Jair's conquest of the region of Argob in Bashan.
layers.text: Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, conquered a group of towns east of the Jordan in the region of Bashan and gave them a new name that included his own.

layers.evidence: Clarke gives the villages or habitations of Jair; T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible give the villages or tent villages of Jair; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives tent-villages. Keil and Delitzsch trace havvoth to a word for life, used of any dwelling place, and render the name Jair's-lives.
layers.text: Havvoth-jair means the villages of Jair. The Hebrew word for the villages he captured (havvoth) is the very word that begins the new name, so Jair simply put his own name on the towns he had taken.

passages.saying: They set out from Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its place in the list of camps in Numbers 33; Clarke places Rithmah in the wilderness of Paran.
layers.text: In Moses' record of Israel's journey through the wilderness, the people left their camp at Hazeroth and made their next camp at Rithmah, in the wilderness of Paran.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the name signifies the juniper tree, from the many such trees there; T. E. Espin and J. F. Thrupp (Barnes' Notes) derive it from retem, the broom-plant; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it the place of the broom; Gill links retem to 1 Kings 19:4; the Companion Bible renders it Juniper.
layers.text: Rithmah comes from retem, the Hebrew word for the broom bush (called juniper in older English Bibles), the same desert shrub Elijah sat under in 1 Kings 19:4. The camp was probably named for the broom that grew there.

passages.saying: today you are as numerous as the stars in the sky
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in verses 9 to 12; Gill explains that their great number was why Moses could not bear them alone.
layers.text: Moses tells Israel that the LORD has made them grow into a nation as countless as the stars. Their great number was why he could no longer carry the burden of leading them alone.

layers.evidence: Gill says the promise to Abraham in Genesis 15:5 was now fulfilled; Clarke calls it the promise God made to Abraham, now amply fulfilled; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Abraham being told to look to the stars; Matthew Henry says Moses owns the fulfilment of God's promise to Abraham.
layers.text: The picture of Israel "as numerous as the stars in the sky" takes up God's promise to Abraham, who was told to count the stars and heard, "So shall your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5). Moses presents that promise as already kept.

passages.saying: from the day that God created man on earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on verses 33 and 34, which say what the great thing is; Keil and Delitzsch explain it so.
layers.text: Moses challenges Israel to search all of history since creation and every corner of the world. Nothing as great as God speaking to them and rescuing them has ever happened or been heard of.

layers.evidence: Gill takes the words back to the creation of the world and of men in it. The Companion Bible notes that the two words for God created (bara Elohim) stand together only three times: Genesis 1:1, Genesis 2:3 and here.
layers.text: Moses' words "from the day that God created man on earth" reach back to the creation account. The Hebrew words here for God created (bara Elohim) are the same pair used in Genesis 1:1, so Israel is to search all history back to the very beginning.

passages.saying: Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Clarke explains testing God as provoking Him by doubting His mercy, goodness, providence and truth.
layers.text: Israel must not put the LORD to the test by doubting His goodness and demanding proof that He is with them, as they had done at Massah when they had no water.

layers.evidence: Gill points to Exodus 17:7 for how Massah got its name; Clarke quotes the people's question, Is the Lord among us or not?, from Exodus 17:1-7; Keil and Delitzsch identify Massah with Rephidim in Exodus 17:1-7.
layers.text: Moses points back to Exodus 17, where the thirsty Israelites quarreled with him and tested the LORD by asking, "Is the LORD among us or not?" Moses named the place Massah because of it.

layers.evidence: Gill calls this verse another passage used by Christ to repel the temptations of Satan (Matthew 4:7). Bullinger's Figures of Speech notes that Moses gave the command to all Israel and the Lord applied it to Himself in reply to the Tempter.
layers.text: When Satan urged Jesus to throw Himself down from the temple, Jesus answered with this verse: "Do not put the Lord your God to the test" (Matthew 4:7). He would not force God to prove His care.

layers.evidence: Gill says Massah was so called from the Israelites tempting the Lord there (Exodus 17:7). The name comes from the same root as the verb test (nasah) used twice in this verse.
layers.text: Massah means Testing. The place was named for the day Israel tested the LORD, and this verse uses the Hebrew verb for testing (nasah) twice before naming it, so some hear the name itself echoing the command.

passages.saying: He brought you water from the rock of flint.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Keil and Delitzsch read it as a list of the desert's terrors and of God's provision in a parched land.
layers.text: Moses reminds Israel that God led them safely through a huge, dangerous desert full of poisonous snakes and scorpions, where there was no water, and gave them water out of hard rock.

layers.evidence: Gill calls them fiery serpents such as bit the Israelites (Numbers 21:6); Clarke, T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) and Keil and Delitzsch all send the reader to Numbers 21:6 for these serpents, and Clarke explains fiery from the burning inflammation of their bite.
layers.text: The venomous snakes recall the snakes the LORD sent among the complaining Israelites in Numbers 21:6. Both verses use the same Hebrew pair, nachash saraph, a burning or fiery serpent, named for its painful, deadly bite.

layers.evidence: Gill says the water from the rock of flint was given both at Horeb and at Kadesh, pointing to Exodus 17:6.
layers.text: Water from the rock may recall Horeb, where God told Moses to strike the rock so that water would come out for the people to drink (Exodus 17:6). A like miracle came later at Kadesh.

passages.saying: Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Clarke stresses how from so small a beginning they had multiplied to more than 600,000.
layers.text: Moses reminds Israel that their ancestors went down to Egypt as a family of only seventy people, and now the LORD has made them a nation too many to count.

layers.evidence: Gill explains the seventy as including Jacob and his sons, pointing to Genesis 46:26; Keil and Delitzsch refer the seventy souls to Genesis 46:26-27; the Companion Bible compares Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5.
layers.text: The number seventy takes up the count of Jacob's household when he moved to Egypt, given in Genesis 46:27, where all the members of his family who went there numbered seventy.

layers.evidence: Gill says God made them as the stars of heaven as He promised in Genesis 15:5; Keil and Delitzsch say the Lord had marvellously fulfilled His promise in Genesis 15:5.
layers.text: The words "as numerous as the stars in the sky" look back to God's promise in Genesis 15:5 that Abraham's offspring would be like the stars. Seventy people had become a multitude, and Moses presents the promise as kept.

passages.saying: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Dead Sea Scroll 4QTestimonia named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: At Horeb the people begged not to hear God's voice or "see this great fire anymore." God answers with a promise: He will raise up a prophet like Moses and "put My words in his mouth."

layers.evidence: Deuteronomy 18:20-22. Benson and Poole speak of a succession of prophets; Keil and Delitzsch include Christ as its culmination; T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) sees a line of prophets culminating in one eminent individual.
layers.text: The near fulfillment is the line of prophets after Moses: the chapter goes straight on to tests for true and false prophets. Commentators see that line reaching its height in Christ, the one great Prophet.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: yaqim (18:15) and qam (34:10) are both qum. Benson and Gill read the verse as still awaiting the prophet; Jewish tradition (Sifre 357) reads it as Moses' unmatched past
layers.text: Yet Deuteronomy closes by saying no such prophet had arisen: "Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses." "Risen" is the same verb, qum, as "raise up." Some Christian commentators read this as Israel still waiting for the prophet like Moses.

layers.evidence: 4QTestimonia, first century BC, quotes Deuteronomy 18:18-19 beside Numbers 24:15-17 (a king) and Deuteronomy 33:8-11 (a priest). Gill on Deuteronomy 18:15 cites John 6:14 for the expectation
layers.text: By Jesus' day people expected "the Prophet." John the Baptist is asked, "Are you the Prophet?" and after the loaves the crowd says, "Truly this is the Prophet." A Dead Sea Scroll had already set this promise beside texts about a coming king and priest.

Peter quotes the promise at the temple and applies it to Jesus, with Moses' warning about anyone who will not listen (Acts 3:22-23). Stephen quotes it again before the council: "God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers."

layers.evidence: Benson, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 17:5 hear Deuteronomy 18:15 in the voice from the cloud
layers.text: At the transfiguration, with Moses standing beside Jesus, the voice from the cloud says, "This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!" Many commentators hear Deuteronomy's "You must listen to him" in those words.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 1:18: the primary reference is still to Moses; Bengel: not even Moses
layers.text: Moses was set apart because the LORD spoke with him "face to face." John says the Son goes further: "No one has ever seen God," but the Son "has made Him known," and "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ."

passages.saying: anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the writers named under each note, and the cross-references from OpenBible.info, with the Septuagint, the Mishnah, Josephus and the Temple Scroll named as ancient witnesses.

layers.text: If an executed criminal's body was hung on a tree, it had to come down and be buried the same day, "because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse." Joshua kept the rule, having the bodies of five kings taken down "at sunset."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qillat (H7045) Elohim taluy (H8518). The Septuagint has cursed by God (hypo theou). Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4, paraphrased
layers.text: The Hebrew, qillat Elohim taluy, reads word for word "curse of God," "hanged one." It can mean cursed by God, as the Greek Old Testament took it, or an offense against God: early Jewish law says leaving the body up would desecrate God's name.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Galatians 3:13 note that Paul leaves out of God (hypo theou), which the Septuagint has; TAGNT confirms Galatians 3:13 has no hypo theou
layers.text: Paul quotes this verse to explain the cross: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." His wording, "Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree," leaves God's name out. The curse He bore opens Abraham's blessing to the Gentiles.

layers.evidence: Acts 5:30 and 10:39. Ellicott on Acts 5:30: the phrase comes from the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 21; TAGNT: kremasantes epi xylou
layers.text: The apostles described the crucifixion in this law's words, "by hanging Him on a tree," and Peter writes, "He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree." The phrase comes from the Greek Old Testament of this law.

layers.evidence: Josephus, Jewish War 4.5.2 (Whiston translation). Barnes, JFB and the Pulpit Commentary on John 19:31 cite Deuteronomy 21:22-23
layers.text: The rule shaped the day Jesus died. The leaders asked that "the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath," and that evening Joseph of Arimathea asked for His body. A Jewish historian of the time says Jews buried even the crucified before sunset.

layers.evidence: The Temple Scroll (11QTemple 64), second century BC, as translated in Torleif Elgvin, The Messiah Who Was Cursed on the Tree, Themelios 22.3
layers.text: Before Jesus, a Dead Sea Scroll already applied this law to men hanged alive, calling those who hang on the tree cursed by God and by men. A crucified Messiah was, as Paul says, "a stumbling block to Jews."

layers.evidence: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 89 (Trypho) and 96 (Justin), ANF translation; Elgvin also cites Trypho's objection
layers.text: In Justin Martyr's second-century Dialogue, Trypho, a Jew, names this verse as his great objection: the law calls anyone crucified accursed. Justin answers that the same verse confirms the hope that rests on the crucified Christ.

passages.saying: turned the curse into a blessing for you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words and the Balaam account in Numbers 22 to 24.
layers.text: Moses reminds Israel that the LORD refused to listen to Balaam, the prophet hired to curse them. Instead God turned the intended curse into a blessing, and He did it because He loved His people.

layers.evidence: Gill on this verse says God overruled Balaam's tongue so that he blessed instead of cursing, and points to Numbers 23:11. Keil and Delitzsch say the LORD turned the curse of Balaam into a blessing, citing Numbers 22 to 24.
layers.text: This line sums up the Balaam story in Numbers 22 to 24. Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but when Balaam opened his mouth, blessing came out instead. Balak cried out, "you have only blessed them!"

passages.saying: The House of the Unsandaled
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the law of a brother's duty to his dead brother's widow in Deuteronomy 25:5-10.
layers.text: A man who refused to marry his dead brother's widow and give his brother an heir was shamed in public. From then on his family would be known in Israel as "The House of the Unsandaled."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call it a name of ridicule meaning the barefooted man, a miserable fellow. T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) reads it as the house of the barefooted one, a sign of the most abject condition. Gill says the mark of infamy fell on his whole family for refusing his brother's widow.
layers.text: In Hebrew the name is beit chaluts hanna'al, the house of the one whose sandal was pulled off. Going barefoot was a picture of poverty and disgrace. He would not keep his brother's family name alive, so his own family carried a name of shame.

passages.saying: blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the command itself and on Amalek's attack described in Deuteronomy 25:17-18.
layers.text: Amalek had attacked Israel's tired stragglers on the way out of Egypt. Once God gave Israel rest from its enemies in the land, Israel was to wipe out Amalek's memory and never forget what Amalek had done.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Exodus 17:14, tie God's vow there to the command in Deuteronomy 25:19. The Companion Bible note on Exodus 17:14 compares Deuteronomy 25:19. Both verses use the same Hebrew for blot out (machah) and memory (zekher).
layers.text: The command repeats almost word for word what God said after Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim: "I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven." What God vowed there, Israel is now told to carry out.

passages.saying: My father was a wandering Aramean
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the setting of the firstfruits offering and on Jacob's story in Genesis 29 to 46.
layers.text: When an Israelite brought the first fruits of his harvest, he was to confess where his people came from. The father is Jacob, called an Aramean because of his long years in Aram with Laban. He went down to Egypt with a small family that grew into a great nation.

layers.evidence: Wesley explains ready to perish as Jacob's want and poverty, pointing to Genesis 28:11, 28:20 and 32:10, or the danger from Esau and Laban. Gill says Jacob was close to perishing when he fled from Esau and was poor and penniless when he came to Laban.
layers.text: The word translated wandering (oved) can also mean close to perishing. It recalls Jacob fleeing from Esau with nothing and serving Laban in hardship. Jacob himself later told God, "with only my staff I came across the Jordan, but now I have become two camps."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on this verse, compare Genesis 34:30, where Jacob himself describes his family as few in number. Both verses use the Hebrew word for men (metim) in the phrase.
layers.text: Few in number may echo Jacob's own words after the trouble at Shechem, when he feared his small household would be wiped out: "We are few in number." The family that once feared for its life is the one God made into a great nation.

passages.saying: as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's place among the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:15-68.
layers.text: If Israel refused to obey the LORD, the curse would shrink the nation. A people who had become as countless as the stars would be cut down to a small remnant.

layers.evidence: Gill, on this verse, says Israel's being as the stars of heaven for multitude was what was promised to Abraham in Genesis 15:5.
layers.text: Some hear in the stars an echo of God's promise to Abraham, when He told him to count the stars and said, "So shall your offspring be." On this reading, disobedience would undo the very growth God had promised and given.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on this verse, render left few in number as a small number and compare Deuteronomy 26:5. Both verses use the same Hebrew phrase, bimtei me'at.
layers.text: Few in number is the same Hebrew phrase (bimtei me'at) used of Jacob's family going down to Egypt (26:5). Some see the echo as pointed: the nation God had grown from that small start could be cut back to a few.

passages.saying: just like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture of a land ruined by the covenant curse.
layers.text: Moses warns that if Israel forsakes the LORD, its land will become a burned, barren waste of sulfur and salt where nothing is sown and nothing grows, like the cities the LORD overthrew in His anger.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call like the overthrow of Sodom an express allusion and point to Genesis 19:24. T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) cites Genesis 19:24-25 and says Israel's ruin would be of the like sort. Gill sends readers to Genesis 19 for the history of this overthrow. Both passages share the Hebrew for sulfur (gophrit) and overthrow (haphakh).
layers.text: This looks back to Genesis 19, when the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah and overthrew the cities and all that grew there. The same Hebrew words for sulfur and overthrow warn that a faithless Israel's land could become as dead as that plain.

passages.saying: He will restore you from captivity and have compassion on you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the promise of Deuteronomy 30:1-5 to a people who return to the LORD in exile.
layers.text: If Israel turns back to the LORD while scattered in exile, He will end their captivity, show them mercy, and gather them again from every nation where He has scattered them.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under paronomasia, noting two similar words wherever the LORD promises to turn the captivity of His people. The Companion Bible note on turn thy captivity also calls it paronomasia, veshab eth-shebuthka.
layers.text: Where the verse says He will restore you from captivity, the Hebrew pairs the verb shav (turn back) with the noun shevut (captivity). Some hear in the like sound a promise that rings with return. The same sound pair comes back wherever God promises to restore His people.

passages.saying: When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words about God assigning lands and borders to the nations.
layers.text: God, the Most High, gave each nation its land and fixed the borders between peoples when He divided mankind. The next verse adds that Israel is the LORD's own share among them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch tie this dividing of mankind to Gen 10:32, where nations formed from Noah's sons; Gill says the Most High directed it (Gen 10:32) and also thinks of Babel; Bullinger points to Gen 10:32 and Wesley to Genesis 10 and 11. Both verses use the verb parad, to separate.
layers.text: Moses looks back to Genesis 10, where the families of Noah's sons spread out after the flood and became separate nations, each in its own land. Both verses use the same verb, parad, to separate. The scattering at Babel in Genesis 11 belongs to the same story.

passages.saying: He found him in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of God finding and guarding Israel in the wilderness.
layers.text: God found Israel helpless in a barren, howling wilderness. He surrounded him, taught him, and guarded him as carefully as a person guards the pupil of his own eye.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say tohu here recalls Gen 1:2 and is used to heighten Israel's helpless state; T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) notes that the word for waste is the one rendered without form in Gen 1:2.
layers.text: The word for the barren waste is tohu, the same word Genesis 1:2 uses for the earth when it was formless. The echo stresses how empty and helpless Israel was when God found him, like the world before He shaped it.

passages.saying: As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the eagle picture the verse itself draws of God's care for Israel.
layers.text: Like an eagle that stirs its nest, hovers over its young, and catches them on its wings, the LORD cared for Israel, carrying them out of Egypt and through the wilderness.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the eagle figure points back to Exo 19:4; Clarke says the same figure is used there; Gill, referring to Exo 19:4, says the Lord bore Israel as on eagles' wings. T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) and Bullinger also compare Exo 19:4. Both verses share the Hebrew words for eagle, wings and carry.
layers.text: At Sinai God reminded Israel that He had carried them on eagles' wings and brought them to Himself (Exodus 19:4). The song unfolds that saying into a full picture of the eagle and its young, using the same Hebrew words for eagle, wings and carrying.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the verb for hovering here is the same word used in Gen 1:2 and likens it to God strengthening Israel by His Spirit. Keil and Delitzsch, on Gen 1:2, explain the Spirit's hovering there by this verse's bird hovering over its young.
layers.text: The eagle hovers (rachaph) over its young, the same verb Genesis 1:2 uses for the Spirit of God hovering over the waters at creation. As the Spirit hovered over the first creation, God hovers over His people to cherish and strengthen them.

passages.saying: But Jeshurun grew fat and kicked
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a well-fed animal turning against its owner.
layers.text: Israel grew fat on God's good gifts and then kicked like a pampered animal. They abandoned the God who made them and scorned the Rock who saved them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch derive Jeshurun from yashar, call it an honourable name, and say its use here carries a stern reproof; Clarke gives the same root; Wesley says it shamed them for falling from their name. Gill, Henry and Bullinger also give the meaning upright.
layers.text: Jeshurun is a poetic name for Israel from yashar, upright, so it means the upright one. The song has just called God upright (32:4). Using the name here stings: the people called to be upright grew fat on His gifts and kicked against Him.

passages.saying: They have provoked My jealousy by that which is not God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's matched threat and on Paul's use of it in Romans 10:19.
layers.text: Israel stirred God's jealousy and anger with idols that are no gods at all. In turn He will stir their jealousy by favoring people they did not count as a people. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:19 about God calling the Gentiles.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call it complete retaliation: a no-god answered by a no-people. T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) says God would mete out the same measure Israel had given Him. Bullinger marks the jealousy, anger, jealousy, anger pattern and the paired no-God and no-people.
layers.text: God answers Israel in matching words. They made Him jealous with a no-god (lo el), so He will make them jealous with a no-people (lo am). The lines run jealousy, anger, jealousy, anger, so the punishment mirrors the sin.

passages.saying: How could one man pursue a thousand, or two put ten thousand to flight
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's question about Israel's defeat and the answer it gives.
layers.text: Moses says Israel's defeat could be explained only one way: the LORD, their Rock, had sold them and handed them over to their enemies. Their losses would show God's judgment, not the enemy's strength.

layers.evidence: Gill says this turns around the promise of Lev 26:8 that obedient Israel would chase its enemies; Keil and Delitzsch also point to Lev 26:8 for the victory Israel could have had. Both verses use radaph (pursue) and revavah (ten thousand).
layers.text: Leviticus 26:8 promised that if Israel obeyed, a few of them would chase great numbers, even ten thousand. This verse recalls that promise with the same words for pursue and ten thousand. Victory against such odds was promised to the faithful, so defeat meant God had given them up.
