passages.saying: Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the lament itself, which names Saul and Jonathan (1:23) and places their death on Mount Gilboa (1:21).
layers.text: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan begins here. The king and his son, the pride of Israel, lie dead on the heights of Mount Gilboa. The refrain that runs through the song is heard for the first time: "How the mighty have fallen!"

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: literally the gazelle, the Eastern type of beauty. The Companion Bible, in its note on 1:18, gives the line as Thy hart, Israel. Keil and Delitzsch disagree and read the word simply as ornament, meaning Saul and Jonathan. In 2 Samuel 2:18 the same Hebrew word, tsevi, in the plural, means gazelles.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for glory here, tsevi, is spelled and sounds the same as the word for gazelle, used of swift Asahel in 2 Samuel 2:18. Some read the line as mourning the fallen as Israel's gazelle, the graceful animal that stood for beauty in the East.

passages.saying: Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Saul’s son Ish-bosheth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 2:8-11, where Abner makes Ish-bosheth king over Israel while the house of Judah follows David.
layers.text: After Saul died, Abner, the commander of his army, took Saul's son Ish-bosheth east across the Jordan to Mahanaim and made him king over Israel. This set up a rival kingdom to David, who reigned over Judah at Hebron.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible: Ish-bosheth means man of shame. With Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown they identify him with the Esh-baal of 1 Chronicles 8:33, with bosheth, shame, written in place of Baal. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch compare Hosea 9:10.
layers.text: Ish-bosheth means man of shame. In 1 Chronicles 8:33 the same son of Saul is called Esh-baal. Bosheth, shame, was written in place of Baal, the name of a shameful idol. Gideon's name Jerubbaal is changed the same way in 2 Samuel 11:21.

passages.saying: So this place, which is in Gibeon, is called Helkath-hazzurim.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 2:12-16: twelve men from each side were matched in a contest at the pool of Gibeon, and they all fell together.
layers.text: At the pool of Gibeon, Abner and Joab each sent out twelve young men to fight. Each man seized his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side, so they all fell together. The place was named after that fight.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes): field of the sharp edges; Keil and Delitzsch compare Psalm 89:43, where the same word, tsur, is the edge of a sword. Gill and Wesley: field of rocks, men who would not give way.
layers.text: Helkath-hazzurim means field of the sharp edges, a name that remembers the swords that struck down all twenty-four men at once. Another reading is field of rocks, for men who stood like rock and died on the spot where they fought.

passages.saying: the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 5:17-20: the Philistines came against the newly anointed king, David asked the LORD, and the LORD gave the victory.
layers.text: When the Philistines came up to attack the new king, David asked the LORD whether to fight and was promised victory. After defeating them he gave the LORD the credit, saying the LORD had broken through his enemies like a flood.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and the Companion Bible all tie Mount Perazim in Isaiah 28:21 to this victory. Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch: the strange thing is that God would now act against His own people.
layers.text: Isaiah 28:21 looks back to this day: "the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim." But this time He would burst out against His own people in Jerusalem, not against their enemies. That is why Isaiah calls it His strange work.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes), Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch all explain Baal-perazim as master or possessor of breaches, named from David's words that the LORD broke through his enemies like a breach of waters.
layers.text: David says the LORD has burst out, parats, against his enemies like a flood bursting, perets, through its banks. So the place is named Baal-perazim, master of burstings-through. The name gives the LORD the credit for the victory.

passages.saying: so he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 6:6-8: Uzzah took hold of the ark when the oxen stumbled, and God struck him down beside it.
layers.text: As the ark was being brought up to the City of David, Uzzah took hold of it when the oxen stumbled, and God struck him dead. David was angry and grieved, and he named the place for what had happened there.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch: Perez-uzzah means the breach or rent of Uzzah. Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) points the reader back to the naming of Baal-perazim in 5:20, where the same verb parats and noun perets are used.
layers.text: Perez-uzzah means the breaking out against Uzzah: the LORD had broken out, parats, in a breaking out, perets, against him. It is the same word that named Baal-perazim, where the LORD broke out against David's enemies (2 Samuel 5:20).

passages.saying: He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, F. F. Bruce, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scroll 4Q174 named as ancient witnesses.

layers.text: King David, settled in a palace of cedar, wants to build a temple for the ark of God. Through the prophet Nathan, God turns the offer around: David's son will build the temple, and God will build David a dynasty and establish its throne forever.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: bayit (H1004) 15 times in 2 Samuel 7. TBESH: house, also household, family. The closing lesson is Keil and Delitzsch's on 7:8-11; Benson, Gill and Clarke on 7:11 make the same turn
layers.text: The chapter turns on bayit, "house," used 15 times. David offers God a house, a temple; God answers, "He Himself will establish a house for you," a dynasty. One commentator draws the lesson: God must build a man's house before the man can build God's.

layers.evidence: Solomon adds: I have built the house for the Name of the LORD (1 Kings 8:20). Keil and Delitzsch on 2 Samuel 7:14 cite that verse and Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) on 7:13 points to 1 Kings 8:16-20. Benson and Gill on 7:14: the discipline clause fits Solomon, not Christ
layers.text: The first fulfillment is Solomon, who dedicated the temple saying, "Now the LORD has fulfilled the word that He spoke." The promise even allows for his failures: "When he does wrong, I will discipline him."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Chronicles 17:13: the omission comes from reading David's seed as the Messiah; Ellicott: probably not a mere abridgment; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes): the writer is not about to record Solomon's sins
layers.text: Chronicles retells the promise without "When he does wrong," and where Samuel has "Your house and kingdom," it reads "My house and My kingdom." Some commentators say Chronicles reads the son as the Messiah; others, that it simply passes over Solomon's sins.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Hebrews 1:5 sees in Solomon a first fulfillment that was only in part; Gill and Bengel: spoken of Solomon, but belonging to Christ. Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) on 2 Samuel 7:14: Hebrews 1:5 applies it to Christ
layers.text: Hebrews quotes "I will be His Father, and He will be My Son" of Christ, and the angel tells Mary her son will have "the throne of His father David" and "His kingdom will never end!" Commentators see in Solomon only a first, partial fulfillment.

layers.evidence: 4Q174 (4QFlorilegium) 1.10-13 on 2 Samuel 7:11-14, read with Amos 9:11 through the shared verb qum (TAHOT; BSB restore), in the Intertextual Bible translation. Herbert Bateman (JETS 38/1, 1995): the shared "I will raise up" links the two, and the scroll expects a future Davidic King-Messiah, the shoot of David.
layers.text: The Dead Sea Scrolls show some Jews reading this as a promise of a coming king. One scroll applies it to the Branch of David and links "I will raise up" to Amos's "I will restore the fallen tent of David," the same verb in Hebrew. Acts 15:16 quotes Amos.

layers.evidence: Numbers 12:7. The Reformation Study Bible on Hebrews 3:6: Moses was in the house, Christ is over it, and God's house is His people (2 Samuel 7:16). Keil and Delitzsch and Benson on 1 Chronicles 17:14: spoken only of the Messiah. Ellicott on Hebrews 3:6: Moses faithful as a servant in God's house, Christ as a son over it.
layers.text: Hebrews sets Moses, faithful "in all My house," beside the Son: "Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house." In 1 Chronicles 17:14 God promises to set David's son over His house and His kingdom forever, words that older commentators say fit only the Messiah.

passages.saying: Who was the one to strike Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 11:14-21: David had ordered Uriah placed where he would be killed, and Joab now reports the losses near the wall.
layers.text: Joab sends word to David of losses near the wall of Rabbah. He expects the king to be angry and to recall how Abimelech died near a wall, so he tells the messenger to add that Uriah the Hittite is dead too, the news David was waiting for.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) all read the question as pointing to Abimelech's death in Judges 9. Hervey adds that it shows the records of that period were known and read in David's day.
layers.text: Joab recalls Judges 9:53, where a woman at Thebez dropped a millstone from the tower onto Abimelech's head. The old story warned soldiers not to go near a besieged wall, and Joab expects David to raise it against him.

layers.evidence: Gill: Jerubbesheth is Jerubbaal, that is Gideon (Judges 6:32), with Besheth, shame, in place of Baal, the name of a shameful idol. Keil and Delitzsch, on 2 Samuel 2:8, note the same change beside Ish-bosheth.
layers.text: Jerubbesheth is Gideon. In Judges 6:32 he is named Jerubbaal, "Let Baal contend with him." Here the Baal part of the name is replaced by besheth, shame, because Baal was a shameful idol.

passages.saying: to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording, read with verse 24, as Gill explains it.
layers.text: After Solomon was born, the LORD sent word through Nathan the prophet that the child should also be called Jedidiah, because the LORD loved him.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that yedid, beloved, in Psalm 127:2 was Solomon's name Jedidiah, given by the LORD in 2 Samuel 12:25. Bullinger's Figures of Speech says the same word is used in the psalm and that the psalm relates to Solomon, as its title shows.
layers.text: Psalm 127, a psalm of Solomon, says He gives sleep to His beloved. The Hebrew word for beloved there is yedid, the word inside Solomon's God-given name Jedidiah, so the line seems to look back to Solomon himself.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all explain Jedidiah as beloved of the Lord, and Matthew Henry and Bullinger say the same. Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) adds that the name shares its root, to love, with the name David.
layers.text: Jedidiah means beloved of the LORD. It joins yedid, beloved, with Yah, a short form of God's name, so the name says what verse 24 says, that the LORD loved the child. It also echoes his father David's name, which carries the same idea of love.

passages.saying: such a thing should never be done in Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Tamar's own plea in the verse, as Gill explains it.
layers.text: Tamar begs her half-brother Amnon not to force himself on her. She tells him that such a shameful act must never be done among God's people Israel.

layers.evidence: Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) calls Tamar's words a verbal quotation of Genesis 34:7 and thinks she knew that passage. Keil and Delitzsch say her words recall Genesis 34:7, where nebalah (folly) is first used of a sin against chastity.
layers.text: Tamar's plea echoes Genesis 34:7, where Shechem's assault on Dinah is called an outrage in Israel, a thing that should not be done. The same Hebrew word, nevalah, is used in both. Her words recall a shameful deed that Israel's own history had already condemned.

passages.saying: Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of the robe, which JFB explains as a mark of royal rank.
layers.text: After Amnon's servant throws Tamar out and bolts the door, the writer notes that she was wearing the special robe worn by the king's unmarried daughters.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the same words occur in Genesis 37:3. Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) and Gill both point to Genesis 37:3 and treat Tamar's garment as the same kind as Joseph's coat, and Keil and Delitzsch also refer to Genesis 37:3. Gill adds that the robe made her shame the more manifest.
layers.text: Tamar's robe is described with the same Hebrew words, ketonet passim, used for the robe of many colors Jacob made for Joseph in Genesis 37:3. The repeated phrase links the two stories, and here the special robe made Tamar's shame all the more plain to see as she was thrown out.

passages.saying: as numerous as the sand on the seashore
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's summary of the nation's growth and plenty, as Keil and Delitzsch describe it.
layers.text: Under Solomon the people of Judah and Israel became very many, and they lived in plenty and gladness, eating, drinking and rejoicing.

layers.evidence: Gill says the promise to Abraham in Genesis 22:17 was here fulfilled. Keil and Delitzsch say the words show that the promise to the patriarchs (Genesis 22:17, compare 32:12) had been fulfilled.
layers.text: Comparing Judah and Israel to the sand on the seashore takes up God's oath to Abraham that his offspring would be as countless as the sand on the seashore. The writer shows that promise come true in Solomon's day.

passages.saying: The pillar to the south he named Jachin
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's account of the two pillars, with Keil and Delitzsch on where they stood.
layers.text: The two bronze pillars were set up at the porch in front of the temple, and each was given a name: the pillar on the south was called Jachin, and the one on the north Boaz.

layers.evidence: Gill gives he will establish for Jachin, and in him, or it is strength, for Boaz; Clarke gives He shall establish and in strength; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) reads the two together as God will establish in strength. Keil and Delitzsch and Matthew Henry give the same meanings.
layers.text: Jachin means he will establish, and Boaz is explained as in him is strength, or in strength. Read together, the names said that God would firmly establish His house and that its strength was found in Him.

passages.saying: the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's account of the cloud and the glory, as Clarke explains it.
layers.text: When the ark was brought into the new temple, the cloud of God's presence filled it, and the priests could not stay to serve, because the glory of the LORD filled the house.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say that as the glory in the cloud filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34-35), so it was now. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) and JFB draw the same comparison, and Gill says the glory took up its abode as in the tabernacle.
layers.text: This repeats the day the tabernacle was finished, when the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle and Moses could not enter. The same cloud and glory now fill Solomon's temple, showing that God accepted it as His dwelling.

passages.saying: You brought them out of Egypt, out of the furnace for iron
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse gives the reason for Solomon's plea, and the furnace stands for Egypt's harsh bondage.
layers.text: Solomon asks God to hear and forgive His people because they belong to Him. They are His own inheritance, whom He rescued from the cruel slavery of Egypt, pictured as a furnace for smelting iron.

layers.evidence: Gill explains the furnace of iron here as Egypt's hard and cruel bondage and sends the reader to Deuteronomy 4:20. The Companion Bible's note on the iron furnace in Deuteronomy 4:20 points to 1 Kings 8:51-53. The Hebrew kur habbarzel (furnace of iron) and nachalah (inheritance) stand in both verses.
layers.text: Calling Egypt a furnace for iron echoes Moses, who told Israel that the LORD had brought them out of the iron furnace to be the people of His inheritance. Solomon uses the same picture and the same word inheritance as he asks God to keep caring for His people.

passages.saying: Not one word has failed of all the good promises
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Solomon's blessing rests on God's promise of rest in the land and on its fulfilment.
layers.text: At the dedication of the temple Solomon blesses the LORD for giving Israel rest, just as He promised. Every good promise God made through Moses has come true, and not one has failed.

layers.evidence: Gill says Solomon seems to have respect to Joshua 23:14. Keil and Delitzsch ground the praise in Joshua 21:44-45 and 23:14. The Companion Bible notes the Hebrew naphal, to fall, and says Solomon knows Joshua 23:14. Both verses say lo naphal davar echad, not one word has fallen.
layers.text: Solomon repeats the witness Joshua gave near the end of his life, that not one of the good promises the LORD had made had failed. In Hebrew both say that no word has fallen (naphal). Generations later, the finished temple is fresh proof of the same faithfulness.

passages.saying: he called them the Land of Cabul
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse records Hiram's displeasure with Solomon's gift and the name it left on the district.
layers.text: Solomon gave Hiram king of Tyre twenty towns in Galilee, but Hiram was not pleased with them. He asked what kind of towns these were, and the district was known as the Land of Cabul from then on.

layers.evidence: Gill, following Hiller, reads Cabul as 'as nothing' and calls this the best sense. Keil and Delitzsch prefer the same sense, adding that the name may first have meant 'pawned land' and was twisted by the people into 'good for nothing'. Josephus, as Gill reports, gave it the Phoenician sense 'not pleasing'.
layers.text: No one is sure where the name Cabul came from, but it was heard as meaning as nothing, or good for nothing. Even if it first meant something else, it sounded like a put-down and matched Hiram's disappointment with the towns.

passages.saying: tore it into twelve pieces
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The twelve pieces stand for the twelve tribes, as the next verse explains.
layers.text: The prophet Ahijah met Jeroboam, tore a new cloak into twelve pieces, and told him to take ten. The torn cloak was an acted sign that God would tear ten of Israel's twelve tribes away from Solomon's house and give them to Jeroboam.

layers.evidence: George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) traces a link between Ahijah's chosen sign and the words spoken to Solomon in 1 Kings 11:11, and points to 1 Samuel 15:26-28. Gill, on 1 Samuel 15:28, says the tearing of the ten tribes from Solomon's kingdom was shown by a like sign. The verb qara (tear) is used in both scenes.
layers.text: This sign recalls Saul's rejection. When Saul grabbed Samuel's robe and it tore, Samuel said, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today." Now a prophet tears a cloak on purpose to show the kingdom being torn from Solomon. Both scenes use the Hebrew verb qara, to tear.

passages.saying: What portion do we have in David
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The cry voices the northern tribes' resentment and their break from David's house.
layers.text: When Rehoboam refused to lighten their burdens, the northern tribes rejected the house of David. They said they had no share in David's family, told Israel to go home, and left David's descendants to rule Judah alone.

layers.evidence: Gill says these seditious words seem borrowed from a seditious man in David's time (2 Samuel 20:1). Keil and Delitzsch call them the words with which Sheba once preached rebellion against David. In Hebrew both cries pair portion (cheleq) with inheritance (nachalah) and send Israel to their tents.
layers.text: The northern tribes repeat, almost word for word, the cry of Sheba, who rebelled against David with the words "We have no share in David" and sent every man to his tent. The resentment that sparked a revolt in David's day now splits the kingdom for good.

passages.saying: the king made two golden calves
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Jeroboam set up the calves to keep his people from going to Jerusalem and so to protect his throne.
layers.text: Afraid that his people would turn back to Rehoboam if they kept going up to worship at Jerusalem, Jeroboam made two golden calves. He told Israel the journey was too much for them and presented the calves as their gods.

layers.evidence: Gill says Jeroboam used the same words Aaron did; Clarke finds it strange that he used the same words Aaron used at the golden calf; Keil and Delitzsch call the words borrowed from Exodus 32:4. In Hebrew the calf (egel), your gods (elohekha) and brought you up (he'elukha) appear in both verses.
layers.text: Jeroboam's words, "Here, O Israel, are your gods," repeat what Israel said over Aaron's golden calf at Sinai: "These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" The northern kingdom begins by repeating the sin of the golden calf.

passages.saying: calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse records the founding of Samaria, which became the capital of the northern kingdom.
layers.text: King Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city on it. Samaria became the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel and the home of its kings.

layers.evidence: Gill says the city took its name Shomeron from Shemer; Keil and Delitzsch say Omri named it after the former owner of the hill; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) speaks of Omri naming his city after Shemer. Shomeron and Shemer are built on the same Hebrew letters, sh-m-r.
layers.text: The city's Hebrew name, Shomeron, comes from Shemer, the man who owned the hill before Omri bought it. So the capital of the northern kingdom carried the name of the hill's former owner.

layers.evidence: George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) suggests Omri also saw the name as fitting the site, since Shomeron would convey to a Hebrew ear the idea of a watch-tower, and he describes the hill as well suited for defense.
layers.text: The name may also have suited the place. To a Hebrew ear Shomeron suggested a watch-tower, and the city stood on a steep hill that was well placed for keeping watch and for defense.

passages.saying: Then Elijah took the child, brought him down from the upper room into the house, and gave him to his mother.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.evidence: Gill on 1 Kings 17:22: the first instance of anyone raised from the dead
layers.text: During a famine Elijah stays with a widow in Zarephath. When her son dies, Elijah stretches himself over the boy and prays, and the LORD restores his life: the first raising of the dead in the Bible. His mother says, "Now I know that you are a man of God."

layers.evidence: Both read kai edoken auton te metri autou: the Septuagint of 1 Kings 17:23 and Luke 7:15 in every edition TAGNT records. Ellicott and JFB on Luke 7:16 recall Elijah
layers.text: Luke tells how Jesus raised a widow's only son at Nain in the words of Elijah's story. Both stories meet a widow at the town gate, and Luke's Greek for "Jesus gave him back to his mother" matches the Greek Old Testament of this verse word for word.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Luke 7:14 sets the long grief and prayer of Elijah and Elisha over the dead beside the Lord's single command. Edersheim contrasts Christ's calm with the intense agitation of an Elijah or an Elisha
layers.text: The differences matter too. Elijah "stretched himself out over the child three times" and pleaded with the LORD; Jesus only touches the coffin and speaks: "Young man," He said, "I tell you, get up!" The crowd cries, "A great prophet has appeared among us!"

layers.evidence: Ellicott, JFB and Barnes on Luke 4:26: a Gentile, Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon; Ellicott sees in it the future calling of the Gentiles
layers.text: Jesus Himself pointed to this widow at Nazareth: "Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon," a Gentile town. He named Naaman the Syrian too, and the synagogue crowd was so enraged that it tried to throw Him off a cliff.

layers.evidence: Edersheim on Nain: southwards lies Shunem. JFB on Luke 7:16: more than bringing back the days of Elijah and Elisha. Barnes, JFB, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Hebrews 11:35 name the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite
layers.text: Elisha later raised a mother's son at Shunem, near Nain, so Luke's story recalls both prophets. Most commentators read Hebrews' "Women received back their dead, raised to life again" as the widow of Zarephath and the woman of Shunem.

layers.evidence: TBESH: Elijah, my God is Jehovah, or Yah is God. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) on 1 Kings 17:1: the name expresses the truth his whole life preached. Joseph Hammond (Pulpit Commentary) on 1 Kings 17:1: the name fits his life and work so closely, as 18:39 shows, that he may have taken it himself.
layers.text: Elijah's name, Eli-yahu, means that the LORD is my God. At Carmel the people's verdict puts his name into words: "The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!" The name sums up the truth his whole life preached.

passages.saying: they leaped around the altar they had made
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse shows Baal's silence despite his prophets' long cries.
layers.text: The prophets of Baal called on Baal from morning until noon, crying for him to answer. No voice came and no one answered, while they danced wildly around the altar they had built.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible renders the verb in verse 21 as leap and points to verse 26, and on verse 26 points back to verse 21. Keil and Delitzsch translate both as limp and call the word in verse 26 a scornful term for the priests' ritual dance. The Hebrew verb is pasach in both verses.
layers.text: The word for the prophets' leaping dance, pasach, is the same verb Elijah used when he asked how long the people would waver between two opinions, literally limp on two sides. The people limped between the LORD and Baal, and Baal's prophets limped around his altar for nothing.

passages.saying: Elijah took twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself: the stones match the number of Jacob's twelve tribes.
layers.text: To rebuild the LORD's altar on Mount Carmel, Elijah used twelve stones, one for each tribe descended from Jacob. Though the kingdom had split in two, he built as if all twelve tribes still belonged together in the worship of the one LORD.

layers.evidence: Gill points to the renaming at Penuel (Genesis 32:28); Keil and Delitzsch cite Genesis 32 and 35:10 and say the reminder showed that the name Israel belonged to the whole nation, not just the ten northern tribes.
layers.text: The verse recalls how God renamed Jacob, saying “Israel shall be your name” (Genesis 32:28; 35:10). By building with twelve stones, Elijah reminds the divided nation that the name Israel was given to their one forefather and belongs to all twelve tribes together.

passages.saying: The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the people's own words after the fire fell in verse 38.
layers.text: When fire from the LORD burned up Elijah's sacrifice, the watching crowd fell facedown and cried out twice that the LORD alone is God. The contest with the prophets of Baal was settled before everyone's eyes.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Elijah's test was based on Leviticus 9 and that the people fell on their faces as they had at the consecration of the altar (Leviticus 9:24). Gill on Leviticus 9:24 names Elijah's sacrifice as the same sign of God's acceptance.
layers.text: The scene repeats the first offerings at the tabernacle, when fire from the LORD consumed the burnt offering and all the people who saw it fell facedown (Leviticus 9:24). On Carmel God answered the same way, showing He accepted the sacrifice and was still Israel's God.

passages.saying: he walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the angel's two meals in verses 5 to 7.
layers.text: After an angel fed him in the wilderness, Elijah traveled on the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights until he came to Horeb, the mountain of God, where the LORD had once given Israel His law.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Elijah fasted just as long as Moses did at Horeb; Gill points to Exodus 24:18 and to Israel's forty years; Keil and Delitzsch compare Moses wandering with Israel forty years. The same number, forty (arbaim), appears in Exodus 24:18 and 34:28.
layers.text: Elijah's forty days and forty nights echo Moses, who stayed with the LORD on this same mountain forty days and forty nights without bread or water. They also recall Israel's forty years in the same wilderness, where God fed His people.

passages.saying: Behold, the LORD is about to pass by
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its sequel in verse 12.
layers.text: At Horeb the LORD told Elijah to stand on the mountain because He was about to pass by. A mighty wind and then an earthquake came first, but the LORD was not in them; He would make Himself known in a quieter way.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch all say God dealt with Elijah here as He had with Moses at Sinai. Keil and Delitzsch take the cave as the cleft of Exodus 33:22; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) calls that possible and Clarke notes it as a conjecture, while Gill doubts it. The verb avar, pass by, is used in all three verses.
layers.text: On this same mountain the LORD once passed by Moses as he hid in a cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:22; 34:6). Now He passes by Elijah there, and the same Hebrew word for passing by (avar) is used. Some take the cave where Elijah spent the night to be that very cleft.

passages.saying: The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Naboth's own words and his appeal to the LORD.
layers.text: King Ahab offered to buy or trade for Naboth's vineyard, but Naboth refused. The land had come down to him from his fathers, and he believed the LORD would not have him give it away.

layers.evidence: Gill ties Naboth's refusal to Leviticus 25:23, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and Bullinger's Companion Bible tie it to both Leviticus 25:23 and Numbers 36:7; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) and Clarke also say the law forbade it. This verse and Numbers 36:7 both speak of the inheritance (nachalah) of the fathers.
layers.text: Naboth's refusal rests on God's law. The land belonged to the LORD and could not be sold for good, and each family was to keep the inheritance of its fathers. Selling to the king would have broken that command, so Naboth chose obedience to God over pleasing the king.

passages.saying: I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the vision and the LORD's words that follow it in the verse.
layers.text: Pressed by Ahab to speak the truth, the prophet Micaiah told of a vision of Israel's army scattered with no one to lead it. It meant Ahab would die in the coming battle and his soldiers would go home.

layers.evidence: George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says the picture of sheep and shepherd was familiar from Moses' prayer in Numbers 27:17, and Keil and Delitzsch say Micaiah described the very state Moses prayed to avert. Both verses use tson (sheep) and roeh (shepherd).
layers.text: The words “like sheep without a shepherd” come from Moses' prayer that God would give Israel a leader after him. Micaiah's vision shows the very thing Moses prayed would not happen: Israel's king gone and his people left without a leader.

passages.saying: Go inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting, as Keil and Delitzsch explain Ahaziah's fall and his inquiry.
layers.text: King Ahaziah of Israel fell through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and was badly hurt. Instead of turning to the LORD, he sent messengers to ask a Philistine god at Ekron whether he would recover.

layers.evidence: Clarke, George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes), JFB, Wesley, Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all give the name as lord or god of flies, and the Septuagint renders it Baal the fly. Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible connect it with the Beelzebul of the Gospels.
layers.text: Baal-zebub means lord of flies. The king of Israel sought an answer from a fly-god of the Philistines rather than from the living God. In the Gospels a similar name, Beelzebul, is used for the prince of demons (Matthew 12:24).

passages.saying: struck the waters, which parted to the right and to the left
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's account of the crossing.
layers.text: At the Jordan, Elijah rolled up his cloak and struck the water. The river parted, and he and Elisha walked across on dry ground just before Elijah was taken up to heaven.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown liken the cloak to Moses' rod at the sea; Wesley and Matthew Henry recall the Jordan yielding to the ark under Joshua; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says the miracle set Elijah on a par with both leaders. Dry ground (charavah) is the word in Exodus 14:21 and Joshua 3:17 too.
layers.text: Elijah's cloak does what Moses' staff did at the sea, and the two men cross on dry ground as Israel crossed the sea and later the Jordan under Joshua. The miracle marks Elijah as a prophet standing in the line of Moses and Joshua.

passages.saying: Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Elijah's offer and Elisha's request in the verse.
layers.text: Before he was taken away, Elijah asked Elisha what he could do for him. Elisha did not ask for wealth or honor but for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, the God-given power he would need to carry on Elijah's work.

layers.evidence: Clarke, George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley all tie the request to the firstborn's double share in Deuteronomy 21:17, and Gill says that view may be most correct. The Hebrew pi shnayim appears in both verses.
layers.text: A double portion (pi shnayim) is the very phrase the law uses for the share of a father's estate given to his firstborn son. Elisha is asking to be treated as Elijah's firstborn spiritual son, the heir who carries on his master's work.

passages.saying: Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain account of Elisha's walk up to Bethel and the taunt he met there.
layers.text: As Elisha walked up the road to Bethel, the center of Israel's calf worship, a crowd of youths came out of the city and jeered at him, calling him baldhead and telling him to go up. The Hebrew word for boys can also mean young men.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Gill, Matthew Henry's Concise, Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all read the taunt as mockery of Elijah's being taken up to heaven; the Companion Bible says it may refer to his translation. The same verb, alah (go up), is used in 2:11 and 2:23.
layers.text: The taunt "Go up" uses the same Hebrew verb, alah, used just before when Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind. The youths were mocking the news of Elijah's going up and daring Elisha to follow him, so their scorn was aimed at the LORD's own work.

passages.saying: every fortified city and every city of importance
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Elisha's prophecy of victory over Moab in 3:16-19.
layers.text: Elisha tells the three kings that the LORD will also give Moab into their hands. Their armies will strike Moab's strong and choice cities, cut down its good trees, stop up its springs, and spoil its good fields by covering them with stones.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words mivtsar (fortified) and mivchor (choice) were meant to make a play on words through their likeness in sound and meaning.
layers.text: In Hebrew, fortified city and city of importance sound alike: ir mivtsar and ir mivchor. Some see a deliberate play here, the matching sounds pressing home that every city of Moab, the strongest and the finest alike, would be struck.

passages.saying: At this time next year, you will hold a son in your arms.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Elisha's promise to the woman of Shunem and her reply.
layers.text: Elisha promises the woman of Shunem, who has no son and whose husband is old, that within a year she will hold a son of her own. She can hardly believe it and begs him not to raise false hopes.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch point to Genesis 18:10 for the phrase and say the Shunammite was given the same favour as Sarah, whose disbelief she shares; Clarke likens the promise to the one about Isaac's birth. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) also compares her doubt with Sarah's in Genesis 18:12.
layers.text: Elisha's words, at this time next year, echo the Hebrew phrase ka'et chayyah from the LORD's promise that Sarah would have a son. Like Sarah, this woman with an old husband finds the promise hard to believe, and like Sarah she receives a son just as promised.

passages.saying: mouth to mouth, eye to eye, and hand to hand
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of Elisha raising the Shunammite's son in 4:32-35.
layers.text: After praying behind a shut door, Elisha lies on the dead boy with his mouth, eyes, and hands on the boy's and bows over him. The child's body begins to grow warm as the LORD brings him back to life.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke (on 1 Kings 17:21), Keil and Delitzsch, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all tie this scene to Elijah raising the widow's son. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) and Keil-Delitzsch also note differences: the verb for stretching out is not the same, and Elisha's miracle came gradually.
layers.text: Elisha follows the pattern of his master Elijah, who stretched himself out over the widow's dead son at Zarephath and cried to the LORD. As God gave that boy back through Elijah, He now gives this boy back through Elisha, Elijah's successor.

passages.saying: Please strike these people with blindness.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of Elisha's prayer when the Aramean troops came to seize him at Dothan.
layers.text: As the Aramean troops sent to capture Elisha came down toward him, he prayed, and the LORD struck them with a blindness that confused them, so that they did not recognize the prophet or the place.

layers.evidence: Gill notes the same word is used of the men of Sodom; Keil and Delitzsch call it the same mental blindness as in Genesis 19:11; Bullinger's Figures of Speech says these are the only two places the word occurs. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also points to Genesis 19:11.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for this blindness, sanverim, appears only here and in Genesis 19:11, where the men of Sodom at Lot's door were struck with it. In both stories God shields His servants by confusing the sight of those who come against them.

passages.saying: My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of King Jehoash visiting the dying Elisha.
layers.text: When Elisha was dying, King Jehoash of Israel came to him and wept. He called the old prophet his father and Israel's chariots and horsemen, meaning that Elisha had been the nation's true defense.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Clarke, Gill, George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all note that the king repeats the very cry Elisha raised when Elijah was taken up (2:12). The Hebrew of the two cries is identical.
layers.text: The king's cry repeats word for word what Elisha himself cried when Elijah was taken up to heaven. Elisha, who had mourned his master with these words, is now mourned with them, honored as Elijah's true successor and Israel's real strength.

passages.saying: They pursued worthless idols and themselves became worthless
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own list of what Israel rejected and what it followed instead.
layers.text: Israel rejected the LORD's statutes, His covenant with their fathers and His warnings. They chased worthless idols and copied the nations around them, the very thing the LORD had told them not to do.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note that the words are verbatim as in Jeremiah 2:5, and the Companion Bible at Jeremiah 2:5 points to this verse. The Hebrew of both lines is the same.
layers.text: The same Hebrew words appear in Jeremiah 2:5, where the LORD asks what fault the fathers found in Him that they "followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves". The history of Israel's fall gives the same verdict as the prophet.

layers.evidence: Gill, George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) and Wesley all explain that the idols are vanity and that their worshippers became vain like them; Rawlinson adds that the word means breath or vapor. The noun hevel and the verb yehbalu share one root, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech refers the same words in Jeremiah 2:5 to paronomasia, a play on words.
layers.text: In Hebrew, Israel went after hevel, a mere breath or vapor, meaning empty idols, and then became empty themselves (yehbalu), a verb from the same root. The repeated sound makes the point: people become like the things they worship.

passages.saying: the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its place in the list of settlers in 2 Kings 17:24-33.
layers.text: The peoples the Assyrians moved into Samaria brought their own gods with them. The Avvites made idols named Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their own children as offerings to their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech.

layers.evidence: George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says the Jews at times altered the names of pagan gods in derision, and calls Anammelech possibly such a contemptuous play upon words: a goddess's name fitted with the male ending. He offers it as possible, not certain.
layers.text: Some suggest the Hebrew writer reshaped these foreign names on purpose, in scorn. Anammelech may be a goddess's name given the male ending melech, king, so that it sounded ridiculous to Hebrew ears.

layers.evidence: Clarke derives Adrammelech from adar, glorious, and melech, king; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) renders it the glorious king; Gill reads it the mighty king and notes that both names end in melech, king, as the name Moloch also signifies.
layers.text: Both names end in melech, the Hebrew word for king, a word also heard in the name Molech, the god of child sacrifice. In Hebrew, Adrammelech can be read as glorious king or mighty king (adar and melech).

passages.saying: He also demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and the history of the bronze snake in Numbers 21.
layers.text: Hezekiah removed the high places, smashed the sacred pillars and cut down the Asherah poles. He even broke up the bronze snake Moses had made, because the Israelites had been burning incense to it.

layers.evidence: Clarke sends the reader to Numbers 21:8-9 for its history, Gill says it is the serpent Moses made in the wilderness, and the Companion Bible says to compare Numbers 21:9. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Numbers 21 also links the two passages.
layers.text: This is the very bronze snake Moses made in the wilderness, when the LORD told him to set a snake on a pole so that anyone bitten who looked at it would live. A sign of God's mercy had been turned into an idol.

layers.evidence: Gill says the name signifies brass, a mere piece of brass; Wesley calls it nothing but a piece of brass; the Companion Bible renders it a brass thing; George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) sets nechushtan, the brass thing, beside nachash, the serpent.
layers.text: Nehushtan means a bronze thing, a mere piece of bronze. It comes from nechoshet, bronze, a word that sounds much like nachash, snake. The name treats the object people burned incense to as nothing more than metal.

passages.saying: the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the charges against Manasseh in 2 Kings 21:1-11.
layers.text: Because of Manasseh's sins, the LORD announced a disaster on Jerusalem and Judah so terrible that the mere report of it would shock everyone who heard it.

layers.evidence: Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) on 1 Samuel 3:11 notes that this phrase occurs again of the destruction of Jerusalem, and the Companion Bible at this verse says to compare 1 Samuel 3:11. Jeremiah 19:3 uses it once more.
layers.text: In Hebrew this is almost the same saying God gave the boy Samuel about the judgment on Eli's house: "the ears of all who hear it will tingle". The shock once announced against Eli's family is now announced against Jerusalem and Judah.

passages.saying: to the south of the Mount of Corruption
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on 1 Kings 11:7, where Solomon built these shrines.
layers.text: Josiah defiled the high places east of Jerusalem that Solomon had built for the gods of the Sidonians, Moabites and Ammonites, so that they could no longer be used for worship.

layers.evidence: Gill says the Mount of Olives was called the mount of corruption by way of reproach, for the idolatry and corrupt worship performed in it, with a small alteration of the letters of the word. Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading mount of anointing and read it as mountain of destruction.
layers.text: Some see a pun here. The hill famous for olive oil would recall mishchah, anointing, and a small change of letters turns it into mashchit, corruption, so a name of blessing becomes a name of shame.

layers.evidence: Wesley, the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech all say the Mount of Olives was called the mount of corruption because of the idolatry practiced there; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown places it on one summit of that ridge.
layers.text: The Mount of Corruption is the Mount of Olives, or one of its peaks, east of Jerusalem. It earned this name of shame because of the idol worship at the shrines Solomon built for foreign gods on that ridge.

passages.saying: One was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its source in Genesis 10:25.
layers.text: Eber had two sons, Peleg and Joktan. Repeating Genesis 10:25, the Chronicler notes that the earth was divided in Peleg's lifetime, which is often taken to mean the peoples were divided by language and land.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible renders Peleg disruption, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech explains the name as division, given because in his days the earth was divided.
layers.text: Peleg means division. The verse ties the name to a verb from the same root: in his days the earth was divided (niflegah). His name kept the memory of that dividing.

passages.saying: Achar, who brought trouble upon Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse sums up the story told in Joshua 7, where Achan kept for himself things devoted to the LORD.
layers.text: In the family of Zerah, Judah's son, the list names Carmi's son Achar. He is remembered for one thing: he brought trouble on Israel by taking for himself things that had been devoted to the LORD, as Joshua 7 tells.

layers.evidence: George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says Achan became Achar to match the Hebrew word for troubler; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley say Achar means troubler; Gill says the name signifies the troubler of Israel. The name and the verb troubled share one Hebrew root.
layers.text: Joshua calls this man Achan, but here he is Achar, a form that means troubler. The verse then says he troubled (okher) Israel, using the same Hebrew root, so his name matches his deed. Joshua 7 ties that word to the Valley of Achor, where he died.

passages.saying: Because I bore him in pain
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse itself gives the mother's reason for the name.
layers.text: Jabez is singled out in Judah's family list as more honored than his brothers. His mother gave him his name because his birth brought her great pain.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible suggests the transposed letters may hint at a change of experience, pain reversed.
layers.text: One reading sees a further hint in the switched letters. Since the word for pain is turned around in his name, it may point to pain being reversed, and the next verse tells how God answered his prayer to be kept from pain.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note the similar-sounding word for sorrow set beside the name; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) say the name signifies grief or sorrow; Wesley speaks of the sorrow in his name; the Companion Bible points out the switched letters.
layers.text: The name Jabez (ya-bets) sounds like the Hebrew word for pain in this verse (otsev), with two of its letters switched around. So the boy's very name carried the memory of the pain his mother felt when he was born.

passages.saying: keep me from harm, so that I will be free from pain
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse records the prayer and says plainly that God granted it.
layers.text: Jabez prayed to the God of Israel to bless him, enlarge his land, be with him, and keep him from harm so that he would not suffer pain. God gave him what he asked.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the closing words a play on the name Jabez; Gill and Wesley say he alludes to his name; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) say the same on verse 9. Keil and Delitzsch add that his life came to contradict his name.
layers.text: The name Jabez sounds like the Hebrew word for pain. His prayer ends by asking that harm would not pain him (otsbi), a word from that same root. He asks that the sorrow in his name would not mark his life, and God granted his request.

passages.saying: which was given this name because its people were craftsmen
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse names Joab as father, meaning founder or head, of the people of this settlement.
layers.text: In Judah's family list, Seraiah's son Joab is named as the father, that is the founder or head, of the people of Ge-harashim. Its people were craftsmen who lived and worked together in one place.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch all render the name the valley of craftsmen; Gill says the word covers carpenters and smiths, and both he and Keil and Delitzsch link it to Nehemiah 11:35.
layers.text: Ge-harashim means valley of craftsmen. The verse explains the name with the same Hebrew word: it was the valley of the harashim because its people were harashim, skilled workers such as carpenters and smiths. Nehemiah 11:35 names the same Valley of the Craftsmen.

passages.saying: So he named him Beriah, because tragedy had come upon his house
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse follows the killing of Ezer and Elead and Ephraim's mourning in verses 21 and 22.
layers.text: After men of Gath killed his sons Ezer and Elead, Ephraim mourned for many days. Later his wife bore another son, and he named the boy after the disaster that had struck his family.

layers.evidence: Gill says Beriah signifies in evil or calamity; Wesley says it means in trouble, since he was born while the family mourned. In Hebrew the name is close to be-raah, in trouble, the phrase the verse uses.
layers.text: The name Beriah sounds like be-raah, in trouble, the very words the verse uses for the tragedy in his house, and it is taken to mean in trouble or in evil. So the boy's name kept alive the memory of his family's grief.

passages.saying: so he named that place Perez-uzzah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse follows Uzzah's death for taking hold of the ark in verses 9 and 10.
layers.text: After the LORD struck down Uzzah for taking hold of the ark, David was angry, and he named the place for what had happened there. The verse adds that the place is still called by that name to this day.

layers.evidence: Wesley explains the name as the breach of Uzza. The verb and noun for breaking out in the verse and the first part of the place name share one Hebrew root.
layers.text: Perez-uzzah means the breach of Uzzah. The name repeats the verse's own words: the LORD had broken out (parats) in a breaking out (perets) against Uzzah, so the place name kept the memory of that judgment.

passages.saying: his name will be Solomon, and I will grant to Israel peace and quiet
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own promise about the son and the peace of his reign.
layers.text: God tells David that a son will be born to him who will be a man of rest. God will give him rest from his enemies on every side, and Israel will have peace and quiet while he reigns, leaving him free to build the temple.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the Lord alludes to the name Shelomoh when He promises shalom in his days; Gill says the name Solomon signifies peace; Keil and Delitzsch say he would rightly bear the name, which means rich in peace, because God would give Israel peace and rest.
layers.text: Solomon's Hebrew name, Shelomoh, is built on the same root as shalom, peace. God links the two in one breath: the boy will be called Solomon, and God will give Israel peace in his days. The name itself announces what his reign will be like.

passages.saying: on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on David's altar at Ornan's threshing floor in 1 Chronicles 21.
layers.text: Solomon began building the LORD's house in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David. It stood on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, the place David had bought and prepared for it.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call Mount Moriah manifestly the mountain where Abraham was to sacrifice Isaac; Clarke says it is supposed to be the same place; Gill, on Genesis 22:2, takes the Mount Moriah of this verse as the mount intended; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also ties the name to Genesis 22:2.
layers.text: The name Moriah takes the reader back to Genesis 22, where God sent Abraham to the land of Moriah to offer Isaac and then provided a ram in his place. The temple, where Israel's sacrifices would be offered, was built on that same mountain.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on this verse, explain Moriah as the appearance of the LORD, named from Abraham's offering, and argue that the verb here means He appeared. Gill, on Genesis 22:2, also derives Moriah from the verb to see.
layers.text: Moriah is explained as meaning the appearing of the LORD, from the verb ra'ah, to see. This verse uses that same verb when it says the LORD had appeared (nir'ah) to David on the mountain.

passages.saying: he named Jachin, and the pillar on the north he named Boaz
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the fuller description of the pillars in 1 Kings 7:15-22.
layers.text: Solomon set up two great pillars at the front of the temple, one on the south side and one on the north, and gave each pillar its own name.

layers.evidence: Wesley's Notes give the meaning of Jachin as He shall establish and of Boaz as In it is strength.
layers.text: Solomon gave the two pillars names with meanings. Jachin means he will establish, and Boaz means in it is strength.

passages.saying: fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's account of fire and glory after Solomon's prayer.
layers.text: When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and burned up the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple. It was God's sign that He accepted the house and its offerings.

layers.evidence: George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says the fire came as at the dedication of the tabernacle in Leviticus 9:24; Bullinger's Figures of Speech says God's fire fell at the first at the tabernacle and again at the temple; Gill names Leviticus 9:24 as an earlier token of God's acceptance; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also points to it.
layers.text: The scene echoes the first sacrifices at the tabernacle, when fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering (Leviticus 9:24). As He did then, God shows by fire that He accepts the new place of worship and the sacrifices offered there.

passages.saying: to David and his descendants forever by a covenant of salt
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Abijah's speech to Jeroboam and Israel before the battle.
layers.text: Before the battle, King Abijah of Judah reminds Jeroboam and the northern tribes that the LORD gave the kingship over Israel to David and his descendants forever, by a covenant that would never be broken.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch read covenant of salt as an irrevocable covenant and point to Leviticus 2:13 and Numbers 18:19; the Companion Bible sends the reader to the same two verses and counts this as the third use; Clarke refers to his note on Numbers 18:19; Wesley, on Numbers 18:19, links that verse with this one.
layers.text: Covenant of salt is the phrase God used for the priests' lasting share of the holy offerings (Numbers 18:19). Salt keeps food from spoiling, so it pictures a covenant that lasts. Abijah applies it to God's promise to David's line, which cannot be undone.

passages.saying: Therefore that place is called the Valley of Beracah to this day
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of Jehoshaphat's victory in verses 20 to 25 and the thanksgiving that followed.
layers.text: On the fourth day, after three days of gathering plunder, the people of Judah met in a valley and praised the LORD for the victory He had given them without a battle. The valley was named for that day of praise.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill all explain Beracah as blessing, named from the people's blessing of the LORD there; Clarke gives the Targum's Valley of Benediction. The noun berakhah and the verb barakh in this verse share one root.
layers.text: Beracah means blessing. The people blessed (berakhu) the LORD in this valley, so it was named the Valley of Blessing (berakhah), from the same Hebrew root. The name still marked the place when Chronicles was written.

passages.saying: they blessed the LORD and His people Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 5 to 7, where the people bring tithes and firstfruits that pile up in heaps.
layers.text: When Hezekiah and his officials saw the great heaps of tithes and firstfruits brought for the priests and Levites, they praised the LORD for His provision and blessed the people of Israel.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under Syllepsis, one word taken in two senses at once: thanks and praise toward God, prayer for blessing toward the people. Gill likewise reads the second blessing as wishing the people all happiness and prosperity.
layers.text: One verb, blessed (barakh), does double duty here. Toward the LORD it means giving Him thanks and praise. Toward His people it means praying for God's good gifts on them. The single word holds both kinds of blessing together.

passages.saying: So the land enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the law of the seventh-year rest for the land and Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years.
layers.text: Judah was carried off to Babylon, and the land lay desolate until seventy years were completed, as Jeremiah had foretold. Israel had often farmed the land in the seventh year when it should have rested, so now it rested through the exile.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the clause is taken word for word from Leviticus 26:34; Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to the same threat by Moses, and the Companion Bible calls it a fulfillment of Leviticus 26. Both verses use ratsah (enjoy), shabbat (Sabbath) and shavat (rest).
layers.text: This echoes the warning of the law: "Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate" (Leviticus 26:34). Israel had denied the land its Sabbath years, so God gave it that rest while His people were in exile.

passages.saying: have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verse 2, which explains that they had taken wives from these peoples for themselves and their sons.
layers.text: After Ezra had arrived and finished his first duties, leaders told him that the people of Israel, even priests and Levites, had married into the surrounding peoples and had not kept apart from their idolatrous practices.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, the Companion Bible and Matthew Henry all tie this complaint to the law against intermarriage in Deuteronomy 7; Gill and Keil and Delitzsch explain the added Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians by the same danger of idolatry.
layers.text: This list echoes the law. Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites and Amorites are among the nations of Deuteronomy 7, of whom God said, "Do not intermarry with them." Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians are added for the same danger of idolatry.

passages.saying: I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Nehemiah's prayer in verses 5 to 11, which calls on God's word through Moses.
layers.text: Nehemiah reminds God of His promise: if His scattered people return to Him and obey His commandments, He will gather them even from the farthest places and bring them back to Jerusalem, the place He chose for His Name.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call Nehemiah's words a free summary with Deuteronomy 30:1-5 chiefly in view, the word for exiles used as in Deuteronomy 30:4; the Companion Bible ties the call to return to Deuteronomy 30:2. Both verses use nadach (banished), qatseh (farthest) and qavats (gather).
layers.text: Nehemiah prays back the promise of Deuteronomy 30, where Moses told a repentant Israel, "Even if you have been banished to the farthest horizon, He will gather you and return you from there." Nehemiah's words follow that promise closely.

passages.saying: You found his heart faithful before You
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verse 7 and the Genesis account of God's covenant with Abraham.
layers.text: This prayer praises God for finding Abraham's heart faithful and making a covenant to give his descendants the land of Canaan. God kept that promise, because He is righteous.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say faithful refers back to Abraham believing the LORD in Genesis 15, and Gill reads it as a true believer, citing Genesis 15:6 and the covenant of Genesis 15:18, which the Companion Bible also cites. Faithful (ne'eman) and believed (he'emin) are forms of one root, aman.
layers.text: This looks back to Genesis 15:6, "Abram believed the LORD." In Hebrew, faithful (ne'eman) and believed (he'emin) come from one root, aman: Abram trusted God, and God found his heart trustworthy. The covenant to give the land recalls the same chapter (Genesis 15:18).

passages.saying: You hurled their pursuers into the depths like a stone into raging waters.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It retells the crossing of the Red Sea in Exodus 14 and 15.
layers.text: The prayer recalls how God split the Red Sea so that Israel crossed on dry ground, and then threw the pursuing Egyptian army into the deep water, where they sank like a stone.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words in the depths like a stone are taken from Exodus 15:5. Gill, on Exodus 15:5, says this sinking like a stone is the detail Nehemiah 9:11 takes up.
layers.text: The prayer borrows its words from the song Israel sang after crossing the sea, where the Egyptians "sank there like a stone." The Hebrew phrase for into the depths like a stone (bimtsolot kemo even) is the same in both places, so the people praise God in Moses' own words.

passages.saying: appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It sums up Israel's rebellions in the wilderness and God's mercy toward them.
layers.text: The people confess that their ancestors refused to listen, forgot God's wonders, and even chose a leader to take them back to slavery in Egypt. Yet God, who is forgiving, gracious and patient, did not abandon them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the clause is taken almost word for word from Numbers 14:4, the rebellion at Kadesh. Gill and the Companion Bible point to Numbers 14:4, and Gill, Wesley and George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) note that the people only resolved on it there, yet the prayer speaks of it as done.
layers.text: This line looks back to the rebellion at Kadesh, where the people said, "Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt." The same Hebrew words for appointing a leader (natan rosh) and going back (shuv) appear in both. They only planned it, but the prayer counts the plan as done.

layers.evidence: Gill says this is how God had proclaimed His name before Moses and points to Exodus 34:6. Keil and Delitzsch call the words gracious and merciful a reminiscence of Exodus 34:6.
layers.text: Calling God gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion repeats what the LORD proclaimed about Himself to Moses on Mount Sinai. The people pray back to God the very words He used to describe His own character.

passages.saying: he was loved by his God, who made him king over all Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Nehemiah uses Solomon's fall as a warning against marrying foreign wives.
layers.text: Nehemiah warns the men who had married foreign wives. Solomon was the greatest king of his day and loved by God, yet his foreign wives led him into sin. If it happened to him, it could happen to them.

layers.evidence: Gill says the words beloved of God allude to Solomon's other name, Jedidiah, meaning beloved of the Lord, given in 2 Samuel 12:24-25. Keil and Delitzsch also say the phrase alludes to 2 Samuel 12:24.
layers.text: Saying Solomon was loved by his God looks back to his birth, when the LORD loved the child and had Nathan name him Jedidiah, which means beloved of the LORD. Even a king given such a name was led astray, which makes Nehemiah's warning sharper.

passages.saying: Mordecai had brought up Hadassah (that is, Esther)
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It introduces Esther as Mordecai's orphaned cousin whom he raised.
layers.text: Esther was an orphan, the daughter of Mordecai's uncle. When her parents died, Mordecai took her in and raised her as his own daughter. She was also very beautiful.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all give Hadassah as myrtle. All of them but Rawlinson take Esther as Persian for star; Rawlinson says that link is thought likely but not yet proven.
layers.text: Esther had two names. Her Hebrew name, Hadassah, means myrtle. Esther, the name she was known by at the Persian court, is commonly taken to mean star in Persian, though that link is less certain than the meaning of Hadassah.

passages.saying: King Xerxes honored Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It records Haman's promotion to the highest post under the king.
layers.text: King Xerxes promoted Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and gave him a seat above all the other officials. Haman became the most powerful man in the empire after the king.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Wesley and the Companion Bible take Agagite to mean a descendant of Agag, the Amalekite king of 1 Samuel 15. Keil and Delitzsch say the name recalls Agag and the link is possible but cannot be proved. Gill and George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) doubt it and think Haman may simply have been a Persian.
layers.text: Haman is called the Agagite. Many take this to mean he came from the line of Agag, the king of Amalek whom Saul spared and Samuel put to death. If so, Haman's hatred of the Jews carries on that old enmity. Others think Agagite may simply be a Persian family name.

passages.saying: the Pur (that is, the lot) was cast before Haman
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, as Keil and Delitzsch explain why Haman turned to the lot.
layers.text: In the first month of King Xerxes' twelfth year, lots were cast before Haman to choose a day for his plan to destroy the Jews. The lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

layers.evidence: Gill, George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes), Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all explain Pur as a foreign word meaning lot, glossed here in Hebrew. Gill, Wesley and Matthew Henry's Concise see God's hand in the lot falling so late. Esther 9:26 says the feast of Purim is named from Pur.
layers.text: Pur was a foreign word, so the writer explains it: that is, the lot. It was cast before Haman to pick a day to destroy the Jews, but it fell months away, giving time for rescue. The word then named the feast of their deliverance: "these days are called Purim, from the word Pur."

passages.saying: And if I perish, I perish!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Esther resolves to risk her life by going to the king unsummoned.
