layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Song 8:6 recalls Paul in Romans 8. Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: no waters can quench Christ's love to us.
layers.text: Christians hear in love "as strong as death" a love stronger still. Some recall Paul here: neither death nor life "will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Others add that no waters can quench Christ's love.

passages.saying: So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the bride's picture of herself as a wall, as T. L. Kingsbury (Barnes' Notes) explains it.
layers.text: The bride says she kept herself pure, firm as a wall with towers. Because of that she won favor in her beloved's eyes and came into a relationship of peace with him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch ask why she says shalom (peace) here rather than the usual word for favor, and answer that she plays on the name Solomon, which she says in the next verse and which 1 Chronicles 22:9 ties to peace.
layers.text: The Hebrew says she became in his eyes like one who finds shalom, peace. The very next verse names Solomon, Shelomoh in Hebrew, a name built on that same word for peace. So the bride has found shalom with Shelomoh, the king whose name means peace.

passages.saying: Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, as John Wesley explains it.
layers.text: The bride tells of a vineyard Solomon owned at Baal-hamon. He let it out to keepers, and each of them was to pay him a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit.

layers.evidence: John Gill says the name signifies the master or lord of a multitude, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives it as owner of a multitude.
layers.text: The place name Baal-hamon means lord of a multitude, or owner of a crowd. Solomon's vineyard lies in a place whose very name speaks of great numbers.

passages.saying: Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's summons to heaven and earth and God's complaint against His children.
layers.text: God calls on heaven and earth to listen as He speaks. He raised Israel like a father raises children, yet they rebelled against Him.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls these the very words of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:1. Barnes finds the same opening in the song of Moses, and Keil and Delitzsch say Isaiah begins as Moses' song begins, only swapping hear and give ear. Clarke and Gill also point to Deuteronomy 32:1.
layers.text: Isaiah opens with the call Moses used to begin his last song, asking heaven and earth to listen, with the two verbs swapped. Moses called them as witnesses against a rebellion still to come. Isaiah calls them again now that the rebellion has come.

passages.saying: Alas, O sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's cry of grief and its list of names for a people weighed down by sin.
layers.text: Isaiah mourns over Israel as a nation weighed down by sin, a family of evildoers who have abandoned the LORD and turned their backs on the Holy One of Israel.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch set the sinful nation against the holy nation (goi kadosh) of Exodus 19:6, and the Companion Bible note on this verse says to contrast Exodus 19:6.
layers.text: At Mount Sinai God called Israel a holy nation. Isaiah turns that title around: the same people have become a sinful nation, the very opposite of what God chose them to be.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch point out the alliteration in hoi goi and say it marks the sinful nation as a nation of woe.
layers.text: The verse opens with two rhyming Hebrew words, hoy goy, meaning alas and nation. Some hear the matching sounds binding the cry of grief to the people, as if this sinful nation had become a nation of woe.

passages.saying: we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's statement that the LORD left survivors.
layers.text: Isaiah says that only the mercy of the LORD of Hosts, who left a few survivors, kept Judah from being wiped out completely.

layers.evidence: Barnes says Judah would have been overwhelmed as Sodom was and compares Genesis 19:24-25. The Companion Bible marks it as a reference to Genesis 19, Gill recalls the cities consumed by fire from heaven, and Keil and Delitzsch note that Gomorrah was utterly destroyed.
layers.text: Sodom and Gomorrah recall the cities the LORD overthrew with sulfur and fire from heaven. Without a remnant, Judah would have shared their total ruin. In the next verse Isaiah even calls Jerusalem's leaders rulers of Sodom.

passages.saying: you will eat the best of the land
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of the land's good to those who obey.
layers.text: God sets a choice before His people. If they willingly obey, they will enjoy the good harvest of their land. If they refuse and rebel, war will destroy them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch contrast the promise of eating with the curse of being eaten by the sword, and say Isaiah used an unusual construction for the sake of the paronomasia, a play on words.
layers.text: The same Hebrew verb, to eat, is used both ways. Obey, and you will eat (tokhelu) the best of the land. Rebel, and you will be eaten (te'ukkelu) by the sword. Some see a deliberate play here: the people will either eat or be eaten.

passages.saying: Your rulers are rebels, friends of thieves
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's charges against Jerusalem's leaders.
layers.text: Jerusalem's leaders defy God, side with thieves and chase bribes, so orphans and widows find no one to defend them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call sorerim alliterative with the rulers' title sarim. The Companion Bible calls sarim sorerim a paronomasia for solemn emphasis and suggests the English, thy rulers are unruly.
layers.text: In Hebrew, “Your rulers are rebels” is just two words, sarayikh sorerim. The leaders' title and their rebellion sound almost the same, much as if we said the rulers are unruly.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch observe that it was not peace (shalom) the rulers hunted after but shalmonim, payments that would satisfy their greed.
layers.text: The rulers chase shalmonim, payoffs or rewards, a word that sounds like shalom, peace. The line can be read as a pointed contrast: instead of pursuing peace, they pursue payment.

passages.saying: the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise to restore judges and counselors and to rename the city.
layers.text: God promises to give Jerusalem honest judges and wise counselors again, as in her early days. Then she will be known for righteousness and faithfulness.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says faithful here means no longer a harlot. Barnes and the Companion Bible both point back to Isaiah 1:21, and Keil and Delitzsch say the names show the city's true nature made plain.
layers.text: Jerusalem's new names say what she will be. In verse 21 the faithful city had become a harlot, though righteousness once lived in her. Once God purifies her, she gets both back as names: City of Righteousness and Faithful City.

passages.saying: when He rises to shake the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of people fleeing into caves before the LORD.
layers.text: When the LORD rises in judgment, idol worshipers will run into caves and holes in the ground, trying to hide from His terrifying majesty.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call larotz ha-aretz a significant paronomasia, like the Latin ut terreat terram. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the pair laarotz and haaretz in Isaiah 2:19 and 2:21 among its examples of paronomasia.
layers.text: In Hebrew, “to shake the earth” is la'arots ha'arets. The verb for making tremble and the word for earth sound almost alike, so the sound itself stresses that the whole earth will shake. The same phrase returns in verse 21.

passages.saying: about to remove from Jerusalem and Judah both supply and support
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and the list of leaders that follows in 3:2-3.
layers.text: The Lord is about to take away everything Jerusalem and Judah lean on. It starts with their food and water, and the next verses add their warriors, judges, prophets and elders.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible calls the pair a paronomasia (a play on words). Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke all note that the two nouns are one word in its masculine and feminine forms, meaning every kind of support.
layers.text: In Hebrew, supply and support are one word said twice: mash'en and mash'enah, its masculine and feminine forms. The pair means every kind of support. A third form, mish'an, follows for the food and water God will remove.

passages.saying: a cloud of smoke by day and a glowing flame of fire by night
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the promise of shelter that completes it in 4:6.
layers.text: Once Zion is cleansed, the LORD will create over the whole mountain and its gatherings a cloud by day and fire by night. Over all its glory He will spread a canopy, a sign that He guards and shelters His people.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley all tie this cloud and fire to the pillar that led Israel out of Egypt. Keil and Delitzsch add that it now rests over Zion as a covering instead of leading a journey.
layers.text: Cloud by day and fire by night recall the pillar that led Israel out of Egypt. The presence that guided and guarded God's people in the wilderness will rest over Zion, no longer leading a journey but covering it like a canopy.

passages.saying: I will sing for my beloved a song of his vineyard
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the song's own explanation in 5:7.
layers.text: Isaiah begins a song for his beloved about the beloved's vineyard on a fertile hill. As the song unfolds, the beloved is the LORD and the vineyard is His people Israel (5:7).

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on 5:1: Isaiah alludes plainly to the Song of Solomon (6:3; 8:11-12) in the words his vineyard and my beloved.
layers.text: Some hear in my beloved and his vineyard an echo of the Song of Solomon: "I belong to my beloved," and "Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon." If so, Isaiah takes up the language of a love song, then tells of a vineyard that failed the one who loved it.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on 5:1 speak of the rhythm, musical euphony and charming assonances of the opening line, and say they cannot be reproduced in translation.
layers.text: Some hear the opening line as musical in Hebrew, with sounds that echo each other: ashirah (I will sing) and shirat (a song of), lididi (for my beloved) and dodi (my beloved). On this reading its rhythm and music are nearly impossible to carry into English.

passages.saying: He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Isaiah sings about a vineyard its owner tended with every care, which still grew only sour grapes. Then he names it: the vineyard is Israel, and the fruit God wanted was justice.

The punchline is two pairs of sound-alike words: God looked for mishpat (justice) and found mispach (bloodshed), for tsedaqah (righteousness) and heard tse'aqah (a cry). Mispach occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, so its exact sense is not certain.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 5:7: the nation is pictured elsewhere under the same figure of a vineyard (Isaiah 27:2; Psalm 80). Barnes on 5:1: the Jewish people are often represented as a vineyard planted by God (Psalm 80; Jeremiah 2:21). The Pulpit Commentary compares Psalm 80:8-16. Calvin: the metaphor is frequently employed by the prophets. The Companion Bible adds Hosea 10:1.
layers.text: Israel as God's vine is a running picture: "You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it."

layers.evidence: Maclaren on Mark 12:1: the picture is based upon Isaiah's song, and our Lord follows the original passage. The Pulpit Commentary: the imagery would be familiar from Isaiah 5:1. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Matthew 21:33: the details, and the basis of the parable, are taken from Isaiah 5:1-7. Ellicott: its opening points to Isaiah 5:1. Gill: the vineyard is Isaiah's.
layers.text: Jesus retells this song as the parable of the tenants, with Isaiah's details: a planted vineyard, a wall, a wine vat, a watchtower. This time the owner sends his beloved son, and the leaders know the story is about them.
Jesus says, "I am the true vine." Where the vineyard of Isaiah 5 gave sour fruit, the true vine bears fruit, and those who remain in Him "bear much fruit."

passages.saying: Go out with your son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the threat described in 7:1-2.
layers.text: As Aram and Israel threaten Jerusalem, the LORD sends Isaiah and his son to meet King Ahaz outside the city, at the aqueduct of the upper pool, where the king was likely seeing to the water supply.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and the Companion Bible all give the name as the remnant shall return; Keil and Delitzsch, the remnant is converted. Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch point to 10:21-22.
layers.text: Shear-jashub means a remnant will return. The boy was a living message to Ahaz: judgment would come, yet God would not wipe out His people. Isaiah later spells it out, "A remnant will return," and says it will return to the Mighty God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on 7:3: father and son together were a personified blessing and curse; the son's name threatened, while Isaiah's own name pointed to salvation.
layers.text: Isaiah's own name is built on the Hebrew word for salvation. Some see father and son, standing before the king together, as a double message: the son's name warned that only a remnant would be left, and the father's name held out the LORD's salvation.

passages.saying: If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." God sends Isaiah to say the invasion "will not happen." All turns on whether Ahaz will trust God, and he refuses even the sign God offers.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:9: a wordplay designed to draw attention to the alternatives set before the king; ta'aminu is the Hiphil and te'amenu the Niphal of aman. TBESH H0539: Niphal made firm, sure; Hiphil to trust, believe. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and Bullinger call it a paronomasia; Keil and Delitzsch find the same play in 2 Chronicles 20:20.
layers.text: The warning uses one Hebrew verb twice: im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu. Ta'aminu, "believe," and te'amenu, "be made firm," are two forms of aman. The pun sets the king's two choices side by side, and the BSB keeps the echo: "stand firm" and "stand at all."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 7:9: the same play upon words is in 2 Chronicles 20:20. Ellicott: an affirmative way of putting Isaiah's words to Ahaz. Maclaren: believing and being established are two forms of the same root-word.
layers.text: Earlier, King Jehoshaphat faced an invasion with the same pair: "Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld" (ha'aminu, te'amenu), Isaiah's warning put positively. His people sang, and "the LORD set ambushes" against the invaders.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: the first occurrence of H0539 is Genesis 15:6 (vehe'emin). Keil and Delitzsch: aman is to be firm and to confirm, in Hiphil to trust, believe. Gill: this is the first time we read of believing.
layers.text: Aman first appears in the Bible when "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness," the verse Paul quotes in Romans and Galatians. Isaiah's pun shows what the word holds: in Hebrew, believing God and being made firm share one root.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Isaiah 28:16: ho pisteuōn ep' autō ou mē kataischynthē. TAHOT: ha-ma'amin is H0539. Barnes, Richard Mayo (Poole's Annotations) and Ellicott on Romans 9:33: Paul applies Isaiah 28:16 to Christ, and Peter uses it too (1 Peter 2:6). Barnes and Ellicott: "shall not be ashamed" follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads "shall not make haste."
layers.text: Isaiah's stone in Zion uses the word again: ha-ma'amin, "the one who believes will never be shaken." The Greek Old Testament reads "put to shame," and Paul and Peter quote it of Christ: "the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame."

layers.evidence: TBESG G0281: amen, from aman, be firm. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch: Isaiah 65:16 is literally the God of Amen, and Ellicott hears an echo of it in Revelation 3:14. Keil and Delitzsch link it to 2 Corinthians 1:20. Barnes: Amen means true, certain, faithful.
layers.text: Amen comes from the same root, "be firm." Isaiah's "God of truth" is literally the God of Amen, and Jesus takes Amen as His title: "the Amen, the faithful and true Witness." So, Paul says, all God's promises are "Yes" in Christ.

passages.saying: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." Isaiah offers him any sign he wants; Ahaz refuses to ask, so the Lord gives a sign anyway: a son to be called Immanuel.

layers.evidence: TBESH H6005: Immanuel, God with us. TAHOT writes the name as two words in 7:14 and 8:8, the same two words (H5973, H0410) that end 8:10.
layers.text: Immanuel is Hebrew for "God with us," as Matthew translates. Isaiah keeps sounding the name: the Assyrian flood will cover "your entire land, O Immanuel!" and the next oracle ends, "For God is with us," in Hebrew the same two words, immanu el.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary, giving Bishop Lowth's view: a double bearing and a double fulfillment. JFB: partly the immediate event, fully the Messiah. Gill: a sign of present deliverance. NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:14 and 7:16.
layers.text: The sign had a near horizon. Before the boy could "reject evil and choose good," the two kings' lands would be laid waste, and soon Assyria took Damascus. Isaiah's next son gets a similar timetable (8:4). So many readers see a double fulfillment, near and far.

layers.evidence: Ellicott: almah strictly denotes one of marriageable age. Barnes: the word is used of Rebekah, and the Septuagint has parthenos. Gill: the Jewish translators of the Septuagint so rendered it long before Matthew. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: from a root to lie hid. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G3933: parthenos renders almah at Genesis 24:43 and Isaiah 7:14.
layers.text: Matthew quotes this verse of Jesus' birth. Isaiah's word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and the Greek Old Testament had already rendered it parthenos, "virgin," here and for Rebekah in Genesis 24:43. Its root means hidden, of a maiden kept from men's gaze.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Ellicott on Isaiah 9:6: the name is applied to the LORD Himself in 10:21. Keil and Delitzsch: the same person as the son of the virgin in chapter 7. TAHOT: El Gibbor is H0410 and H1368 in both verses.
layers.text: Two chapters on, the child returns: "unto us a son is given," named "Mighty God," El Gibbor, who will "reign on the throne of David." A chapter later Isaiah uses El Gibbor of the LORD Himself: a remnant will return "to the Mighty God."

layers.evidence: Gerald Bilkes and Gerrit Scott Dawson (Ligonier) tie Jesus' closing promise in Matthew 28:20, "I am with you always," to His name Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23). R. T. France (Themelios) traces "God with us" (1:23) through the Gospel to "I am with you always" (28:20).
layers.text: Matthew gives the name near his start, "God with us," and Jesus' last words echo it: "surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age." In between He promises, "where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Hebrews 2:13: the words are from Isaiah 8:18, with Isaiah representing Christ. The Pulpit Commentary: Isaiah is himself a sign, a type of the Immanuel to come. Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown also trace the words to Isaiah 8:18.
layers.text: Isaiah says he and his children are "signs and symbols in Israel," and Hebrews puts his words in Christ's mouth: "Here am I, and the children God has given Me." The prophet's sign-children become a picture of Christ and the family He brings to God.

passages.saying: Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the tablet of 8:1-2.
layers.text: Isaiah's wife, called the prophetess, gives birth to a son. The LORD tells Isaiah to give him the same name He had Isaiah write on a large scroll before witnesses (8:1-2).

layers.evidence: Barnes, Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, the Companion Bible and Matthew Henry all read the name as words of haste and plunder. Barnes and the Companion Bible tie it to the plunder of Damascus and Samaria in 8:4.
layers.text: Maher-shalal-hash-baz strings four Hebrew words together: hurry, plunder, hasten, prey. Verse 4 explains it: before the boy can say Father or Mother, Assyria will carry off the wealth of Damascus and the shalal, the plunder, of Samaria.

passages.saying: state a proposal, but it will not happen. For God is with us
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the challenge to the nations in 8:9.
layers.text: Isaiah dares the nations to plot against Judah. Their plans will be thwarted and their orders will come to nothing, because God is with His people.

layers.evidence: Gill: for God is with us is the interpretation of the name Immanuel. Barnes: in Hebrew, For Immanuel. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way.
layers.text: The closing words, "For God is with us," are in Hebrew ki immanu El, the very name Immanuel. The flood of Assyria may cover "your entire land, O Immanuel," yet the name promised in 7:14 is why every enemy plan must fail.

passages.saying: the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: the children were the LORD's gift, given as signs and types in the history of salvation.
layers.text: Isaiah presents himself and his sons before the LORD. God gave them to him for a purpose: while Judah would not listen, the prophet and his children stood among the people as living signs from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.

layers.evidence: Barnes: they were signs by the names given them; Shear-jashub means the remnant shall return, and Isaiah's name signifies the salvation of Jehovah. JFB: Isaiah means salvation of Jehovah, and his children's names were signs. Keil and Delitzsch: the sons' names spoke of wrath and grace, the father's of salvation. Gill: the sons were signs in their very names.
layers.text: The signs were partly in their names. Isaiah means the salvation of the LORD. His son Shear-jashub means a remnant will return (7:3), and Maher-shalal-hash-baz speaks of plunder seized in haste (8:1-4). The prophet's family carried God's message of judgment and rescue.

passages.saying: as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: the past tense describes a future rescue as the prophet saw it in vision.
layers.text: Isaiah celebrates a coming rescue as if it had already happened. God will smash the yoke, the bar across the shoulders and the rod that the oppressor laid on His people, just as He once broke the power of Midian.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, JFB, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley all refer the day of Midian to Gideon's victory (Judges 7). Barnes: a deliverance not by human strength but by the power of God. Keil and Delitzsch: won by a handful of warriors, fitting a rescue of only a small remnant.
layers.text: The day of Midian recalls Gideon's victory in Judges 7, when the LORD routed the vast Midianite army through only three hundred men with horns and torches. Isaiah promises a rescue just as plainly God's own work, not won by human strength.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: its burden (subbolo) and its oppressor (noges) both recall the Egyptian bondage (Exodus 2:11; 5:6), and the deliverance Isaiah celebrates would be the counterpart of the one from Egypt.
layers.text: The word for oppressor here, noges, is the word used for Pharaoh's taskmasters, and some hear the burden as recalling Israel's forced labor in Egypt. On this reading the rescue Isaiah foresees is pictured as a new exodus, freeing God's people from slavery once more.

passages.saying: He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: its reference to the Messiah has been almost universally conceded.
layers.text: Isaiah gives the reason for the coming joy: a child will be born, a son given to God's people, and the government will rest on His shoulders. The verse looks ahead to the promised King, the Messiah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: as the Angel of the LORD answered Manoah that His name was peli and so showed His divine nature, so the Child is pele, beyond human conception, Himself a wonder. The Companion Bible and JFB also point to Judges 13:18.
layers.text: The first title, pele (wonder), may echo the Angel of the LORD in Judges 13:18, who said His name was peli, beyond comprehension. Read this way, the Child too bears a name that marks Him as One whose nature is beyond human understanding.

layers.evidence: Gill: these are not names He would commonly be called by, but He answers to every one. Wesley: not a description of His name but of His nature. Keil and Delitzsch take pele (wonder) and yo'etz (counselor) as separate names and say El gibbor attributes divinity to Him. Clarke renders Abi ad the Father of eternity.
layers.text: These are not everyday names but titles that say who the Child is. Pele means a wonder, yoets a counselor, El Gibbor mighty God, Avi-ad father of eternity, and Sar Shalom prince of peace. Together they describe a King who is wise, divine, eternal and the bringer of peace.

passages.saying: under his pomp will be kindled a fire like a burning flame
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: a threat of punishment on the Assyrian for his insolence and pride.
layers.text: Because the king of Assyria boasted against God, the Lord GOD of Hosts will send a wasting disease on his well-fed warriors and set a fire burning under all his pomp. The proud army will be consumed.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible and Figures of Speech list yekad yekod kikod as paronomasia, a run of like-sounding words. Keil and Delitzsch: by Isaiah's art of painting in tones we can hear the crackling and hissing of the fire.
layers.text: The words for the fire crackle in Hebrew: yeqad yeqod kiqod, three words built from one root meaning to burn. The repeated sound lets the hearer almost hear the fire that will consume the glory of Assyria.

passages.saying: A remnant will return
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: the survivors of the invasion would forsake their idols and worship the true God.
layers.text: Only a remnant of Jacob will come through the judgment, but that remnant will not be lost. They will turn from idols and false trust and come back to the Mighty God.

layers.evidence: Gill: said in allusion to Shearjashub, the name of Isaiah's son, which signifies the remnant shall return and was given him as an assurance of it. Companion Bible: Hebrew Shear-jashub, see 7:3. Keil and Delitzsch (on 10:20) speak of the promise in the name Shear-yashub being fulfilled.
layers.text: "A remnant will return" is she'ar yashuv in Hebrew, the very name of Isaiah's son Shear-jashub (7:3). The boy's name was a living promise, and here Isaiah spells out what it meant: a remnant would come back to God.

passages.saying: as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: the two comparisons picture the complete destruction of the Assyrian army.
layers.text: The LORD of Hosts will turn on Assyria with a whip. The oppressor who beat God's people will himself be struck down, as God struck His people's enemies in the past.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and the Companion Bible all point to Judges 7:25. Barnes: the rock was probably named for Oreb, slain there, and the Assyrian's ruin would be as signal and total as Midian's.
layers.text: The rock of Oreb is where Oreb, a prince of Midian, was killed after God routed Midian's army in Gideon's day (Judges 7:25). Assyria's defeat will be just as sudden and complete.

layers.evidence: Gill: Moses' rod lifted over the Red Sea when the Egyptians were drowned. JFB cites Exodus 14:16. Keil and Delitzsch: stretched out like the wonder-working staff of Moses. Barnes: as God overthrew the Egyptians in the Red Sea, so He would the Assyrian.
layers.text: The staff raised over the sea recalls Moses lifting his staff over the Red Sea (Exodus 14:16), when the waters opened for Israel and then closed over Pharaoh's army. God will deal with Assyria as He dealt with Egypt.

passages.saying: Cry aloud, O Daughter of Gallim! Listen, O Laishah! O wretched Anathoth!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: the nearby towns raise a cry of alarm at the enemy's approach.
layers.text: Isaiah pictures the Assyrian army marching town by town toward Jerusalem. He calls on the villages north of the city to cry out in alarm as the enemy draws near, and grieves for Anathoth in its distress.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls the Hebrew a paronomasia, a play on like sounds, and says poor here means afflicted. Keil and Delitzsch: the prophet takes the name as an omen of its fate. Clarke, reading answer her with the Syriac, also sees a play on the town's name.
layers.text: "O wretched Anathoth" is aniyyah anatot in Hebrew. The word for wretched, meaning afflicted, sounds like the town's own name, as if Anathoth's name foretold its distress when the invader passed by.

passages.saying: They will swoop down on the slopes of the Philistines to the west
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of Ephraim and Judah, now reconciled (verse 13), acting together against old enemies.
layers.text: Once Israel and Judah are united, they will together overcome the neighbors who had long troubled them: the Philistines to the west, the peoples of the east, and Edom, Moab and Ammon.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say katef (shoulder) was the name of the Philistine coastland sloping to the sea, and that here, with an implied allusion to that name, it means the shoulder of the Philistine nation. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the picture of an attack on the shoulders is the more apt because the same Hebrew word is used of a coast.
layers.text: The word for slopes is katef, which means shoulder. It named the Philistine coastland sloping down to the sea, but it also pictures Israel swooping like a bird of prey onto the enemy's shoulder, striking from behind.

passages.saying: He will split it into seven streams for men to cross with dry sandals
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the figurative language of removing every barrier between God's scattered people and home.
layers.text: The LORD promises to dry up the gulf of the Sea of Egypt and break the great river into shallow streams, so that His scattered people can come home with nothing blocking the way.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all tie the dried-up sea, the hand waved over the waters and the strong wind to the Red Sea crossing in Exodus 14:21; Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch read the passage the same way. Both verses use the Hebrew words for hand, sea and wind.
layers.text: This echoes the Red Sea crossing. Moses stretched his hand over the sea and the LORD drove it back with a strong wind; here God waves His hand and sends a scorching wind to open a dry path. The return home is pictured as a second exodus.

passages.saying: For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the song's opening confession that salvation comes from God alone.
layers.text: The people God has rescued declare that God Himself is their salvation. Because of that they will trust Him and not be afraid, for He is their strength and the reason for their song.

layers.evidence: Gill says these clauses are taken out of Exodus 15:2; Barnes says the song is evidently composed in imitation of Moses' hymn after the Red Sea; Keil and Delitzsch call the verse the echo of Exodus 15:2, on which Psalm 118:14 is also founded. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible agree. The key Hebrew words are the same.
layers.text: These words repeat the song Moses and Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.” Those God rescues in the future praise Him in the very words of the first exodus.

passages.saying: With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the familiar picture of wells and springs as a source of life and refreshment.
layers.text: God's salvation is pictured as springs of water. His people will draw from it freely and gladly, like thirsty travelers who find wells in the desert.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown describe the water rite at the Feast of Tabernacles and say this is the allusion in Jesus' words on the last day of the feast. Barnes, on John 7:37, links the rite to this verse and thinks Jesus cried out while it was being performed.
layers.text: In Jesus' day, at the Feast of Tabernacles, water was carried from the pool of Siloam to the altar with great rejoicing, a rite linked to this verse. On the last day of that feast Jesus called the thirsty to come to Him and drink, presenting Himself as the true spring.

passages.saying: Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain call to praise God and spread the news of His deeds.
layers.text: The redeemed call for songs of praise to the LORD for the glorious things He has done, and they want His deeds made known through the whole earth.

layers.evidence: Barnes says this is the same expression as in the song of Moses at Exodus 15:21 and that Isaiah evidently had it in view; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say it alludes to Exodus 15:21; the Companion Bible marks a reference to Exodus 15:1 and 15:21. Gill also sees a reference to Exodus 15:1.
layers.text: The call to sing to the LORD for His glorious deeds echoes the song of Miriam and Israel after the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 15:21). God's people in the coming day praise Him just as Israel did when He brought them out of Egypt.

passages.saying: it will come as destruction from the Almighty.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the address to Babylon and the prophets' term for God's day of judgment.
layers.text: Babylon is told to wail, because the Day of the LORD, His day of judgment, is near. It will strike with a destruction that comes from God Almighty Himself.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say that in this play on words Isaiah repeats words of Joel 1:15; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), on Joel 1:15, says the words form a kind of terrible proverb that Isaiah adopted from Joel.
layers.text: Joel 1:15 says the same thing in nearly the same Hebrew, sound play included: the Day of the LORD is near and comes as destruction from the Almighty. Isaiah appears to take up the earlier prophet's warning and turn it against Babylon.

layers.evidence: Gill calls keshod mishaddai a beautiful paronomasia; Barnes calls it a paronomasia or pun that cannot be kept in translation; the Companion Bible marks Paronomasia on keshod and mishshaddai. Keil and Delitzsch and Bullinger's Figures of Speech also treat it as a play on words.
layers.text: In Hebrew the day comes ke-shod mi-Shaddai, as destruction from the Almighty. The word for destruction, shod, sounds like Shaddai, the Almighty, so the very sound of the line says that this ruin comes from God.

passages.saying: The waters of Dimon are full of blood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of slaughter so great that it colors the local waters.
layers.text: So many in Moab will be slain that the waters of Dimon run red with blood, and God warns that still more will come, a lion upon those who escape.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Dibon is called Dimon here to sound more like dam, blood; the Companion Bible marks a Paronomasia on Dimon and dam, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse among its examples of Paronomasia.
layers.text: Dimon is most likely the town of Dibon from verse 2, spelled here with an m so that its name echoes dam, the Hebrew word for blood. The place whose waters run red now has a name that sounds like blood.

passages.saying: Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains the verse as the overthrow of Damascus by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 16:9).
layers.text: God announces that Damascus, the capital of Syria, will be destroyed and left a heap of ruins. This came true when the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser took the city and carried its people away.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the rare word me'i was used on purpose to sound like me'ir, from a city. Bullinger marks a Paronomasia here in both the Companion Bible and Figures of Speech, noting that the unusual form alludes to the word city.
layers.text: In Hebrew, Damascus is removed from being a city, meir, and becomes a ruin, mei. An unusual form of the word for ruin may have been chosen so that it sounds like meir with its last letter broken off, a picture of a shattered city.

passages.saying: The cities of Aroer are forsaken
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains that the towns would be emptied as their people were killed, captured or forced to flee.
layers.text: The towns around Aroer will be deserted, their people killed, captured or fled. Flocks will graze and rest where the towns once stood, with no one left to frighten them away.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch see a significant play upon the sound in arei Aroer, cities of Aroer. The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech both list the phrase as a Paronomasia.
layers.text: In Hebrew, the cities of Aroer is arei Aroer. The word for cities and the town's name sound almost the same, which may tie the name of the town to the fate of the cities around it.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the name of Aroer was ominous, since a Hebrew word like it means to lay bare or pull down, and what the name indicated would happen to its cities.
layers.text: Some hear in the name Aroer a Hebrew word meaning to lay bare or pull down. On that reading the name itself became a warning: the towns around it would be stripped and left empty.

passages.saying: One of them will be called the City of the Sun
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the verse as a promise that many in Egypt would fear the LORD and embrace the true religion.
layers.text: Isaiah foresees a day when cities in Egypt will speak the language of God's people and pledge themselves to the LORD, a sign of Egypt turning from its idols to the true God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch hold that the received reading Ir ha-Heres plays on Ir ha-Cheres, Heliopolis, foretelling the end of its idolatry. Clarke reports the view that the prophet wrote heres for cheres on purpose. Barnes and the Companion Bible allow that a copyist may have changed the letter instead.
layers.text: Most Hebrew copies read Ir ha-Heres, city of destruction, while some read Ir ha-Cheres, city of the sun, which this translation follows. The two differ by one letter. Many see a deliberate play: Egypt's city of the sun, Heliopolis, home of sun worship, would become a city where idols are torn down.

passages.saying: Watchman, what is left of the night?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain the question as Edom's anxious wish to know whether its night of trouble will soon be over.
layers.text: Someone from Seir, the mountain country of Edom, calls to the prophet as to a watchman, anxiously asking how much longer the night of trouble will last.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Dumah means deep silence and turns the name Edom into an emblem of its fate. The Companion Bible reads Dumah as Edom, meaning silence, prophetic of its end. Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown report the same reading from earlier scholars.
layers.text: Dumah means silence. It sounds like Edom with its first sound moved to the end, and the call comes from Seir, Edom's land. So the heading names Edom by a word that foretells its fate: a deathlike silence, like a long night.

passages.saying: roll you into a ball, and sling you into a wide land
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a ball thrown far; Barnes explains that God would cast Shebna so far into a distant land that he could not return.
layers.text: God tells Shebna, the proud steward of the palace, that He will wind him up like a ball and hurl him into a wide country. There he will die, and there his splendid chariots will end up, while he himself is a disgrace to his master's house.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the figure Paronomasia here (zanoph, yiznaphka, zenephah), and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse among its examples of Paronomasia. Gill gives the literal sense: wrapping he will wrap thee with a wrapping.
layers.text: The Hebrew repeats one root three times in a row: tsanof yitsnafekha tsenefah, roughly winding He will wind you a winding. The echoing sounds stress how tightly Shebna will be wound up, like a ball, before he is hurled away.

passages.saying: The earth will be utterly laid waste and thoroughly plundered.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the doubled verbs; Barnes calls the verse an emphatic repetition of verse 1 showing the certainty of the threat.
layers.text: Isaiah repeats the warning of verse 1 in stronger words: the earth will be completely emptied and stripped bare. It is certain, because the LORD has spoken this word.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks Paronomasia here for emphasis, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse among its examples of Paronomasia. Keil and Delitzsch say tibboq and tibboz are intentionally written in an unusual way to rhyme with the words before them.
layers.text: Each verb is doubled in Hebrew for emphasis, and the pairs rhyme: hibboq tibboq, hibboz tibboz (utterly laid waste, thoroughly plundered). The second word of each pair seems to be given an unusual form so it rhymes with the first. The verb for laying waste is the same one used in verse 1.

passages.saying: The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and fades
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of withering; Barnes says the figure is taken from a plant that lacks moisture and soon withers.
layers.text: Under God's judgment the earth droops like a plant without water. The world fades, and even its most exalted people waste away.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse among its examples of Paronomasia, giving avelah, navlah, umlelah and umlalu, and Keil and Delitzsch say Isaiah 33:9 contains the same play upon sounds.
layers.text: The Hebrew verbs rhyme: avelah navelah (mourns and withers), umlelah navelah (languishes and fades; navelah is the same word both times), and umlalu (waste away). The same play on sounds is heard in Isaiah 33:9.

passages.saying: The treacherous betray; the treacherous deal in treachery.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between distant songs of praise and the prophet's grief over treachery.
layers.text: Isaiah hears songs from the ends of the earth giving glory to the Righteous One, yet he cries out that he is wasting away, because traitors go on betraying.

layers.evidence: Clarke prints the Hebrew and calls it a strange connection of uncouth sounds; Keil and Delitzsch note the play upon the word bagad; Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse under Polyptoton, a variety of inflections heaped together to enhance the sense.
layers.text: The second half of the verse is a knot of repeated sounds in Hebrew: razi li, razi li, oi li, then bogedim bagadu uveged bogedim bagadu. Five words built on bagad, to betray, are piled together to stress how complete the treachery is.

passages.saying: Terror and pit and snare await you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the hunting images of the verse, which the commentaries read as dangers no one can escape.
layers.text: Terror and pit and snare are a hunter's tools. Whoever escapes one danger is caught by the next, so no one on earth can slip away from God's judgment.

layers.evidence: Barnes says Jeremiah probably copied the description from Isaiah; Clarke notes Jeremiah repeats it in the same words; Keil and Delitzsch and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also point to Jeremiah 48:43-44, where the same three Hebrew words appear.
layers.text: Jeremiah later repeats this saying almost word for word against Moab: Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab. What Isaiah announced over the whole earth is applied to one nation's coming fall.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it an elegant play on words; Barnes and Clarke call it a paronomasia, Barnes noting that pach sounds in each word; the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech mark the same figure in verses 17 and 18.
layers.text: Terror and pit and snare are pachad, pachat and pach in Hebrew, three words that sound almost alike. The next verse runs through all three again in order. The echoing words make the trap feel inescapable: each sound leads straight into the next.

passages.saying: For the windows of heaven are open
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of escape cut off on every side, from heaven above and the earth below.
layers.text: Anyone who escapes the first danger is caught by the next. Heaven's windows open and the earth's foundations shake, picturing a judgment that comes from above and from below.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it an allusion to the opening of the windows of heaven at the Flood; Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say it is taken from Genesis 7:11; the Companion Bible, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley also tie it to the Flood. Both verses use the same Hebrew words for windows and opened.
layers.text: The picture of heaven's windows standing open echoes the Flood, when the floodgates of the heavens were opened in Noah's day. The same Hebrew words are used, so the coming judgment is pictured as a new flood over the whole earth.

passages.saying: O LORD, You are my God! I will exalt You
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's praise of God for carrying out plans made long ago, which the commentaries read as His faithfulness to His promises.
layers.text: Speaking for God's people, the prophet praises the LORD as his own God, because God has done wonderful things, carrying out plans He made long ago and keeping every promise faithfully.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks I will exalt Thee as a reference to Exodus 15:2; Keil and Delitzsch say Thou hast wrought wonders is taken from Exodus 15:11. Both verses come from the song Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea.
layers.text: This praise echoes the Song of Moses at the Red Sea, where Israel sang of God, I will exalt Him, and praised Him for performing wonders. A new rescue is celebrated in the words of the first great one.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says two of the three Hebrew words form a Paronomasia, not as a pun but for solemn emphasis; Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse under Paronomasia, giving aromimcha and odeh shimcha.
layers.text: In Hebrew, "I will exalt You; I will praise Your name" is only three words: aromimkha, odeh shimkha. Two of them, aromimkha and shimkha, end with the same sound, imkha. Some take the chime not as wordplay for its own sake but as solemn emphasis, meant to catch the reader's attention.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say it is Isaiah's custom to place derivatives of the same word side by side for the greatest possible emphasis, here emunah and omen; Barnes notes that omen is the word from which Amen comes.
layers.text: The verse ends with two words from one Hebrew root, emunah and omen, both meaning faithfulness or sureness. Setting them side by side stresses that what God planned long ago He has made firmly true. The same root gives us the word amen.

passages.saying: the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the feast imagery, which the commentaries read as joy and abundant provision offered to every nation.
layers.text: On His mountain the LORD will spread a rich feast of the best food and finest aged wine, open to all peoples. It pictures the joy and abundance of the blessings God provides.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a Paronomasia, saying the words are heaped together to show the greatness of the feast; Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse under Paronomasia; Keil and Delitzsch call the ring of the verse joyful music; Gill says the heap of repeated words shows the plenty.
layers.text: The menu rings in Hebrew: mishteh shemanim, mishteh shemarim, shemanim memuchayim, shemarim mezukkakim. Rich foods (shemanim) and aged wines (shemarim) differ by one sound, and the repeated, chiming words pile up to picture how lavish God's feast will be.

passages.saying: But Moab will be trampled in his place
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast between God's hand resting on Zion and Moab, standing for all the enemies of God's people, trodden down.
layers.text: While God's hand rests on Zion to protect it, Moab, standing for the enemies of God's people, will be trampled down in its own land like straw trodden into a dung pile.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch suggest that bemo is a play upon the name Moab, and madmenah a play on the Moabite town Madmen of Jeremiah 48:2; the Companion Bible marks Moab, mathben, bemo, Madmenah as the figure Homoeopropheron, a run of like-sounding words.
layers.text: The Hebrew rings with m sounds around Moab's name: Moab, matben (straw), bemo (in), madmenah (dung pile). The small word bemo may echo Moab itself, and madmenah may hint at Madmen, a town of Moab, so Moab's own name seems to sound through its disgrace.

passages.saying: Your name and renown are the desire of our souls
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words of waiting and longing, which the commentaries read as longing for God Himself to act.
layers.text: God's people say they have waited for the LORD while walking in the path of His judgments, and that their deepest longing is for God Himself, His name and His renown.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible calls remembrance a reference to the Pentateuch, the same word as memorial in Exodus 3:15; Keil and Delitzsch explain the name and remembrance from Exodus 3:15, God made known by revealing Himself.
layers.text: Name and renown are shem and zekher, the pair God used at the burning bush: This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered. The people long for God to show Himself again as the God He revealed to Moses.

passages.saying: Sing about a fruitful vineyard.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the song that follows in verses 3 to 5, where the LORD speaks as the vineyard's keeper.
layers.text: In that day, after God has judged His enemies, His people will sing about His vineyard. It is a fruitful vineyard, and the LORD Himself is its keeper.

layers.evidence: Gill, on this verse, says this vineyard is very different from the one in Isaiah 5:5, though Israel too was compared to a vineyard in Isaiah 5:1. Clarke, on verse 4, says this song gains much light when set beside the one in chapter 5. Both songs use kerem, vineyard.
layers.text: This vineyard song looks back to the one in Isaiah 5 and can be read as its reverse. There God said He would take away His vineyard's hedge, tear down its wall and command the clouds not to rain on it. Here the LORD Himself keeps the vineyard, waters it continually and guards it night and day.

passages.saying: Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verse 9, where the speakers ask whether the prophet takes them for weaned infants.
layers.text: Jerusalem's drunken leaders mock Isaiah. They ask whether he takes them for babies just weaned, since all he gives them is one little rule after another, a bit here and a bit there.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Barnes point to the repeated Hebrew sounds that mock the prophet, and Keil and Delitzsch hear in them the babbling of drunken scoffers. Bullinger's Companion Bible names the figures epizeuxis and paronomasia. Barnes on verse 13 says God makes it as they said it was. The words are tsav (command), qav (line) and ze'eir (a little).
layers.text: In Hebrew the mockery sounds like a nursery lesson: tsav latsav, tsav latsav, qav laqav, qav laqav, ze'eir sham, ze'eir sham. The scoffers mimic the prophet as if he taught small children. In verse 13 God hands the same words back to them, now as a word of judgment.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, in their comment on verses 14 to 17, say qav is given a different turn in verse 17, as a play upon verses 10 and 11. Barnes on verse 10 explains qav as a cord or measuring line.
layers.text: Some see the word qav, line, coming back in verse 17 with a new turn. The scoffers mocked the prophet's line on line. Now God says, "I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level." He will build by that line, and their refuge of lies will be swept away.

passages.saying: the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two places of past victory and its words strange and disturbing.
layers.text: God will rise up in power as He did in the old battles at Perazim and Gibeon, but this time against His own people. That is why Isaiah calls it His strange work and His disturbing task.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Barnes, Gill, Wesley and Bullinger's Companion Bible all tie Perazim to 2 Samuel 5:20. For Gibeon, Keil and Delitzsch, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to David's victory in 1 Chronicles 14; Gill and Wesley mention both it and Joshua 10, and the Companion Bible cites Joshua 10:10.
layers.text: Mount Perazim recalls Baal-perazim, where the LORD gave David victory over the Philistines. Gibeon recalls either David's next rout of them, from Gibeon to Gezer, or Joshua's great victory there. Now God will fight that way against Jerusalem itself.

layers.evidence: Barnes derives Perazim from parats, to break forth as waters do; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the same; Gill says the place took its name from the LORD breaking forth like a breach of waters. 2 Samuel 5:20 uses parats and perets beside the name.
layers.text: Perazim means breaches or bursts. David named the place after the LORD burst out against his enemies like a flood breaking through. Isaiah uses the name as a warning: God can break out just as suddenly, and this time against Jerusalem.

passages.saying: Woe to you, O Ariel, the city of Ariel where David camped!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the phrase the city where David camped, which marks out Jerusalem.
layers.text: Isaiah pronounces woe on Ariel, a name for Jerusalem, the city where David camped. The people may keep their yearly round of feasts, but God will still bring the city into distress.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes, Clarke and Bullinger's Companion Bible give both senses, lion of God and altar hearth of God, citing Ezekiel 43 for the altar. Keil and Delitzsch prefer hearth of God. Clarke and Barnes read the second Ariel in verse 2 as the altar hearth.
layers.text: Ariel can be read as lion of God, a title of strength. But in Ezekiel 43:15 the same word means the altar hearth where offerings burned. Verse 2 turns the name: Ariel will be to God like an ariel, an altar hearth, a place of fire before Him.

passages.saying: there will be mourning and lamentation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on verse 3, where God says He will besiege the city.
layers.text: God will bring Jerusalem into distress under siege. The city will be full of mourning, and it will become like an altar hearth before Him.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown renders the pair groaning and moaning, saying this keeps the Hebrew paronomasia (play on sound). Keil and Delitzsch translate it the same way.
layers.text: Mourning and lamentation are a rhyming pair in Hebrew, ta'aniyyah va'aniyyah. Some render them groaning and moaning to keep the play on sound in English.

passages.saying: Stop and be astonished; blind yourselves and be sightless
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on verse 10, where the LORD pours out a spirit of deep sleep.
layers.text: Isaiah tells the people to go on staring in stunned confusion and blinding themselves. They reel like drunks, though not from wine. Their stupor is spiritual: they will not see what God is doing.

layers.evidence: Barnes says this phrase holds a paronomasia that cannot be carried into translation, built on the verb sha'a, which means to spread over, as when the eyes are smeared shut. Keil and Delitzsch note that both words come from that one verb and say the self-chosen blindness becomes a God-appointed punishment.
layers.text: The second pair of commands is a play on one Hebrew verb: hishta'ash'u and sho'u, blind yourselves and be sightless. The repeated verb can be read this way: the blindness they chose for themselves becomes the blindness God sends on them.

passages.saying: therefore I have called her Rahab Who Sits Still
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes reads the verse as a warning that an alliance with Egypt would fail to defend Judah from the invader.
layers.text: Judah's leaders were sending riches to Egypt to buy help against Assyria. God says Egypt's help is worthless and empty, and He gives her a mocking name to fit.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible take Rahab as a name for Egypt meaning pride, arrogance or boasting. Barnes renders the whole name the blusterer that sitteth still; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Arrogance that sitteth still.
layers.text: This Rahab is not the woman of Jericho but a poetic name for Egypt meaning pride or boasting, as in Psalm 87:4. God calls her Rahab hem shavet, the Boaster who sits still: Egypt talks loudly about helping, but when the time comes she will do nothing.

passages.saying: “No,” you say, “we will flee on horses.” Therefore you will flee!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that Judah hoped to gain the help of Egypt's cavalry through the alliance.
layers.text: God had offered Judah rescue through repentance and quiet trust, but they chose to rely on horses from Egypt. So the horses they trusted would only carry them in flight, and their enemies would chase them down even faster.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note that nus rhymes with sus and call this a play upon the words that shows God's law of retribution. The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech list both pairs, nanus, sus, t'nusun and kal, yikkallu, as paronomasia.
layers.text: Judah says "we will flee on horses" (nanus, sus), and God answers, "Therefore you will flee!" (tenusun). They boast of riding swift ones (qal), so their pursuers will be swift (yiqqallu). Each boast comes back on them as its own punishment.

passages.saying: You will sing as on the night of a holy festival
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the song as joy over the sudden destruction of Sennacherib's army.
layers.text: When God destroys the Assyrian army, His people will sing for joy, like worshipers keeping a sacred feast by night or pilgrims going up to the temple to the sound of the flute.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch see an unmistakable allusion to the Passover in the night of this feast, citing Exodus 12:42. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown likewise compares this night of song with the Passover night that celebrated the deliverance from Egypt.
layers.text: The night of a holy festival points to Passover, the night the LORD kept a vigil to bring Israel out of Egypt. Jerusalem's rescue from Assyria will feel like that first Passover: God's people singing inside while He strikes the enemy outside.

passages.saying: it has been made ready for the king
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the verse as the complete destruction of the Assyrian army, pictured as a pyre in the valley of Hinnom lit by God's breath.
layers.text: Topheth, the place of burning in the valley outside Jerusalem, pictures the doom prepared for Assyria's king and army. The LORD Himself will set it ablaze, His breath like a torrent of burning sulfur.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch judge that lammelekh is in all probability a play upon lammolekh, while the king meant is the king of Asshur. Wesley says the fire here alludes to the burning of children to Moloch.
layers.text: For the king is lammelekh in Hebrew, likely a play on lammolekh, to Molech, the god whose fires burned children at Topheth (2 Kings 23:10). The place of Molech's fires has been made ready for Assyria's king.

passages.saying: He will pass over it and preserve it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the picture as God protecting Jerusalem the way a bird defends its young.
layers.text: Like mother birds hovering over their nest, the LORD of Hosts will shield Jerusalem from the Assyrians, rescue it and keep it safe.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all connect pasoach here with the Passover in Exodus 12, and Wesley says the destroying angel shall pass over Jerusalem. Keil and Delitzsch note that the Passover took its name from this passing over.
layers.text: Pass over is pasoach, the verb of the first Passover, when God said, "I will pass over you." As He spared Israel's homes when He struck Egypt, He will spare Jerusalem when He strikes Assyria.

passages.saying: For a fool speaks foolishness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that the fool acts in accordance with his nature, so a righteous ruler would keep such men out of power.
layers.text: In the righteous kingdom Isaiah describes, people will be known for what they are. A fool gives himself away by what he says and does: he plots evil, speaks falsely about the LORD, and leaves the hungry and thirsty without help.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech mark nabal nebalah here as paronomasia. Barnes points to 1 Samuel 25:25 for this sense of fool.
layers.text: The Hebrew reads naval nevalah: a fool (naval) speaks folly (nevalah). The man and his words share one root. Abigail pairs the same two words about her husband Nabal in 1 Samuel 25:25: "His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him."

passages.saying: The weapons of the scoundrel are destructive
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording; Wesley explains the lying words as unjust decrees against the poor even when their cause is good.
layers.text: The scoundrel's methods are evil. He plots to ruin the poor with lies, and he does it even when the needy person's case is just and right.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes and Bullinger (Companion Bible, and Figures of Speech under Paronomasia) all mark a sound play in kelai kelav. Keil and Delitzsch add that this form of the word for the scoundrel is used for the sake of its likeness in sound to the word for his instruments.
layers.text: In Hebrew the verse opens with two words that sound almost the same: kelai, the scoundrel, and kelav, his weapons or tools. Isaiah used this form of the word for scoundrel to echo the word for his tools.

passages.saying: But hail will level the forest
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Isaiah's use of hail for God's judgment and of the forest for the Assyrian army (Isaiah 10:18-19, 33-34), as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains.
layers.text: God's judgment will fall like a hailstorm on the forest, a picture Isaiah uses for the massed Assyrian army, and the city will be brought very low. Interpreters differ on which city is meant.

layers.evidence: Barnes gives the Hebrew barad beredeth and calls it a paronomasia that cannot be expressed in a translation. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes the same paronomasia, for emphasis, and his Figures of Speech lists the verse under Paronomasia, or rhyming words.
layers.text: The Hebrew opens with u-varad, and it will hail, followed by be-redet, in the coming down. The two words sound alike, and the echo may add force to the picture of the storm striking the forest.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, in their comment on Isaiah 32:15-20, call the word for the city a play upon the word and a counterpart to the word for the forest.
layers.text: The verse also sets the forest, ha-ya'ar, beside the city, ha-ir. Some hear a play on sound here: the two Hebrew words sound alike, which may tie the fall of the forest to the humbling of the city.

passages.saying: a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the builder's tools named in the verse; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains the line and plumb stones as God measuring out exact justice on Edom.
layers.text: Edom will become a ruin where only wild birds live. The Lord will measure it out for destruction as carefully as a builder uses a line and plumb weight, but to tear down instead of to build.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that tohu and bohu are the very words used for the unformed, empty earth in Genesis 1:2. Keil and Delitzsch say Edom is thrown back into a state like the shapeless chaos of creation, and on Genesis 1:2 say the pair, where used together elsewhere, is taken from that passage.
layers.text: The words for chaos and destruction here are tohu and bohu, the same pair used in Genesis 1:2, where the earth was formless and void. God will undo Edom until it is like the empty earth before He shaped it.

passages.saying: Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Hezekiah's own song of thanks after his healing (38:9-20).
layers.text: Hezekiah looks back on his deadly illness and sees that his bitter suffering was for his good. In love God pulled him back from death and threw all his sins behind His back, forgiven and out of sight.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls mar li mar a paronomasia and renders it my anguish is changed into ease. Keil and Delitzsch say the word mar is doubled here to give it superlative force.
layers.text: Hezekiah's Hebrew is mar li mar, bitter to me, bitter: one short word said twice to show how deep his anguish went. Some older scholars also hear a play on sound, taking the first mar to mean changed, so that his bitterness was turned into peace.

passages.saying: The islands see and fear
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the setting of 41:1-7, where God raises up a conqueror and the nations panic.
layers.text: Faraway lands see what God is doing through the conqueror He has raised up, and they are terrified. From the ends of the earth they tremble and gather to face the danger together.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch point out the play on ra'u and yira'u, which pairs seeing and fearing. Bullinger lists the verse among his examples of paronomasia (rhyming words) in Figures of Speech.
layers.text: Isaiah's Hebrew pairs two words that sound almost alike: the islands ra'u, see, and yira'u, fear. The echo ties the seeing and the fearing closely together.

passages.saying: who makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the setting of 43:14-21, a promise of rescue from Babylon.
layers.text: Before giving His promise, the LORD names Himself as the God who opens a road through the sea and a path through mighty waters. What He has done before assures His people that He can rescue them again.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes, Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, and the Companion Bible all tie these lines to the Red Sea. Keil and Delitzsch call the redemption out of Egypt a type and pledge of the return from Babylon.
layers.text: God is the One "who makes a way in the sea" and brings out chariots and horses "to lie down, never to rise again". This recalls the Red Sea, where Israel crossed on dry ground and Pharaoh's army drowned. That old rescue is the pledge of a new one (43:18-19).

passages.saying: Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the promise of 44:1-5, which follows the judgment of 43:22-28.
layers.text: God speaks to Israel as the One who made them and formed them from the womb, and He promises to help them. After all their sin and punishment, His chosen servant need not be afraid.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry's Concise, Clarke and Gill say the name means upright. Clarke derives it from yashar, Keil and Delitzsch trace it to that root, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown hear an allusion to it. The name occurs elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:15; 33:5, 26.
layers.text: Jeshurun is a rare poetic name for Israel. It comes from the Hebrew yashar, upright, and means the upright one. Apart from this verse it appears only in Moses' song and blessing (Deuteronomy 32:15; 33:5, 26).

passages.saying: He did not create it to be empty, but formed it to be inhabited
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's description of Himself as Creator in 45:18.
layers.text: The LORD who made heaven and earth explains why He made the world: not to lie empty, but as a home for people to live in. He alone is God.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that tohu is the word used of the earth in Genesis 1:2, and the Companion Bible calls it the same word as in Genesis 1:2. Keil and Delitzsch read tohu here as a desert and compare Genesis 1:2. Bullinger's Figures of Speech also links the two verses.
