layers.text: The Hebrew word for empty is tohu, the same word Genesis 1:2 uses for the earth when it was formless. Isaiah looks back to the creation story to show God's purpose: He never meant the earth to stay a waste but shaped it as a home to be lived in.

passages.saying: Your descendants would have been as countless as the sand
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's lament in 48:18-19 over what obedience would have brought.
layers.text: God tells Israel what obedience would have brought: descendants as many as the grains of sand, and a name never cut off from His presence. Their sin had held this blessing back.

layers.evidence: Gill says the sand is the number promised to Abraham in Genesis 22:17; the Companion Bible marks a reference to Genesis 22:17 and 32:12.
layers.text: Descendants as countless as the sand recalls God's promise to multiply Abraham's descendants like "the sand on the seashore" (Genesis 22:17). Obedience would have brought Israel the full measure of that old promise.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the play on me'eykha and me'otav very conspicuous, and they take me'otav as the grains of sand.
layers.text: Some hear a play in the Hebrew on two words that sound alike: me'eykha, your body, and me'otav, its grains. The children born of Israel's body would have been as many as the sand's grains, and the echo may bind the two together.

passages.saying: He made water flow for them from the rock
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the song the freed exiles are told to sing in 48:20-21.
layers.text: The people redeemed from Babylon are to sing that God led them through dry places without thirst and made water flow from the rock. Though spoken as already done, it promises God's full care on the way home.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls the allusion undoubted and names Exodus 17:6 and Numbers 20:11. Gill and the Companion Bible point to Exodus 17:6. Clarke calls it an allusion to the miraculous exodus, and Keil and Delitzsch say the miracles of the Egyptian redemption are renewed.
layers.text: These words recall the wilderness, when God gave Israel water from the rock that Moses struck (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). The return from Babylon is told in the language of the first exodus: the God who cared for their fathers will care for them.

passages.saying: Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own appeal to Abraham, one man whom God called, blessed and multiplied.
layers.text: God tells His discouraged people to remember Abraham and Sarah. Abraham was only one man when God called him, yet God blessed him and made his family a great people. The same God can bless and multiply His small remnant again.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch tie the blessing and multiplying to Genesis 12:1-2; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Genesis 12:1; the Companion Bible marks a reference to the Pentateuch at Genesis 12. Both verses use the same verb for bless, barakh.
layers.text: This looks back to Genesis 12, where God called Abram away from his homeland and promised, "I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you." Isaiah uses the same Hebrew verb for bless (barakh). The God who made one man a nation can do it again.

passages.saying: He will make her wilderness like Eden
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise that the LORD will comfort Zion and rebuild her ruins.
layers.text: The LORD promises to comfort ruined Zion. He will turn her wasteland into a place as lovely and fruitful as Eden, and fill it again with joy, thanksgiving and singing.

layers.evidence: Barnes links the garden of the LORD to the garden God planted in Genesis 2:8; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call it the restoration of the primeval paradise (Genesis 2:8); the Companion Bible marks Eden as a reference to Genesis 2 and 3. Both verses use gan (garden) and Eden.
layers.text: Eden and the garden of the LORD point back to Genesis 2, where God planted a garden in Eden and placed the first man there. Isaiah pictures Zion's restoration as paradise given back: ruined land made like the garden God Himself first planted.

passages.saying: For the moth will devour them like a garment
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of moth-eaten cloth set against God's lasting righteousness.
layers.text: Those who mock God's people will wear away like cloth eaten by moths and worms. But God's righteousness and salvation will last forever, through all generations.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch (on verses 7 and 8) say the double figure of verse 8 forms a play upon words that cannot well be reproduced, and explain its two insect names, ash and sas, as words for the moth.
layers.text: In Hebrew the two lines are built alike: the moth (ash) will eat them, and the worm (sas) will eat them. Some hear the two short insect names echo each other, a sound play English cannot copy. Something as small as a moth is enough to bring proud scoffers down.

passages.saying: Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to the arm of the LORD and its memory of Egypt's defeat.
layers.text: God's exiled people cry out for the LORD's mighty arm to wake up and act as it did long ago. They remember how He struck down Rahab, a poetic name for Egypt, and pierced the dragon, a picture of Pharaoh.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech says Egypt is called Rahab on account of its pride, the word having that meaning; Wesley explains the name from Egypt's pride or strength; Gill gives the pride and haughtiness of its people as the first reason for the name.
layers.text: Rahab here is a poetic name for Egypt, spelled differently in Hebrew from Rahab of Jericho. The word rahab means pride or arrogance, so the name marks Egypt as the proud power that God cut down when He brought Israel out.

passages.saying: Was it not You who dried up the sea
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's question about God's past act of drying up the sea for His redeemed.
layers.text: The prophet reminds God that He once dried up the sea and made a road through its depths so His redeemed people could cross. The same power can rescue them now.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all identify the dried sea as the Red Sea and cite Exodus 14:21. Isaiah's verb for dried up (charav) shares its root with the dry ground (charavah) of Exodus 14:21.
layers.text: This points back to the Red Sea in Exodus 14, when the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land, and Israel walked through. The God who opened that road for the redeemed can open a way home for them again.

passages.saying: For you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise that the LORD will lead the returning exiles and guard their rear.
layers.text: The exiles will leave Babylon calmly, not as panicked fugitives. The LORD Himself will march at their head, and the God of Israel will guard them from behind.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note that the word bechippazon recalls the hurried departure from Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:3; Exodus 12:39); Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown make the same contrast with leaving Egypt and cite Deuteronomy 16:3. The Companion Bible also marks a reference to the Pentateuch here.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for hurry here, chippazon, is the word the Law uses for the night Israel left the land of Egypt in haste. This new exodus will be different: no frantic rush this time, but an orderly march with God in charge.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch compare God going both before and behind His people to Exodus 14:19; Gill sees an allusion to the pillar of fire and cloud that went before and behind Israel.
layers.text: This likely recalls the Red Sea, where God's angel and the pillar of cloud moved from in front of Israel to stand behind them (Exodus 14:19). In the same way the LORD will lead His returning people from the front and guard them from the rear.

passages.saying: He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Targum of Isaiah named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Isaiah describes the LORD's servant suffering for wrongs that are not His own. Watch the pronouns: the wounds are His, the transgressions are ours, and the peace and the healing come to us.

layers.evidence: Peter's word is molops, a bruise or wound left by a blow (TBESG, from Abbott-Smith). The Septuagint uses it here; it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Isaiah's chabburah is a bruise or welt (TBESH). Ellicott on Isaiah 53:5, and the Pulpit Commentary, Clarke and the continuation of Poole's Annotations on 1 Peter 2:24, tie Peter's use to the servants he addressed, who might be scourged.
layers.text: Peter quotes this line to household servants who could be beaten even for doing good: "By His stripes you are healed." Isaiah's "we" becomes "you," and Peter's word for stripes means a welt, a mark many of his readers knew on their own backs.

layers.evidence: Isaiah 53:4 has choli, sickness, and makob, pain (TBESH); the Septuagint renders the first as sins. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 8:17: Matthew follows the Hebrew. Gill and Matthew Henry on Isaiah 53:4: Matthew applies it to bodily healing, while the Septuagint and Peter read sins. The continuation of Poole's Annotations on Matthew 8:17: the verse was twice fulfilled in Christ.
layers.text: The New Testament reads this song two ways at once. Matthew quotes 53:4 of Jesus' healings, where the Hebrew speaks of sickness. The Greek Old Testament made it sins, and Peter writes, "He Himself bore our sins." The Servant carries both.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: the same verb, daka (H1792), in 53:5 and 53:10. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, Barnes and Gill tie the bruising of 53:10 back to 53:5 and to the LORD's purpose. Matthew Henry on 53:10: men thought Him smitten of God for some sin of His own (53:4); He was smitten of God, but for our sin.
layers.text: "Crushed" is the Hebrew daka, and it returns five verses later: "it was the LORD’s will to crush Him." Onlookers thought God was striking Him (53:4). The chapter answers that He was crushed for our iniquities, and that even this served God's purpose.

layers.evidence: Gill, the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott on Luke 22:37.
layers.text: On His last night Jesus applies the chapter to Himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me," He says, and quotes 53:12, "He was numbered with the transgressors." The next day He was crucified between two criminals.

layers.evidence: Gill on Acts 8:34: some apply it to the people of Israel, wrongly, since the Servant is set apart from the people for whose transgressions he was stricken. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Isaiah 52:13: an individual is plainly described. The Pulpit Commentary on 52:13 parts the individual Servant from Israel, the collective one.
layers.text: An Ethiopian official asked, "who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?" Isaiah calls Israel God's servant (49:3), and medieval Jewish commentators read the song that way. Yet this Servant is "stricken for the transgression of My people." Philip answered with Jesus.

layers.evidence: Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 52:13 and 53:5 (English translation of 1871, on Sefaria). TBESH lists both senses of chalal, to pierce and to profane
layers.text: An early Jewish paraphrase in Aramaic, the Targum, names the Servant of 52:13 as the Messiah. In 53:5 it reads the word for "pierced" as "profaned" and applies it to the sanctuary. The Hebrew letters allow both senses.

passages.saying: In a surge of anger I hid My face from you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between a moment of anger and everlasting kindness.
layers.text: God admits that in a burst of anger He turned away from His people for a short time. But His compassion on them rests on a kindness that lasts forever.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say shetseph rhymes with ketseph (wrath) and that the wrath is only a vanishing moment beside God's everlasting kindness; Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the pair among its examples of paronomasia (words alike in sound).
layers.text: The Hebrew for a surge of anger is beshetsef qetsef, a rhyming pair. The rare word shetsef echoes qetsef, wrath. The ringing phrase sums up a brief outburst of anger, which the verse sets against God's everlasting kindness.

passages.saying: For to Me this is like the days of Noah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparison of God's oath to Zion with His oath after the Flood.
layers.text: God compares His promise to Zion with His promise after the Flood. Just as He swore the waters would never again cover the earth, He now swears He will not be angry with His people or rebuke them.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Genesis 8:21 and 9:11 and say God kept that promise; Gill points to the covenant with Noah sealed by the rainbow (Genesis 9:9); Wesley says the covenant with Zion is as certain as the one made with Noah. Both verses speak of the waters and of never again.
layers.text: This recalls God's covenant with Noah in Genesis 9, where He promised that "never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth." That promise has held ever since, so His new oath of peace to His people is just as sure.

passages.saying: I will make with you an everlasting covenant
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to listen and its promise of the covenant love shown to David.
layers.text: God calls His people to listen and come to Him so that they may truly live. He promises them an everlasting covenant built on the faithful love He once promised to David.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the 'true mercies' probably allude to 2 Samuel 7:16. The Companion Bible ties the everlasting covenant to 2 Samuel 7:8-16, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites 2 Samuel 7:15-16 for 'sure', and Bullinger's Figures of Speech points to the promise in 2 Samuel 7.
layers.text: This covenant looks back to God's promise to David in 2 Samuel 7: His loving devotion (chesed) would never be removed from David's line, and David's house would endure forever. Isaiah calls this devotion ne'emanim, sure, from the same root, aman, used there for that lasting house.

passages.saying: they are dreamers lying around, loving to slumber
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's pictures of blind watchmen and silent watchdogs.
layers.text: Israel's leaders were meant to watch over the people and warn them of danger. Instead they are blind and silent, like guard dogs that never bark, and they would rather lie around and sleep.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch set 'seers' (chozim) against 'ravers' (hozim) and compare another play on words in Isaiah 19:18. Barnes notes that hozim, to dream or talk in one's sleep, is kindred to chazah, to see.
layers.text: Prophets were meant to be seers (chozim), men who see what God shows them. Isaiah calls these watchmen dreamers (hozim), a word that sounds almost the same. Instead of seeing visions from God, they only doze and talk in their sleep.

passages.saying: Your portion is among the smooth stones of the valley
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of offerings poured out to stones from the valley.
layers.text: The people chose smooth stones from the valley as their gods and poured out drink offerings and grain offerings to them. God asks whether He should simply relent and let such worship pass.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it an elegant play on words between smooth stones and portion, and Barnes a paronomasia. Keil and Delitzsch say chalaq (smooth) plays on chelek (portion) and set the stones against the LORD as Israel's portion. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse as a paronomasia.
layers.text: Isaiah plays on two words that sound alike: chalaq, smooth, and chelek, portion. The people chose smooth stones from the valley as their gods, so those stones would be their portion, in place of the LORD, whom the faithful call their portion.

passages.saying: you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise that violence and destruction will end in Zion's land.
layers.text: God promises that violence, ruin and destruction will never again be heard of in Zion's land. Her walls and gates will be known for salvation and praise instead.

layers.evidence: Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain both names: God's salvation serves as the city's walls, and praise fills the gates. Keil and Delitzsch and Barnes also read Salvation as the city's true defense.
layers.text: Zion will give her walls and gates new names. Her walls will be called Salvation (yeshuah), because God's saving help will be her true defense. Her gates will be called Praise (tehillah), because gates once broken by enemies will be filled with praise to God.

passages.saying: to give them a crown of beauty for ashes
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's list of gifts of joy given in place of the signs of mourning.
layers.text: God promises to comfort those who mourn in Zion, exchanging every sign of grief for a sign of joy. His people will stand strong like oaks of righteousness, planted by the LORD to show His glory.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it a beautiful play on words, peer for epher; Barnes calls it a paronomasia; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown a play on sound and meaning. Clarke, the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech also mark the paronomasia.
layers.text: The mourners receive pe'er instead of efer, a crown of beauty for ashes. The two Hebrew words sound alike and use the same three letters in a different order. The ashes thrown on the head in grief are exchanged for a festive headdress.

passages.saying: you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between Zion's old names and her new ones.
layers.text: Zion will no longer be seen as abandoned, nor her land as a wasteland. God gives them new names, because He delights in His people and their land will be His bride.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that Hephzibah was Hezekiah's wife and calls her a type of Jerusalem. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes), on 2 Kings 21:1, says Isaiah may well have used her name in Isaiah 62:4 as a compliment to her. Keil and Delitzsch note the same woman without pressing a link.
layers.text: Hephzibah was also the name of King Hezekiah's wife, the mother of Manasseh, in Isaiah's own day (2 Kings 21:1). Isaiah may have used the queen's name on purpose, making it a picture of Jerusalem, the bride in whom the LORD delights.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Wesley, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch all give Hephzibah as 'my delight is in her' and Beulah as 'married', and Gill notes that the verse's last clause explains both names.
layers.text: The old names, Azuvah (Forsaken) for Zion and Shemamah (Desolate) for her land, give way to new ones. Hephzibah means my delight is in her, and Beulah means married. The verse explains both: the LORD delights (chafetz) in her, and her land will be married (tibba'el).

passages.saying: you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording; Barnes explains the names as the honorable names God's redeemed people will bear.
layers.text: God's people will be known as the holy people whom the LORD has redeemed, and Zion will be called Sought Out, a city God will never again abandon.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain derushah as one whose welfare men, and still more Jehovah, zealously promote, and call Not Forsaken the antithesis to azubah, Forsaken, in 60:15 and possibly also in 62:4. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read Sought Out as answering to Not Forsaken, with the image of a wife from 62:4.
layers.text: Zion's new names undo her old one. In verse 4 she had been called Forsaken (azuvah). Now she is Sought Out (derushah), a city God seeks and prizes, and A City Not Forsaken (lo ne'ezavah), built from the same verb azav, to forsake.

passages.saying: Who is this coming from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the vision of verses 1-6; Matthew Henry's Concise reads it as the Messiah returning in triumph over His enemies, Edom being a type.
layers.text: The prophet sees a mighty Warrior marching from Edom and its city Bozrah in red-stained garments. He announces that He is mighty to save. He is the Lord returning in triumph over His people's enemies, of whom Edom was a type.

layers.evidence: Wesley sees an allusion to the conqueror's garments, Edom signifying red and Bozrah a vintage; Clarke and the Companion Bible give the same two meanings, and the Companion Bible's note on verse 2 ties adom, red, to the name Edom.
layers.text: Edom means red, and verse 2 asks why the Warrior's clothes are red (adom). Bozrah, Edom's chief city, sounds like the Hebrew word for grape harvest. So the very names fit the scene: He comes from the land of red, stained like one who has trodden grapes in the winepress.

passages.saying: Then His people remembered the days of old, the days of Moses.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the questions of verses 11-14; Barnes says they recall that God never wholly forsook His people and plead that He act the same way now.
layers.text: In their distress God's people look back to the days of Moses and ask where the God is who once led Israel through the sea and set His Holy Spirit among them. The memory becomes a plea for Him to act again.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the sea is the Red Sea, a deliverance constantly recalled in Scripture; Wesley says God divided the sea for them; Keil and Delitzsch note that the raised staff and hand of Moses divided the Red Sea, citing Exodus 14:16.
layers.text: The question points back to the Red Sea crossing, when God told Moses to lift his staff, stretch his hand over the sea and divide it, so Israel could walk through on dry ground. Verse 12 finishes the memory: God divided the waters before them.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the phrase as a reference to the Pentateuch, Numbers 11:17; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Numbers 11:17 and 25 for the Spirit given in the midst of the people.
layers.text: The One who set His Holy Spirit among them may recall the wilderness, when the LORD shared the Spirit resting on Moses with the seventy elders. Isaiah uses the same Hebrew verb, sum (set or put), and the same word Spirit (ruach) as Numbers 11:17.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the real Hebrew meaning of the name Mosheh is extrahens, one who draws out, that is, a liberator, though they do not read this verse as a play on it. Exodus 2:10 gives the origin of the name.
layers.text: Moses got his name because Pharaoh's daughter said, "I drew him out of the water" (Exodus 2:10); in Hebrew, Mosheh means one who draws out, a deliverer. The people now look back to the days of Moses, when God brought them through the sea.

passages.saying: If only You would rend the heavens and come down
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the prayer's own words; Gill explains it as a plea for a visible display of God's power against His people's enemies.
layers.text: The people pray that God would tear open the heavens and come down in power to rescue them, so that even the mountains would shake at His presence.

layers.evidence: Clarke sees an allusion to God's appearing on Mount Sinai, and Wesley calls it possibly an allusion to His coming down there; the Companion Bible says the reference is to Sinai and compares Judges 5:4-5, which Barnes also quotes. Isaiah's harim nazollu closely echoes harim nazlu in Judges 5:5.
layers.text: The prayer likely looks back to Mount Sinai, when the LORD came down and the mountains shook. The Song of Deborah used almost the same Hebrew words: "The mountains quaked before the LORD, the One of Sinai" (Judges 5:5). The people ask God to come down like that once more.

passages.saying: I will destine you for the sword
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's threat and its stated reason; Wesley explains that a great number would perish by the sword.
layers.text: Because they ignored God's call and chose what He hates, the idol worshipers of verse 11 will be handed over to the sword and bow down to be slaughtered.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say God's word umanithi contains a play upon the name of Meni; Barnes says both words come from manah, to number; the Companion Bible calls it a Paronomasia with the god's name, and Gill, Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agree.
layers.text: Verse 11 names the idol Meni, Destiny, whose name comes from the verb manah, to number or assign. God answers with that same verb: umaniti, I will destine you for the sword. They poured wine for the idol of fate, so the LORD Himself would assign their fate.

passages.saying: but the food of the serpent will be dust
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of peace; Keil and Delitzsch say peace and harmony will prevail even in the animal world.
layers.text: In the new heavens and new earth even the animals will live at peace. The wolf feeds with the lamb and the lion eats straw, while the serpent eats dust, and nothing will harm or destroy on God's holy mountain.

layers.evidence: Barnes says there is evidently an allusion to the sentence on the serpent in Genesis 3:14; Keil and Delitzsch say the serpent will be content with the food assigned it there; Gill reads it of the old serpent, the devil, as threatened in Genesis 3:14.
layers.text: When everything else is healed, the serpent still eats dust. This echoes God's curse on the serpent in Eden: "dust you will eat, all the days of your life." That sentence stands, but the serpent will no longer harm anyone on God's holy mountain.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the prophet here repeats Isaiah 11:6-9 almost word for word in shortened form; the Companion Bible points to Isaiah 11:6, 7 and 9.
layers.text: Isaiah repeats his own earlier promise of peace from chapter 11. The lion eating straw like the ox comes from 11:7, and the closing line, "They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain," is word for word 11:9. Only the line about the serpent is new.

passages.saying: they have chosen their own ways and delighted in their abominations
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparisons; Wesley says such formal services were no more acceptable to God than murder or idolatry.
layers.text: God rejects the worship of people whose hearts are set on their own ways. Their offerings of ox, lamb, grain and incense are as hateful to Him as murder, unclean offerings or idol worship.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech notes the words are repeated in another sense, first of men's acts and then of God; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown set they have chosen against I will choose in verse 4; Keil and Delitzsch call God's choosing their ill-treatment the law of retribution.
layers.text: The key verbs return in verse 4 with God as the one acting. They chose (bachar) their own ways and delighted (chaphets) in abominations. So God says He will choose their punishment, because they chose what He did not delight in. Their choice is answered by His.

passages.saying: I have put My words in your mouth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain the touch on the mouth as God's sign that He frames in Jeremiah's mouth what he is to speak.
layers.text: The LORD touched Jeremiah's mouth as a sign and told him, "Behold, I have put My words in your mouth." Jeremiah, who had said he did not know how to speak, would not bring his own message but God's.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible, on the words I have put My words, says this is inspiration and points to Deuteronomy 18:18. Both verses use the same three Hebrew words: natan (put), devarai (My words) and peh (mouth).
layers.text: These words match God's promise in Deuteronomy 18:18 of a prophet like Moses: "I will put My words in his mouth." The Hebrew phrase is the same, so Jeremiah is given what that promise describes: God's own words to speak, not his own.

passages.saying: to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that prophets are said to do what God sends them to declare will be done.
layers.text: God sets Jeremiah over nations and kingdoms as His prophet. By announcing God's word he would declare judgment, uprooting and tearing down, and also restoration, building and planting.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) calls the pair an instance of the alliteration common in the prophets; JFB notes the play on similar sounds in the Hebrew for root out and pull down; Keil and Delitzsch call natash and natats assonant verbs joined to heighten the sense, with four words of ruin before two of building.
layers.text: In Hebrew the first two verbs sound almost alike: lintosh, to uproot, and lintots, to tear down. Only the last sound changes. This ringing pair leads four words of ruin, and only after them come two words of hope, to build and plant.

passages.saying: I am watching over My word to accomplish it.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew text from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Young Jeremiah protests, "I am only a child!" God touches his mouth, puts His words there, and sends him "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant." Then He asks, "Jeremiah, what do you see?"

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Jeremiah 1:12: the almond blossoms in January or February and is the harbinger of spring. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: literally the wakeful tree, waking from winter's sleep before the others. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch note the play on the name.
layers.text: Jeremiah sees "a branch of an almond tree," shaqed, and God answers that He is shoqed, "watching." The almond is the first tree to blossom after winter, so its name means something like "the wakeful tree." God is awake over His word.

layers.evidence: Benson on Amos 8:1-2 says qets (end) sounds like qayits (summer fruit) and names Jeremiah 1:11 as the same kind of play. Keil and Delitzsch on Jeremiah 1:13: Jeremiah's second vision, the boiling pot, turns on a like-sounding word, just as Amos 8:2 does. The continuation of Poole's Annotations on Jeremiah 1:11 links the almond rod to Amos's summer fruit as a sign of God's readiness to smite.
layers.text: Amos had a vision built the same way: "Amos, what do you see?" "A basket of summer fruit," qayits. Then God says the end, qets, "has come for My people Israel." Both visions turn an everyday object into a message through the sound of its name.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Jeremiah 31:28 recalls the wakeful or watching tree and the two-fold work of the call. Keil and Delitzsch and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Jeremiah 1:10: what is said there of Jeremiah's word is said of the LORD Himself in 31:28. TAHOT: all three forms are H8245.
layers.text: The almond's verb returns beside the new-covenant promise: "Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down," so "I will watch over them to build and to plant," the two tasks of Jeremiah's call. God watches over rebuilding as He watched over judgment.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Barnes, Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Hebrews 8:8: the quotation in Hebrews 8:8-12 is from Jeremiah 31:31-34.
layers.text: Three verses later comes what He is watching to build, "a new covenant": "I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts." Hebrews quotes the whole passage and says of Jesus, "the covenant He mediates is better."

passages.saying: Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains getting ready (girding the loins) as haste and courage in doing the Lord's work.
layers.text: God tells Jeremiah to get ready, stand up and speak everything He commands. He must not shrink back in fear of the people, or God Himself will leave him terrified before them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call it a play on words; the Companion Bible and Figures of Speech mark a paronomasia in alternating pairs (tehath, mippeneyhem; ahiteka, liphneyhem); JFB notes that dismayed and confound are the same Hebrew word, literally to break.
layers.text: Intimidated and terrify are one Hebrew verb used twice: do not be dismayed (techat) before them, or I will dismay you (achittekha) before them. If Jeremiah gave way to fear of people, God would leave him truly broken before them.

passages.saying: followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains the question: God gave no cause for complaint, so why did they turn to idols?
layers.text: God asks what wrong their ancestors ever found in Him that they wandered so far away. He had given them no cause, yet they chased worthless idols and became worthless themselves.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks What iniquity as a reference to Deuteronomy 32:4; Keil and Delitzsch explain the word avel (wrong) from that verse, where the LORD is a God of faithfulness in whom is no iniquity. JFB also compares Deuteronomy 32:4.
layers.text: God's question, "What fault did your fathers find in Me," echoes the Song of Moses, which calls Him "A God of faithfulness without injustice" (Deuteronomy 32:4). Fault and injustice are the same Hebrew word, avel. No wrong was ever found in Him.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech quotes walked after vanity and are become vain and refers it to paronomasia; JFB says an idol is vanity itself and its worshippers acquire its character, becoming vain as it is; the Companion Bible says vanity stands for idols and idolaters always become like the gods they worship.
layers.text: In Hebrew the noun and the verb match: they went after hevel, emptiness, meaning worthless idols, and vayyehbalu, they became empty themselves. Those who chase what is worthless grow like it, for people become like what they worship.

passages.saying: I had planted you like a choice vine from the very best seed.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that God gave Israel the fullest instruction and privileges, yet it degenerated into idolatry.
layers.text: God had planted Israel like a choice vine from the very best seed, giving it every advantage. Yet Israel turned into a rotten, wild vine, falling into idolatry instead of bearing good fruit.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) identifies the noble vine as a Sorek vine and points to Isaiah 5:2; Clarke and Gill point to Isaiah 5:1 for the same image of Israel as God's planted vine; JFB also lists Isaiah 5:1. Both verses use the verb nata (plant) with soreq (choice vine).
layers.text: Isaiah's song of the vineyard uses the same picture: God "planted the finest vines" yet got only sour fruit (Isaiah 5:2). Both verses use the same Hebrew word, soreq, for the prized vine, and both mourn a choice planting gone bad.

passages.saying: If a man divorces his wife and she leaves him to marry another
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that Israel was joined to the Lord in covenant like a wife, then turned to idols.
layers.text: God compares His people to an unfaithful wife. By the law, a divorced wife who married another man could not go back to her first husband. Israel had gone after many lovers, the idols, so how could she expect simply to come back to the LORD?

layers.evidence: Gill says the first husband might not take her back according to the law in Deuteronomy 24:4; JFB says it was unlawful (Deuteronomy 24:1-4); Wesley says he cannot take her again according to the law, yet God is ready to be reconciled. Both texts use shalach (send away) and shuv (return).
layers.text: The question rests on the law of Deuteronomy 24:1-4: a husband who sent his wife away could not take her back after she married another, for that would bring sin on the land. Yet the LORD goes beyond that law and calls faithless Israel to return (3:12, 3:22).

passages.saying: Return, O faithless Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that the north means the lands where the ten tribes were captive, and notes how tender the call is.
layers.text: Jeremiah is sent to call toward the north, where the exiled northern tribes lived, "Return, O faithless Israel." God promises to stop looking on them in anger, for He is merciful and will not be angry forever.

layers.evidence: JFB notes that the Hebrew for Return, backsliding is Shubah, Meshubah, a play on sounds. Meshuvah (faithless, turning away) is formed from shuv (turn, return).
layers.text: Some hear a play on sounds in the Hebrew call, shuvah meshuvah, which means roughly: turn back, you who turned away. The word for Israel's sin of turning from God is built on the same word God uses to call her home.

passages.saying: Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) explains that God's call is at once followed by the people's acceptance of His mercy.
layers.text: God again calls His faithless people to return and promises to heal their unfaithfulness. The people answer at once, "Here we are. We come to You, for You are the LORD our God."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Hosea 14:5 (14:4 in English Bibles) was in the prophet's mind when he wrote of healing backslidings; JFB points to Hosea 14:4 for heal meaning forgive. Both verses join rapha (heal) with meshuvah (turning away).
layers.text: God's promise seems to echo Hosea's: "I will heal their apostasy" (Hosea 14:4). Jeremiah uses the same two Hebrew words, erpa (I will heal) and meshuvah (turning away), likely taking up the earlier prophet's promise to Israel.

passages.saying: If you will return, O Israel, return to Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The LORD's answer to Israel's confession at the end of chapter 3, as the commentaries read it.
layers.text: The LORD calls Israel to come back, and to come back to Him. That means putting their detestable idols out of His sight and no longer wavering between Him and other gods.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the repeated return a play on words: to return to the land, Israel must first return to God in repentance. R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) notes the same two senses of return here, literal (back to the land) and spiritual (away from sin).
layers.text: The verse uses the Hebrew word for return (shuv) twice. One reading hears two senses in it: if Israel wants to return home to the land, it must first return to the LORD in repentance.

passages.saying: then the nations will be blessed by Him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse finishes the condition begun in verse 1 and states its result for the nations.
layers.text: If Israel swears by the living LORD alone, honestly and justly, the nations will see what God has done for His people. They will seek their blessing in Him and boast in Him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the promise alludes to the promises to the patriarchs (Genesis 12:3; 18:18; 22:18), though here the blessing is found in the LORD Himself. Gill ties it to Genesis 22:18, the nations blessed in Christ.
layers.text: The nations being blessed echoes God's promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring, using the same Hebrew verb. If Israel truly turned back, that old promise would reach the nations, who would find their blessing in the LORD.

passages.saying: Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries agree the circumcision called for is of the heart, not the flesh.
layers.text: Judah's men were already circumcised in the body, so God calls for a change of heart. They must cut away the stubborn sin in their hearts, or His anger will burn like a fire no one can put out.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the command as a reference to Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6. Keil and Delitzsch explain it from Deuteronomy 10:16 and note that some manuscripts even bring the wording into line with that verse.
layers.text: Jeremiah seems to take up Moses' command in Deuteronomy to circumcise the foreskin of the heart, using the same Hebrew words. Judah was already circumcised in the flesh; God called for the impurity of the heart itself to be put away.

passages.saying: a voice resounds from Dan, proclaiming disaster from the hills of Ephraim
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Dan was the northern border town, and the hills of Ephraim lay just north of Judah.
layers.text: Messengers bring news of the invader first from Dan in the far north, then from the hills of Ephraim close to Judah. The enemy is coming nearer and nearer to Jerusalem.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) sees a play on the double meaning of aven, used in verse 14 for wickedness and here for misery. Gill notes the word for affliction means iniquity, showing the ruin came because of their sins.
layers.text: The word for disaster here (aven) is the same word used one verse earlier for Jerusalem's wicked thoughts. It can mean both wickedness and trouble, and the verse likely plays on both: the sin the city kept in its heart becomes the very ruin now announced from the north.

passages.saying: I looked at the earth, and it was formless and void
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The first of four visions that each begin with I looked, describing the coming desolation of Judah.
layers.text: In a vision Jeremiah sees what the coming judgment will do to the land. It lies empty and ruined, and the sky above has gone dark.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch all point to Genesis 1:2: the same pair of words, tohu and bohu, describes the earth before God brought it into order.
layers.text: Formless and void (tohu and bohu) are the words of Genesis 1:2, describing the earth before God gave it shape and light. Jeremiah pictures judgment as creation running backward: the land emptied and the heavens dark again.

passages.saying: The whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries read the second half as a limit God sets on the judgment.
layers.text: The whole land will be laid waste, yet God will not wipe His people out completely. A remnant will be left, and the land will one day be lived in again.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks it as a reference to Leviticus 26:44. Keil and Delitzsch say the limit is founded on that promise. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares Leviticus 26:44.
layers.text: God's refusal to make a full end rests on His covenant promise in Leviticus 26:44. There He said that even when His people were in their enemies' land, He would not destroy them completely or break His covenant with them.

passages.saying: If you can find a single person, anyone who acts justly
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries read the search as showing how widespread the city's corruption was.
layers.text: God tells searchers to comb Jerusalem's streets and squares for just one person who does what is right and seeks the truth. If one can be found, He will forgive the city.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Wesley and Gill all compare Abraham's plea for Sodom in Genesis 18, where God would spare the city for ten righteous people. Wesley notes that Jerusalem is offered pardon for only one.
layers.text: The search for one just person recalls Abraham pleading for Sodom, when God agreed to spare the city if ten righteous people were found there. Jerusalem is offered pardon for just one, yet none is found, which makes it look worse than Sodom.

passages.saying: sworn by gods that are not gods. I satisfied their needs
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries read the verse as God's reason why He cannot simply overlook Judah's sin.
layers.text: God asks why He should forgive a people who left Him and swore by false gods. He filled their needs, and they answered His kindness with adultery and visits to houses of prostitution.

layers.evidence: Gill points out a beautiful play on words in the Hebrew between the word for swearing and the word for feeding. The Companion Bible notes that some Hebrew copies read the second word as made them swear.
layers.text: Two Hebrew words that look and sound almost alike stand close together: the people swore (shava) by false gods, though the LORD had filled them (sava) to the full. Some Hebrew copies even read the second word as made them swear.

passages.saying: I am bringing a distant nation against you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries identify the distant nation as Babylon.
layers.text: God warns that He is bringing a strong and ancient nation from far away against His people. They will not know its language, and its soldiers will not understand their cries for mercy.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the verse alludes to Deuteronomy 28:49. Keil and Delitzsch also compare Deuteronomy 28:49 for the foreign tongue.
layers.text: The warning echoes the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:49, where Moses said the LORD would bring a nation from far away whose language Israel would not understand. What Moses had warned of was now at the door.

passages.saying: Sound the ram’s horn in Tekoa
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Tekoa and Beth-haccerem lay south of Jerusalem, away from the enemy coming from the north.
layers.text: Jeremiah warns the people of Benjamin to flee Jerusalem. Alarm horns and fire signals are to go up in the towns to the south, because a great disaster is coming from the north.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks it as a paronomasia, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists it too. Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill also note the play. R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) adds that Tekoa was chosen not only for the sound but because it was the last town on the edge of the desert.
layers.text: In Hebrew the command to blow the horn in Tekoa is a sound play: tiqu (blow) and bitqoa (in Tekoa). The town whose name echoes the blast also stood south of Jerusalem near the desert, the way people fleeing a northern enemy would run.

passages.saying: They are called rejected silver, because the LORD has rejected them
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse ends the picture of the prophet as a tester of metal in verses 27 to 29.
layers.text: Jeremiah has tested the people like a refiner tests silver, but no pure metal comes out. They are worthless dross, and the LORD has thrown them away.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a paronomasia on nim'as and ma'as: rejected silver, rejected people.
layers.text: Some see a wordplay on one Hebrew word used twice. The people are called rejected (nimas) silver because the LORD has rejected (maas) them, so what people call them may echo what God has done.

passages.saying: Will you steal and murder, commit adultery and perjury
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Part of Jeremiah's temple sermon, which the next verse completes.
layers.text: Jeremiah asks whether the people really think they can steal, murder, commit adultery, lie under oath and worship Baal, and then come into God's house and feel safe.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the list as a reference to the commandments in Exodus 20. Gill calls them sins against the second table of the law, and the idolatry that follows sins against the first.
layers.text: Jeremiah's list walks through the Ten Commandments, using the same Hebrew verbs for steal, murder and commit adultery, and then names false oaths and other gods. The people broke God's covenant law and still trusted His temple to protect them.

passages.saying: the place in Shiloh where I first made a dwelling for My Name
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The tabernacle stood at Shiloh from Joshua's day until the ark was lost in Eli's day.
layers.text: God tells the people to look at Shiloh, where His tabernacle first stood, and see what He did to it because of Israel's sin. Having His house among them would not save Jerusalem either.

layers.evidence: Gill, R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all point to Psalm 78 for what God did to Shiloh, with Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adding 1 Samuel 4, where the ark was taken by the Philistines.
layers.text: God points back to the fall of Shiloh, which Psalm 78:60 describes: "He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men." If He did that to His first dwelling place, the temple in Jerusalem was not safe either.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the phrase as a reference to Deuteronomy 12:5 and 12:11.
layers.text: Making a dwelling for His Name may echo the language of Deuteronomy 12:11, where Moses spoke of the place the LORD would choose for His Name. Shiloh had been that chosen place, and still it fell.

passages.saying: they pour out drink offerings to other gods to provoke Me to anger
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture of every member of the family taking part in idol worship.
layers.text: Whole families in Judah join in false worship. Children gather wood, fathers light the fire, and women bake cakes for the Queen of Heaven. They pour out drink offerings to other gods, and this provokes the LORD to anger.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists Jeremiah 7:18-19 as one word used in two senses: first of the people provoking God, then of the punishment they bring on themselves. The Companion Bible marks the same figure (Ploke) on verse 19.
layers.text: They worship other gods "to provoke Me to anger," and God answers, "But am I the One they are provoking?" Some see the same Hebrew verb (ka'as, to provoke or vex) coming back with a second sense: the anger they stir up really falls on themselves, to their own shame.

passages.saying: I will take away their harvest, declares the LORD
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of Judah as a fruitless vine and fig tree facing judgment.
layers.text: The LORD says He will take away Judah's harvest and sweep the people away. Judah is like a vine with no grapes and a fig tree with no figs and withered leaves, and whatever He gave them will be lost to them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain the phrase as a combination of asaf (gather, glean, carry away) and suf (make an end, sweep off) that heightens the sense. The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech both list it as a paronomasia, 'asoph 'asiphem.
layers.text: The verse opens with two Hebrew words that sound alike, asof asifem. The first comes from asaf, to gather or glean, as at harvest; the second is read as from suf, to make an end. Together they may say God will gather His people in and sweep them away completely.

passages.saying: let us flee to the fortified cities and perish there
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the people's own words in the verse as they give up hope of escape.
layers.text: As the enemy comes, the people of Judah urge one another to flee into the walled cities, though they expect to die there. They admit that the LORD has given them poisoned water to drink because they sinned against Him.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech says the people propose to rest quietly in their sin and are answered with the same word in a different sense, the silence of death. The Companion Bible marks the same figure (Ploke) on silence. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read the first word as let us be silent there; R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) notes it literally means be put to silence.
layers.text: The Hebrew for perish there, nidmah (from damam, to be still), can also mean let us be silent there. Some see a play: the people mean to wait quietly behind the walls, but the same root returns in "the LORD our God has doomed us," literally has silenced us. Their quiet becomes the silence of death.

passages.saying: for every brother deals craftily, and every friend spreads slander
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's warning to guard against neighbors and brothers alike.
layers.text: Deceit has spread so far in Judah that no one can trust a neighbor or even a brother. Every brother cheats and every friend goes about spreading slander.

layers.evidence: Gill says every brother will play the Jacob, as Jacob twice supplanted Esau, and that the same word is used here. R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) calls it an allusion to the name of Jacob (Genesis 27:36). Keil and Delitzsch see an allusion to Jacob's underhand dealing with his brother Esau.
layers.text: Deals craftily translates aqov ya'qov, a doubled verb meaning to supplant or trip up by the heel. Ya'qov is spelled with the same Hebrew letters as the name Jacob (Ya'aqov), recalling Esau's complaint that Jacob cheated him twice. Every brother in Judah has become a thorough Jacob.

passages.saying: These gods, who have made neither the heavens nor the earth, will perish
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, given to Judah as a reply to idol worshipers.
layers.text: Jeremiah gives the people of Judah a short reply for the nations: the idols, which did not create the heavens and the earth, will disappear from the earth and from under the heavens.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech both list not made and shall perish as a paronomasia ('abadu ye'badu). Figures of Speech adds that, unlike the rest of Jeremiah, this verse is written in Chaldee (Aramaic), as a message to the Gentiles.
layers.text: This is Jeremiah's only verse written in Aramaic, the language of Babylon, perhaps as a message to the nations. The gods who did not make (avadu) the heavens and the earth will perish (yevadu). Some hear a play in the two verbs, which sound almost alike, tying what the idols never did to their end.

passages.saying: I was like a gentle lamb led to slaughter
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on the plot by the men of Anathoth told in 11:21.
layers.text: Jeremiah says he was like a trusting lamb being led to slaughter. He did not know that men of his own town were plotting to kill him and wipe out his name.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the language is exactly that applied to the Messiah in Isaiah 53:7, each prophet showing some feature of His sufferings. The Companion Bible calls Jeremiah here a type of Christ and points to Isaiah 53:8, where the Servant is cut off from the land of the living.
layers.text: Jeremiah pictures himself as a lamb led to slaughter whom his enemies want cut off from the land of the living. Isaiah gives the same picture of the suffering Servant, who was "led like a lamb to the slaughter." In this Jeremiah's suffering foreshadows Christ's.

passages.saying: He is like a tree planted by the waters
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of the one who trusts in the LORD (17:7).
layers.text: The one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree whose roots reach a stream. Heat and drought do not harm it; its leaves stay green and it keeps bearing fruit.

layers.evidence: Gill says Psalm 1:3 seems to be alluded to here. Keil and Delitzsch call the picture an extension of Psalm 1:3-4, of the man who delights in the law of the Lord. The Companion Bible marks it as a reference to Psalm 1:1-3.
layers.text: This echoes Psalm 1:3, where the one who delights in God's law is "like a tree planted by streams of water." Jeremiah gives the same picture to the one who trusts the LORD, in contrast to the man who trusts in man and is like a shrub in the desert (17:5-6).

passages.saying: Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, its twin in Jeremiah 7:32, and the child sacrifices described in 19:4-5.
layers.text: God says a day is coming when the valley outside Jerusalem where children were burned as offerings will no longer go by its old names, Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom. It will be known as the Valley of Slaughter.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch all explain the new name by the slaughter of Jerusalem's people in that valley. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown contrasts it with the children once killed there, and Gill, R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown draw the same contrast on the twin verse 7:32.
layers.text: The new name, Valley of Slaughter (Hebrew haregah, killing), turns the place against those who used it. Where parents had killed their children for idols, the people of Jerusalem would themselves be killed in great numbers when the city fell.

passages.saying: And in this place I will ruin the plans of Judah and Jerusalem
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in the valley where Judah sought help from idols (19:2-5).
layers.text: In the very valley where Judah practiced idolatry, God would bring the nation's plans to nothing. Its people would fall by the sword before their enemies, and their bodies would be left for birds and wild animals to eat.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the verb plays on the jar's name, Gill calls it an elegant play on words, and R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) notes the verb is the one the jar's name comes from, so it could be rendered pour out. Keil and Delitzsch and R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) also say the name imitates the sound of liquid pouring from the jar.
layers.text: Jeremiah carried a clay jar, in Hebrew a baqbuq, a name that echoes the gurgle of liquid pouring out. Here God says He will empty out (baqqoti) Judah's plans, using the verb behind the jar's name. Their schemes would be poured out and come to nothing. Then Jeremiah was to smash the jar (19:10).

passages.saying: The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account in 20:1-6 of Pashhur's punishment of Jeremiah and the LORD's answer.
layers.text: Pashhur, a priest and chief officer in the temple, had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks. The next day, when he released him, Jeremiah told him that the LORD no longer called him Pashhur, but Magor-missabib.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) says Jeremiah probably took the phrase as his watchword from Psalm 31:13. Keil and Delitzsch say Jeremiah 20:10 repeats the psalm word for word, the prophet using the psalmist's language in a similar trial.
layers.text: Magor-missabib means terror on every side, words also found in Psalm 31:13, where the psalmist is slandered and plotted against. Jeremiah, who suffered the same way, uses the phrase five times (6:25; 20:3, 10; 46:5; 49:29) and seems to have taken it up from the psalm.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Gill, Wesley, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all render Magor-missabib as terror or fear on every side, and Gill and R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) see verse 4 explaining the name. They differ on what Pashhur itself means, so the note leaves that open.
layers.text: Magor-missabib means terror on every side. Verse 4 explains the name with the same word, magor, terror: "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends." The man who punished God's prophet would see his friends fall and go to Babylon himself.

passages.saying: The wind will drive away all your shepherds
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the shepherd language for Judah's rulers in Jeremiah 22 and 23.
layers.text: Judah's leaders, called its shepherds, would be swept away as if by a wind, and the allies Judah courted as lovers would go into captivity. Then Judah would be ashamed and humiliated because of all its wickedness.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the verb was chosen for the word-play with shepherds, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it a happy play on words, and R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) renders it literally as shall depasture thy pastors.
layers.text: The verb translated drive away is ra'ah, to graze a flock, the same root as ro'im, shepherds. So the verse says, in effect, the wind will shepherd your shepherds. The rulers who should have fed God's flock would themselves be grazed bare and carried off.

passages.saying: and have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the woe on the shepherds in 23:1.
layers.text: God speaks against the shepherds, Judah's rulers, who should have cared for His people. They scattered His flock, drove it away and neglected it, so He will punish them for the evil they have done.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this a play on the double sense of visit, and Gill explains that because the rulers did not visit the flock in kindness, God would visit them in justice.
layers.text: The Hebrew verb paqad can mean to look after someone or to call someone to account. The shepherds have not attended to the flock, so God says, "I will attend to you," using the same verb, this time in judgment. Their neglect comes back on them.

passages.saying: And this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Judah's rulers have been shepherds who "destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture." God promises to "raise up for David a righteous Branch," a King who "will administer justice and righteousness in the land."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6667: Zedekiah, Jehovah is righteous, renamed from Mattaniah by Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott on Jeremiah 23:6 and 2 Kings 24:17 and George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) on 2 Kings 24:17 tie it to Jeremiah 23's promised King. Keil and Delitzsch: probably chosen in hope of the righteousness promised to God's people. The Pulpit Commentary: one possibility. Ellicott: his reign was a miserable failure.
layers.text: Judah's last king was Zedekiah, a name the king of Babylon gave him, meaning the LORD is righteous. Yet "Zedekiah did evil in the sight of the LORD." He bore a name close to the promised one and failed it; the true King will be "The LORD Our Righteousness."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6780: a sprout or shoot, used of the Messiah from David's tree. Keil and Delitzsch: tsemach denotes the Messiah. The continuation of Poole's Annotations ties it to the Branch of Jeremiah 33:15, and Ellicott to the Branch of Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12.
layers.text: "Branch" is tsemach, a sprout: the future King springing from David's family tree. Jeremiah repeats it, "I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch," and after the exile Zechariah hears, "I am going to bring My servant, the Branch."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Jeremiah 23:6: in 33:16 the same name is given to Jerusalem. Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on 33:16: Christ and His church are one, so they share the name.
layers.text: When Jeremiah repeats the promise, the name moves from the King to His city: Jerusalem "will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." The King and His people share one name.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) and the continuation of Poole's Annotations see the King called Yahweh, and the continuation of Poole's Annotations links the name to 1 Corinthians 1:30. Keil and Delitzsch: he by whom Jahveh deals righteousness. Ellicott applies it to imputed righteousness.
layers.text: Christians have long read the name of Christ, whom Paul calls "our righteousness," in whom "we might become the righteousness of God." Some hear the King called the LORD Himself; others, the one through whom the LORD gives righteousness.

passages.saying: What burden? I will forsake you, declares the LORD.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the ban on the mocking phrase in 23:34-38.
layers.text: When the people, a prophet or a priest mockingly ask Jeremiah what the latest burden from the LORD is, he is to answer that the LORD will forsake them.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) see a play on the double sense of massa, and Keil and Delitzsch say the idea of burden is kept up in God's answer. R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) gives the other reading, Ye are the burden, and Keil and Delitzsch explain it as the Septuagint's different division of the same letters, while keeping the Hebrew text.
layers.text: The Hebrew word massa means both a solemn message from God and a heavy load. Mockers asked for the latest burden, sneering at Jeremiah's warnings. God answers in kind: He will cast them off like a load. One ancient translation divides the letters differently, so the people are the burden.

passages.saying: I will surely forget you and will cast you out of My presence
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse as the penalty for repeating the forbidden phrase in 23:38.
layers.text: Because the people kept mocking God's word as a burden after He forbade it, He would forget them and cast them out of His presence, along with Jerusalem, the city He gave to them and their fathers.

layers.evidence: Gill and Keil and Delitzsch see a deliberate play between the verb for forget and massa, burden, which Keil and Delitzsch derive from nasa, to lift. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) translate the verb as lift up or take up, as Keil and Delitzsch note the Septuagint, Vulgate and Syriac did, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says this alludes to the mockers' word burden.
layers.text: The Hebrew for "I will surely forget you" (nashiti ... nasho) sounds like nasa, to lift, the root of massa, the burden the mockers kept naming. Some ancient translations read it as lift up: God would lift them like a load and throw them off. Either way, their mocking word lands on them.

passages.saying: And after all of them, the king of Sheshach will drink it too.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the cup vision of 25:15-26 and on 51:41, where Sheshach stands in parallel with Babylon.
layers.text: Jeremiah is told to make the nations drink the cup of God's anger, beginning with Jerusalem and Judah. After all the kingdoms near and far have drunk it, the king of Sheshach, that is, Babylon, the very power God used to judge them, must drink it last.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain the name by the Atbash code, in which letters are swapped in reverse alphabetical order, and R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) reports Jerome calling it Babel written in cipher. JFB and Gill also report this reading, though JFB prefers, and Gill finds not improbable, a link to the name of a Babylonian god.
layers.text: Sheshach is a name for Babylon, as 51:41 shows by setting the two side by side. Many read it as Babel in a simple code that swaps each Hebrew letter for its mirror at the other end of the alphabet: b becomes sh and l becomes k, so Babel (b-b-l) becomes Sheshach (sh-sh-k).

passages.saying: I will restore you from captivity
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its place in Jeremiah's letter to the exiles in Babylon (29:1-14).
layers.text: In his letter to the exiles in Babylon, Jeremiah passes on God's promise: He will let Himself be found by them, gather them from every nation and place where He drove them, and bring them back to the land from which He sent them into exile.

layers.evidence: JFB on this verse calls the phrase a play upon sounds, shabti and shebith.
layers.text: In "I will restore you from captivity," the Hebrew verb is shavti, from shuv (turn back), and the noun is shevut (captivity). The two words sound nearly alike, and the echo may add weight to God's promise to turn back the captivity.

passages.saying: Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; these two men appear nowhere else in Scripture.
layers.text: Jeremiah's letter names two false prophets among the exiles, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who were prophesying lies in God's name. God will hand them over to Nebuchadnezzar, and he will put them to death before the exiles' eyes.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a paronomasia in Kolayah, curse and roasted. Keil and Delitzsch: the word roasted is probably an allusion to the name Kolaiah. R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes): a play on words, which may be why their death became a proverb.
layers.text: Ahab's father was named Kolaiah (qo-la-yah). In the next verse the exiles turn the two men into a curse, qelalah, because the king of Babylon roasted them, qalam, in the fire. Kolaiah, qelalah and qalam sound alike, so the name echoes in their curse and in their punishment.

passages.saying: Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on God's answer to Rachel in 31:16-17.
layers.text: God describes a cry of grief heard in Ramah. Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeps for her children and refuses comfort, because they are gone, killed or carried into exile. In the next verses God tells her to stop weeping, for her children will return.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a reference to Genesis 35:19. JFB recalls Rachel dying in sorrow as she gave birth to Benjamin (Genesis 35:18-19). Wesley, Clarke and Matthew Henry all picture her as risen from her grave to weep.
layers.text: Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin and was buried on the way to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem. Jeremiah pictures her as if rising from that grave to weep over her lost descendants. Matthew later applies this verse to Herod's killing of the boys of Bethlehem.

passages.saying: Nothing is too difficult for You!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the field purchase that prompts the prayer (32:6-16).
layers.text: With Jerusalem under siege, God has told Jeremiah to buy a field. Jeremiah begins his prayer by praising the God who made the heavens and the earth by His great power and outstretched arm, and he confesses that nothing is too difficult for Him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible tie Jeremiah's words to Genesis 18:14, and JFB adds that God's reply in 32:27 matches the prayer. All three verses use the same Hebrew verb, pala, to be too wonderful or too hard.
layers.text: Jeremiah's words can be read as an echo of God's question to Abraham when Sarah laughed at the promise of a son: "Is anything too difficult for the LORD?" God then answers Jeremiah with the same question: "Is anything too difficult for Me?"

passages.saying: this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.
