layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the promise of the righteous Branch in 33:15.
layers.text: When God makes a righteous Branch sprout for David, Judah will be saved and Jerusalem will live in safety. The city that was about to fall to Babylon will be given a new name: The LORD Our Righteousness.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: the name passes from the sprout of David to Jerusalem, which reflects the righteousness the Messiah bestows. R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes), the Companion Bible, JFB and Gill likewise see the King's name given to the city. Clarke and Wesley hold that the name belongs to Christ, not to the city.
layers.text: The name, Yahweh tsidqenu, means the LORD is our righteousness. In 23:6 it is the name of the coming King from David's line. Here the same name is given to Jerusalem, because the city will reflect the righteousness her King gives her.

passages.saying: If you can break My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its conclusion in 33:21.
layers.text: God says His covenant with David and with the Levitical priests is as firm as His covenant with day and night. No one can stop day and night from coming at their appointed time, and no one can break His promise that David will always have a son to reign.

layers.evidence: Gill: this order of nature was formed into a covenant and promise to Noah after the flood (Genesis 8:22). The Companion Bible marks a reference to Genesis 8:22. Keil and Delitzsch: it is called a covenant because God pledged after the flood that it would continue.
layers.text: After the Flood God promised that "day and night shall never cease." Jeremiah calls that fixed order God's covenant with the day and the night. As surely as that promise has held ever since, God's covenant with David will never be broken.

passages.saying: So now I proclaim freedom for you, declares the LORD
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 8 to 16, where Jerusalem freed its Hebrew slaves and then took them back, and on this verse's threat.
layers.text: During Babylon's siege the people of Jerusalem set their Hebrew slaves free, as God's law required, and then forced them back into slavery. So God declares that He will hand the people over to the sword, plague and famine, and make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech call the double liberty an antanaclasis, one word used in two senses. JFB and Clarke also read the second liberty as a punishment matching the offense. The Hebrew deror (freedom) appears twice, each time with qara (proclaim).
layers.text: God answers their broken promise by using one word, deror (freedom), in two senses. They would not proclaim freedom for their slaves, so He proclaims a different freedom for them: "freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine!" The punishment mirrors the sin.

passages.saying: in Heshbon they devise evil against her
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words about the Moabite towns of Heshbon and Madmen.
layers.text: Moab has lost its glory. Enemies gathered in the town of Heshbon plan to wipe Moab out as a nation, and the town of Madmen will be silenced as the sword pursues it.

layers.evidence: Clarke, JFB and Keil and Delitzsch all note the double play, cheshbon with chashevu and madmen with tiddommi. Gill, R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) and Bullinger's Figures of Speech note it too, and the Companion Bible marks Heshbon, hashbu as a paronomasia. Gill and JFB say the name Heshbon comes from the word for devising or counsel.
layers.text: Two place names are echoed by the verbs beside them. In Heshbon (cheshbon) the enemy plans (chashevu) evil against Moab, using the root the town's name comes from. And Madmen (madmen) will be silenced (tiddommi). The names themselves seem to announce the judgment.

passages.saying: Put salt on Moab, for she will be laid waste
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of empty cities; Gill, JFB, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley all read the word rendered salt as wings, and Keil and Delitzsch note that it elsewhere means a flower.
layers.text: Moab will be ruined, and her cities left empty with no one living in them. The word rendered salt elsewhere means a flower, and many commentators read it here as wings: Moab would need wings to escape what is coming.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say natso is spelled with an aleph to obtain similarity of sound and means to flee. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists natso and tetse among his examples of paronomasia: may fly and flee away.
layers.text: The Hebrew pairs two verbs that sound alike, natso and tetse. Many read them as Moab fleeing and getting away, as if on wings, while others take them as "she will be laid waste" instead. Either way, one verb seems to be spelled to echo the sound of the other.

passages.saying: Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's three dangers and the chain of escapes spelled out in the next verse.
layers.text: The LORD warns the people of Moab that terror, a pit and a snare lie in wait for them. Whoever escapes one danger will only fall into the next, so there is no way out.

layers.evidence: Gill says the words seem to be taken from Isaiah 24:17, with what Isaiah said of the whole earth applied to Moab. Keil and Delitzsch say the wordplay and the way it is worked out are taken from Isaiah 24:17. Clarke and JFB refer readers to their notes on Isaiah 24:17-18.
layers.text: Jeremiah takes up Isaiah's warning to the whole world: "Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of the earth." Isaiah's next verse has the same chain of escapes. What Isaiah said of all the earth is here aimed at Moab in particular.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch name the play on pachad (fear), pachat (pit) and pach (spring-trap). The Companion Bible marks the same words in verse 44 as a paronomasia.
layers.text: The three dangers almost rhyme in Hebrew: pachad (terror), pachat (pit) and pach (snare). The next verse links them in a chain: whoever runs from the panic falls into the pit, and whoever climbs out is caught in the snare. Escaping one danger only leads into the next.

passages.saying: fire has gone forth from Heshbon and a flame from within Sihon
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of fugitives halting at Heshbon and a fire coming out of that same city.
layers.text: Moab's refugees stop in the shadow of Heshbon, too worn out to run any further, but they find no safety there. A fire of war breaks out from Heshbon itself and consumes Moab, down to its proud and noisy warriors.

layers.evidence: Clarke, JFB, Keil and Delitzsch, Gill, R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible all trace this verse to the old song in Numbers 21. Keil and Delitzsch call the words about fire going out from Heshbon a verbatim repetition of Numbers 21:28, and JFB and the Companion Bible tie verse 46 to Numbers 21:29.
layers.text: These lines echo an old song from Moses' day about Sihon of Heshbon conquering Moab: "For a fire went out from Heshbon, a blaze from the city of Sihon." The next verse repeats its cry, "Woe to you, O Moab!" What Moab suffered then will come on it again.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say these words were taken from Balaam's utterance about Moab in Numbers 24:17 with some changes. JFB says Jeremiah copies Balaam's prophecy with alterations, and the Companion Bible marks the line as a reference to Numbers 24:17.
layers.text: Balaam once foretold that a ruler rising from Israel would "crush the skulls of Moab" in days to come. Jeremiah gives those words to the fire, which "devours the foreheads of Moab and the skulls of the sons of tumult." Balaam's old word about Moab is coming true.

passages.saying: Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, which close the long prophecy against Moab in chapter 48.
layers.text: After a long run of judgments on Moab, God ends with mercy: in the latter days He will restore Moab from captivity. The verse then marks the end of the judgment on Moab.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Moab's conversion to the Christian faith must be the main end of this prophecy. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says gospel blessings to the Gentiles in the last days are intended. Gill sees it fulfilled when Moabites turned to the Gospel; the continuation of Poole's Annotations and Wesley read it of calling them into the Messiah's kingdom; Matthew Henry says it looks further, to gospel times.
layers.text: Many see the promise to restore Moab "in the latter days" reaching past any return from exile to the age of the Messiah, when the gospel goes out to the nations and Moab's people, too, are brought into God's kingdom.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible marks a paronomasia (a play on similar sounds) at bring again the captivity, and his Figures of Speech lists this verse among the passages where turn and captivity are two similar words. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, commenting on the same phrase at Jeremiah 29:14 (not on this verse), calls turn … captivity a play upon sounds, shabti … shebith.
layers.text: In Hebrew the promise to restore Moab from captivity reads ve-shavti shevut, two similar-sounding words placed side by side (shavti and shevut). Some see a deliberate sound play here, as wherever God promises to turn back a people's captivity.

passages.saying: Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the residents of Pekod
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in chapter 50, a prophecy against Babylon.
layers.text: God commands the army He has raised to attack Babylon, here called the land of Merathaim and the residents of Pekod, and to destroy it completely, doing all that He has commanded.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the prophet sums up Babylon's crimes and punishment in two names formed for the occasion. R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes), Clarke and the Companion Bible also give Merathaim as double rebellion; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible give Pekod as visitation, that is, punishment.
layers.text: Babylon is called by two names chosen for their meaning. Merathaim means double rebellion, and Pekod means visitation, in the sense of God coming to punish. Together they sum up her sin and her sentence: a land deeply rebellious against God, now due for His judgment.

passages.saying: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of Hosts is His name
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, set against Babylon's hold on captive Israel in the verse before.
layers.text: Israel's Redeemer is the mighty LORD of Hosts. He will take up His people's case like an advocate in court, bringing rest to the earth and turmoil to Babylon, their oppressor.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note a play on the similar sounds of the two Hebrew verbs to make the contrast more vivid; Keil and Delitzsch likewise say the two verbs, which have similar sounds, express a contrast.
layers.text: The Hebrew sets two similar-sounding verbs side by side: hirgia, to give rest, and hirgiz, to bring turmoil. The near rhyme sharpens the reversal. The earth that Babylon kept in unrest will now have rest, while Babylon itself will tremble.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) points out the triple repetition of the same word in the Hebrew and renders it literally as pleading He will plead their plea.
layers.text: The words “He will fervently plead their case” use the same Hebrew word three times: riv yariv et rivam, literally pleading He will plead their plea. The repetition may stress how fully the Lord, as Israel's Redeemer, will take up His people's cause.

passages.saying: I will stir up against Babylon and against the people of Leb-kamai
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, which continues the prophecy against Babylon from chapter 50.
layers.text: The LORD announces that He will stir up the spirit of a destroyer, a picture of an invading army, against Babylon and against the people of Leb-kamai.

layers.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) calls Leb-kamai the cipher for Kasdim, that is, Chaldea; the Companion Bible cites a Masoretic note calling it a cryptogram for the Chaldees; Gill reads it as a description of the Chaldeans, who rose up against God. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown grant the letters give Chaldeans but doubt the code was intended.
layers.text: Leb-kamai means the heart of those who rise against Me. It also works as a letter code: swap each Hebrew letter for its partner at the other end of the alphabet and it spells Kasdim, the Chaldeans. Read this way, the name both points to Babylon's people and brands them as rebels against God.

passages.saying: He has multiplied mourning and lamentation for the Daughter of Judah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words about the fall of Jerusalem and Judah's strongholds.
layers.text: The Lord, once Israel's protector, has acted like an enemy toward His own people. He has swallowed up their palaces and strongholds and filled Judah with mourning and grief.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note a play of similar sounds in the original to heighten the effect; Keil and Delitzsch say two forms from the same stem are joined for emphasis; the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech mark it as paronomasia.
layers.text: Mourning and lamentation in Hebrew are ta'aniyyah va'aniyyah, two words from the same root that sound almost alike, much like sorrow and sadness in English. The echoing pair makes the grief heavier.

passages.saying: All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words about passers-by mocking ruined Jerusalem.
layers.text: Travelers passing the ruined city clap, hiss and shake their heads at Jerusalem. They mock her as no longer the beautiful, joyful city she was once called.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the writer had Psalm 50:2 in mind and took the joy of the whole earth from Psalm 48 (verse 3 in Hebrew numbering); Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite both psalms and say the enemies quote Israel's very words in scorn; Gill points to Psalm 48:2.
layers.text: The mockers borrow Zion's own praises from the Psalms: “perfect in beauty” from Psalm 50:2 and “the joy of all the earth” from Psalm 48:2. Words once sung in her honor are now thrown back at her in scorn.

passages.saying: He has made me dwell in darkness like those dead for ages
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, part of the sufferer's lament in chapter 3.
layers.text: The sufferer says God has made him live in darkness, as if he were already in the grave among those long dead, cut off and forgotten.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the verse a verbatim reminiscence from Psalm 143:3; Barnes, commenting on Psalm 143:3, says the same Hebrew words are used in Lamentations 3:6.
layers.text: This line repeats, almost word for word, the prayer of Psalm 143:3, where the psalmist says the enemy has made him dwell in darkness like those long dead. The same four Hebrew words appear in both, so the sufferer voices his pain in an old prayer of distress.

passages.saying: Panic and pitfall have come upon us
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two pairs of words, terror and trap, ruin and breaking, describing Jerusalem's fall.
layers.text: The people cry that terror and a trap have overtaken them. Their land has been laid waste and their city broken.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the figure paronomasia on pachad vapachath and renders it scare and snare; Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse the same way.
layers.text: In Hebrew, panic and pitfall are pachad and pachat, two words that sound almost alike, much like scare and snare in English. The same sound pair is used in Isaiah 24:17 and Jeremiah 48:43.

passages.saying: They dropped me alive into a pit
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of being thrown alive into a pit, read as an attempt on the speaker's life.
layers.text: The speaker tells how his enemies threw him alive into a pit and cast stones on him, trying to end his life.

layers.evidence: Clarke says that from here to the chapter's end the prophet speaks of his own sufferings in the dungeon, citing Jeremiah 38:6; the Companion Bible compares Jeremiah 38:6. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch read it more broadly, of the sufferings of the captive people or of all the godly.
layers.text: These words can recall the day Jeremiah's enemies let him down into a cistern, where he sank in the mud. The Hebrew word bor (pit here, cistern there) is the same in both places. Some read the verse more broadly, as a picture of the suffering of God's people.

passages.saying: like that of a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words that this was only the appearance of the likeness of the LORD's glory.
layers.text: Ezekiel sees a brightness around the One on the throne like a rainbow in the clouds. It is only a likeness of the LORD's glory, yet he falls on his face in awe.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks it as a reference to Genesis 9:16; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the bow the symbol of God's covenant of mercy, as in Noah's day; Matthew Henry's Concise calls it the emblem of the covenant. Clarke and G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) also read it as the token of God's mercy.
layers.text: The rainbow around God's throne recalls the bow He set in the clouds after the Flood as the sign of His covenant. As Ezekiel is sent to announce judgment on Jerusalem, God's mercy and faithfulness to His promise still surround His throne.

passages.saying: I will make your face as hard as their faces
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's matching of the prophet's face and forehead with the people's.
layers.text: God warns Ezekiel that Israel will not listen, but promises to make him just as firm as they are stubborn, so that he will not be outfaced or afraid.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that Ezekiel means one strengthened by God and that he proved so in firmness against opposition; the Companion Bible gives the Hebrew hazak, strong or hard, and says to compare the name Ezekiel.
layers.text: Ezekiel's name means God strengthens. Here God makes his face and forehead hard (chazaq), from the same root as his name, so he can stand before a people whom verse 7 calls hard (chizqe) of forehead. The prophet lives up to his name.

passages.saying: The end has come! The end has come! It has roused itself against you.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's repeated cry that the end has come, announcing Judah's coming destruction.
layers.text: Ezekiel cries out again and again that the end has come for the land. The repetition stresses how near and certain the coming destruction is.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it a paronomasia, a play upon letters and words; Keil and Delitzsch say the verb for waking was suggested by its sound play with the end; the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech both list qets, haqqets and heqits as paronomasia.
layers.text: In Hebrew the end is qets, and the verb for roused itself is heqits, which sounds almost the same. The end is pictured as if it had been asleep and has now woken up to come against the people.

passages.saying: they were bowing to the east in worship of the sun
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of men turning their backs on the temple to bow toward the east.
layers.text: In the inner court of the temple, about twenty-five men turn their backs on the LORD's house and bow toward the rising sun. They worship the creation instead of the Creator.

layers.evidence: Gill says the word is compounded of to corrupt and to worship, showing they corrupted themselves and God's house, as the Targum also renders it; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says a corrupt form is used to express the corruption of such worship. Keil and Delitzsch instead take it as a copyist's error.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for bowing down here has an unusual form. Some read it as mixing in shachat, to corrupt, or as a form bent on purpose, as if their sun worship was itself corruption. Others think the odd spelling is simply a copyist's slip.

passages.saying: whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a weak wall coated with whitewash, applied to the false prophets' promises of peace.
layers.text: The false prophets led God's people astray by promising peace when judgment was coming. Like workers smearing whitewash on a flimsy wall, they made the people's empty hopes look solid instead of exposing them.

layers.evidence: G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) says the Hebrew word for the plaster plays upon the word rendered folly in Jeremiah 23:13. Keil and Delitzsch say tafel was chosen with an allusion to its figurative sense of something silly or absurd, citing Jeremiah 23:13 and Lamentations 2:14.
layers.text: The word for whitewash, tafel, sounds like tiflah, the word for the "offensive thing" (or folly) of Samaria's prophets in Jeremiah 23:13. Tafel itself can mean tasteless or foolish. So the prophets' coat of plaster pictures their foolish message.

passages.saying: saw a vision of peace for her when there was no peace
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, which names the plasterers of verses 10 to 15 as the false prophets.
layers.text: The ones who whitewashed the wall are the prophets of Israel who promised Jerusalem peace. They claimed visions of safety for the city, but no peace was coming, and God declares their work will fall.

layers.evidence: Gill sees here an allusion to the name of Jerusalem, which some take to mean they shall see peace. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes also mark peace as a reference to the meaning of the name Jerusalem.
layers.text: The name Jerusalem sounds like it holds the word shalom, peace, and some have read it as meaning they shall see peace. The verse likely plays on this: these prophets saw a vision of peace for the city whose very name was heard as peace, yet there was no peace for her.

passages.saying: So I spread My cloak over you and covered your nakedness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's marriage language; the commentaries take the covenant as the one made with Israel at Sinai.
layers.text: God pictures Israel as a young woman, grown but naked and alone. He took her as His own like a bridegroom, covered her shame, and bound Himself to her by an oath and a covenant, which He did with Israel at Mount Sinai.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley all explain spreading the skirt as the custom of espousal and point to Ruth 3:9; Gill and Keil and Delitzsch also refer to Ruth 3:9. Both verses use the same Hebrew pair, to spread and the corner of a garment.
layers.text: Spreading the corner of a garment over a woman was a way of taking her as wife. Ruth asked Boaz for exactly this, in the same Hebrew words. Here the LORD Himself does it for helpless Israel, covering her and making her His own in covenant.

passages.saying: the sacrifice of every firstborn in the fire
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse within God's review of Israel's rebellion in chapter 20.
layers.text: God says He let Israel defile themselves through their own offerings, above all by giving their firstborn children in the fire to idols. This came on them as a judgment, so that they would come to know that He is the LORD.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase points back to Exodus 13:12, with the words to the LORD left out because it describes a perversion of that law. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note the same expression there, and Gill says the same word is used.
layers.text: In Hebrew, the sacrifice of every firstborn reads literally as making every firstborn pass through. These are the words of the law in Exodus 13:12, where Israel was told to present to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb. Israel twisted that command and gave their firstborn to idols instead.

passages.saying: What is this high place to which you go?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse and the hilltop worship described in verse 28.
layers.text: God asks Israel what the high place is that they keep going to. These hilltop shrines were places of worship He had forbidden, yet the people kept using them and still called them by that name in Ezekiel's day.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a paronomasia here, used for emphasis and to contrast the idolatrous high place with Zion. Keil and Delitzsch reject the further idea that Ezekiel built the word bamah out of the words for go and what.
layers.text: In Hebrew, God's question begins mah habbamah. The word for what (mah) echoes the end of the word for high place (bamah). Read as a sound play, this gives the question extra force and sets these hilltop shrines against God's true holy mountain in verse 40.

layers.evidence: G. Currey (Barnes' Notes), Wesley and Gill all explain Bamah as the Hebrew word for high place. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) calls the name a brand of God's displeasure and a memorial of the people's guilt, and Clarke says it was so called to mark it with infamy.
layers.text: Bamah is simply the Hebrew word for a high place, a hilltop shrine. The name was still in use in Ezekiel's day, so the word itself stood as a reminder of worship God had condemned and Israel had never given up.

passages.saying: I will make you pass under the rod
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the shepherd picture in the verse and God's promise of judgment and renewal in verses 33 to 38.
layers.text: Like a shepherd counting his sheep, God will make His people pass under His rod, looking over each one. He will bring them into the bond of His covenant and separate out those who rebel against Him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all tie the phrase to Leviticus 27:32, and Clarke says it alludes to the custom of tithing the sheep. Both verses use the same Hebrew words for passing under the rod.
layers.text: Pass under the rod uses the same Hebrew words as the law of the tithe in Leviticus 27:32, where every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's rod is holy to the LORD. God will count His people one by one, as a shepherd counts his flock, and claim them as His own.

passages.saying: Should we rejoice in the scepter of My son?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse within the song of the sword in verses 8 to 17.
layers.text: This verse belongs to a song about the sword of the LORD, sharpened and polished for slaughter. It is no time for rejoicing, because the sword will show no respect even for Judah's royal scepter.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all take the scepter here as the scepter promised to Judah in Genesis 49:10. Keil and Delitzsch add that the clear echo of the same prophecy in verse 27 supports this.
layers.text: The scepter here is Judah's royal scepter, promised in Jacob's blessing: "The scepter will not depart from Judah." That promise would not shield Judah from this judgment. The sword of Babylon would treat its scepter like any common stick.

passages.saying: until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, spoken against the last king of Judah in verses 25 to 27.
layers.text: God will overturn the kingdom of Judah completely. The throne will not be restored until the coming of the One to whom the right to rule truly belongs, the Messiah, and God will give it to Him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the allusion to Genesis 49:10 generally acknowledged, while noting it explains the prophecy rather than the word Shiloh. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it strikingly parallel, the Companion Bible gives it as a reference to the Pentateuch, and Clarke points to the famous prophecy.
layers.text: The promise that the throne waits until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs echoes Jacob's blessing on Judah, where the scepter stays until Shiloh comes. Both verses use the same Hebrew words for until he comes, and both point to the Messiah, the rightful King from Judah.

passages.saying: I will hand you over to brutal men, skilled in destruction
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, part of the word against the Ammonites in verses 28 to 32.
layers.text: God tells the Ammonites He will pour out His anger on them and blow on them with the fire of His fury, like a smith at a furnace. He will hand them over to cruel men who are experts at destroying.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown renders the phrase artificers of destruction, alluding to Isaiah 54:16. Keil and Delitzsch call the allusion indisputable, say it alone explains why the two words are joined, and read God's blowing on the fire in the same verse in the light of Isaiah 54:16.
layers.text: Skilled in destruction is literally craftsmen of destruction. It joins two words found together in Isaiah 54:16, where God says He created the craftsman who fans the coals into flame and also the destroyer. Here God hands Ammon over to such destroyers.

passages.saying: Among you are slanderous men bent on bloodshed
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse within the list of Jerusalem's sins in verses 6 to 12.
layers.text: God charges Jerusalem with harboring slanderers whose lies lead to the death of the innocent, people who feast at idol shrines on the mountains, and people who commit shameful sexual sins.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the charge of slander points back to the ban in Leviticus 19:16; the Companion Bible and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown give the same reference. Both verses pair the Hebrew words for slander and blood.
layers.text: This charge echoes the law in Leviticus 19:16, which uses the same Hebrew words for slander and blood (blood is rendered life there): "You must not go about spreading slander among your people. You must not endanger the life of your neighbor." Jerusalem was breaking that very command.

passages.saying: stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse after the charges against Jerusalem's leaders and people in verses 25 to 29.
layers.text: God looked for someone in the land who would repair the broken wall and stand before Him to plead for the people, so that He would not have to destroy the land. He found no one.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the gap to Psalm 106:23, Gill points to Moses praying that God would not destroy Israel and cites the same psalm, and G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) recalls Moses standing in the gap. Both verses use the Hebrew for standing in the breach.
layers.text: Stand in the gap uses the same Hebrew words as Psalm 106:23, which recalls how Moses stood before Him in the breach to turn God's wrath away from destroying Israel. God looked for someone like that in the land, but found no one.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Abraham's plea for Sodom was in Ezekiel's mind and that the closing words of the verse allude to Genesis 18:28. Gill also compares the missing intercessor with Abraham pleading for Sodom.
layers.text: The closing words also recall Abraham pleading for Sodom. There God said, "If I find forty-five there, I will not destroy it." Ezekiel uses the same Hebrew words for find and destroy, but this time God found no one to plead for the land.

passages.saying: Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own explanation of the two sisters in the parable of chapter 23.
layers.text: In this parable God pictures His people as two sisters whom He took as His own. The older, Oholah, stands for Samaria, the northern kingdom of Israel. The younger, Oholibah, stands for Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, G. Currey (Barnes' Notes), Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Clarke, Wesley, Matthew Henry and Bullinger all explain the names this way, from the Hebrew ohel, tent, with the tent standing for the sanctuary.
layers.text: Oholah means her tent, and Oholibah means my tent is in her. The tent stands for a place of worship. Samaria set up shrines of its own making, while Jerusalem had the temple where God Himself chose to dwell. That made Jerusalem's unfaithfulness all the worse.

passages.saying: the desire of your eyes, and the delight of your soul
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, which explains the sign of Ezekiel's wife's death in verses 15 to 24.
layers.text: God tells Israel He is about to let His own temple be desecrated, the sanctuary they took pride in and loved most. The sons and daughters they had left behind in Judah would also die by the sword.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties the desire of your eyes here to Ezekiel's wife in verse 16, Wesley says the temple was as much their desire as his wife was his, and Gill calls her its emblem. The same Hebrew phrase is used in both verses.
layers.text: The desire of your eyes repeats the very words God used for Ezekiel's wife in verse 16. Her sudden death, which he was told not to mourn openly, was a sign: the temple, just as dear to the people, would be taken from them too.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase is taken from Leviticus 26:19 and explain that Israel based its strength on the temple. The Companion Bible, on Leviticus 26:19, notes the same phrase in this verse.
layers.text: The pride of your power is the same Hebrew phrase as in the law's warning in Leviticus 26:19, where God said to a rebellious Israel, "I will break down your stubborn pride." Ezekiel likely borrows it: Israel trusted in the temple as its strength, and now God was about to break that pride.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under paronomasia, or rhyming words, and imitates the rhyme in English as your eyes' admiration and your soul's commiseration.
layers.text: In Hebrew, the desire of your eyes (machmad) and the delight of your soul (machmal) are rhyming words that differ by a single sound. Some hear the matching sounds as underlining how deeply the people loved the temple that God was about to desecrate.

passages.saying: I will cut off the Cherethites
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on verse 15, which gives the Philistines' revenge and old hostility toward Israel as the reason.
layers.text: God announces judgment on the Philistines for their long hatred of Israel. He will stretch out His hand against them, cut off the Cherethites, a Philistine people of the southern coast, and destroy the rest of those living along the sea.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it a beautiful play on words in the Hebrew; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives hichratti cherethim; Keil and Delitzsch say Ezekiel, like Zephaniah 2:5, used this name for the sake of the paronomasia; the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech list it as paronomasia.
layers.text: In Hebrew, I will cut off is hikhratti, and the Cherethites are the Kerethim. The people's name sounds like the very verb of their doom, so God's sentence echoes their own name: the Kerethim will be cut off.

passages.saying: You were in Eden, the garden of God.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse within the lament of verses 11 to 19, which describes the king's splendor to show how great his fall would be.
layers.text: In a lament over the king of Tyre, God pictures his former glory as if he had lived in Eden, the garden of God, clothed in every kind of precious stone set in gold, all made ready on the day he was created.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Ezekiel compares the prince of Tyre with the first man in Paradise and his fall with Adam's; G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) says he is like Adam in paradise and like Adam in his fall; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown speaks of images drawn from the first man in Eden. Clarke and Gill also compare him to Adam.
layers.text: This looks back to Genesis, where God planted a garden in Eden and put the first man there (Genesis 2:8). The king is pictured like Adam: placed in paradise, blameless at first, then cast out when wickedness was found in him.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible holds that the one in Eden here can only be Satan, the serpent of Genesis 3, since he is said to be created, not born of woman.
layers.text: Some Bible teachers see more than a human king here. Because this one is said to have been created and to have been in Eden, they take it as a look behind the king of Tyre at Satan, who was in the garden as the serpent (Genesis 3:1).

passages.saying: The young men of On and Pi-beseth will fall by the sword
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on the identification of On with Heliopolis and Pi-beseth with Bubastis.
layers.text: Ezekiel foretells that the young men of On and Pi-beseth, two cities of Egypt, will die in battle, and the people of those cities will be carried off as captives.

layers.evidence: Gill says it is called Aven, or vanity, because of its idolatrous worship; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the name was changed slightly to mean vanity or iniquity in allusion to its idolatry; Keil and Delitzsch say the form was probably chosen on purpose to mark an idol-city. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) mentions the view too.
layers.text: On was the great city of sun worship where Joseph's father-in-law served as priest (Genesis 41:45). Here the Hebrew spells its name Aven, a word meaning wickedness or emptiness, a scornful twist that brands it a city of idols.

passages.saying: the envy of all the trees of Eden
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the parable of the cedar in verses 3 to 18, where the tree stands for Assyria and its fall is a warning to Pharaoh.
layers.text: In a parable for Pharaoh, Assyria is pictured as a great cedar. God says He made it beautiful with many branches, so splendid that all the trees in the garden of God envied it. Its glory came from God, though it would later be cut down.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the garden of God here is the garden of Paradise and that Eden in this chapter is Paradise, as in 28:13; the Companion Bible marks Eden here as a reference to Genesis 2.
layers.text: The trees of Eden in the garden of God point back to the garden God planted in Eden at creation (Genesis 2:8). Ezekiel measures Assyria's glory against paradise itself: even the trees of God's own garden envied this cedar, yet foreigners would cut it down.

passages.saying: like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on verse 31, which says the people hear the prophet's words but do not put them into practice.
layers.text: God tells Ezekiel that the people treat his preaching like entertainment. They enjoy listening the way they would enjoy a fine singer of love songs with a skilled instrument, but they do not do what he says.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a paronomasia between agabim here, which it reads as a song for the pipes, and the lovers (agabim) of verse 31; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown renders the two literally as making love and a song of loves.
layers.text: The same Hebrew word, agavim, appears in this verse and the one before. In verse 31 the people express love (agavim) with their mouths; here the prophet is to them like a song of agavim, a love song. Some see the word for their empty love returning to describe how they hear him: as a pleasant song.

passages.saying: I will make with them a covenant of peace
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of peace and safety from wild beasts, as Gill explains.
layers.text: God promises to make a covenant of peace with His flock under the shepherd He will raise up. He will remove the wild animals that threatened them, so they can live safely even in the wilderness and sleep in the forest.

layers.evidence: Both verses say God will make evil beasts cease from the land, with the same Hebrew words. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this the original promise of the law in Leviticus 26:6; Keil and Delitzsch say Leviticus 26:4-6 is the passage Ezekiel had in mind, with its rain and harvest too.
layers.text: God's promise to rid the land of wild animals repeats, almost word for word, the covenant blessing of Leviticus 26:6, and the rain and fruitful trees that follow echo Leviticus 26:4. Under the coming Shepherd, the blessings promised in the law will be given in full.

passages.saying: I will give you over to bloodshed and it will pursue you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verse 5 and this verse; Wesley explains that Edom loved bloodshed, so vengeance follows it.
layers.text: Edom had handed Israel over to the sword in its time of disaster. Because Edom did not hate bloodshed, God swears that bloodshed will now pursue Edom itself. What it did to others will be done to it.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes a play on similar sounds, Edom and dam (blood), since Edom means red. Keil and Delitzsch say the wording was probably chosen for the play on dam and Edom, so that Edom becomes what its name suggests.
layers.text: In Hebrew, blood is dam, which sounds like Edom, a name meaning red. Because Edom loved bloodshed, God says He will turn it over to blood and blood will pursue it. Edom will become what its own name suggests.

passages.saying: This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on this verse and 36:34; Gill takes the speakers to be travellers who saw the land before and after.
layers.text: When God restores Israel, people passing by will say that the land once left in ruins has become like the garden of Eden, and that its broken cities are rebuilt, fortified and full of people.

layers.evidence: The verse uses the same two words, gan (garden) and Eden, as Genesis 2:8, where God planted a garden in Eden. Gill explains the likeness as delight and fruitfulness; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links it with Isaiah 51:3; Keil and Delitzsch say the waste land is to become a paradise.
layers.text: The garden of Eden is the garden God planted at creation (Genesis 2:8). Ezekiel promises that the land laid waste by judgment will become like that first paradise again, so fruitful and lovely that everyone can see it is God's work.

passages.saying: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 37:8-10; Gill notes the bones had been formed into bodies but breath was still lacking.
layers.text: In the valley of dry bones, the bodies have come together but have no breath. God tells Ezekiel to prophesy to the breath and call it from every direction to enter the dead so that they may live.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the command to breathe into these slain points back to Genesis 2:7, and that the two steps, bodies first and then breath, follow the creation of man in Genesis 2. Both verses use the verb naphach, to breathe.
layers.text: The call to breathe into the slain recalls creation, when God first formed Adam's body and then "breathed the breath of life into his nostrils" (Genesis 2:7). Both use the same verb for breathing. Raising Israel from death is pictured as a new creation.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that the same word is used for wind, breath and spirit, and may be applied to the Spirit of God. Clarke says ruach here carries both its main meanings, wind or breath and soul, so the line can read breath from the four breaths or wind from the four winds.
layers.text: The Hebrew word ruach can mean breath, wind or spirit, and the vision plays on all three. Ezekiel speaks to the breath, calls it from the four winds, and God then promises, "I will put My Spirit in you" (37:14). Wind and breath can picture the life-giving work of God's Spirit.

passages.saying: After a long time you will be summoned.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) explains that God is drawing Gog on toward his ruin.
layers.text: God tells Gog that after a long time he will be called up. In the latter years he will invade a land whose people were gathered back from many nations to the mountains of Israel and now live securely.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reads the verb as visited in wrath and sees a probable allusion to Isaiah 24:21-22. Keil and Delitzsch say the first clause recalls Isaiah 24:22 so strongly that the echo cannot be mistaken, and take it as a visit of punishment.
layers.text: "After a long time you will be summoned" echoes Isaiah 24:22, where hostile powers are shut up and "punished after many days." Both speak of many days and use the verb paqad, to call up or to visit in judgment. The echo hints that Gog is being called up for his own punishment.

passages.saying: So it will be called the Valley of Hamon-gog.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that Gog found a grave where he expected plunder.
layers.text: Gog came to seize Israel's land, but God gives him only a grave there. Gog and his whole army will be buried in a valley east of the Sea, the graves will block the travelers' way, and the valley will be renamed after them.

layers.evidence: G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) calls Ezekiel 39:11-15 a play upon words on passengers, with the triple sense of passing in to invade, passing by and passing through. Keil and Delitzsch, by contrast, deny that the valley takes its name from the searchers of verse 15.
layers.text: The Hebrew verb for passing (avar) keeps returning. The grave lies in the Valley of the Travelers, it blocks those who travel through, and men later pass through the land searching for bones (39:15). Some see a play here: invaders who passed into the land are buried where others pass by.

layers.evidence: The verse says Gog and all his hordes (hamon) are buried there, then names the valley Hamon-gog. Gill says hamon means a multitude and the name will keep the memory alive; Wesley explains it as the multitude of Gog; Keil and Delitzsch say the valley is named from Gog's multitude buried there.
layers.text: Hamon means multitude or horde. Because Gog and all his hordes (hamon) are buried there, the valley is renamed Hamon-gog, the horde of Gog. The new name stands as a lasting memorial of the army God destroyed.

passages.saying: Even the city will be named Hamonah.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 39:12-16; Gill explains the cleansing as burying every remaining bone.
layers.text: A city near the burial valley will also be named Hamonah. By burying every last body of the fallen invaders, Israel will cleanse the land.

layers.evidence: Hamonah comes from hamon, the word for Gog's hordes in 39:11. Gill says the name signifies a multitude, taken from the burial nearby; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it commemorates the overthrow of the enemy's multitudes; Keil and Delitzsch render it multitude or tumult.
layers.text: Hamonah means multitude. It comes from the same word as the hordes (hamon) of Gog buried in the Valley of Hamon-gog (39:11), so the city's very name will remind people of the vast army God overthrew.

passages.saying: I saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 47:1-5; Clarke traces the water's course from the threshold past the altar.
layers.text: Ezekiel is brought back to the temple entrance and sees water flowing out from under the threshold toward the east, running down the temple's south side, south of the altar. In the verses that follow it grows into a deep river that brings life.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown pairs this water with Revelation 22:1; Clarke says John had this chapter in view when he described the paradise of God in Revelation 22; G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) says Ezekiel's description is taken up in Revelation. Gill also notes that Revelation 22:1 agrees.
layers.text: Ezekiel's river flowing out from God's house is taken up at the close of the Bible, where John is shown "a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb". Both show life pouring out from where God dwells.

passages.saying: the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse gives the city's measure and the new name it will bear.
layers.text: Ezekiel's vision of the restored land ends with the city. Its perimeter is 18,000 cubits, and from that day on the city will be named for the LORD's presence in it.

layers.evidence: Gill, the Companion Bible, Clarke, G. Currey (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley all give the name as Jehovah Shammah, the LORD is there. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) adds that the glory which had departed from the temple is received again in Ezekiel's vision.
layers.text: The city's new name in Hebrew is Yahweh Shammah, which means the LORD is there. Ezekiel had watched God's glory leave the temple (Ezekiel 10), but his book closes with a city whose very name says that the LORD dwells in it.

passages.saying: He carried these off to the land of Shinar
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says who gave the victory and where the temple articles were taken.
layers.text: The Lord handed King Jehoiakim of Judah over to Nebuchadnezzar. The king of Babylon took some of the articles from God's temple and put them in the treasury of his own god in Babylonia.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible calls the land of Shinar a reference to the Pentateuch, citing Genesis 11:2. Gill notes that Shinar is where the tower of Babel was built and that an idol's temple now stood in the same place. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke call Shinar the old name of Babylon.
layers.text: Daniel uses the old name for Babylonia, the land of Shinar. That name takes the reader back to Genesis, where people settled in Shinar and built the tower of Babel. Now the articles from God's house are placed in an idol's temple in that same land.

passages.saying: The chief official gave them new names
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse lists each young man's new name.
layers.text: The official in charge gave the four young men from Judah new names. Daniel became Belteshazzar, Hananiah became Shadrach, Mishael became Meshach, and Azariah became Abednego.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Matthew Henry note that the Hebrew names held the name of God, and they, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley say the new names pointed to Babylon's idols. Clarke, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown give the meanings of the Hebrew names.
layers.text: Each Hebrew name honored Israel's God: Daniel means God is my judge, Hananiah the LORD has been gracious, Mishael who is like God, and Azariah the LORD helps. The new names drop God's name, and some honor Babylon's gods, such as Belteshazzar after Bel and Abednego, servant of Nego.

passages.saying: whose name is Belteshazzar after the name of my god
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse tells how Daniel came in after the other wise men had failed.
layers.text: When Babylon's wise men could not explain his dream, Nebuchadnezzar at last told it to Daniel. The king describes Daniel as a man with the spirit of the holy gods in him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch all say the god meant is Bel, whose name is built into Belteshazzar. Keil and Delitzsch add that the king meant Daniel had been brought into fellowship with Bel. Gill notes that Daniel's God was the one glorified.
layers.text: The king himself explains Daniel's court name: Belteshazzar was given after the name of his god, Bel, the chief god of Babylon. The name was meant to tie Daniel to Bel, yet it is Daniel's God who is made known and glorified through him.

passages.saying: this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse gives the four words written on the wall.
layers.text: Daniel reads out the words the hand wrote on the palace wall: mene, mene, tekel, parsin. They mean numbered, weighed and divided, and in the next verses he explains them as God's verdict on the king.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say all three words carry a double sense that Daniel's reading brings out, and that tekel, to weigh, matches a verb meaning to be light. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists mene with menah, numbered, among its rhyming words (paronomasia).
layers.text: Daniel draws a double sense out of the words. Mene, numbered, becomes menah: God has numbered the days of the reign and ended it. Tekel, weighed, also sounds like a word for being light, so the king is weighed and found too light.

passages.saying: PERES means that your kingdom has been divided
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse gives the meaning of the last word on the wall.
layers.text: Peres means that Belshazzar's kingdom has been broken apart and handed over to the Medes and Persians. That same night the king was killed and Darius the Mede received the kingdom.

layers.evidence: Gill calls Peres and Persians an elegant play on words, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Peres alludes to Persia, and Wesley says the word means both broken off and Persian. Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible also see a reference to the Persians in it.
layers.text: Peres means divided, and the same letters, read as paras, name Persia. So one word gives both the sentence and those who carry it out: the kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.

passages.saying: the Ancient of Days took His seat
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse describes God taking His seat to judge.
layers.text: In Daniel's vision, thrones are set in place and God, the Ancient of Days, sits down to judge. His clothing is white as snow, His hair like pure wool, and His throne blazes with fire on burning wheels.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible links the throne's wheels to Ezekiel 1:15-20, 1:26-28 and 10:9-13, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Ezekiel 1:15-16. Keil and Delitzsch say the LORD appeared in human form on Ezekiel's throne, as in Daniel 7:9.
layers.text: Some see an echo of Ezekiel's first vision in this blazing throne on wheels. There the LORD's throne rose above the living creatures and their wheels, fire shone all around, and the One seated on it looked like a man. Daniel too sees God in a form like a man, on a throne of fire.

passages.saying: I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea, explained as "four kings who will arise from the earth." Then the Ancient of Days takes His throne, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds and is given an everlasting kingdom.

layers.evidence: TBESH: bar, son; enash, man, human being. Keil and Delitzsch: like a man, not a beast; clouds are the chariot on which God comes to judge (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1).
layers.text: In Aramaic "son of man" is bar enash, simply a human being. After the beasts comes a human figure, yet he arrives with "the clouds of heaven," and in Scripture clouds carry God Himself: "the LORD rides on a swift cloud." Human, and coming as God comes.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott on Daniel 7:14: in biblical Aramaic pelach is used only of the service and homage due to God. All 10 biblical uses are religious, though later Aramaic (Targum Onkelos) also uses it of farm work. Barnes on Daniel 7:14 compares Matthew 28:18.
layers.text: He is given a kingdom so "that the people of every nation and language should serve Him." The Bible uses this verb, pelach, only for religious service, as in "the God whom we serve." Jesus' last words echo the scene: all authority "has been given to Me."

layers.evidence: Gill on Mark 14:62, and Benson and Keil and Delitzsch on Daniel 7:13, tie Jesus' answer to this verse; His words also echo Psalm 110:1.
layers.text: Asked at His trial if He is the Christ, Jesus answers "I am," joining this verse to Psalm 110: "you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven." The high priest tears his clothes and cries blasphemy.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: the Son of Man occurs 80 times in the Gospels (NA28). TAHOT: ben adam occurs 94 times in Ezekiel; Ellicott: above ninety times. Matthew Henry's Concise: Christ usually called Himself the Son of man. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: the title implies His lowliness and His exaltation.
layers.text: Son of Man was Jesus' favorite name for Himself, used about 80 times in the Gospels. It could sound humble: God calls Ezekiel "son of man" more than 90 times. But Jesus used it with authority: "the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch report some who read the figure as the people of Israel. Gill: the Messiah, as most Christian interpreters allow.
layers.text: The angel's explanation shares the kingdom: "the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom." Some medieval Jewish and modern commentators read the figure as Israel; most Christian interpreters see the Messiah, who shares His kingdom with His people.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and the continuation of Poole's Annotations on Revelation 1:14: the description matches the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9.
layers.text: John sees "One like the Son of Man" whose hair is "white like wool, as white as snow," as Daniel described the Ancient of Days. The one who came to the throne shares the look of the One on it. And "He is coming with the clouds."

passages.saying: the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which names Jeremiah's prophecy and its seventy years.
layers.text: In the first year of Darius, Daniel studied the sacred scrolls and learned from God's word through Jeremiah that Jerusalem would lie in ruins for seventy years. Those years were nearly over.

layers.evidence: Barnes quotes Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10 as the prophecy Daniel read; JFB points to the same two passages; Gill notes Daniel uses Jeremiah's very word for the desolations. Clarke and the Companion Bible also cite Jeremiah 25 and 29, and Matthew Henry names Jeremiah.
layers.text: Daniel is reading Jeremiah's prophecy that the land would lie desolate while the nations served Babylon for seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10). He even uses Jeremiah's word for the ruins. Seeing the seventy years almost complete, he turns God's promise into prayer.

passages.saying: Ships of Kittim will come against him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, JFB and Keil and Delitzsch all link the verse to the Roman embassy that turned Antiochus IV back from Egypt.
layers.text: Ships from the west would stop the king of the north, and he would lose heart. Turning back, he would vent his rage on the holy covenant and favor those who abandoned it. Many Bible teachers see this fulfilled when Roman envoys forced Antiochus Epiphanes out of Egypt.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the expression is derived from Numbers 24:24; the Companion Bible marks the phrase as a reference to the Pentateuch at Numbers 24:24. The same Hebrew words for ships and Kittim stand in both verses.
layers.text: Daniel's ships of Kittim echo Balaam's last oracle, where ships come from Kittim, that is Cyprus, to subdue Asshur and Eber (Numbers 24:24). The same Hebrew words for ships and Kittim stand in both verses, here for the western ships that turn this proud king back.

passages.saying: I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own explanation of the name; Wesley, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Gill read it of Jehu's line losing the throne.
layers.text: God tells Hosea to name his first son Jezreel, because He will soon punish Jehu's royal line for the blood it shed at Jezreel and bring the kingdom of Israel to an end.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the blood can only be Jehu's deeds recorded in 2 Kings 9 and 10; JFB and the Companion Bible list those chapters, including 2 Kings 10:11; Gill and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) describe the same slaughter. Clarke reads it more broadly of Jehu's cruelties at Jezreel.
layers.text: The bloodshed of Jezreel points back to Jehu's purge in 2 Kings 9 and 10, when he killed Ahab's family and friends at Jezreel. God had ordered that judgment, but Jehu acted for his own ends and kept Jeroboam's idols, so the guilt now falls on his own house.

layers.evidence: Gill says the name signifies God will sow or scatter; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and JFB give God will scatter, Clarke God will disperse, Matthew Henry dispersion; the Companion Bible gives both senses and points to Hosea 2:22-23. Keil and Delitzsch hold the sowing sense is taken up only in Hosea 2.
layers.text: Jezreel means God sows. Sowing scatters seed, so the boy's name warned that God would scatter Israel among the nations. Later Hosea turns the same name into hope, when God promises to sow His people again in their land (Hosea 2:22-23).

passages.saying: I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Wesley, Keil and Delitzsch, JFB and the Companion Bible take the bow as Israel's military strength.
layers.text: When judgment comes, God will break Israel's bow, that is, its military power, in the Valley of Jezreel, the great battlefield of the land.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the paronomasia between Israel and Jezreel unmistakable in this verse; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Jezreel resembles Israel in form and sound and reverses the promise in Israel's name.
layers.text: In Hebrew, Israel (Yisra'el) and Jezreel (Yizre'el) sound almost alike. The nation named Israel would be broken in the valley named Jezreel, so the place of its defeat would echo its own name and reverse the promise that name once carried.

passages.saying: Name her Lo-ruhamah, for I will no longer have compassion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own explanation of the name; Clarke, Gill and JFB read it of the coming end of the northern kingdom.
layers.text: Gomer bears a daughter, and God tells Hosea to name her Lo-ruhamah, because He will no longer show compassion to the house of Israel or forgive them.

layers.evidence: Gill says the name signifies she has not obtained mercy and the next words explain it; Clarke gives not having obtained mercy; the Companion Bible gives not compassionated. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible note how Paul (Romans 9:25) and Peter (1 Peter 2:10) render it; JFB and Matthew Henry agree.
layers.text: Lo-ruhamah means not pitied, or shown no compassion. God explains the name at once with a verb from the same Hebrew root (racham): He will no longer have compassion on Israel. Paul and Peter later take up the name for people once without mercy who now receive it.

passages.saying: Name him Lo-ammi, for you are not My people
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own explanation of the name; Keil and Delitzsch, Gill and Wesley read it as God disowning the northern tribes.
layers.text: God names Gomer's third child Lo-ammi, declaring that Israel is no longer His people and He is no longer their God.

layers.evidence: Clarke says God probably refers to Exodus 3:14 and paraphrases, I will not be your eheyeh; the Companion Bible renders the clause, I am not I am to you. Both rest on the verb ehyeh, used in Hosea 1:9 and in Exodus 3:14.
layers.text: The last words read literally, I will not be to you. The verb is ehyeh, the word God used for His own name, I AM, when He spoke to Moses at the burning bush. So the sentence can be heard as God saying He will no longer be I AM for them.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Clarke and Wesley all render Lo-ammi as not my people; Clarke notes that the reason follows at once, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) calls this name the last degree of chastisement. JFB, Matthew Henry, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible agree.
layers.text: Lo-ammi means not my people (lo, not; ammi, my people). God explains it in the same breath with the very words of the name. It is the heaviest of the three names, because it speaks of the covenant bond itself being broken.

passages.saying: like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of a countless Israel and a new name, as Clarke explains.
layers.text: Though God had just said Israel was not His people, He promises that their number will still be beyond counting, like the sand of the sea. In the very place where they were disowned, they will be called sons of the living God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note the almost verbal agreement with the promises in Genesis 22:17 and 32:12; the Companion Bible marks a reference to both; Gill ties it to the promise made to Abraham, and Clarke and JFB cite Genesis 32:12. The Hebrew for sand of the sea that cannot be counted matches Genesis 32:12.
layers.text: God promised Abraham and Jacob descendants like the sand of the sea, too many to count (Genesis 22:17; 32:12). Hosea repeats that promise almost word for word right after the sentence of judgment, showing that the judgment does not cancel what God swore to the fathers.

passages.saying: For great will be the day of Jezreel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a reunited people coming home, as Wesley explains.
layers.text: The people of Judah and Israel, long divided into two kingdoms, will be gathered together under one leader and come up out of the land where they were scattered. That day of Jezreel will be great.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say both clauses recall the twelve tribes leaving Egypt and that the phrase going up out of the land is borrowed from Exodus 1:10. The same Hebrew words for go up and the land stand in both verses.
layers.text: The words "will go up out of the land" use the same Hebrew phrase Pharaoh used when he feared Israel would leave the country (Exodus 1:10). Some see the return of the reunited people under one leader pictured here as a new exodus.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the prophet alludes to the meaning of the name, the seed of God, whom God had sown among the nations; JFB says Jezreel here means God will sow, not God will scatter as in 1:4; the Companion Bible and Wesley agree. Keil and Delitzsch think the sense is only lightly hinted at here.
layers.text: Jezreel means God sows. In 1:4 the name recalled bloodshed and the judgment that would scatter Israel like seed. Here it turns to its good sense: the God who scattered His people will sow them again in their own land, and that day will be great.

passages.saying: Say of your brothers, ‘My people,’ and of your sisters, ‘My loved one.’
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to use the new names once the promise of 1:10-11 comes true, as JFB explains.
layers.text: When the restoration promised in 1:10-11 comes, God's people are to speak to one another as His family, calling their brothers My people and their sisters My loved one.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the names of ill omen are changed into their opposite by leaving out the Hebrew word for not. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) gives Ammi as my people and Ruhamah as tenderly pitied; the Companion Bible gives Pitied One; Gill and Clarke read the names the same way.
layers.text: Hosea's children had been named Lo-ammi, Not My People, and Lo-ruhamah, No Compassion (1:6, 9). Here the names are reversed by dropping lo, the Hebrew word for not. Ammi means My people, and Ruhamah, given here as My loved one, means she is shown compassion.

passages.saying: make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise that God will restore what Israel lost, as JFB explains.
layers.text: After leading Israel through the wilderness, God will give back her vineyards and turn the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope. Israel will respond to Him as she did in her youth, when He brought her out of Egypt.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch see an evident allusion to Joshua 7, from which the valley got its name; Gill says it was named from Achan, who was stoned there in Joshua's day; the Companion Bible refers to Joshua 7:26. JFB and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) draw the same link.
layers.text: The Valley of Achor is where Achan was stoned for taking what was devoted to God, just as Israel entered Canaan (Joshua 7:24-26). Once that sin was judged, God gave Israel victory. In the same way God will turn His people's trouble into an opening of hope.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to the song Israel sang at the Red Sea and cites Exodus 15:1; JFB calls it a second exodus song; Keil and Delitzsch say Israel then answered the Lord with the song at the Red Sea. The Companion Bible and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) also point to Exodus 15.
layers.text: The words "as in the day she came up out of Egypt" point back to the exodus, when Israel answered God's rescue with the song at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:1). Restored Israel will again respond to her Redeemer with grateful praise.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) gives the name as literally troubling and JFB as trouble, adding that trouble and hope are rightly blended here; the Companion Bible gives Achor as trouble and hope as an expectation no longer of trouble. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch give the same meaning.
layers.text: Achor means trouble. God promises to turn the Valley of Trouble into a gateway of hope, so the place whose very name meant trouble becomes the way into new blessing.

passages.saying: you will call Me ‘my Husband,’ and no longer call Me ‘my Master.’
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the chapter's picture of God as Israel's husband, as Wesley explains.
layers.text: When God restores His people, Israel will call Him my Husband and no longer my Master. She will own Him in love as her true husband.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Baali, good in itself, became unfit for the LORD after being given to false gods; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says God refuses the title because of its likeness to Baal; JFB says the word had been perverted to name the images of Baal. Gill also calls it an ambiguous word used for the idol.
layers.text: In Hebrew she will call God Ishi, my husband, and no longer Baali, my master. Baal was an ordinary word for a husband or lord, but it was also the name of the idol Baal. So God sets aside even a proper title that would bring the idol to mind.

passages.saying: I will remove from her lips the names of the Baals
