passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the promise that God Himself will remove the idols' names, as E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains.
layers.text: God Himself will take the names of the Baals off Israel's lips, so the idols are no longer called on or even remembered. The end of her idolatry will be His own work of grace.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say this promise rests on the command in Exodus 23:13; Gill sees a reference to that law; the Companion Bible marks it as a reference to Exodus 23:13. Both verses use the Hebrew words for name, mouth and mention.
layers.text: The law said, "You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips" (Exodus 23:13). Israel broke that command, but here God promises to make it true in her: He will remove the Baals' names from her lips.

passages.saying: and they will respond to Jezreel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of nature answering God's people, as JFB explains.
layers.text: In a chain of answers, the earth will bring forth grain, new wine and oil, and these will answer Jezreel, God's restored people. God will supply what His people need.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch read Jezreel here as the nation which God sows, as 2:23 explains; Gill says the name now means the seed of God, confirmed by the words I will sow her; the Companion Bible gives the seed of God as stated in 2:23; JFB says the sense is God will plant, not God will scatter.
layers.text: The chain of answers ends with Jezreel, a name meaning God sows. The next words explain it: "I will sow her as My own in the land" (2:23). The people once scattered in judgment are now God's own planting, and the harvest flows to them.

passages.saying: I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people,’ and they will say, ‘You are my God.’
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: God tells Hosea to marry an unfaithful wife, a living picture of Israel "departing from the LORD," and later to love her again, "as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods." Their children's names carry God's message.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Ellicott on Hosea 1:4: the massacre of Ahab's family by Jehu. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and Ellicott: Jezreel sounds like Israel. TBESH: Lo-ruhamah, no mercy; Lo-ammi, not my people.
layers.text: Each name is a sermon. Jezreel, which sounds like "Israel," recalls Jehu's massacre of Ahab's family there: "I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu." Lo-ruhamah means "no mercy," and Lo-ammi "not my people": "you are not My people."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Hosea 1:9: the Hebrew reads lo' 'ehyeh lakhem, I will not be yours; an allusion to Exodus 3:12, 14 and in effect a negation of it. The Reformation Study Bible: literally "I am not 'I am' to you," a reference to the divine name of Exodus 3:14. TAHOT: all three are H1961.
layers.text: Literally, 1:9 ends with God saying He will not be (ehyeh) theirs. Ehyeh is the word God spoke at the burning bush: "I will surely be with you" and "I AM WHO I AM." Hosea's line turns that promise around.

layers.evidence: TBESH H3157: Jezreel, God sows. Ellicott on Hosea 1:4: Jezreel means God shall sow; on 2:21-23, the name is to represent a Divine seed. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes): God changes the name's meaning to God shall sow. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: no longer God will scatter but God will plant. Benson: the word sow alludes to and explains Jezreel. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way.
layers.text: Then God turns the names inside out. Jezreel means "God sows," so the name of judgment becomes a harvest: the grain, wine and oil "will respond to Jezreel," and God says, "I will sow her as My own in the land." The God who scattered now plants.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: salvation is announced by simply turning the names into their opposites, dropping the lo (not). TAHOT: ammi (H5971) and ruhamah (H7355) in 2:1 and 2:23.
layers.text: The other two names simply lose their "not": "Say of your brothers, ‘My people,’ and of your sisters, ‘My loved one,’" in Hebrew ammi and ruhamah. Where they were told "You are not My people," "they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’"

layers.evidence: TBESH H5911: Achor, the valley of trouble where Achan was stoned; H5916 akhar, to trouble. The Pulpit Commentary on Joshua 7:25: Joshua uses akhar for both Achan's sin and his punishment. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch on Hosea 2:15. NET Bible notes on Hosea 2:15.
layers.text: Even a place name is redeemed. The Valley of Achor, "trouble," was named for Achan's sin: "Why have you brought this trouble upon us?" Joshua asked. "Today the LORD will bring trouble upon you!" Now God will "make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope."

layers.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary on Romans 9:25: first said of the ten tribes; the apostle legitimately applies it to the Gentiles. Ellicott: typically and prophetically applied to the Gentiles.
layers.text: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes coming back to God. Paul applies his words to those God called "not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles," and Peter tells his readers, "Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God."

passages.saying: do not go up to Beth-aven
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's warning to Judah about Israel's idol shrines.
layers.text: Hosea warns Judah not to copy Israel's unfaithfulness. Judah must not go to worship at the shrines of Gilgal and Beth-aven, nor swear by the LORD's name while serving idols there.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), JFB, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech all take Beth-aven here as a name put for Bethel after Jeroboam set up a golden calf there (1 Kings 12:28-29). Gill and JFB say it was given in contempt, and Keil and Delitzsch note Hosea took it from Amos 5:5.
layers.text: Beth-aven means house of wickedness, or house of nothing. Hosea uses it here for Bethel, whose name means house of God. Once the golden calf was set up there, the house of God had become a house of idols, so the prophets called it by a name for what it had become.

passages.saying: like those who move boundary stones
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparison and the threat of wrath poured out like water.
layers.text: Judah's leaders had become like people who move a neighbor's boundary stone, breaking through the limits God had set. So God would pour out His wrath on them like a flood.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the unusual phrase is formed after Deuteronomy 19:14 and 27:17. Gill, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), JFB, the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech also point to these laws, and Pusey quotes the curse of 27:17.
layers.text: The law of Moses forbade moving a neighbor's boundary marker and put a curse on anyone who did (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17). Hosea uses the same Hebrew words. Judah's princes had broken through the limits God set, so they stood under that curse.

passages.saying: Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of sickness and a wound that Assyria could not heal.
layers.text: When Israel and Judah saw how sick and wounded they were, they turned to the king of Assyria for help instead of to the LORD. But he could not cure them or heal their wound.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch render Jareb as striver, a title Hosea gave the Assyrian king. JFB and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explain it as one who pleads a cause, or an avenger, and Clarke notes the Vulgate and Targum render it avenger. The Companion Bible instead suggests Jareb may be a birth-name of the Assyrian king Sargon II.
layers.text: Older translations read King Jareb here, where the BSB has the great king. Jareb comes from a word meaning to strive or plead a case, so the title means something like the contender. Israel hoped he would take up their cause, but he could not heal their wound.

passages.saying: in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of God withdrawing until the people seek Him.
layers.text: Like a lion going back to its den, God would withdraw from His people until they admitted their guilt. Their suffering would then drive them to seek Him earnestly.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase rendered in their affliction recalls the same words in Deuteronomy 4:30, and compare Deuteronomy 4:29-30. The Companion Bible marks seek My face as a reference to Deuteronomy 4:29.
layers.text: Moses foretold that when Israel was in distress far from home, they would seek the LORD and return to Him (Deuteronomy 4:29-30). Hosea echoes that promise, using the same Hebrew phrase for being in distress.

passages.saying: He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to return and its pairing of tearing and healing.
layers.text: The prophet calls the people to return to the LORD. The God who struck them in judgment is the same God who will heal them and bind up their wounds.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the word heal alludes to Deuteronomy 32:39, where God promised His people healing, and that the reviving in the next verse applies the same verse. Gill also grounds the tearing and healing on Deuteronomy 32:39.
layers.text: In the Song of Moses the LORD says, "I wound and I heal." Hosea's call rests on that old promise: the same God who struck Israel is the One who will heal them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch point out that torn and heal pick up the same words in 5:13 and 5:14, and that let us return answers I will return in 5:15. Clarke says the people are referring to what God said in 5:14.
layers.text: The people answer God's own words from just before. He said He would tear them like a lion (5:14), and Assyria could not heal them (5:13). Now they confess that the LORD has torn them, and that He is the one who will heal.

passages.saying: As surely as the sun rises, He will appear
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to know the LORD and its pictures of dawn and rain.
layers.text: The people urge one another to press on to know the LORD. He will surely come to them, as certainly as the sun rises each morning and as the spring rains water the land.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the verb for seeking early in 5:15 is formed from shachar, the dawn, as the play on the word in 6:3 plainly shows. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) links the two verses: they seek Him in the morning, and He goes forth as the morning.
layers.text: In 5:15 God says that in their affliction they will earnestly seek Him. That verb comes from shachar, dawn, and pictures rising at daybreak to seek Him. The answer comes in the same word: His coming is as sure as the dawn (shachar).

passages.saying: like Adam, have transgressed the covenant
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's charge of covenant breaking and unfaithfulness.
layers.text: God charges His people with breaking His covenant. In the very land He had given them, they were unfaithful to Him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Clarke and Matthew Henry read like Adam and compare his breaking of God's command in Eden; Clarke and Pusey add that Israel, like Adam, would be cast out. JFB prefers like men, and Gill gives both readings.
layers.text: The Hebrew adam can also mean simply man, but here it most likely points to Adam. As Adam broke God's command in the garden and was driven out, Israel broke God's covenant in the good land He gave them, and they too would be driven out.

passages.saying: An eagle looms over the house of the LORD
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the trumpet alarm and the eagle picture in the verse.
layers.text: The prophet is told to sound the alarm. An enemy is about to swoop on God's people like an eagle on its prey, because they have broken His covenant and rebelled against His law.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the simile of the eagle points back to the threat of Moses in Deuteronomy 28:49. Gill sees some reference to the same verse, and JFB lists it for the Assyrian eagle.
layers.text: Moses warned that if Israel refused to obey the LORD, He would bring a nation from far away to swoop down on them like an eagle (Deuteronomy 28:49). Hosea's eagle is that warning coming true, for the people had broken the covenant.

passages.saying: For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's farming picture of sowing and reaping, read as a proverb for wasted labor and coming judgment.
layers.text: Israel's trust in idols and foreign help is like sowing wind: it comes back as a destroying storm. Their crop will not grow, and if it ever yields any grain, foreigners will eat it up.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call tsemach and qemach a play upon the words. Bullinger's Companion Bible and his Figures of Speech both list it as paronomasia and suggest the English 'the flower will yield no flour.'
layers.text: In Hebrew, "what sprouts fails to yield flour" can be heard as a rhyme: the tsemach (sprout) gives no qemach (flour). The matching sounds may make the empty harvest ring in the ear, much as English might say the flower yields no flour.

passages.saying: They will return to Egypt.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between Israel's many sacrifices and the LORD's refusal to accept them.
layers.text: Israel kept offering sacrifices, but they were only meat for their own meals, and the LORD took no pleasure in them. Instead of forgiving, He would punish their sins and send them back into bondage, as in Egypt.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all tie this threat to Moses' warning in Deuteronomy 28:68.
layers.text: "They will return to Egypt" takes up one of the last curses Moses warned of: "The LORD will return you to Egypt in ships." God had freed Israel from Egypt, and now their unfaithfulness would undo that rescue and send them back into slavery.

passages.saying: They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparison of Israel's present sin with the days of Gibeah.
layers.text: Israel had sunk as deep into corruption as in the worst days of its past, at Gibeah. God would not overlook it; He would remember their guilt and punish their sins.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech all read the days of Gibeah as the outrage of Judges 19.
layers.text: The days of Gibeah point back to Judges 19, when wicked men of Gibeah surrounded a house and abused a Levite's concubine until she died. Hosea says Israel's corruption now runs as deep as that infamous crime.

passages.saying: But they went to Baal-peor, and consecrated themselves to Shame
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of grapes and early figs set against Israel's turn to Baal-peor.
layers.text: God recalls His delight in Israel at the start, like a traveler finding grapes in the desert or the first ripe figs of the season. Yet they gave themselves to the idol at Baal-peor and became as vile as the thing they loved.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible point to Numbers 25:3. Gill says this refers to the history in Numbers 25, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Keil and Delitzsch also read it as the idolatry with Baal-peor.
layers.text: Baal-peor recalls Numbers 25, when Israel, near the end of the wilderness years, joined the women of Moab in worshiping Baal of Peor and the LORD's anger burned. Hosea sets that early fall right beside God's first delight in His people.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words evidently refer to Deuteronomy 32:10. Gill points to the same verse for God finding and caring for Israel in the wilderness.
layers.text: God finding Israel like grapes in the wilderness echoes the Song of Moses, where the LORD found His people "in a desert land" and guarded them as the apple of His eye. Both passages picture God's tender choice of a helpless people.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Hosea turns the name Baal into Bosheth, shame. Gill says Baal and Bosheth are put for each other, as with Eshbaal and Ishbosheth. Keil and Delitzsch say Bosheth is the name given to the idol of Baal-peor.
layers.text: Hosea names Baal-peor, then calls the idol simply Shame (bosheth). Baal means lord or master, and Scripture sometimes swaps it for bosheth, as when Saul's son Eshbaal is also called Ish-bosheth. The idol is named for the disgrace it brought.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say this verb was chosen to show Israel ought to have been the Nazirite of the LORD. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says they made themselves, as it were, Nazirites to shame.
layers.text: The verb for consecrated themselves (nazar) is the word behind the Nazirite, a person set apart to God by a special vow. Israel was meant to be set apart for the LORD, but they set themselves apart to Shame instead, a Nazirite vow turned upside down.

passages.saying: I will no longer love them; all their leaders are rebellious.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's charge against Gilgal and its rulers, explained from Gilgal's history as a holy place turned to idolatry.
layers.text: Gilgal, once a place of God's great mercies, had become a center of Israel's idolatry. For their evil deeds God would drive them out of His house and love them no longer, because every one of their leaders had rebelled.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call sarim and sorerim a play on similar sounds, Gill calls it an elegant play on words, and Keil and Delitzsch and Bullinger's Figures of Speech also note it.
layers.text: In Hebrew, "all their leaders are rebellious" is a jingle: sarehem sorerim. The words for leaders (sarim) and rebels (sorerim) sound almost alike, much as English might say their rulers are unruly.

passages.saying: Ephraim is struck down; their root is withered; they cannot bear fruit.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a blighted tree applied to Ephraim and its children.
layers.text: Picturing Israel as a stricken tree with a dried-up root, God says Ephraim will bear no fruit. Even the children they do have, the ones they treasure most, will be lost in the coming judgment.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the figures of root and fruit here are suggested by the name Ephraim, which means fruitful.
layers.text: The name Ephraim means fruitful; Joseph gave it because God had made him fruitful (Genesis 41:52). Some see Hosea turning the name around here: fruitful Ephraim is struck like a tree whose root has dried up, so that it cannot bear fruit.

passages.saying: The people of Samaria will fear for the calf of Beth-aven.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of the calf idol's worshipers and priests mourning its loss.
layers.text: Far from protecting its people, the calf idol will need protecting. The people of Samaria will be anxious for it, and its people and priests, who once delighted in it, will mourn as their prized idol is carried away into exile.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the glory departing here as a reference to 1 Samuel 4:21-22. Both verses use the same Hebrew words for glory and for going into exile.
layers.text: Hosea says the calf's glory has been taken into exile. Some hear in this the cry when the ark was captured, which uses the same Hebrew words: "The glory has departed from Israel." This time the glory that departs is the calf's.

layers.evidence: Gill says Bethel is called Bethaven, the house of iniquity, by way of contempt. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the House of God was turned into the house of vanity. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Bullinger's Figures of Speech say the same.
layers.text: Bethel means house of God, but Hosea calls it Beth-aven, house of wickedness or emptiness. The new name mocks the shrine where King Jeroboam had set up a golden calf: the house of God had become a house of idols.

passages.saying: Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's tracing of Israel's sin back to the days of Gibeah.
layers.text: Israel's sin is not new. Ever since the crime at Gibeah they have kept on in the same wickedness, and the kind of war that once fell on the wrongdoers at Gibeah will now overtake them.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all take Gibeah here as the crime of Judges 19 and the war against Benjamin in Judges 20.
layers.text: The days of Gibeah and the battle in Gibeah recall Judges 19 and 20. After the men of Gibeah committed a terrible crime, Benjamin refused to hand them over, and the other tribes went to war and nearly wiped Benjamin out.

passages.saying: Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the farming picture of sowing, plowing and rain that runs through the verse.
layers.text: Hosea calls Israel to sow righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion. They must break up the hard, unplowed ground of their hearts and seek the LORD now, until He comes and sends righteousness on them like rain.

layers.evidence: Gill gives "teach you righteousness" as another rendering of the same words, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) prefers it, noting that the Hebrew verb seldom means to rain but constantly means to teach.
layers.text: The verb behind "sends righteousness upon you like rain" is yoreh. It can mean to send rain, but far more often it is the word for teaching. So the line can also be read as a promise that the LORD will come and teach His people righteousness.

passages.saying: out of Egypt I called My son
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Exodus, when God brought young Israel out of Egypt.
layers.text: God looks back to Israel's beginning as a nation. When Israel was young and helpless, God loved him and brought him out of slavery in Egypt as His own son.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the verse rests on Exodus 4:22-23; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible point to the same words to Pharaoh. Matthew 2:15 later quotes the line about Jesus.
layers.text: Calling Israel God's son goes back to the Exodus story. God sent Moses to tell Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son,” and to let His son go. Matthew 2:15 later quotes this verse about Jesus.

passages.saying: How could I give you up, O Ephraim?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's anguished questions and God's stated compassion.
layers.text: God speaks with deep feeling about rebellious Israel. They deserved to be wiped out, yet He asks how He could hand them over. His heart turns within Him and His compassion is stirred, so He will spare them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) say Hosea has in mind Deuteronomy 29:23 (29:22 in the Hebrew), where Moses threatened idolatrous Israel with the same end; the Companion Bible lists it as a reference to the Law, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites it too.
layers.text: Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah. Moses had warned that if Israel turned to idols, its land would become like those cities (Deuteronomy 29:23). God names them to show what Israel deserved, then holds back His wrath.

passages.saying: In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Genesis accounts of Jacob's birth and his wrestling with God.
layers.text: Hosea points the nation back to its forefather Jacob. Before he was born he grasped his twin brother's heel, and as a grown man he wrestled with God. His descendants, who carry his name, are measured against his story.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Hosea has Genesis 25:26 in mind; the Companion Bible cites the same verse, Gill points to the birth story there, and Clarke refers readers to it.
layers.text: This line retells Jacob's birth in Genesis 25:26, when he came out of the womb holding his twin brother Esau's heel and was given the name Jacob because of it.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that 'akab gives the name Jacob and sarah the name Israel; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also ties the heel to the name Jacob and the wrestling to the name Israel.
layers.text: Both verbs echo Jacob's two names. Grasped the heel is 'aqav, which echoes Ya'aqov, Jacob, the name Genesis 25:26 ties to that heel. Wrestled is sarah, the verb Genesis 32:28 uses to explain the name Yisra'el, Israel.

passages.saying: he wept and sought His favor; he found Him at Bethel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Genesis accounts of Jacob's struggle and of God meeting him at Bethel.
layers.text: Hosea continues Jacob's story. Jacob struggled with the angel and prevailed, not by force alone but by weeping and pleading for God's blessing. God also met him at Bethel and spoke with him there.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the pleading to Genesis 32:26; Keil and Delitzsch say the clause draws on that verse and shows the fight was won by prayer; Clarke and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) note that Genesis does not mention the tears.
layers.text: He wept and sought His favor looks back to the night Jacob wrestled and would not let go, saying, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” Genesis does not mention tears. Hosea adds them, and this is often read to mean Jacob won by weeping and pleading, not by strength alone.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible point to Genesis 28 at Bethel; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) includes both meetings there, in Genesis 28 and 35, while Keil and Delitzsch refer it only to the second (Genesis 35:9), not the first. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible note that Bethel had since become a seat of idolatry.
layers.text: Bethel recalls where God met Jacob as he fled from Esau, in the dream of a ladder reaching to heaven. Jacob named the place Bethel, house of God (Genesis 28:19). God met him there again on his return (Genesis 35). By Hosea's day Bethel housed a golden calf.

passages.saying: the LORD is His name of renown
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the divine names the LORD and the God of Hosts.
layers.text: Hosea names the God who met Jacob. He is the LORD, the God of Hosts, who commands every power in heaven and on earth. The LORD is the name by which He wants to be remembered.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the wording is taken from Exodus 3:15; the Companion Bible cites the same verse, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) quotes it in full.
layers.text: Renown here is zekher, memorial, the way someone is remembered. It echoes Exodus 3:15, where God gave Moses His name and said, “This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation.”

passages.saying: A merchant loves to defraud with dishonest scales in his hands.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of rigged scales, which God's law forbade (Leviticus 19:36).
layers.text: Hosea describes Ephraim as a crooked trader. He cheats with rigged scales and loves to take advantage of others, the very opposite of the love and justice God asks for.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it a play on the double sense of Canaan; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Keil and Delitzsch, Gill, Clarke and Matthew Henry all note that the word for merchant is Canaan.
layers.text: The word for merchant is kena'an, which is also the name Canaan, because the Canaanites were famous traders. Just after recalling Jacob, who wrestled with God, Hosea calls his descendants Canaan: they now cheat like the people whose land they were given.

passages.saying: I will again make you dwell in tents
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own reminder of the Exodus and its promise of tents.
layers.text: God reminds Israel that He has been their God ever since He brought them out of Egypt. He says He will again make them live in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all tie the verse to the Feast of Tabernacles and Leviticus 23:42-43; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Wesley and Bullinger's Companion Bible agree. Clarke alone doubts the feast is meant and reads the verse only as a threat.
layers.text: The appointed feast is the Feast of Booths, when Israel lived in booths for seven days to remember how God sheltered them after the Exodus (Leviticus 23:42-43). Living in tents again recalls that wilderness journey, when God both humbled His people and cared for them.

passages.saying: their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the two place names and the farming picture of stones cleared from a field.
layers.text: Gilead, east of the Jordan, and Gilgal, west of it, stand for the whole northern kingdom, and both are full of idol worship. Their many altars will end up like the piles of stones farmers clear out of plowed fields.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch see a play upon the name Gilgal in the heaps of stones (gallim); Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the word heaps alludes to Gilgal; Bullinger's Companion Bible and Figures of Speech mark a paronomasia on Gilead, Gilgal and gallim.
layers.text: Hosea plays on the place names. Gilgal (gil-gal) and Gilead (gil-ad) share the sound of gallim, heaps of stones. The altars at these places would become just what the names suggest: rubble heaps.

passages.saying: Jacob fled to the land of Aram
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Genesis account of Jacob's years with Laban.
layers.text: Hosea reminds proud Israel of its forefather's humble start. Jacob ran away to Aram and worked there as a hired hand, tending sheep to win a wife.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Genesis 28:5 and 29:20, 28; Bullinger's Companion Bible marks references to Genesis 28:5 and 29:18; Keil and Delitzsch say the words point to Jacob's hardships in Genesis 29 to 31; Gill also traces the verse to Genesis 28 and 29.
layers.text: This retells Jacob's story from Genesis. He fled from Esau to his uncle Laban in Aram and worked seven years for Rachel, then seven more (Genesis 29:20, 30). The nation that carried his name had a lowly beginning.

passages.saying: by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Exodus account of Moses leading Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness.
layers.text: God used a prophet to bring Israel out of Egypt, and through a prophet He kept them safe on the way. Israel owed its freedom to a prophet's work, yet it now ignored the prophets God sent.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and Bullinger's Companion Bible all identify the prophet as Moses; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible point to Deuteronomy 18:15, and Keil and Delitzsch to 18:18. Clarke takes the second prophet in the verse as Joshua.
layers.text: The prophet here is Moses, who led Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness. Moses spoke of himself as a prophet when he promised that God would raise up another prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15).

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note the same Hebrew word in verse 12; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) contrasts Jacob keeping sheep with Israel being kept; Keil and Delitzsch set Jacob's guarding of cattle against God's guarding of Israel through Moses; Bullinger's Companion Bible reads kept, as in verse 12.
layers.text: One Hebrew verb, shamar, links the two verses. Jacob tended sheep to win a wife, and Israel was preserved, literally kept, by God through a prophet. The man who guarded flocks had descendants whom God guarded like a flock.

passages.saying: you know no God but Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between the LORD who rescued Israel and the idols it served.
layers.text: God has been Israel's God ever since He rescued them from Egypt. They were to acknowledge no other god, because no one else can save them.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible marks a reference to Exodus 20:2-3; Clarke says this was God's first self-revelation to Israel and the first commandment He gave. Gill adds that knowing no other god was enjoined in the law.
layers.text: These words echo the opening of the Ten Commandments, where God names Himself as the One who brought Israel out of Egypt and then forbids any other gods (Exodus 20:2-3). Hosea holds the first commandment up to a people worshiping calf idols.

passages.saying: when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's chain of pasture, fullness, pride and forgetting.
layers.text: When Israel enjoyed rich pasture in the land, they ate their fill. Being full made them proud, and their pride led them to forget God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the reproof almost word for word from Deuteronomy 8:11 and following; Bullinger's Companion Bible cites Deuteronomy 8:12-14 and 32:15. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill point to Moses' similar warnings in Deuteronomy 6:11-12 and 32:15.
layers.text: Moses had warned that when Israel ate and was satisfied in the good land, their hearts would grow proud and they would forget the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:12-14). Hosea traces the same steps to show that the warning had come true.

passages.saying: Although he flourishes among his brothers, an east wind will come
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of the scorching desert wind and the Assyrian invasion it stands for.
layers.text: Ephraim may flourish among the tribes, but God will send a scorching east wind from the desert, a picture of the Assyrian invader. It will dry up his springs and carry off his treasures.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it a paronomasia on Ephraim from the root parah, to be fruitful; Keil and Delitzsch call it an evident play upon the name; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Gill and Bullinger's Companion Bible also tie fruitful here to the name Ephraim.
layers.text: The Hebrew for he flourishes, yafri, plays on the name Ephraim (efrayim), which Joseph chose because God had made him fruitful (Genesis 41:52). Even the tribe whose name speaks of fruitfulness could not escape the withering east wind.

passages.saying: The field is ruined; the land mourns.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains that the locusts ate up every green thing in the fields.
layers.text: The locusts have ruined the fields, and the very ground seems to mourn. The grain, the new wine and the olive oil, the chief crops of the land, have all failed.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the figure paronomasia (a play on sounds) in shuddad... sadeh. Clarke, commenting on 1:7, lists suddad sadeh in 1:10 among the sound plays Joel delights in.
layers.text: In Hebrew, "The field is ruined" is just two words, shuddad sadeh, which sound almost alike. The echo makes the ruin ring in the ear, and the same verb shuddad returns in "the grain is destroyed" later in the verse.

passages.saying: it will come as destruction from the Almighty
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain the day as the day of the LORD's anger, a foretaste of His final judgment.
layers.text: Joel cries out because the Day of the LORD is near, a time when God comes in judgment. It will come as ruin sent by the Almighty Himself, a foretaste of His final judgment of all people.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the words form a sort of terrible proverb, adopted from Joel by Isaiah in Isaiah 13:6. Keil and Delitzsch, on Isaiah 13:6, say Isaiah there repeats words of Joel 1:15, play on words included.
layers.text: Isaiah 13:6 gives the same warning against Babylon in almost the same words, ending "it will come as destruction from the Almighty." The saying became a fixed warning, and some hold that Isaiah took it up from Joel.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it an elegant play on words, wasting from the Waster. Keil and Delitzsch call keshod mishshaddai a play upon the words, deriving both from shadad. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says shod is formed from the same root as Shaddai. The Companion Bible also marks paronomasia here.
layers.text: In Hebrew, destruction is shod and the Almighty is Shaddai. The two words sound alike and are often traced to the same root, so the line rings: mighty ruin from the Mighty One. The God who rules all things is the One who sends this judgment.

passages.saying: The land before them is like the Garden of Eden
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains the contrast between the fruitful land before the invaders and the wilderness they leave behind.
layers.text: The invading swarm moves like a wildfire. Before it the land is lush and fruitful, but behind it lies a desert wasteland, and nothing escapes it.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the garden of Eden here as a reference to Genesis 2:8. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the land was like that Paradise of God where He placed our first parents. Keil and Delitzsch say the land had resembled the garden of paradise of Genesis 2:8.
layers.text: The Garden of Eden is the garden the LORD God planted for the first man in Genesis 2:8. Joel's picture shows the invaders turning a land as rich as that first paradise into a desert wasteland.

passages.saying: So rend your hearts and not your garments
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain it as a call for inward sorrow, not merely the outward sign of torn clothes.
layers.text: God calls His people to true repentance. Tearing their clothes was an outward sign of grief, but He wants broken hearts that turn back to Him, because He is merciful and willing to hold back the disaster He had warned of.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Joel points to God's mercy in the words of Exodus 34:6, by which He made known His nature to Moses, adding that He relents. Gill says these traits are taken from Exodus 34:6, and the Companion Bible marks a reference to Exodus 34:6-7. Clarke also points to Exodus 34:6-7.
layers.text: Joel gives the reason to return in God's own words to Moses in Exodus 34:6, where the LORD proclaimed His name: "slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion." Joel then adds that He relents from sending disaster.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech says rend is used only once here with two meanings: figuratively of the heart and literally of the garments.
layers.text: Some note that Joel uses the verb rend only once for both hearts and garments, but in two senses: garments are torn literally, as a sign of grief, while hearts are torn in a figure. God asks for the inward tearing of the heart.

passages.saying: for the LORD has done great things
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains the great things as God driving the invaders away and restoring the land.
layers.text: The land itself is told not to be afraid but to rejoice, because the LORD has acted mightily, driving off the invader and making the land fruitful again.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes): the enemy had done great things, now God had done great things. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown set the great things of the haughty foe in 2:20 against those done by the LORD. Keil and Delitzsch say the LORD destroyed the foe that did great things. The Companion Bible: greater than the foe himself.
layers.text: Verse 20 ends with the same Hebrew words as this verse, "has done great things". Many read verse 20 of the proud invader and its havoc. Here the same words are given to the LORD, whose great deeds answer and outdo the enemy's. Some read verse 20 of God as well.

passages.saying: He has given you the autumn rains for your vindication
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Wesley explains the former rain as the autumn rain that readies the soil for the grain.
layers.text: Zion's people are told to rejoice in the LORD, who is giving back the rains the land needs: the autumn rains at sowing time and the spring rains before harvest, as in former days.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch read the first moreh as the teacher for righteousness and think Joel used moreh, not the usual yoreh, for the early rain later in the verse for the sake of the echo. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes that moreh mostly means teacher. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read both as rain.
layers.text: The word translated autumn rains, moreh, appears twice here and usually means teacher. Many older readers took the first as a teacher who leads to righteousness and the second as rain. On that view Joel may have used this rarer word for rain to echo the first. Others read both as rain.

passages.saying: I will pour out My Spirit on all people
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise and on Peter's statement in Acts 2 that it began to be fulfilled at Pentecost.
layers.text: God promises a time when He will pour out His Spirit on all kinds of people, not only on a few prophets. Sons and daughters, old men and young men, will all receive His Spirit and speak His message.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Moses' wish in Numbers 11:29 was to be fulfilled by this promise. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Numbers 11:29 to contrast the privileged few of old with people of all ages and ranks.
layers.text: When two men prophesied in the camp, Moses said he wished all the LORD's people were prophets with His Spirit on them. Joel's promise answers that wish. God will put His Spirit not on a chosen few but on all people.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all point to Peter's quotation of this verse in Acts 2:17 as the start of its fulfillment. Matthew Henry's Concise and the Companion Bible say the same.
layers.text: On the day of Pentecost, Peter quoted this promise to explain what the crowd in Jerusalem was seeing. "This is what was spoken by the prophet Joel," he said (Acts 2:16-17). The Spirit coming on the believers was this promise beginning to come true.

passages.saying: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of rescue for all who call on the LORD in the day of judgment.
layers.text: When the LORD's day of judgment comes, anyone who calls on Him in faith will be rescued. On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be survivors, the remnant whom the LORD Himself calls.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say these words point to Obadiah 17, where the saying occurs word for word. The Companion Bible compares Obadiah 17 and says the LORD had said this by Joel and other prophets. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown instead takes them to refer to Joel's own earlier words.
layers.text: The words "as the LORD has promised" may point back to Obadiah 17, which makes the same promise in almost the same Hebrew words: "on Mount Zion there will be deliverance." If so, Joel is reminding his hearers of a promise God had already given.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says this verse is applied to Jesus in Romans 10:13. Keil and Delitzsch say Paul quoted it there to show that the Gentiles share in salvation, and Clarke says Paul's use of it shows its wider meaning. Gill points to Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13.
layers.text: Peter quotes this promise at Pentecost (Acts 2:21), and Paul quotes it in Romans 10:13. Paul uses it to show that anyone, Jew or Gentile, who calls on the Lord Jesus will be saved.

passages.saying: bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's charge against the nations that scattered Israel and divided the LORD's land.
layers.text: God will gather the nations that scattered His people and divided up His land. He will judge them for the way they treated Israel, His own inheritance.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown sees an allusion to the judgment on Judah's foes in Jehoshaphat's time. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the imagery may come from that deliverance, and the Companion Bible calls 2 Chronicles 20:21-26 typical of this judgment.
layers.text: The name likely also recalls the day of King Jehoshaphat, when armies from Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir came against Judah and the LORD Himself defeated them. That victory is a small picture of the greater judgment God will bring on all the nations that attack His people.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible renders the name Jehovah hath judged and calls the pairing yehoshaphat vnishpatti a play on words. Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill and Keil and Delitzsch all give the name as the judgment of the LORD or the LORD judges.
layers.text: Jehoshaphat means the LORD judges, and the valley's name tells what God will do there: "There I will enter into judgment against them." In Hebrew the name Yehoshaphat and the verb nishpatti, I will enter into judgment, come from the same root, shaphat, to judge.

passages.saying: Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to the hostile nations to arm every man for war.
layers.text: God summons the hostile nations to war. Every farm tool is to become a weapon, and even the weak are to claim they are strong, so eager will the nations be to attack God's people. Yet they gather only to be judged.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all set this command beside Isaiah 2:4 as its opposite, and all but Gill also name Micah 4:3. The Companion Bible notes that Joel's command comes first and the peaceful reversal follows.
layers.text: This command is the mirror image of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3, where the nations "will beat their swords into plowshares." Here the nations arm for war against God's people. There, under the Messiah's reign of peace, weapons become farm tools again.

passages.saying: Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the prophet's cry at the vast crowds gathering for judgment.
layers.text: The prophet sees huge crowds of nations pouring into the valley where God will judge them. The repeated word stresses how many there are, and the Day of the LORD is near for them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch derive charuts from a verb meaning to decide irrevocably and say it defines the name Jehoshaphat more precisely. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the word means cut, then decided. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill also identify this valley with the Valley of Jehoshaphat.
layers.text: The valley of decision is another name for the Valley of Jehoshaphat (verses 2 and 12). The Hebrew word charuts comes from a root meaning to cut, and so to decide once for all. The first name says the LORD judges. This one adds that His verdict is fixed and final.

passages.saying: a spring will flow from the house of the LORD
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a land overflowing with blessing after God's judgment.
layers.text: After God's judgment, His land will overflow with blessing: wine on the mountains, milk on the hills and water in every streambed. A spring will flow from the LORD's house and water even the dry Valley of Acacias.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Ezekiel 47, say Joel had already described this river of salvation and Ezekiel's vision grows out of it. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible link Joel 3:18 with Ezekiel 47:1 and Zechariah 14:8, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Zechariah continues the image.
layers.text: Later prophets take up this picture of water flowing from God's house. Ezekiel sees a river flowing from under the temple threshold and bringing life (Ezekiel 47:1-12). Zechariah sees living water flow out from Jerusalem (14:8), and Revelation shows the river of life from God's throne (22:1).

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the name is taken from Israel's last encampment in Moab before entering Canaan, and the Companion Bible marks it as a reference to Numbers 33:49. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes that Shittim was Israel's last station before the land of promise, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown places it on the border of Moab beyond the Jordan.
layers.text: Shittim, the Hebrew name behind the Valley of Acacias, was also the place of Israel's last camp on the plains of Moab, just before they crossed the Jordan into the Promised Land. Naming it recalls that border place at the edge of the land, and shows God's blessing flowing out even that far.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Shittim means acacias, which grow only in arid regions. Keil and Delitzsch say the name was chosen to denote a very dry valley, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) calls it a dry valley where the acacia grows. The Companion Bible also renders it the acacias.
layers.text: The Valley of Acacias is Shittim in Hebrew. Acacias grow in dry, barren ground, so the name pictures a parched valley. The spring from God's house will water even a place like this, showing that His blessing reaches the driest land.

passages.saying: The LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a lion's roar and a land drying up, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Amos opens by picturing the LORD like a roaring lion, speaking in judgment from Zion, where His temple stood. At His voice the shepherds' pastures mourn and even the green top of Mount Carmel withers.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Amos joins his prophecy to the end of Joel's; Keil and Delitzsch say the first half of the verse is taken word for word from Joel; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that in Joel the LORD roars on Israel's behalf but here against her. The Companion Bible also compares Joel 3:16.
layers.text: Amos begins with the very words of Joel 3:16, where the LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem, so his message picks up where Joel's left off. In Joel that roar shelters God's people. Here it is turned against Israel itself.

passages.saying: the Valley of Aven and the one who wields the scepter in Beth-eden
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words and on their fulfilment when Assyria took Damascus (2 Kings 16:9).
layers.text: The LORD announces judgment on Aram and its capital Damascus. He will break open its gates, cut off its rulers, and send its people into exile to Kir. Assyria carried this out when it took Damascus.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) renders the place literally as vale of vanity and calls Beth-eden a significant name meaning house of pleasure; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Aven means vanity, from the idol worship there, and Eden means pleasantness; Keil and Delitzsch give valley of nothingness, or of idols, and house of delight. Gill gives idol and pleasure house.
layers.text: Aven means vanity or nothingness, a word also used for idols, so the Valley of Aven is a valley of vanity, likely named for its idol worship. Beth-eden means house of pleasure. The LORD will cut off both the ruler of the valley of vanity and the king in his house of pleasure.

passages.saying: broke a covenant of brotherhood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's charge against Tyre, the Phoenician trading city, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: The LORD judges Tyre, the great Phoenician trading city, because it handed over whole communities of captives, most likely Israelites, to Edom as slaves, and so broke a covenant of brotherhood.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Wesley all take the brotherly covenant as the league of Hiram of Tyre with David and Solomon; Clarke points to 1 Kings 5:12, while noting some take it as the kinship of Israel and Edom. Gill gives both views.
layers.text: The covenant of brotherhood most likely recalls the treaty of friendship that Hiram king of Tyre made with David and Solomon, when Tyre supplied cedar for the temple. By selling Israelite captives to Edom, Tyre betrayed that old bond with Israel.

passages.saying: he pursued his brother with the sword
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's charge against Edom, Israel's kin nation, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: The LORD judges Edom, the nation descended from Esau, because it attacked Israel, its brother nation, with the sword, smothered all pity, and kept its anger burning without end.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Esau's posterity kept up his grudge against Jacob (Genesis 27:41); the Companion Bible marks the verse as a reference to Genesis 27:41; Gill says Edom kept its wrath as Esau their father proposed to do.
layers.text: Edom came from Esau and Israel from his twin brother Jacob, so the brother here is Israel. Edom's endless anger carries on Esau's grudge against Jacob over the blessing, when Esau planned to kill his brother. The old family hatred lived on in the nation.

passages.saying: Their king will go into exile
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words about Ammon's rulers going into captivity together.
layers.text: The LORD's judgment on Ammon ends with its king and his officials carried off into exile together, leaving no leaders to rally the nation against its conqueror.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) sees in the word malcham a subordinate allusion to Ammon's god Molech or Malchom and notes Jeremiah 49:3 uses almost the same words of that god; Clarke thinks it should be read as Milcom. Gill mentions this view; Keil and Delitzsch and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown keep the plain sense their king.
layers.text: The Hebrew for their king is malkam, which sounds almost the same as Milcom, the chief god of the Ammonites. So the line may also hint that Ammon's idol, not only its king, would be carried into exile. Jeremiah later says nearly the same words of Milcom.

passages.saying: They lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of feasting at altars, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: The rich in Israel stretch out at their altars on cloaks taken from the poor as security for debts, and in the house of their god they drink wine paid for with unjust fines.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch all point to the law that a poor man's pledged cloak be returned before sunset (Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-13); the Companion Bible marks the verse as a reference to Exodus 22:26.
layers.text: God's law said a poor man's cloak taken as security must be returned by sunset, because it was his only covering at night. These people keep such cloaks and lie on them at their altars, breaking God's law even as they worship.

passages.saying: though his height was like that of the cedars
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's reminder of the conquest of Canaan, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: God reminds ungrateful Israel that He Himself destroyed the Amorites before them, a people as tall as cedars and as strong as oaks, wiping them out completely, fruit and roots alike.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Amos applies to the whole nation what the spies reported about the giants (Numbers 13:32-33); E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) links it to the spies' report and Israel feeling like grasshoppers; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Numbers 13:32-33; Gill calls the Amorites of the race of the giants.
layers.text: Amorites as tall as cedars recall the spies' report that the people of Canaan were giants, beside whom Israel felt like grasshoppers. The very foes who frightened Israel's fathers were destroyed by God, so the land was His gift and not their own victory.

passages.saying: you made the Nazirites drink wine
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two charges, as the commentaries explain them.
layers.text: Israel answered God's gifts with contempt. They pushed the Nazirites, people set apart to God by a vow, into drinking wine, and they ordered the prophets to stop prophesying.

layers.evidence: Clarke says wine was expressly forbidden in the Nazirite law (Numbers 6:1-3); Keil and Delitzsch say the Nazirites were commanded to abstain from wine and point to Numbers 6; the Companion Bible marks the verse as a reference to Numbers 6:2-3. Gill says it was contrary to their vow.
layers.text: The Nazirite law in Numbers 6 required anyone under that vow to keep away from wine and even from grapes. By making Nazirites drink wine, Israel deliberately broke down the living signs of holiness God had raised up among them.

passages.saying: As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's shepherd picture, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: When a lion takes a sheep, a shepherd may rescue only a couple of leg bones or a bit of an ear. In the same way, only a scrap of the people living at ease in Samaria will be rescued when judgment falls.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the piece of ear was brought to the owner so the shepherd need not pay for the loss, citing Exodus 22:13; Gill says the remains were taken to show the master the sheep was torn by a beast of prey.
layers.text: A shepherd who lost a sheep to a wild beast brought what was left to the owner as proof it had been torn (compare Exodus 22:13). Two leg bones or a scrap of ear proved only that the sheep was gone. Such will be the few rescued from Samaria.

passages.saying: I struck you with blight and mildew
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's list of crop disasters God sent as warnings.
layers.text: God reminds Israel that He struck their crops with blight and mildew and sent locusts to eat their gardens, vineyards, fig trees and olive trees. Yet even then they did not turn back to Him.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says both words stand together in Deuteronomy 28:22 among the scourges of disobedience. Keil and Delitzsch say the blight is threatened there, and the Companion Bible marks a reference to Deuteronomy 28:22.
layers.text: Blight and mildew, shiddafon and yeraqon in Hebrew, are the same pair of words Moses named in Deuteronomy 28:22 among the curses for breaking the covenant. Hearing them would remind Israel of the warnings God had given long before.

passages.saying: I sent plagues among you like those of Egypt
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's list of plague and defeat in war sent as warnings.
layers.text: God reminds Israel that He sent plague among them as He once did in Egypt, let their young men fall by the sword and their horses be captured, and filled their camps with the stench of the dead. Yet they did not return to Him.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) quotes Deuteronomy 28:60 here, with Exodus 15:26 for the earlier promise. Keil and Delitzsch and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also point to Deuteronomy 28:60, and the Companion Bible marks it as a reference.
layers.text: Moses had warned that if Israel turned from God, He would bring on them the diseases of Egypt they had dreaded (Deuteronomy 28:60). Amos shows that warning coming true: the people once promised freedom from Egypt's diseases were now struck with plagues like Egypt's.

passages.saying: Some of you I overthrew as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparison with Sodom and its picture of a narrow escape.
layers.text: God says He had already brought ruin on parts of Israel, as He overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and those who survived were like a burning stick pulled from the fire just in time. Yet still they did not return to Him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words are taken from Deuteronomy 29 (verse 22 in Hebrew, 23 in English), where the ruined land is compared to Sodom and Gomorrah. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible also point to Deuteronomy 29:23.
layers.text: Amos uses nearly the same Hebrew words as Moses in Deuteronomy 29:23, where a land laid waste for forsaking the LORD is compared to the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. Read this way, Amos is showing Israel that this warning had already begun to fall on them.

passages.saying: Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Amos 1:1 dates Amos to the days of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel. A few decades later Assyria captured Samaria and carried the Israelites away into exile (2 Kings 17:6).
layers.text: Amos speaks to the northern kingdom of Israel. Its people made trips to old holy places like Bethel and Gilgal while they "trample on the poor." God says, "Seek Me and live!" The shrines they trusted cannot save them; they too will fall.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Gilgal (H1537) and galoh yigleh, it will surely go into exile (H1540, twice), in Amos 5:5. Gilgal and galah come from different roots, so the link is one of sound, not word history. Joshua 5:9 gives the Bible's own account of the name: there God rolled away (galal) the reproach of Egypt.
layers.text: In Hebrew the line is a run of matching sounds: ha-gilgal galoh yigleh, "Gilgal will surely go into exile." The name Gilgal and galah, the verb for going into exile, share the sounds g and l, so the town's name rings with its fate.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Bet-el (H1008) and aven (H0205) in Amos 5:5; Bet aven (H1007) in Hosea 4:15, beside Gilgal, and 10:5. Joshua 7:2 names a real Beth-aven near Bethel, but E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary take Hosea's Beth-aven, with its calf (Hosea 10:5), as a name for Bethel, where Jeroboam set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-29).
layers.text: Bethel means "house of God." Amos says it "will come to nothing," and nothing is aven, a word for emptiness and wickedness. Many think Hosea made it a nickname: "do not go up to Beth-aven," house of wickedness, not house of God.

passages.saying: you will never live in the stone houses you have built
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's link between oppressing the poor and losing ill-gotten wealth.
layers.text: Because the rich trample the poor and force them to hand over grain, God says they will not live in the fine stone houses they built or drink the wine of the vineyards they planted.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the threat is taken from Deuteronomy 28:30 and 39. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it the original prophecy of Moses, and the Companion Bible marks a reference to the same verses.
layers.text: Moses warned in Deuteronomy 28:30, "You will build a house but will not live in it," and in 28:39 that those who planted vineyards would not drink the wine. Amos tells the rich of Israel that this covenant curse is about to fall on them.

passages.saying: you will now go into exile as the first of the captives
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's sentence on the idle rich described in 6:1-6.
layers.text: Because Israel's leaders lounged at feasts and did not grieve over the nation's ruin, they will be the first carried into exile, and their feasting and lounging will come to an end.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase at the head of the captives was chosen with direct reference to the first of oils in 6:6. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties it to their being first in rank (6:1) and in ointments (6:6). Reshit (first, finest) and rosh (head) come from the same Hebrew root.
layers.text: The leaders were the notable men of the foremost (reshit) nation (6:1), and they anointed themselves with the finest (reshit) oils (6:6). Now they will go into exile at the head (rosh) of the captives. They keep their place at the front, but now it is the front of the line into exile.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say seruchim points back to the couches of 6:4 and forms a play upon words with mirzach. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Amos joined similar harsh sounds on purpose to express the revelers' scream.
layers.text: The closing words, mirzach seruchim, the revelry of the sprawlers, are a play on sounds. Their harsh, hissing sounds seem chosen to echo the noisy feasting of those who sprawled on their couches (6:4), and that revelry will pass away.

passages.saying: you who rejoice in Lo-debar and say
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's boast of victory won by our own strength.
layers.text: Amos rebukes Israel's leaders for celebrating their recent victories and boasting that they won them by their own strength, instead of giving the glory to God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) read the Hebrew by its meaning: lo davar is a nothing, a thing with no existence, and horns are the symbol of strength and military power.
layers.text: Here Lo-debar is written lo davar, which means no thing, and Karnaim means horns, a common picture of strength. So the boast is empty: they rejoice in a nothing and claim to have taken horns by their own strength. Older translations render both words by their meaning instead of as town names.

passages.saying: I saw a basket of summer fruit
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Lord's own explanation of the vision in verse 2.
layers.text: In a fourth vision the Lord shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit. Fruit picked at the close of summer must be eaten at once, and in the same way Israel is ripe for judgment and its end is near.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Adam Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all point out the sound-play between qayits (summer fruit) in verse 1 and qets (end) in verse 2. Gill, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Bullinger's Companion Bible and Figures of Speech note it too.
layers.text: The vision turns on two Hebrew words that sound almost alike. Amos sees qayits, ripe summer fruit, and the Lord answers that the qets, the end, has come for Israel. The ripe fruit itself carries the message: the nation is ripe, and its end is here.

passages.saying: The end has come for My people Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: God shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit and asks what he sees. The answer becomes the message: Israel's time is up. The next verses say why: they "trample the needy" and cheat the poor with dishonest scales.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qayits (H7019) in 8:1 and 8:2, qets (H7093) in 8:2. Keil and Delitzsch and Gill note the paronomasia. Late summer fruit, such as figs, was the last crop of the farming year, which gives the picture its point; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes): when it was gathered, the circle of husbandry came to its close.
layers.text: Summer fruit is qayits; the end is qets. The two words sound almost alike, so the vision works like a spoken pun: Amos sees qayits and hears qets. Summer fruit was the last harvest of the year, and Israel's season is ending.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qets (H7093) in Ezekiel 7:2 and 7:6; heqits, it has awakened (H6974), in 7:6. Ezekiel 7:2 repeats the words of Amos 8:2, the end has come, and speaks to the land of Israel, which by Ezekiel's day meant Judah. The Pulpit Commentary hears an echo of Amos and, with Keil and Delitzsch, notes the pun in 7:6.
layers.text: Over a century later Ezekiel brings the cry to "the land of Israel," which by then meant Judah: "The end! The end has come." He adds a pun of his own: the end (qets) "has roused itself" (heqits) against you. The end has woken up.

Jeremiah's first vision is built the same way: "Jeremiah, what do you see?" An almond branch, shaqed, and God is shoqed, "watching over My word." The prophets heard God's message in the names of ordinary things.

passages.saying: Let us reduce the ephah and increase the shekel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain sense of the merchants' own words about measures, weights and scales.
layers.text: Israel's grain dealers resent the New Moon and the Sabbath because those holy days stop their trade. They long to sell again, giving short measure for the grain, demanding extra silver with heavy weights and using rigged scales, so the poor get less and pay more.

layers.evidence: Gill says this cheating was contrary to the law in Deuteronomy 25:13. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it a double fraud against Deuteronomy 25:13-14. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) quotes Deuteronomy 25:13-15 and says such dealings were expressly forbidden by God.
layers.text: The law of Moses forbade keeping two differing weights or measures, one heavy and one light, and called for honest ones so that Israel might live long in the land. These merchants break that command on purpose, shrinking the ephah and enlarging the shekel to cheat the poor.

passages.saying: Though they dig down to Sheol, from there My hand will take them
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain sense of the verse's two extreme pictures, the deepest depth and the highest height.
layers.text: God warns that no one can escape His judgment. Even if people could dig down to the realm of the dead or climb up to heaven, His hand would reach them there and bring them down.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch judge that Amos most likely had Psalm 139:7-8 in mind here. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill both point to Psalm 139:8.
layers.text: In Psalm 139 David says that if he goes up to the heavens or makes his bed in Sheol, God is there. Amos likely has that psalm in mind, naming the same pair, Sheol and heaven, to show that no place, however high or deep, puts the guilty out of God's reach.

passages.saying: I will restore the fallen tent of David
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture of a fallen house that God raises and rebuilds.
layers.text: After the judgment, God promises to raise up David's royal house again. Though it has fallen into ruin, He will repair its broken walls, restore what was destroyed, and rebuild it as it was in the days of old.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words as in the days of old point back to God's promise in 2 Samuel 7:11-16 to build David a lasting house, and they contrast the hut with the palace David built. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown likewise notes that Amos says tent or booth, not house, to show how low the kingdom had fallen.
