layers.text: God had promised David a house and kingdom that would last forever. Amos pictures that royal house brought so low that it is only a fallen tent, a hut (sukkah) rather than a palace. God vows to rebuild it as in the days of old, which some read as pointing back to His promise to David.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Adam Clarke all note that James quotes this passage in Acts 15:16-17. Gill and the Companion Bible say the same.
layers.text: At the council in Jerusalem, James quotes this promise and the next verse (Acts 15:16-17). He shows that Gentiles turning to the Lord and being welcomed among God's people, without first being circumcised, fits what God said about rebuilding David's fallen tent.

passages.saying: the plowman will overtake the reaper
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain sense of the farming pictures in the verse.
layers.text: God promises a coming time of overflowing plenty. Harvests will be so large that plowing for the next crop starts before the reaping is done, and the grape harvest will run on into sowing time. Even the mountains and hills will seem to flow with sweet wine.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the verse is formed after Leviticus 26:5, with Amos moving the action to the workers. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the image is taken from that promise in the law. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it a fulfilment of Leviticus 26:5.
layers.text: In the law God promised that if Israel obeyed, threshing would last until the grape harvest and the grape harvest until sowing time. Amos takes up that blessing and makes it greater still: the workers themselves will catch up with one another, the plowman with the reaper.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the second half of the verse is taken from Joel 3:18. Gill also points to Joel 3:18.
layers.text: The promise that the mountains will drip with sweet wine repeats, almost word for word in Hebrew, a promise in Joel. Both prophets use the picture for the day when God restores His people and the land overflows with blessing.

passages.saying: I will restore My people Israel from captivity
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain sense of the restoration promise.
layers.text: God promises to restore His people. They will rebuild their ruined cities and live in them, plant vineyards and drink the wine, and make gardens and eat their fruit, enjoying the work of their own hands.

layers.evidence: Adam Clarke sets this promise against the threat of Amos 5:11, saying that after their restoration the people will labor for themselves. The Companion Bible also compares Amos 5:11.
layers.text: Earlier Amos warned the rich oppressors that they would plant lush vineyards but never drink their wine. Here God reverses that judgment for His restored people: they will plant vineyards and drink the wine themselves.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists Amos 9:14 among the passages where the Lord says He will turn the captivity of His people, and notes this use of two similar words.
layers.text: In Hebrew, the promise to restore the people from captivity is veshavti et-shevut, two similar-sounding words side by side: shavti (I will turn back) and shevut (captivity). The same ringing pair comes again and again in the Psalms and the prophets when God restores His people.

passages.saying: O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of Edom's high rocky home and its proud boast.
layers.text: Edom lived among high, rocky mountains that seemed impossible to attack, and its people grew proud and felt safe. God says that pride has fooled them, for no height will keep them from being brought down.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Petra, in Hebrew sela, meaning rock, was Edom's capital, with houses cut in the rocks. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Edom's chief city was called Selah or Petra, rock.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for rock here is sela. Sela, which means rock, was also the name of Edom's rock stronghold (2 Kings 14:7), often identified with Petra, whose Greek name also means rock. So the proud dwellers in the rocks may point to the people of Edom's famous rock city.

passages.saying: Because of the violence against your brother Jacob
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's stress on the brother tie between Edom and Jacob.
layers.text: Edom will be covered with shame and cut off forever because it did violence to Judah, the nation descended from Jacob, Edom's own brother. Wrong done to a brother is all the worse.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch trace Edom's hostility to Esau's hatred of Jacob in Genesis 27:41. Gill says the verse alludes to Esau's violence against Jacob. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Esau's descendants followed their father's hatred. The Companion Bible cites Genesis 27:41-44.
layers.text: Edom descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. Calling Judah your brother Jacob recalls the old grudge Esau held when he vowed to kill his brother Jacob. That family hatred lived on in Esau's descendants, who turned on Judah in its day of disaster.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) sets the verse beside God's command in Deuteronomy 23:7 not to abhor an Edomite, for he is a brother. The Companion Bible lists Deuteronomy 23:7 as a reference for this verse.
layers.text: The law told Israel, "Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother." Obadiah turns that same family tie against Edom. Israel was told to treat Edom as a brother, yet Edom did violence to its own brother Jacob.

passages.saying: the house of Jacob will be a blazing fire
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of fire consuming stubble, which Gill explains as Israel overcoming Edom with ease.
layers.text: Obadiah pictures the people of Jacob and Joseph as a fire and Edom, the house of Esau, as dry stubble. They will burn it up, and no one of Esau's house will survive, because the LORD has spoken.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible notes compare Numbers 24:19 for the same word for one who remains. Gill on Numbers 24:19 says it means none of Edom would be left, and points to Obadiah 1:18.
layers.text: The promise that "no survivor will remain from the house of Esau" may recall Balaam's prophecy about Edom in Numbers 24:18-19, where a ruler from Jacob would destroy the survivors. Both verses use the same Hebrew word for a survivor, sarid.

passages.saying: The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between Mount Zion and the mountains of Esau, and its closing promise of the LORD's kingdom.
layers.text: Rescuers from among God's people will go up to Mount Zion and rule over Edom's mountains. In the end the kingdom will belong to the LORD Himself.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the title of saviour was familiar from Judges 3:9 and 3:15. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes call them earthly deliverers as in Judges 3:9 and 3:15. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties them to the judges raised up as deliverers. Gill notes the judges were called saviours (Nehemiah 9:27).
layers.text: The deliverers who go up to Mount Zion recall the deliverers God raised up in the days of the judges, such as Othniel in Judges 3:9. The same Hebrew word, moshia (deliverer), names both. As He did then, God will again give His people rescuers.

passages.saying: In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two matching lines of calling and being heard, with Sheol as a picture of being near death.
layers.text: Jonah thanks God that in deep trouble, as near to death as if he were already in the grave, he cried out, and the LORD heard and answered him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the first clause recalls Psalm 120:1 (and Psalm 18:6), though freshly worded. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the psalmist thanked God in the same words, though in a different order.
layers.text: Jonah's opening line closely matches Psalm 120:1, "In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me." The same Hebrew words for distress, calling and answering appear in both, in a slightly different order. Jonah prays in the words of the psalms.

passages.saying: all Your breakers and waves swept over me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words You cast me and Your breakers, which make God the one behind the storm.
layers.text: Jonah says God threw him into the deep sea. The sailors did the throwing, but Jonah sees God's hand in it, and he calls the waves that rolled over him God's own waves.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the line seems borrowed from Psalm 42:7. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the sons of Korah used these self-same words. Keil and Delitzsch call it a reminiscence of the psalm (42:8 in Hebrew numbering), lived out literally by Jonah. Gill also says the prophet borrows the expressions.
layers.text: The words "all Your breakers and waves swept over me" repeat Psalm 42:7 exactly in Hebrew. The psalmist felt waves of trouble roll over him in spirit; Jonah felt them in the real sea, and he still calls them God's waves.

passages.saying: I have been banished from Your sight
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's turn from feeling banished to the word yet and a renewed look toward the temple.
layers.text: Sinking in the sea, Jonah thought God had driven him away from His care for good. Yet he resolved to look once more toward God's holy temple in prayer.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words come from Psalm 31:22 (31:23 in Hebrew), with nigrashti put in place of nigrazti. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Jonah substitutes a stronger word for David's I am cut off. Gill and Clarke also point to Psalm 31:22.
layers.text: Jonah's cry echoes David in Psalm 31:22, "I am cut off from Your sight!" The Hebrew verbs differ by one letter: David said nigrazti, cut off, and Jonah says nigrashti, driven out, a stronger word for being expelled.

passages.saying: The waters engulfed me to take my life
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's three pictures of the sea closing in: the waters, the deep and the seaweed.
layers.text: Jonah describes drowning. The water closed over him until his life was at stake, the deep surrounded him, and seaweed wrapped around his head.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the clause recalls Psalm 69:1 (69:2 in Hebrew), strengthened by a verb from Psalm 18:4. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says words that were figures of distress for others were realities for Jonah.
layers.text: Jonah's words borrow David's cry in Psalm 69:1, "the waters are up to my neck." Both say the waters came up to the nefesh, a word for the throat or the life. What David used as a picture of trouble, Jonah went through for real.

passages.saying: As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Gill explains that Jonah's prayer, prompted by remembering God's mercy, reached God and was answered.
layers.text: As Jonah sank toward death in the sea and his strength gave way, he turned his mind to the LORD. His prayer rose up and reached God in His temple.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Jonah 2:7 is formed after Psalm 142:4 (Hebrew numbering; 142:3 in English Bibles) or Psalm 143:4, with life in place of spirit because Jonah was drowning. Jonah 2:7 and Psalm 142:3 both open with behit'atef alay.
layers.text: Jonah's words "As my life was fading away" may borrow the Hebrew of Psalm 142:3 (behit'atef alay), where David says "my spirit grows faint within me." Psalm 143:4 says the same. If so, Jonah speaks of his life rather than his spirit, because he was sinking toward death in the sea.

passages.saying: Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Gill explains that idol worshippers forsake the God of their mercies.
layers.text: Jonah says that people who devote themselves to empty idols turn away from the loving devotion God would show them. In the next verse he sets himself apart from them by promising to thank and worship the LORD.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call Jonah's wording a reminiscence of Psalm 31 (their Hebrew verse 7; verse 6 in English Bibles). Both verses join the verb shamar, to keep or cling to, with havlei shav, worthless vanities.
layers.text: Some hear in the phrase "those who cling to worthless idols" an echo of the Hebrew of Psalm 31:6 (havlei shav, empty vanities), where David says he hates such people and trusts in the LORD. Jonah sets such people against himself: they forsake His loving devotion, but he will thank the LORD.

passages.saying: Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Jonah runs from God's call, is swallowed by a great fish, and finally preaches in Nineveh. The city repents and God spares it, to Jonah's anger.

layers.evidence: TBESH lists both senses of haphak. The Pulpit Commentary: the word used for the destruction of Sodom. BibleProject: it can also mean transformation, so Jonah's words came true, but not as he intended.
layers.text: "Overturned" is haphak, the verb used when God overthrew Sodom (BSB "destroyed"). But it can also mean to be turned or changed. Nineveh was overturned, just not as Jonah expected: it turned around.

layers.evidence: Gary Yates (JETS 2016) notes Jonah goes down (yarad) in 1:3, 1:5 and 2:6, a downward descent of disobedience to the brink of Sheol.
layers.text: The story moves step by step downward: Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into its hold, and down to the roots of the mountains, the same verb (yarad) each time, until God raises his life from the pit.

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Jonah 1:1: Jonah means dove. Maclaren: Jonah becomes a kind of representative of Israel.
layers.text: Jonah means "dove." Hosea calls the northern kingdom "a silly, senseless dove," and some readers see the runaway prophet as a picture of Israel itself.

Jesus names "the sign of the prophet Jonah": as Jonah was three days and three nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth. Nineveh repented, "and now One greater than Jonah is here."

Jonah sailed from Joppa to avoid preaching to Nineveh. Centuries later Peter, whom Jesus called "Simon son of Jonah" (John's Gospel has "son of John"), is staying in Joppa when God sends him to the Gentile Cornelius.

passages.saying: Who knows? God may turn and relent
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Clarke explains it as a hopeful perhaps that God may turn and spare them.
layers.text: The king of Nineveh orders fasting and prayer in the hope that God may yet hold back His anger and the judgment He announced, so the city will not perish. He has no promise, only hope in God's mercy.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the Ninevites use the same form of words that God gave Judah through Joel. Keil and Delitzsch note that yashuv venicham, turn and relent, stands as in Joel 2:14. Both verses open with mi yodea, who knows.
layers.text: The king's words, "Who knows? God may turn and relent," echo Joel 2:14, where the prophet calls Judah to repent: both open with the same four Hebrew words, mi yodea yashuv venicham. A pagan king voices the very hope God held out to His own people.

passages.saying: I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Gill explains that Jonah had foreseen the Ninevites would repent and be forgiven.
layers.text: Angry that Nineveh was spared, Jonah tells the LORD this is why he first ran toward Tarshish: he knew God's mercy would spare the city if it repented, and he did not want that.

layers.evidence: Gill and Bullinger say Jonah has in view God's proclamation in Exodus 34:6; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says he repeats to the letter God's words through Joel (Joel 2:13). Keil and Delitzsch compare both. Jonah 4:2 and Joel 2:13 share the same list, including relenting from disaster.
layers.text: Jonah recites God's own description of Himself, first proclaimed to Moses in Exodus 34:6, calling Him "a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion." Like Joel 2:13 he adds that "He relents from sending disaster." Words meant for praise become his complaint.

passages.saying: it grew up to provide shade over Jonah’s head to ease his discomfort
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Keil and Delitzsch explain that God made the plant grow miraculously fast to shade Jonah's head.
layers.text: While Jonah waited outside Nineveh, the LORD made a plant spring up quickly to shade his head and relieve his misery, and Jonah was very glad of it.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible marks a paronomasia, a play on similar sounds, between tzel, shade, and le-hatztzel, to deliver. The two words come from different roots but sound alike. The NET Bible notes suggest the narrator may have chosen the ambiguous consonants for a play on natsal, rescue, and tsalal, shade.
layers.text: The vine grew to be a shade (tsel) over Jonah's head, to deliver him (lehatsil) from his distress, here translated "to ease his discomfort." The two Hebrew words sound alike, and some see a deliberate play on them.

passages.saying: he grew faint and wished to die
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Gill explains that with the plant withered Jonah had no shelter from the sun.
layers.text: With the plant withered, God sent a scorching east wind, and the sun beat on Jonah's head until he grew faint. Once again he said he would rather die than live.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note that Jonah 4:8 uses the same Hebrew as 1 Kings 19:4, he asked that his soul might die. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) on 1 Kings 19:4 sets Elijah's request beside Jonah's. Both verses read vayyish'al et-nafsho lamut.
layers.text: When Jonah wished to die, the Hebrew is the very phrase used of Elijah under the broom tree in 1 Kings 19:4: literally, he asked that his soul might die. Both prophets asked to die, but Elijah was worn out and in despair, while Jonah was angry that God had spared Nineveh and taken his shade.

passages.saying: Roll in the dust in Beth-leaphrah.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Micah came from Moresheth in Judah's foothills. He mourns the towns around his home one by one as disaster, most likely an invading army, sweeps through them toward Jerusalem: it "has approached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem itself."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Beth-le'aphrah (H1036) and aphar, dust (H6083), in 1:10. TBESH gives the name as house belonging to Aphrah or house of dust. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, Ellicott, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and the Pulpit Commentary note the puns in Micah 1:10-15, though the sense of some is uncertain.
layers.text: Micah mourns town by town with puns on their names. Beth-leaphrah sounds like "house of dust," so its people must roll in the dust (aphar). English cannot keep these puns, and the sense of a few is uncertain, but the names echo the grief.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Akhziv (H0392) and akhzav (H0391) in 1:14; Mareshah (H4762) and hayyoresh, the one who takes possession (H3423), in 1:15. Jeremiah 15:18 uses akhzav for a stream that fails, rendered mirage.
layers.text: The puns run on. "The houses of Achzib will prove deceptive": Achzib (akhziv) will be akhzav, the word Jeremiah uses for a stream that fails, "water that is not there." To Mareshah God will bring "a conqueror," ha-yoresh, which echoes its name.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Micah 1:10 begat al-taggidu and 2 Samuel 1:20 al-taggidu begat use the same words, Gath (H1661) and tell (H5046), in reverse order. Some also hear a sound-play between gat and taggidu.
layers.text: Micah's lament for the towns opens, "Do not tell it in Gath," the words of David's lament for Saul and Jonathan: "Tell it not in Gath." Micah borrows David's famous funeral song to grieve for his own neighbors.

passages.saying: The dwellers of Zaanan will not come out.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's warning of exile and siege as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Micah warns that the people of Shaphir will be led into exile stripped and shamed. The people of Zaanan will stay shut inside their walls, and mourning Beth-ezel will be no support or shelter to anyone.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Bullinger's Companion Bible read these names as deliberate plays: Shaphir as beauty, Zaanan echoing yatsa (come out), Beth-ezel as the house beside or nearby. Gill also says Zaanan's not coming out alludes to its name.
layers.text: Each town is judged by its own name. Shaphir means beautiful, yet its people leave in shameful nakedness. Zaanan sounds like the word for come out, yet its people do not come out. Beth-ezel means house nearby, yet it cannot stand by its neighbors.

passages.saying: the dwellers of Maroth pined for good
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast of hoped-for good with calamity from the LORD.
layers.text: The people of Maroth longed anxiously for better days, but disaster sent by the LORD came instead, sweeping through the land until it reached the very gate of Jerusalem.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) gives Maroth as bitterness and says the town was probably chosen for its meaning; Bullinger's Companion Bible calls it Bitter town; Keil and Delitzsch give the name as bitternesses among the ten towns whose names are made into plays on words.
layers.text: Maroth means bitterness. The town called Bitterness longs for good, but calamity comes down from the LORD instead, so its bitter name comes true. The words good (tov) and calamity (ra) stand in sharp contrast.

passages.saying: Harness your chariot horses, O dweller of Lachish.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the call to flee and the charge that sin began at Lachish.
layers.text: Lachish is told to hitch its swift horses to its chariots and flee. This city was the first in Judah to take up the idolatry of the northern kingdom, and from there the sin spread to Jerusalem.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say rekesh is used as ringing with Lachish; Bullinger's Companion Bible marks larekesh and Lakish as a paronomasia, calling the city Horse-town.
layers.text: In Hebrew the word for the swift horses, rekesh, rings with the city's name, Lachish. The sound ties the town to the horses it must harness, not to ride out to battle but to run away from the enemy.

passages.saying: the houses of Achzib will prove deceptive to the kings of Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of Judah losing its towns to the invader.
layers.text: Judah will have to give up Moresheth-gath, Micah's home town, to the invader. The town of Achzib will fail Israel's kings who depended on it, like a stream that runs dry.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Bullinger's Companion Bible all explain Achzib as a lie or false town that will prove false. Keil and Delitzsch, Gill and Clarke also note the play between Achzib and akhzav.
layers.text: Achzib sounds like akhzav, a deceitful thing, a word used for a brook that dries up in summer. The town with the deceitful name will live up to it, failing the kings who looked to it for help just when they needed it.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the picture rests on the sound of Moresheth and the word for the betrothed, and that the gifts are like a father's gift to a married daughter. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) also reads them as bridal gifts with which a daughter was sent away for good.
layers.text: The farewell gifts may be the dowry a father sent with a daughter leaving home to marry. Some hear in Moresheth the Hebrew for a betrothed bride: Judah would give up Micah's home town like a bride sent away to another, never to return.

passages.saying: I will again bring a conqueror against you, O dweller of Mareshah.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's threat of a conqueror and flight to Adullam.
layers.text: God will bring a conqueror to take possession of Mareshah. The glory of Israel, its leading men, will be driven to Adullam, a place where fugitives hid.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Micah names Adullam because of its cave, a refuge for Israel's great men; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the name recalled David's cave of refuge; Bullinger's Companion Bible says the nobles would flee there as David had done (1 Samuel 22:1).
layers.text: Adullam recalls the cave where David hid when he was running for his life. Israel's glory, likely its nobles, will again take refuge there, just as David once did.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) all see a play between Mareshah, inheritance, and the heir or possessor God brings. Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, and Bullinger's Companion Bible say the same.
layers.text: Mareshah sounds like the Hebrew for possession or inheritance, and God will bring against it hayyoresh, the one who takes possession. So the town whose name echoes possession will itself be taken over by a new owner, the conqueror.

passages.saying: taunt you with this bitter lamentation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's mocking proverb and the people's own lament over lost fields.
layers.text: When judgment comes, the people will be mocked with a song of mourning. They will cry that they are ruined, because God has taken away their land and handed their fields to their enemies.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the word divideth was the more bitter because it reversed the first division of the land at the entrance into Canaan, citing the same word in Numbers 26:53 and in Joshua.
layers.text: The word for allotting the fields here is chalaq, the same Hebrew verb used when God had the land of Canaan divided among Israel's tribes. Some see that first division turned around here: the land once divided to Israel is divided to their enemies.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible marks venahah nehi nihyah as polyptoton and paronomasia; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the repetition represents the continuous wail; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the words are varied forms of a word imitating sounds of woe. Bullinger's Figures of Speech also lists it as a lamentation of lamentations.
layers.text: In Hebrew the bitter lamentation is three echoing words: nahah, nehi, nihyah, a wail upon a wail. The repeated sound imitates a long, steady cry of grief over the land being lost.

passages.saying: Do not preach these things; disgrace will not overtake us.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the speakers' own words in the verse, which commentators read as a command to silence God's prophets.
layers.text: False prophets, speaking for people who wanted only pleasant messages, ordered God's true prophets to stop preaching judgment. They insisted that disgrace would never overtake them.

layers.evidence: JFB says the similarity of sound and word shows God taking the people at their own word. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes the word is literally drop not and that God recites their ban back to them. Clarke renders it do not cause it to rain.
layers.text: The Hebrew verb for preach here is nataf, to drip, picturing words falling like rain. It comes three times in one breath: do not drip, they drip, do not drip. Some read the repetition as turning the people's own word back on them, as God takes them at their word.

passages.saying: Arise and depart, for this is not your place of rest
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the command to leave and the reason given, the land's defilement.
layers.text: Micah tells the people to get up and go, because the land will no longer be their place of rest. Their sin has defiled it, and that defilement will bring severe destruction and exile.

layers.evidence: Keil says the verse builds on Deuteronomy 12:9-10, where entering Canaan is pictured as coming to rest. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) quotes that passage, JFB cites Deuteronomy 12:9, and the Companion Bible marks a reference to it.
layers.text: The word for rest, menuchah, is the word Moses used for the promised land: the resting place and the inheritance God was giving Israel. Micah turns that promise around. The people had defiled the land, so it would no longer be their rest.

passages.saying: he would be just the preacher for this people!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast between the rejected true prophets and the welcome liar.
layers.text: The people silence God's true prophets, yet if a lying windbag came promising them plenty of wine and strong drink, they would welcome him gladly. That is the kind of preacher they want.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Micah uses the same word the scorners used when they said drop not. Gill calls the false prophet a dropper and points back to 2:6. The Companion Bible reads it literally as dropper of words, as in 2:6.
layers.text: Preacher here is again the drip word, nataf. In verse 6 the people told God's prophets not to drip. Now Micah says a liar who would drip about wine and strong drink would be just the dripper for them. Their own word is turned back on them.

layers.evidence: JFB notes the Hebrew for spirit also means wind: a man professing the spirit of inspiration but really walking in wind. Gill gives both readings of the word, a man pretending to the Spirit of God or one who walks with the wind and is full of wind and vanity.
layers.text: The Hebrew word ruach means both wind and spirit. Some read a double edge here: such a man claims to speak by the Spirit, but he only walks in wind, and his message is as empty as air.

passages.saying: each man will sit under his own vine and under his own fig tree
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the familiar picture of sitting at ease under one's own vine and fig tree.
layers.text: In the last days God's people will live in peace and plenty, each family safe at home with no one to make them afraid. This is sure because the LORD Himself has promised it.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says this had been Israel's lot in the peaceful days of Solomon, citing 1 Kings 4:25. Gill calls it a proverbial phrase for security and points to the same verse, as JFB also does.
layers.text: This picture echoes the words used of Solomon's reign, when Judah and Israel dwelt securely, each man under his own vine and his own fig tree. Micah promises that settled peace again, and more, when the LORD reigns over the nations in the last days.

passages.saying: And you, O watchtower of the flock
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the promise that the former dominion will return to the Daughter of Zion.
layers.text: Micah speaks to Zion as the watchtower of God's flock and the stronghold of Jerusalem. He promises that the kingdom it once had under David will be given back to it.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says the name refers back to Genesis 35:21, its only other use, and is used here of Bethlehem. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Jacob fed his sheep there, near Bethlehem. JFB and Clarke prefer to read the tower as Jerusalem itself.
layers.text: Watchtower of the flock is Migdal-eder in Hebrew, a name found elsewhere only in Genesis 35:21, where Jacob pitched his tent beyond the Tower of Eder, near Bethlehem, after burying Rachel. Some see the name tying Zion's restored kingdom to Bethlehem, the town Micah names in 5:2.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the name Tower of Ader is interpreted tower of the flock. JFB gives Eder as the Hebrew for flock and describes the high towers built in large pastures to oversee the flock. Gill gives the Hebrew words Migdal Eder and speaks of a shepherd's tower where the shepherds watch.
layers.text: Watchtower of the flock translates the Hebrew name Migdal-eder: migdal means tower and eder means flock. Shepherds built such towers in open pasture to watch over their sheep, so the name pictures watchful care over God's flock.

passages.saying: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the promise of a Ruler from Bethlehem, which Matthew 2:6 quotes as fulfilled in Jesus.
layers.text: Micah foretells that Israel's Ruler will come from Bethlehem, a town too small to count among Judah's clans, yet His origins reach back to eternity. Matthew 2:6 shows this fulfilled in the birth of Jesus.

layers.evidence: Keil says Micah most probably alluded to God's word to Samuel in 1 Samuel 16:1, to show David as a type of the Messiah. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) links the words to Me with the same verse, where God provided Himself a king among the sons of Jesse of Bethlehem.
layers.text: The words for Me likely echo God's choice of David. God sent Samuel to Jesse of Bethlehem, saying, "I have selected from his sons a king for Myself." As God once chose David from little Bethlehem, He would raise up David's greater Son from the same town.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says going forth is set against going forth: one out of Bethlehem, one from eternity. JFB calls it a plain antithesis to come forth out of thee. Keil notes the word for goings forth corresponds to the verb come forth earlier in the verse.
layers.text: Micah uses the Hebrew root yatsa, to go out, twice. The Ruler will come forth (yetse) from little Bethlehem, yet His origins, literally His goings forth (motsaot), are from the days of eternity. One going forth is His birth in time; the other reaches back into eternity.

layers.evidence: JFB, Gill and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) all give Bethlehem as house of bread and Ephrathah as fruitful. Gill calls it a proper birthplace for Christ, the bread of life. Keil gives the same meanings, and Wesley derives Ephrathah from fruitfulness.
layers.text: Bethlehem means house of bread, and Ephrathah means fruitful. Both names speak of the fertile fields around the town. Believers have long found it fitting that Jesus, the bread of life, was born in the house of bread.

passages.saying: until she who is in labor has given birth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the link with the Ruler from Bethlehem in the verse before.
layers.text: God would give Israel over to its enemies until the mother of the promised Ruler gave birth to Him. After that, the rest of His brothers would return and be joined with the children of Israel.

layers.evidence: Keil says Micah could speak of this because Isaiah had already foretold the Messiah's birth in Isaiah 7:14. JFB names the virgin mother of Isaiah 7:14, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) the Virgin who would bear Immanuel.
layers.text: She who is in labor points back to Isaiah, Micah's fellow prophet, who foretold that the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son. Israel would be given up until the mother of the promised Ruler from Bethlehem gave birth to Him.

passages.saying: the land of Nimrod with the blade drawn
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's shepherd picture: those who shepherd God's people will overcome the invader.
layers.text: Micah promises that the shepherd-leaders raised up against the invader will rule Assyria and the land of Nimrod with the sword. When the enemy marches into Judah's land, it is the coming Ruler, the true Shepherd, who will deliver His people.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the land is called after Nimrod, founder of the first empire (Genesis 10), to show its hostility to God's kingdom. The Companion Bible, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), JFB, Clarke and Gill also tie the phrase to Nimrod's kingdom in Genesis 10, though they differ on whether it means Assyria or Babylon.
layers.text: The land of Nimrod points back to Genesis 10, where Nimrod the mighty hunter founded the first kingdom, beginning at Babylon. Whether Micah means Assyria itself or Babylon beside it, the name marks Israel's foes as heirs of that first proud empire set against God.

passages.saying: remember what Balak king of Moab counseled
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the setting: God is answering His people's complaint by recalling His past kindness.
layers.text: In His case against His people, God asks them to remember how He protected them on the way into the promised land. If they recall it, they will see that the LORD has always acted rightly and faithfully toward them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch point to Numbers 22 to 24, where Balak's plan to destroy Israel through Balaam's curses was frustrated. Clarke says Balaam was sent for to curse but was made to bless; JFB cites Numbers 22:5; the Companion Bible and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) also refer to the Balaam account.
layers.text: God points His people back to Numbers 22 to 24. Balak king of Moab sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel, but God would not let him, and every curse came out as a blessing. It was a rescue Israel had done nothing to earn.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call Shittim Israel's last camp beyond the Jordan and Gilgal the first camp in Canaan (Joshua 4:19-20). Clarke sees a reference to the miraculous crossing of the Jordan; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and JFB also describe Gilgal as the first camp in the promised land.
layers.text: From Shittim to Gilgal sums up the last stage of the journey. Shittim, where Israel sinned with Moab, was their last camp east of the Jordan. Gilgal was their first camp in the land, reached after God stopped the river so they could cross on dry ground (Joshua 3 and 4).

passages.saying: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the answer to the people's question in verses 6 and 7 about what offerings would please God.
layers.text: The people had asked what costly offering would please God. The answer is that God had already told them: deal fairly with others, love showing kindness and faithfulness, and live in humble fellowship with Him.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says God had shown this when He said through Moses what He required of Israel, quoting Deuteronomy 10:12-13. JFB compares Deuteronomy 10:12, and Keil and Delitzsch note the same turn of phrase as in Deuteronomy 10:12.
layers.text: Micah's question, "what does the LORD require of you", echoes Moses in Deuteronomy 10:12: "what does the LORD your God ask of you". God had already shown His people what is good in His law, so they had no need to ask what sacrifice would buy His favor.

passages.saying: You will sow but not reap
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's place in the threatened punishment of verses 13 to 16.
layers.text: Because of their dishonesty and violence, the people will lose the fruit of their work. They will plant, press olives and tread grapes, but invaders and hard times will take the harvest, the oil and the wine before they can enjoy them.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Micah renews the threats of the law (Leviticus 26:16; Deuteronomy 28:38-41). JFB and the Companion Bible point to Deuteronomy 28:38-40, and Keil and Delitzsch say the words about not anointing with oil are taken verbatim from Deuteronomy 28:40.
layers.text: These losses repeat the covenant curses Moses warned of in Deuteronomy 28:38 to 40: sowing much but harvesting little, planting vineyards but drinking no wine, and having olive trees but no oil to anoint with. Micah even uses Moses' own Hebrew words for not anointing with oil.

passages.saying: The day for rebuilding your walls will come
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the address to Zion that follows her confession of sin and hope in God in verses 8 to 10.
layers.text: After judgment, God promises Jerusalem a day of restoration. Her broken walls will be built again, and on that day her boundary will be extended. The next verse tells of people coming to her from distant lands.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the figure Paronomasia (a play on like-sounding words) in yir'chok here. Keil and Delitzsch say the verb for being far was chosen for the sake of its assonance with choq. The two differ on whether choq means a boundary or an ordinance.
layers.text: The verse ends with two Hebrew words that sound alike: yirchaq, it will be far, and choq, a set limit or boundary. The echo makes the promise ring out: on the day Zion's walls are rebuilt, the old limit will be pushed far away.

passages.saying: As in the days when you came out of Egypt
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse as the LORD's answer to the prayer of verse 14.
layers.text: The LORD answers the prayer for His flock. Just as He worked mighty miracles when He brought Israel out of Egypt, He promises to work wonders again to rescue His people.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch link the wonders (niphla'oth) to Exodus 3:20 and 15:11, the wonders with which the Lord struck Egypt. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the word is used especially of the miracles of the deliverance from Egypt, citing Exodus 3:20.
layers.text: The word for wonders here is the one God used when He promised to strike Egypt "with all the wonders I will perform among them" (Exodus 3:20). The plagues and the sea crossing become the pattern for the rescue still to come.

passages.saying: They will lick the dust like a snake
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of the nations' complete humbling before God in verses 16 and 17.
layers.text: The nations that opposed God's people will be utterly humbled. Like snakes and crawling things driven from their holes, they will come trembling out of their strongholds and turn in fear to the LORD.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call licking the dust like the serpent an allusion to Genesis 3:14. Gill ties it to the curse on the serpent, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says it pictures those who share the serpent's doom, and the Companion Bible also cites Genesis 3:14.
layers.text: Licking the dust like a snake recalls God's curse on the serpent in Eden: "dust you will eat, all the days of your life." The nations that fought against God's people will share the humbling of that cursed serpent.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Micah's crawlers of the earth recalls the crawlers of the dust in Deuteronomy 32:24. The Companion Bible gives Deuteronomy 32:24 as a reference using the same word, and JFB also cites it.
layers.text: Micah's word for "reptiles slithering on the ground" is the word Moses used in his song for "vipers that slither in the dust" (Deuteronomy 32:24). The humbled nations are pictured as snakes crawling in the dust.

passages.saying: Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's string of praises, each naming something God does with sin.
layers.text: Micah closes his book in praise. No god compares with the LORD, who forgives the sins of the remnant He calls His own, does not stay angry forever, and delights to show steadfast love.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words are formed after Exodus 34:6-7, where God revealed Himself after the golden calf. The Companion Bible gives Exodus 34:7 as the reference, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the praise is taken from God's revelation of Himself after that great transgression at Sinai.
layers.text: The words "who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression" echo what God proclaimed to Moses after the golden calf: "forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin" (Exodus 34:7). Micah praises the same pardoning God who forgave Israel at Sinai.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the question looks back to Exodus 15:11 and contrast God's unmatched exaltation then with His unmatched grace now. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Moses made the like appeal to God after the deliverance at the Red Sea.
layers.text: "Who is a God like You" echoes the song Moses sang after the Red Sea: "Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?" (Exodus 15:11). There God was praised as unmatched in power over Egypt; here He is praised as unmatched in mercy toward sinners.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Micah identified his own name with this praise, his name being the herald of his message: who is like the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch think a play on the prophet's name is doubtful.
layers.text: The name Micah means Who is like the LORD? His book closes with nearly the same question, Who is a God like You? Some see the prophet's own name echoed here as the heart of his message: no one is like the LORD, who pardons sin.

passages.saying: You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture of sin trodden down and sunk in the sea, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: God will have compassion on His people again. He will tread down their iniquities and throw all their sins into the deep sea, forgiving them so fully that they never rise again.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch compare this to God drowning Pharaoh in the depths of the sea (Exodus 15:5, 10); E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says that as not one Egyptian was left at the Red Sea, so not one sin will be left. Both verses use metsulot, depths.
layers.text: The depths of the sea recall the Red Sea, where Pharaoh's army went down into the depths like a stone (Exodus 15:5), and the Hebrew word for depths is the same. As not one pursuer rose again, God will sink His people's sins for good.

passages.saying: as You swore to our fathers from the days of old
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's link between God's faithfulness and His promises to the patriarchs.
layers.text: Micah closes his book sure that God will keep faith with Jacob and show loyal love to Abraham, keeping the promises He made to the patriarchs long ago.

layers.evidence: Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both point to the oath of Genesis 22:16; Gill says it confirmed the promises of Abraham's many offspring, of the land and of the Messiah. Both verses use the verb shava, swear.
layers.text: The oath to the fathers looks back to Genesis 22:16-18, where, after Abraham offered Isaac, God swore by Himself to bless him and to bless all nations through his offspring. Micah's hope rests on that sworn promise.

passages.saying: The LORD is a jealous and avenging God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's repeated titles for God as jealous and avenging, as the commentaries explain them.
layers.text: Nahum begins his message against Nineveh by declaring that the LORD guards His honor and His people with jealous love, and that He will surely repay His enemies, keeping wrath in store for them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Nahum opens with the words God used of His holiness in the Ten Commandments; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Bullinger also point to Exodus 20:5, and JFB compares it. Nahum's qanno is a form of the word qanna, jealous, used in Exodus.
layers.text: Calling the LORD a jealous God echoes the Ten Commandments, where He says, "I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5). The jealous love that guards His people now turns against Nineveh, their oppressor.

passages.saying: The LORD is slow to anger and great in power
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's pairing of God's patience with His power to punish.
layers.text: God's patience is not weakness. He is slow to anger yet mighty, and He will not let the guilty go free. Storm and whirlwind are His path, and the clouds are like dust under His feet.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch trace slow to anger to Exodus 34:6 and not leaving unpunished to Exodus 34:7; JFB cites Exodus 34:6-7, and Bullinger calls it a reference to the Pentateuch. Both verses use the doubled verb naqah, acquit.
layers.text: These words come from God's own description of Himself to Moses: slow to anger, yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished (Exodus 34:6-7). Even the doubled Hebrew verb, naqqeh lo yenaqqeh, is the same. Nahum holds both truths together: God is patient, yet He punishes.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Nahum takes up Jonah's words about God's attributes toward Nineveh to show their other side; Bullinger also compares Jonah 4:2. Both verses read erekh appayim, slow to anger.
layers.text: Jonah complained that God was slow to anger when He spared Nineveh (Jonah 4:2). Nahum uses the same words about the same city, and some read this as a deliberate echo: God's patience has an end, and Nineveh's guilt will now be punished.

passages.saying: He rebukes the sea and dries it up
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of nature failing before God, which the commentaries apply to Nineveh.
layers.text: The LORD rules all creation. At His rebuke seas and rivers dry up, and even the rich lands of Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon wither. If nature cannot stand before Him, neither can Nineveh.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch see an allusion to the drying up of the Red Sea, citing Psalm 106:9, where God rebuked the Red Sea and it dried up; Gill says He did this at the Red Sea; Bullinger refers it to Exodus 14; Clarke and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) agree.
layers.text: God rebuking the sea and drying it up recalls the Red Sea, which He pushed back with a strong wind to make dry land for Israel (Exodus 14:21). The God who did that for His people can surely bring down Nineveh.

layers.evidence: Clarke sees an allusion to the Red Sea and the Jordan; Gill and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) both name the Jordan crossing, and Bullinger compares Joshua 4:23.
layers.text: The rivers running dry recall the Jordan, which the LORD dried up so Israel could cross into the land, just as He had done at the Red Sea (Joshua 4:23).

passages.saying: the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to Judah after the enemy's defeat, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Messengers hurry over the mountains to Judah with good news: the Assyrian oppressor is cut off. Judah can celebrate its feasts and keep its vows again, for the wicked will never again invade it.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, JFB, Keil and Delitzsch and Bullinger all link this verse to Isaiah 52:7, though they differ on which prophet echoes the other. Both verses use the same Hebrew words for feet, bringing good news (mevasser), proclaiming and peace (shalom).
layers.text: Isaiah uses the same picture in nearly the same Hebrew words: "How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news" (Isaiah 52:7). Here the news is Nineveh's fall; in Isaiah it is God's reign and salvation.

passages.saying: She is emptied! Yes, she is desolate and laid waste!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of the plundered city and its terrified people.
layers.text: Nineveh is stripped bare, emptied of people and treasure and left in ruins, while those inside melt with fear. Knees shake, bodies tremble, and every face goes pale.

layers.evidence: Bullinger notes the expression occurs only here and in Joel 2:6 and holds that Nahum refers to Joel. Both verses read qibbetsu pa'rur, using the same rare word for the glow that drains from the face.
layers.text: The closing words, every face grows pale, use a Hebrew expression found only here and in Joel 2:6, where nations turn pale before the army of the day of the LORD. The terror Joel described now falls on Nineveh.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it an elegant play on words; Clarke says the words share a sound and grow longer as the desolation grows; JFB notes the rising syllables; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Bullinger, who names it paronomasia, agree.
layers.text: The opening cry is three Hebrew words that sound alike and grow longer each time: buqah, mevuqah, mevullaqah, meaning emptiness, desolation and devastation. The echoing, swelling sounds make Nineveh's ruin feel complete.

passages.saying: all who see you will recoil from you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself read with verse 6, as Gill explains the onlookers' horror and the lack of mourners.
layers.text: After God exposes and shames Nineveh, everyone who sees the ruined city will turn away in horror. No one will grieve for her or comfort her, because her cruelty to others has earned her this end.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Nahum had Isaiah 51:19 before his mind; Keil and Delitzsch note the same words are used there of Jerusalem. Both verses ask who will grieve (yanud) and speak of comforting (nacham).
layers.text: Nahum's questions echo Isaiah 51:19, spoken over suffering Jerusalem: "Who will grieve for you? Who can comfort you?" Now the same questions fall on Nineveh, the city that had crushed others, and no one will mourn her.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say ro'ayikh, those who see you, in verse 7 contains a play upon ro'i, spectacle, in verse 6. Both come from the verb ra'ah, to see.
layers.text: In verse 6 God says He will make Nineveh a spectacle, in Hebrew ro'i, something to stare at. Verse 7 names the onlookers with a word from the same root, ro'ayikh, those who see you. The city becomes a sight, and everyone who sees it runs away.

passages.saying: makes himself rich with many loans
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse in its setting, the nations gathered by the Chaldean in verse 5, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain.
layers.text: The nations the Babylonians conquered will one day mock their conqueror. They will pronounce woe on the one who grew rich on what was never his, piling up other people's goods like a lender hoarding pledges, and ask how long it can last.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Habakkuk follows Isaiah 14:4 in his wording, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the opening words carry the mind back to Isaiah. Both verses speak of lifting up (nasa) a mashal, a taunt, against Babylon's ruler.
layers.text: The taunt the nations take up recalls Isaiah 14:4, where God's people are told, "you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon." Habakkuk uses the same Hebrew wording, lifting up a mashal, and aims it at the same proud empire.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain that avtit, found only here, means a mass of pledges but, heard aloud, can be taken as two words, av tit, a mass of dirt, and count it among the riddles this verse mentions. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the word translated thick clay, as if it were two words, also means a strong pledge.
layers.text: The word for many loans, avtit, appears only here and means a heap of pledges. Heard aloud it can also sound like two words, av tit, a thick mass of mud, which is why older English Bibles say thick clay. Read that way, the plunderer's hoard is a heavy load of dirt that will bring him down.

passages.saying: Will not your creditors suddenly arise
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) stresses the suddenness of the judgment.
layers.text: The one who plundered the nations will be caught off guard. Those he wronged will suddenly rise up against him and shake him from his place, so that the plunderer becomes plunder himself.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call it a double meaning: biters who come to demand interest (neshek). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) note that bite is the word used of charging interest, and Gill gives the rendering usurers or creditors. The root is nashakh, to bite.
layers.text: The word for your creditors, noshekhekha, literally means those who bite you, and the same root gives neshek, the Hebrew word for interest on a loan. The conqueror who squeezed the nations like a cruel moneylender will meet lenders who bite back and demand it all with interest.

passages.saying: the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse as the reason for the woe on cities built with blood, as Keil and Delitzsch explain.
layers.text: God promises that proud empires built on bloodshed will come to nothing, and in their place the whole world will come to know the LORD's glory. That knowledge will cover the earth as completely as water covers the sea.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the thought is formed after Isaiah 11:9 with small changes; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say it is adapted from Isaiah 11:9; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Habakkuk embodies Isaiah's words. Gill and Clarke also point to Isaiah 11:9. Both verses use male, to fill, and kasah, to cover.
layers.text: Habakkuk repeats Isaiah 11:9 almost word for word in Hebrew: "the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water." He adds the word glory: the LORD's glory will be known everywhere once proud Babylon falls.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a reference to Numbers 14:21, the first place this promise appears; Keil and Delitzsch call Numbers 14:21 the primary passage. Both verses use male, fill, and kavod, glory.
layers.text: Behind this promise stands God's oath in Numbers 14:21, spoken as He judged unbelieving Israel in the wilderness: "as surely as the whole earth is filled with the glory of the LORD." Habakkuk shows that same glory made known as God judges Babylon.

passages.saying: utter disgrace will cover your glory
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the image of the cup passed from hand to hand, as E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains.
layers.text: The conqueror who made the nations drunk so he could gloat over their shame will now drink the cup of judgment from the LORD's own hand. The glory he sought will be buried under disgrace.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the rare form qiqalon was chosen for the play on qi qalon, vomit of shame, so that hearers would catch the second sense, since heavy drinking ends in vomiting.
layers.text: The verse opens with shame, qalon, in place of glory and closes with a rare word for utter disgrace, qiqalon. Some hear in qiqalon a hint of qi qalon, vomit of shame. The one who got others drunk ends up drunk on God's cup, his glory covered with his own disgrace.

passages.saying: he makes idols that cannot speak
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain.
layers.text: An idol is worthless, however skillfully it is carved or cast. It teaches only lies, and the man who made it is foolish to trust in his own handiwork, for he can make an idol but cannot make it speak.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible names this a paronomasia: elilim illemim, nothings that say nothing. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the pair under Paronomasia, or rhyming words. Clarke likewise renders the phrase dumb nothings.
layers.text: The closing words, idols that cannot speak, are elilim illemim in Hebrew, two words that sound almost alike. Elilim, a scornful word for idols, suggests nothings, and illemim means mute. Some hear a deliberate jingle mocking them as nothings that say nothing.

passages.saying: let all the earth be silent before Him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast with the dumb idols of 2:18-19, which Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke draw out.
layers.text: After mocking idols that cannot speak, Habakkuk turns to the living God. The LORD reigns from His holy temple in heaven, and the whole earth should fall silent before Him in awe and submission.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) on this verse: these are the words with which David, in Psalm 11:4, sets God on His throne in heaven against the oppression of man. Hebrew be-heikhal qodsho, in His holy temple, stands in both verses.
layers.text: "The LORD is in His holy temple" are also David's words in Psalm 11:4, where the LORD watches from His heavenly throne while the wicked seem to prevail. Some see Habakkuk echoing them, meeting the violence of Babylon and its idols with the same confidence.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13 say the command is formed after Habakkuk 2:20; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) on Zephaniah 1:7 says it was renewed from Habakkuk; Gill on Zechariah 2:13 notes the like phrase, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible cross-refer. Hebrew has, hush, stands in all three.
layers.text: The word for "be silent" here is has, a one-word "Hush!" The same hush returns in Zephaniah, "Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD," and in Zechariah, "Be silent before the LORD, all people." Some commentators think the later prophets took up Habakkuk's word.

passages.saying: God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's place names, which Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reads as an appeal to God's glory shown at Sinai.
layers.text: Habakkuk pictures God coming from the south, from Teman and Mount Paran, the desert lands south of Judah. His splendor covers the sky and the earth is full of His praise. He is the same God who came to His people long ago.

layers.evidence: Gill says Deuteronomy 33:2 is the passage alluded to; Keil and Delitzsch say the opening has its roots in the song of Moses; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Habakkuk renews its imagery; the Companion Bible marks a reference to it. Both verses use bo, came, and name Paran.
layers.text: "God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran" echoes Moses' blessing: "The LORD came from Sinai" and "He shone forth from Mount Paran." Habakkuk recalls God coming in glory to give the law, and looks for Him to come again to save His people.

passages.saying: the ancient mountains crumbled; the perpetual hills collapsed
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of God halting to survey the earth, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains it.
layers.text: God takes His stand and surveys the earth, and at His look the nations startle. Even the oldest mountains and hills, which seemed unmovable, give way before Him, for His ways are everlasting.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch compare God coming down on Sinai, when the mountains shook (Judges 5:5); Clarke says it may refer to the quaking of Sinai (Exodus 19:18); Gill compares Sinai too, though he prefers a figurative reading of kingdoms.
layers.text: The mountains giving way recall Sinai, where "the whole mountain quaked violently" when the LORD came down, and Deborah's song: "The mountains quaked before the LORD, the One of Sinai." As God shook the mountains then, so He will at His coming.

passages.saying: Were You angry at the rivers, O LORD?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the phrase chariots of salvation, which Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes as the implied answer.
layers.text: Habakkuk asks whether God's anger burned against the rivers and the sea when He rode out with His horses and chariots. The answer is no: His chariots are chariots of salvation, and He rode out to rescue His people.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch tie the verse to the dividing of the Red Sea and the Jordan; Clarke and Wesley name the Red Sea, and Gill gives both. Keil and Delitzsch add that the picture reaches beyond them to God judging the world. Yam, sea, is in both verses.
layers.text: The rivers and the sea recall Israel's two great crossings: the Red Sea, when "the LORD drove back the sea," and the Jordan, when "the flowing water stood still." Read this way, God was not angry with the waters; He parted them to bring His people through.

passages.saying: The mountains saw You and quaked
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's personified mountains and deep, as Clarke explains them.
layers.text: When God appears, the mountains writhe as if in pain, torrents of water sweep past, and the deep roars and lifts its waves like hands raised high. All creation reacts to His presence.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Psalm 77:16 call the psalm the primary passage that Habakkuk reworked, noting the same verb for writhing and the reshaped line about water. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on this verse and Barnes on Psalm 77:16 cross-refer the two passages.
layers.text: "The mountains saw You and quaked" may follow Asaph's song of the Exodus: "The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and swirled." Both say ra'ukha, they saw You, and yachilu, they writhed. Asaph's poured down water (zormu mayim) may lie behind Habakkuk's torrents (zerem mayim).

passages.saying: Sun and moon stood still in their places
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the battle picture of God's arrows and spear, as the Companion Bible renders it.
layers.text: As God goes out to battle like a warrior, the sun and moon halt in their places, while His arrows fly like light and His spear flashes like lightning.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible point to Joshua 10:12-13, and amad, stood still, is in both. Gill says it is generally taken so, but he and Keil and Delitzsch read instead that sun and moon withdrew from sight.
layers.text: "Sun and moon stood still in their places" recalls Joshua's long day at Gibeon, when "the sun stood still and the moon stopped" until Israel won. Most older commentators read it this way; some take it instead as sun and moon hiding their light before God's flashing weapons.

passages.saying: You trampled the sea with Your horses
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of God's horses crossing the sea, which E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains.
layers.text: God is pictured as a warrior driving His horses straight through the sea and the heaving mass of great waters. What stands in His people's way becomes His road to rescue them.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) hears Asaph's His path in the sea (Psalm 77:19); Keil and Delitzsch on Psalm 77 note that Habakkuk sends God's horses through its great waters; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Psalm 77:19; Gill and Clarke see the Red Sea crossing. Hebrew bayyam, in the sea, and mayim rabbim, great waters, stand in both verses.
layers.text: "You trampled the sea with Your horses" recalls the Red Sea, where God made a road for Israel. Asaph sang, "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters," and Habakkuk uses the same Hebrew for sea and for great or mighty waters, yam and mayim rabbim.

passages.saying: He makes my feet like those of a deer
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the deer image, which Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains as God-given swiftness and safety.
layers.text: Even facing loss and invasion, Habakkuk ends in trust. The Lord God is his strength, and He makes him sure-footed and swift like a deer, able to stand safely on the high places.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch say the verse is drawn from Psalm 18 (Keil and Delitzsch use the Hebrew number, 18:34). Keil and Delitzsch add that Habakkuk changed David's verb to darakh, tread, after Deuteronomy 33:29, which the Companion Bible also cites.
layers.text: "He makes my feet like those of a deer" is David's line in Psalm 18:33, nearly word for word. David says God "stations me upon the heights"; Habakkuk says He makes me walk, or tread, on them, the verb of Moses' blessing: "you shall trample their high places."

passages.saying: I will completely sweep away everything from the face of the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain wording, which heads the chapter's warnings of judgment.
layers.text: The LORD declares that He will sweep away everything from the face of the earth. This opening line sums up the judgment that the rest of the chapter goes on to describe.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible calls asoph aseph a paronomasia for emphasis, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech glosses the pair as to end, I end; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the two words are conformed in sound and blend their meanings; Keil and Delitzsch explain that one form comes from asaph and the other from suph, verbs of kindred meaning.
layers.text: The opening words are asoph aseph. They sound nearly the same but come from two different verbs, one meaning to gather or take away and the other meaning to bring to an end. Together they say God will take away and make a full end, and the echo drives the warning home.

passages.saying: I will sweep away man and beast
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own list, which spells out the everything of verse 2.
layers.text: God lists what the sweeping judgment will reach: people and animals, birds and fish, and the idols together with those who worship them. Mankind itself will be cut off from the land.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the list stands in unmistakable relation to God's threat in Genesis 6:7, and that by playing on it Zephaniah shows the judgment will be as general and terrible as the flood.
layers.text: Naming man, beast, and birds, and cutting off mankind from the face of the earth, echoes God's words before the flood in Genesis 6:7. The echo signals that this judgment will be as sweeping and as terrible as the flood.

passages.saying: swear by the LORD but also swear by Milcom
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of two kinds of false worship.
layers.text: Judgment will fall on those who worship the stars from their flat rooftops and on those who swear loyalty to the LORD while also swearing by an idol. God will not share His people's devotion with a false god.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch both read malkam as their king; the Companion Bible glosses it king-god or king-idol and notes the Syriac and Vulgate read Milcom. JFB, Gill and Wesley identify the idol with Molech; Keil and Delitzsch with Baal.
layers.text: In the Hebrew text the idol's name reads malkam, which means their king. Bible teachers link this king to Molech, also called Milcom, or to Baal, who was also hailed as king. Either way, these people pledged themselves to the LORD yet called on a rival king.

passages.saying: Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a sacrificial feast, read as the coming slaughter of the guilty.
layers.text: Everyone must fall silent before God, because His day of judgment is near. He has prepared a sacrifice, the slaughter of a guilty people, and has set apart His invited guests, the invading armies He calls to carry out that judgment.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the command is formed after Habakkuk 2:20; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Zephaniah renewed this summons to hushed silence from Habakkuk. Both verses use the same Hebrew word, has, meaning hush.
