layers.text: The command to hush before the Lord repeats Habakkuk 2:20, where all the earth is told to be silent before the LORD in His holy temple. Here the prophet takes up that summons as the Day of the LORD draws near.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the description of the judgment as zebach, a sacrifice, is taken from Isaiah 34:6; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the image was probably suggested by Isaiah's words there. Both verses use the same Hebrew word for sacrifice.
layers.text: Picturing judgment as a sacrifice the LORD has prepared likely picks up Isaiah 34:6, where the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah and a great slaughter in Edom. Here the same image is turned against Judah itself.

passages.saying: Wail, O dwellers of the Hollow
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's address to Jerusalem's merchant quarter.
layers.text: The people of the Hollow, a low-lying quarter of Jerusalem where traders did business, are told to wail. Its merchants and all who deal in silver will be cut off when judgment comes.

layers.evidence: Gill notes the word for merchant signifies a Canaanite; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reads it as irony, Jerusalem's merchants being very Canaanites in greed and idolatry; Keil and Delitzsch say these are Judean merchants who resembled the Canaanites in their business. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) agrees.
layers.text: The word translated merchants is literally people of Canaan, since the Canaanites were known as traders and their name was used for merchants. Calling Jerusalem's own traders Canaanites also hints that they had become like the Canaanites themselves, some say in greed and idolatry.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) suggests the name Maktesh was chosen to echo Mikdash, sanctuary, turning their false hopes in the temple into true fears.
layers.text: Some also hear a sound-play here. The people thought of themselves as a Mikdash, a holy sanctuary, because God's temple stood among them, but they would become a Maktesh, a mortar where they would be crushed.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Keil and Delitzsch, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all take Maktesh as mortar and see in the name the people being pounded in judgment. Gill and the Companion Bible explain the name from the district's hollow, basin-like shape.
layers.text: The Hollow is Maktesh in Hebrew, which means mortar, the bowl in which grain is pounded. The name suited this sunken district, and it pictured its fate: the people living there would be crushed like grain under a pestle.

passages.saying: They will build houses but not inhabit them
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording, which follows the complacent unbelief of verse 12.
layers.text: Those who thought God would do nothing will lose everything. Their wealth will be plundered and their homes ruined, and they will never enjoy the houses they build or the wine of the vineyards they plant.

layers.evidence: Gill says this agrees with what was threatened in the law of Moses at Deuteronomy 28:30; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it the fulfilling of Deuteronomy 28:30 and 39; the Companion Bible marks it a reference to the Pentateuch. Keil and Delitzsch and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) also point to Deuteronomy 28.
layers.text: Building houses but never living in them, and planting vineyards but never drinking the wine, is the curse the law warned of in Deuteronomy 28:30 and 39 for a people who turned from the LORD. Now that warning is about to come true.

passages.saying: That day will be a day of wrath
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's string of paired words for the coming day.
layers.text: The prophet piles up pairs of words to describe the Day of the LORD: wrath, trouble and distress, ruin and desolation, darkness and thick cloud. It will be the day God's anger against sin is poured out in full.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Zephaniah describes the day as the darkest cloudy night after Joel 2:2. The Hebrew of the two lines is identical, word for word.
layers.text: The words "a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness" are the same as in Joel 2:2, which describes the coming Day of the LORD. The prophet takes up Joel's words for the Day of the LORD that he says is near (verse 14).

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the similar sounds of Shoah, Umeshoah express the dreary monotony of desolation; Keil and Delitzsch note the same pair is joined in Job 30:3 and 38:27.
layers.text: Destruction and desolation are shoah and meshoah in Hebrew, two words that sound almost alike. Some hear in the near echo a heavy, dreary sound that matches the empty ruin it describes.

passages.saying: they will walk like the blind
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of people groping blindly under God's judgment, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: On the day of the LORD, God will hem in those who sinned against Him. They will stumble about like blind people, unable to find any way out, and their lives will be thrown away as if worth no more than dust.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the allusion to Deuteronomy 28:29 unmistakable. The Companion Bible marks the phrase as a reference to the Pentateuch at Deuteronomy 28:29. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says God forewarned them in the law and quotes that verse. Both verses use the same word for the blind, ivver.
layers.text: Walking like the blind recalls one of the curses Moses warned Israel about if they abandoned the covenant: "at noon you will grope about like a blind man in the darkness." Zephaniah announces that the long-threatened curse is now coming.

passages.saying: For Gaza will be abandoned
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Zephaniah turns from Judah to its old enemies, the Philistine cities on the coastal plain, and announces that each will fall. Even this message ends with hope for Judah's remnant: "the LORD their God will attend to them."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Azzah (H5804) with azuvah (H5800), and Eqron (H6138) with te'aqer (H6131), in the one verse. Keil and Delitzsch, the Pulpit Commentary and Gill point out both plays; Ashkelon and Ashdod have no clear pun.
layers.text: Two of the city names already sound like their fate. Gaza, azzah, will be azuvah, "abandoned," and Ekron, eqron, te'aqer, "uprooted." English loses it, but a Hebrew listener would hear the warning in the names themselves.

layers.evidence: Gill says Gaza was a strong and fortified place, as its name signifies. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) glosses Azzah as strong and says these boastful names carried their own sentence with them.
layers.text: Gaza's Hebrew name, Azzah, means strong. The city whose name boasted of its strength is told it will be abandoned, so its own proud name carries its sentence.

layers.evidence: Zechariah 9:5-7 names Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod, as Zephaniah does, and begins with judgment. The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David took it; afterward they lived on within Israel (1 Kings 9:20-21). Keil and Delitzsch, the Pulpit Commentary and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown read the comparison as Ekron being taken into God's people.
layers.text: A later prophet also foresees judgment on these cities, then goes further: God will cleanse them, "they too will become a remnant for our God," and "Ekron will be like the Jebusites," who stayed on and lived among Israel after David took their city.

passages.saying: the seacoast will become a land of pastures
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which turns the Philistine coast of verse 5 into grazing land.
layers.text: The Philistine coastland, once crowded with towns and fighting men, will be emptied of its people. Where cities stood there will be open pasture, with shepherds' wells and pens for their sheep.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls keroth a play on sounds alluding to the name Cherethites, so that the land becomes what the name implies. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the place of the Cherethites shall be cheroth of shepherds, places they dug. The Septuagint even rendered the word as Crete.
layers.text: In verse 5 the coastal people are the Cherethites, keretim in Hebrew. Here their land becomes keroth, places dug out by shepherds (the BSB says wells). The land of the keretim turns into keroth, and the people's name is likely echoed in the diggings that replace them.

passages.saying: I am it, and there is none besides me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between the city's boast and its ruin, with Nineveh named in verse 13.
layers.text: Nineveh, the proud capital of Assyria, felt so safe that it thought no city could rival it. Zephaniah sees it already in ruins, a resting place for wild animals, mocked by everyone who passes by.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the phrase is plainly adopted from Isaiah 47:8. Keil and Delitzsch say the words describing the city's security and boast are borrowed from Isaiah's description of Babylon and express self-deification. The Hebrew of the boast is the same in both verses.
layers.text: Nineveh's boast repeats the words Isaiah gave to proud Babylon, who sits securely and says, "I am, and there is none besides me." Both cities claim for themselves what only God can truly say, and both are brought to ruin.

passages.saying: I will restore pure lips to the peoples
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Hebrew of the verse, a purified lip, read with the judgment on the nations in verse 8.
layers.text: After judging the nations, God promises to purify the lips of the peoples, which had called on idols. Then all of them will call on the name of the LORD and serve Him together, side by side.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) contrasts the one impure lip of the world before Babel with the one purified lip promised here; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the promise to the confusion of languages at Babel in Genesis 11. Both verses use the Hebrew word safah, lip or language.
layers.text: The word for lips here is the word for the one language of the world at Babel. There the LORD confused the language of a rebellious world and scattered it. Here He reverses Babel, giving the nations pure lips so that they all call on His name together.

passages.saying: From beyond the rivers of Cush My worshipers, My scattered people
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse naming Cush, south of Egypt, the farthest southern land Israel knew.
layers.text: Even from beyond the rivers of Cush, at the far southern edge of the known world, God's worshipers, His scattered people, will come bringing Him an offering. No place is too distant for His worship to reach.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Zephaniah took the expression from beyond the rivers of Cush from Isaiah 18:1 to name the most remote nations. The three Hebrew words are the same in both verses.
layers.text: The phrase "beyond the rivers of Cush" is the same three Hebrew words found in Isaiah 18:1 (there rendered "along the rivers of Cush"). Zephaniah may be borrowing Isaiah's phrase to stand for the most distant nations, saying that worship will come to God even from there.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Zephaniah had Isaiah 66:20 in view and gave its thought more briefly, and they and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read the scattered worshipers as the offering brought to God, as in Isaiah. Both verses use minchah, an offering or gift.
layers.text: Isaiah 66:20 pictures the nations bringing Israel's brothers to the LORD as a gift, like an offering at His house. Zephaniah echoes it briefly, and the Hebrew can be read the same way: God's scattered worshipers are themselves the offering, brought to Him from the farthest lands.

passages.saying: I will save the lame and gather the scattered
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promises of judgment on oppressors and rescue for the weak and scattered.
layers.text: God promises to deal with all who have oppressed His people, to rescue the lame and weak, and to gather those who were scattered. Where they were put to shame, He will make them praised and honored.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say this is taken almost verbatim from Micah 4:6, and Clarke calls Micah 4:6 a parallel place. Both verses use the same Hebrew words for the lame (tsoleah) and the outcast (niddachah), and the verb qavats, gather or assemble.
layers.text: This promise repeats, almost word for word in Hebrew, the LORD's promise in Micah 4:6 to gather the lame and assemble the outcast. Zephaniah likely takes up the earlier prophet's words, renewing the same hope for a weak and scattered people.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the last clause points back to Deuteronomy 26:19, and Bullinger's Companion Bible marks it as a reference to that verse. Both verses pair the Hebrew words for praise and name.
layers.text: God's promise to give the disgraced praise and fame, literally praise and a name, looks back to Deuteronomy 26:19, where He promised to set Israel high in praise and name above all the nations. What He pledged through Moses, He will surely do.

passages.saying: when I restore your captives before your very eyes
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promises to bring in, gather and honor God's people.
layers.text: At that time God will bring His people home and gather them. He will make them famous and praised among all the peoples of the earth, and they will see Him restore them with their own eyes.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists Zephaniah 3:20 among the passages, beginning with Deuteronomy 30:3, where the Lord's promise to turn back the captivity uses two similar words, a figure he calls paronomasia.
layers.text: Behind the words restore your captives, the Hebrew sets two like-sounding words side by side, shuv (turn back) and shevut (captivity): God will turn back the captivity. Scripture uses this ringing pair many times when God promises to end a captivity, most often His own people's.

passages.saying: I have summoned a drought on the fields and on the mountains
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting, God's answer in verse 9 to why their harvests failed.
layers.text: Because the people left God's house unbuilt, the LORD says He Himself called down the drought on their land and hills, their grain, new wine and oil, their people and animals, and all the work of their hands.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say verses 10 and 11 depict the curse with an evident play upon the punishments threatened in the Law, naming Leviticus 26:19-20, Deuteronomy 11:17 and Deuteronomy 28:23-24.
layers.text: The withheld dew, failed crops and drought of verses 10 and 11 may echo the warnings of the Law. Moses had said that if Israel turned from the LORD, He would shut the heavens so no rain fell and the land would not yield its produce.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it an elegant play on words; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that choreb (drought) sounds like chareb (waste), said of God's house in 1:4 and 1:9; Keil and Delitzsch say the word was carefully chosen so the punishment matches the sin. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) also sees it.
layers.text: The people let God's house lie charev, in ruins (verses 4 and 9), so He summoned chorev, a drought. The two Hebrew words sound alike to show that the punishment fit the sin: they left His house waste, and a wasting drought came on all that was theirs.

passages.saying: Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's questions to those who remembered Solomon's temple.
layers.text: Haggai asks the oldest people, who had seen Solomon's temple before it was destroyed, how the new temple looks to them. Next to the glory of the first house, it seems like nothing.

layers.evidence: Gill, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all connect this question with the elders of Ezra 3:12 who had seen the first temple and wept when the new foundation was laid, and Gill and Pusey say some of them were still living when Haggai spoke.
layers.text: Haggai's question is aimed at the people Ezra describes: older priests, Levites and family heads who had seen the first temple and wept aloud when the new foundation was laid. Some of them were still alive to hear him, and the LORD goes on to encourage them.

passages.saying: I will shake the heavens and the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse and its setting in Haggai's call to finish rebuilding the temple.
layers.text: God promises that in a little while He will once more shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land. This encouraged the people rebuilding the temple: every power that frightened them would fall before the kingdom of the Messiah, who was to be linked with this very house.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke all tie this shaking to the quaking of Sinai when the law was given (Exodus 19:18). Keil and Delitzsch add that Hebrews 12:26 rightly reads the verse this way.
layers.text: The words once more look back to Sinai, where the whole mountain quaked violently as the LORD came down to give the law. God promises a greater shaking still, of heaven and earth together. Hebrews 12:26 reads the verse in just this way.

passages.saying: I will fill this house with glory
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its promise that the second temple would outshine the first (Haggai 2:9).
layers.text: God will shake all nations, their treasures will come, and He will fill the rebuilt temple with glory. Many older Christian interpreters read the words rendered their treasures as the Desire of all nations, the Messiah, whose own presence in this temple would be its greatest glory.

layers.evidence: Gill says the words allude to the glory that filled Moses' tabernacle and Solomon's temple. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) calls it the received expression for God's presence there (Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:11). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares the cloud of glory that filled the first temple. Keil and Delitzsch grant the word glory was chosen with reference to those events.
layers.text: Filling the house with glory recalls the day the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle, and later the day it filled Solomon's temple. God promises that this plain second temple would also be filled with glory.

passages.saying: If one who is defiled by contact with a corpse touches any of these
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the question and answer in the verse, set beside the first question in Haggai 2:12.
layers.text: Haggai puts a second question of the law to the priests: if someone made unclean by touching a dead body touches food, does the food become unclean? They rightly answer yes. Uncleanness spreads by touch far more easily than holiness does.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all ground the priests' answer in Numbers 19:22, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill also point to Numbers 19:11 for the uncleanness caused by a dead body.
layers.text: The priests answer straight from the law in Numbers 19. Touching a dead body made a person unclean for seven days, and whatever that person touched became unclean too. Haggai then applies the rule to the people, whose sin made their work and offerings unclean.

passages.saying: with blight, mildew, and hail, but you did not turn to Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in Haggai 2:15-19, which sets the lean years beside the blessing to come.
layers.text: God tells the people that the blight, mildew and hail that ruined their harvests came from Him as discipline for their sins, while His house lay in ruins. Even so, they did not turn back to Him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the words a reminiscence of Amos 4:9, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says they are appropriated from it, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Amos had spoken in these self-same words.
layers.text: This verse borrows the words of Amos 4:9, where God said, “I struck you with blight and mildew,” yet Israel did not return to Him. Haggai repeats them and adds hail: generations later, the same discipline had met the same refusal to turn back.

passages.saying: I will make you like My signet ring
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse and on how a signet ring served as its owner's seal and authority.
layers.text: When God overthrows the thrones of the nations, He will take Zerubbabel, His chosen servant, and make him like His signet ring, a treasured seal kept close and used with the owner's authority. Zerubbabel is also seen as a type of the Messiah, who came from his line.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says God here reverses to Zerubbabel the sentence on Jeconiah in Jeremiah 22:24. A writer quoted by Clarke points to the same threat against Zerubbabel's forefather, and Keil and Delitzsch explain the signet image from Jeremiah 22:24. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible also cross-reference it.
layers.text: Through Jeremiah, God told King Jehoiachin, also called Coniah, that even if he were a signet ring on God's right hand, He would pull him off. Now God tells Jehoiachin's descendant Zerubbabel, "I will make you like My signet ring," which can be read as reversing that sentence.

passages.saying: Turn now from your evil ways and deeds
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the call to return in Zechariah 1:2-6.
layers.text: Zechariah warns the returned exiles not to be like their ancestors. The earlier prophets called them to turn from their evil ways, but they would not listen to God, and judgment followed.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes that Jeremiah sums up these calls to turn as the words of all the prophets (Jeremiah 25:3-8) and judges that this summary was chiefly in Zechariah's mind. Keil and Delitzsch see here the warnings of the earlier prophets generally.
layers.text: The former prophets' call, "Turn now from your evil ways and deeds," matches Jeremiah's own summary of what all the prophets had preached (Jeremiah 25:5). Zechariah may have had that summary in mind as he warned a new generation not to repeat the old refusal.

passages.saying: with which You have been angry these seventy years
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on the LORD's comforting answer in Zechariah 1:13.
layers.text: In Zechariah's vision the angel of the LORD pleads for Jerusalem and the towns of Judah, asking how long God will withhold mercy after seventy years of anger. Many Christian interpreters see this Angel as the Lord Christ, interceding for His people.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown identify these as the seventy years foretold in Jeremiah 25:11 and 29:10. Keil and Delitzsch agree and add that nearly seventy years had also passed since the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple.
layers.text: These seventy years recall Jeremiah's prophecy that the nations would serve the king of Babylon for seventy years, after which God would bring His people home (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10). With that span now run out, the angel asks God to show the promised mercy.

passages.saying: I will be a wall of fire around it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture of God as both the city's wall and its glory; Clarke explains the wall of fire as God's own defense, which no adversary may break through.
layers.text: God promises that Jerusalem will not need stone walls for its safety. The LORD Himself will be a wall of fire around the city to guard it, and His glory will dwell within it.

layers.evidence: Gill compares God's protection here to the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel through the wilderness. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that Isaiah 4:5 joins the same glory and defense, alluding to the pillar of cloud and fire.
layers.text: Fire around the city and glory in its midst can recall the pillar of fire in which the LORD went before Israel in the wilderness, guarding and lighting His people by night. Isaiah 4:5 had already promised that same fire and glory over Zion.

passages.saying: whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of the eye's pupil, which Matthew Henry's Concise explains as God's tender love for His people.
layers.text: God declares that the nations who plundered His people will be judged, for anyone who harms them touches the apple of His eye, the most tender and closely guarded part. He takes an attack on them as an attack on Himself.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks the phrase as a reference to Deuteronomy 32:10. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill both point to the same verse, Gill quoting it to show how carefully God keeps His people.
layers.text: The apple of His eye echoes the Song of Moses, where the LORD found Israel in the wilderness and guarded him as the apple of His eye. Zechariah uses a different Hebrew word for the pupil, but the picture of God's watchful care is the same.

passages.saying: for I am coming to dwell among you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to rejoice and its reason, the LORD coming to dwell among them, as Keil and Delitzsch explain.
layers.text: Zion is called to sing and rejoice because the LORD Himself is coming to live among His people. The joy rests on God's own presence in their midst.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes that Zion is invited with this same word elsewhere, quoting Zephaniah 3:14-15, always for the renewed presence of God. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also lists Zephaniah 3:14 as a parallel.
layers.text: The call to Zion to shout for joy and be glad uses the same two Hebrew verbs as Zephaniah 3:14, and Zephaniah's next words give the same reason for joy: the LORD would be in Zion's midst. Zechariah may be renewing that call for the people back from exile.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) asks what this coming to dwell among them is but the Incarnation, quoting John 1:14. Keil and Delitzsch say it begins with the Son of God's coming in the flesh and is completed at His return. Gill instead applies it to Christ's spiritual presence in the last days.
layers.text: This promise is seen as first fulfilled when the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us, God living among His people in Jesus. It will be completed when He returns and the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3).

passages.saying: the LORD will take possession of Judah as His portion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words for inheriting and portion, which Wesley explains as God claiming and delighting in His own.
layers.text: The LORD will again claim Judah as His own possession in the Holy Land and will once more choose Jerusalem. His earlier choice of His people has not been cancelled.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the first half of the verse rests on Deuteronomy 32:9. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes that Israel is called God's portion only there and that Zechariah unites two rare idioms. The Companion Bible marks it as a reference to the same verse.
layers.text: Judah as His portion echoes the Song of Moses, which calls the LORD's people His portion and Jacob His allotted inheritance (Deuteronomy 32:9). Zechariah uses the same word for portion, chelek, and a verb from the same root as the word for inheritance.

passages.saying: Be silent before the LORD, all people
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's command to be silent and its reason, which Wesley explains as reverent waiting for God to fulfill His word.
layers.text: All people are told to be silent in awe before the LORD, because He has roused Himself from His holy dwelling in heaven to act for His people and judge their enemies.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the call to silence follows Habakkuk 2:20, and Gill calls it a like phrase. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) renders the word literally as hush and points to Habakkuk 2:20. The Companion Bible compares both Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7.
layers.text: Be silent is a single Hebrew word, has, much like our hush. Habakkuk used it when he called all the earth to be silent before the LORD in His holy temple (Habakkuk 2:20), and Zephaniah used it to warn that the Day of the LORD is near (Zephaniah 1:7).

passages.saying: with Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's court setting, which Keil and Delitzsch explain from the accuser's place at the right hand.
layers.text: In a vision Zechariah sees a courtroom scene. Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD, and Satan stands at his right hand, the place of an accuser, to bring charges against him.

layers.evidence: Clarke and the Companion Bible both call this a paronomasia, a play on satan and lesitno. Gill says the name Satan, meaning adversary, comes from the very word used here. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also explains Satan as the Hebrew term for an adversary in a law court.
layers.text: In Hebrew the accuser's title and his action come from one root. Ha-satan, the adversary, stands there le-sitno, to oppose or accuse him. The name Satan means adversary or accuser, and here he does exactly what his name says.

passages.saying: Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two grounds for the rebuke, God's choice of Jerusalem and His rescue of Joshua, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains.
layers.text: The LORD rebukes Satan and rejects his charges against Joshua. The ground is God's own choice of Jerusalem, and Joshua is like a burning stick pulled from the fire, already rescued by God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain the phrase as one who has narrowly escaped destruction and refer to Amos 4:11 for the figure. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible both point to Amos 4:11, and Gill does the same.
layers.text: A firebrand snatched from the fire is a stick pulled out just before it burns up. Amos used the same picture, with the same Hebrew words for firebrand and snatched, for Israel barely spared in judgment (Amos 4:11). Here it marks Joshua, back from exile, as one who narrowly escaped destruction.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Jude 9 relates to this scene, with the very same phrasing. The Companion Bible compares Jude 9. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Jude, notes that Michael uses the same rebuke that the Angel of the LORD used against Satan in pleading for Joshua.
layers.text: The words spoken to Satan here, “The LORD rebukes you,” are echoed in Jude 9, where Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, would not bring a slanderous charge but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” In both scenes the accuser is left to the Lord's own rebuke.

passages.saying: I am going to bring My servant, the Branch
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of My servant, the Branch, which Wesley explains as the Messiah.
layers.text: God tells Joshua and his fellow priests that they are a sign of something greater to come. He is about to bring His servant, called the Branch, the promised Messiah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Zechariah formed the name Tsemach, Sprout, chiefly from Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible both identify the Branch as the Messiah and point to the same verses in Jeremiah.
layers.text: Branch translates tsemach, a sprout or shoot. Jeremiah had promised that God would raise up for David a righteous Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15). Zechariah takes up that word almost as a name for the coming Son of David and calls Him My servant.

passages.saying: See the stone I have set before Joshua
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording, which Wesley explains as God pointing to a particular stone and pardoning the land's iniquity at once.
layers.text: God points to a stone He has set before Joshua, with seven eyes on it and an inscription He Himself will engrave. He promises to take away the land's iniquity in a single day.

layers.evidence: Clarke, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all read the stone in light of Isaiah 28:16 and see it fulfilled in Christ, and Gill points to the same verse. Keil and Delitzsch disagree, holding that a stone set before Joshua can hardly be the Messiah.
layers.text: The stone God sets before Joshua is often linked with the stone God promised to lay in Zion, a tested and precious cornerstone (Isaiah 28:16). The New Testament applies that cornerstone to Christ (1 Peter 2:6), and many read Zechariah's stone, like the Branch before it, as pointing to Him.

passages.saying: invite your neighbor to sit under your own vine and fig tree
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of shared rest, which Wesley explains as neighbors inviting one another to enjoy the fruit of vine and fig tree.
layers.text: In the day God removes the land's sin, His people will live in peace and plenty, each one inviting a neighbor to come and sit with him under his own vine and fig tree.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Micah made this picture of Solomon's peaceful days a symbol of the peace of Christ's time. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites 1 Kings 4:25 and Micah 4:4, and the Companion Bible notes the same wording as in Micah 4:4.
layers.text: Every family resting under its own vine and fig tree was the picture of peace in Solomon's days (1 Kings 4:25). Micah used it for the peace of the coming kingdom (Micah 4:4). Zechariah adds that neighbors will invite one another to share it once God removes the land's iniquity.

passages.saying: I see a solid gold lampstand
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains how the bowl, pipes and lamps work together in the vision.
layers.text: Zechariah is shown a lampstand made all of gold. A bowl of oil sits on top, and pipes carry the oil from the bowl to the seven lamps on the lampstand.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Keil and Delitzsch, Gill and Clarke all identify it with the tabernacle lampstand of Exodus 25 and point out the added bowl and pipes. Both verses use the same Hebrew phrase, menorat zahav, a lampstand of gold.
layers.text: The gold lampstand recalls the one Moses was told to make for the tabernacle (Exodus 25:31). Both are called a lampstand of gold, but this one has things the first lacked: a bowl of oil on top and pipes feeding the lamps, supplied by two olive trees.

passages.saying: To build a house for it in the land of Shinar
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains that building a house there means wickedness will stay there for good.
layers.text: The angel explains that the basket holding the woman called Wickedness is being carried to Shinar. A house will be built for it there and it will be set on its base, so wickedness is taken out of Judah and settled far away.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the land of Shinar recalls Genesis 11:2, the first attempt to build a world power against God. Keil and Delitzsch say that by Genesis 10:10 and 11:2 Shinar is where Nimrod founded the first empire and men built the tower of Babel. The Companion Bible marks it as a reference to Genesis 10:10 and 11:2.
layers.text: Shinar is the old name for the land of Babylon. In Genesis it is the plain where people settled and then built the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2). Wickedness is carried off to the land where mankind first joined together against God.

passages.saying: Here is a man whose name is the Branch
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke, like the other commentaries, sees the crowned Joshua as a type of the Messiah called the Branch.
layers.text: Zechariah is to tell Joshua the high priest, who has just been crowned, that a man named the Branch will sprout up from His place and build the temple of the LORD. The crowned priest is a picture of this coming Messiah.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) quotes Jeremiah 33:15 to explain the Branch growing up. Keil and Delitzsch say that, according to Jeremiah 33:15, the Messiah is called Tsemach because the LORD makes a righteous growth spring up for David. Both verses use the noun tsemach and the verb tsamach.
layers.text: The title Branch takes up Jeremiah's promise, "I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch" (Jeremiah 33:15). Jeremiah uses the same noun and verb, so the Branch here is the promised Son of David, the Messiah.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible calls this paronomasia: a branch shall branch forth. Keil and Delitzsch say the name Tsemach is explained by the words that follow, He will sprout up. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the verb keeps the image of the Branch.
layers.text: His name and what He does come from the same Hebrew root. His name is tsemach, the Branch, and He will yitsmach, branch out. The name explains itself: the Branch will branch out from His own place.

passages.saying: He will be a priest on His throne
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that the Messiah will be both king and priest, since the priest is said to sit on his throne.
layers.text: The Branch will build the LORD's temple, be clothed in royal splendor, and rule from His throne. He will also be a priest on that throne, so the offices of king and priest meet in one person, with peace between them.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains the priest on His throne with the words of Psalm 110:4. Keil and Delitzsch, commenting on Psalm 110, say Zechariah's prophecy of the Branch looks back to that psalm and is the key to it, since the One who builds the temple unites priest and king.
layers.text: A King who is also a Priest recalls Psalm 110, where David's Lord is told, "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek" (Psalm 110:4). Zechariah's Branch is that same King and Priest.

passages.saying: as a memorial to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and the gracious son of Zephaniah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that the crown was laid up in the temple as a memorial of this sign.
layers.text: After the crowning, the crown is to be kept in the LORD's temple as a memorial to the men who brought silver and gold from the exiles, and to the son of Zephaniah, whose house Zechariah visited to receive the gift.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Hen means favor and is another name for Josiah. Keil and Delitzsch take chen as the ordinary word for favor, the kindness he showed by receiving the exiles from Babylon into his house.
layers.text: Where 6:10 names Josiah son of Zephaniah, this verse has the Hebrew word chen, meaning favor or grace. Some take it as Hen, a second name for Josiah. Others read it as the favor he showed by taking the exiles into his house, so the verse speaks of "the gracious son of Zephaniah."

passages.saying: Jerusalem will be called the City of Truth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain the City of Truth as a city where truth and faithfulness toward the LORD have their home.
layers.text: The LORD promises to return to Zion and live in Jerusalem. Then the city will be known for truth and faithfulness to Him, and the temple hill will be called holy because the Holy One lives there.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) quotes Isaiah 1:26 here. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains the City of Truth as faithful to her God and cites Isaiah 1:21 and 1:26. The Companion Bible renders it a city of fidelity and compares Isaiah 1:21 and 1:26.
layers.text: The new name likely echoes Isaiah's promise that Jerusalem would be called "the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City" (Isaiah 1:26). The city that had been unfaithful will become what its new name says, true and faithful to God.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) traces how Ezekiel saw the LORD's glory leave the temple and the city (Ezekiel 11:23) and later return. Keil and Delitzsch say the LORD had forsaken His dwelling, as Ezekiel saw, and is now about to make His home in Jerusalem again.
layers.text: "I will return to Zion" answers Ezekiel's vision before Jerusalem fell, when "the glory of the LORD rose up from within the city" and left it (Ezekiel 11:23). The God whose glory departed now promises to come back and dwell in Jerusalem.

passages.saying: Tyre has built herself a fortress
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of Tyre's island fortress and its great riches.
layers.text: Tyre, the rich Phoenician city on its island, built strong walls for herself and piled up silver and gold as if they were as common as dust and mud in the streets. She trusted in her walls and her wealth.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains that Tyre (Zor) means the rock and that she built herself a mazor, a word meaning both stronghold and siege. Bullinger's Companion Bible calls zor mazor a paronomasia that cannot be reproduced in English, and his Figures of Speech lists the verse as an example of the figure.
layers.text: In Hebrew, Tyre is Tsor, meaning rock, and fortress is matsor. The two words sound alike, so it is as if the Rock built herself a rock-like fort. The word matsor can also mean siege, which may hint that her walls would one day be surrounded and fall.

passages.saying: His dominion will extend from sea to sea
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between weapons of war and the King's reign of peace.
layers.text: God will take away the chariots, war horses and battle bows of His own people. The coming King will proclaim peace to the nations, and His rule will reach across the whole earth without the help of weapons.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the statement rests upon Psalm 72:8, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it fulfils that psalm. The Companion Bible and Gill also point to Psalm 72:8. The Hebrew of the two lines is the same apart from the opening word for ruling.
layers.text: The last line uses the very words of the prayer for the king in Psalm 72:8: "from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth." The humble King riding into Zion is the One whose worldwide reign that psalm prayed for.

passages.saying: because of the blood of My covenant
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of release grounded in God's covenant.
layers.text: God speaks to Zion. Because of the covenant He made with her, sealed with blood, He will set her captive people free and bring them up out of a dry pit where they would otherwise have died.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to the blood sprinkled on the people at Sinai, called the blood of the covenant in Exodus 24:8. Keil and Delitzsch and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown tie the phrase to the same verse, and so do E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible.
layers.text: The blood of the covenant recalls Sinai, where Moses sprinkled blood on the people and said, "This is the blood of the covenant" (Exodus 24:8). Because God had bound Himself to His people with covenant blood, He would not leave them in captivity.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a reference here to Genesis 37:24. Keil and Delitzsch see an evident allusion to Joseph lying in a pit with no water, the kind used as a prison, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also cite Genesis 37:24 for this kind of dry dungeon pit.
layers.text: The waterless pit echoes the pit Joseph's brothers threw him into, which "was empty, with no water in it" (Genesis 37:24). A dry pit like that served as a prison, and God promises to bring His captive people up out of it.

passages.saying: The cornerstone will come from Judah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's four pictures of strength that come from Judah itself.
layers.text: Judah will no longer depend on foreign rulers. From Judah itself will come the cornerstone and the tent peg that hold the nation firm, the battle bow that defends it, and every ruler it needs.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Gill both read the peg in light of Isaiah 22:23, where Eliakim is fastened like a nail in a sure place; Gill calls Eliakim a type of Christ. Keil and Delitzsch note that Isaiah 22:23 had already used the peg for a person, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible cite the same verse.
layers.text: The tent peg recalls Isaiah 22:23, where God promised to drive His servant Eliakim "like a peg into a firm place," so that his father's house could rest on him. The leader from Judah will be that kind of firm support for God's people.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the cornerstone to the Messiah of Isaiah 28:16, and Keil and Delitzsch say the word means cornerstone here as in Isaiah 28:16. Gill and the Companion Bible also see the Messiah in it.
layers.text: The word for cornerstone here is the one Isaiah 28:16 uses when God lays in Zion "a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation." Many Christian readers see the Messiah, who came from Judah, as this cornerstone.

passages.saying: I will whistle for them to gather
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of gathering grounded in God's redemption.
layers.text: God will call His scattered people home with a simple whistle and gather them, because He has redeemed them. They will grow as numerous as they were in the past.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes that God had once used this summons to call enemies to chastise His people and now uses it to gather them. The Companion Bible and Keil and Delitzsch point to the same word in Isaiah 5:26 and 7:18.
layers.text: In Isaiah, God whistles for foreign armies to come against His people like swarms of flies and bees (Isaiah 5:26; 7:18). Many see the same whistle turned around here: God whistles to call His own redeemed people home.

passages.saying: They will pass through the sea of distress
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's images of sea and river and on the fall of Assyria and Egypt.
layers.text: God will lead His people home through every barrier, as if through a hostile sea. He will strike its waves and dry up the Nile, and the proud powers of Assyria and Egypt that held His people will fall.

layers.evidence: Clarke and Wesley call the verse an allusion to the Red Sea crossing. Keil and Delitzsch say the smiting of the waves plays upon the dividing of the Red Sea in Exodus 14:21, and Gill, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the same.
layers.text: Passing through the sea and striking its waves recalls the Exodus, when the LORD drove back the Red Sea and turned it into dry land so Israel could cross (Exodus 14:21). God promises a new exodus to bring His scattered people home.

passages.saying: I took for myself two staffs, calling one Favor and the other Union
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Keil and Delitzsch explain that the named staffs point to the blessings the flock receives through the shepherd's care.
layers.text: The prophet acts out the part of a shepherd sent by God. He tends a flock headed for slaughter, caring especially for its weakest sheep, and he takes two shepherd's staffs and gives each one a name.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain No'am as favor and Chovlim as a participle of the verb to bind, meaning a binding or bond; Bullinger glosses the names Graciousness and Union; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown tie the second staff to the brotherhood of Judah and Israel broken in 11:14.
layers.text: The first staff is named No'am, meaning favor or pleasantness, for God's kindness that guarded His flock from the nations. The second is Chovlim, from a verb meaning to bind, for the bond uniting Judah and Israel. Breaking each staff (11:10, 14) takes that blessing away.

passages.saying: So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the shepherd story of 11:4-14; Keil and Delitzsch explain the request for wages as a call for the flock to show whether it valued his care.
layers.text: The shepherd asks the people to pay him whatever they think his work was worth, or to keep their money if they wish. They weigh out thirty pieces of silver, a payment that shows how little they valued him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the sum an allusion to the compensation for a slave in Exodus 21:32; Clarke, Gill, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and Bullinger likewise call thirty pieces the price of a slave or servant under that law.
layers.text: Thirty shekels of silver was the sum the law of Moses fixed as payment to a master when an ox gored his servant (Exodus 21:32). By paying the shepherd exactly that amount, the people valued him at the price of a slave, an insult rather than a reward.

layers.evidence: Gill points to Matthew 26:15 as the fulfilment of this prophecy; Wesley says it was fulfilled when Judas was paid to betray Christ; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the high priest fixed on the very price Zechariah named; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Matthew Henry agree.
layers.text: The same sum returns in the Gospels. When Judas offered to hand Jesus over, the chief priests set out for him thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). The Good Shepherd was priced just as Zechariah's rejected shepherd was, and this is read as the prophecy fulfilled.

passages.saying: who stretches out the heavens and lays the foundation of the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's heading and its titles for God; Bullinger notes that the Lord's almighty power guarantees that His word will be carried out.
layers.text: This verse opens a new message about Israel. Before speaking, God names Himself as the Creator who spreads out the sky, sets the earth on its foundations, and shapes the spirit inside every person, so that no one doubts He can do what He promises.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say these titles of God are formed after Isaiah 42:5; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call Isaiah 42:5 a similar preface that reminds readers of God's creating power. Both verses use the same Hebrew verb for stretching out the heavens.
layers.text: These titles for God follow Isaiah 42:5, where the LORD stretched out the heavens, spread out the earth, and gives breath and life to its people. The word for life there is ruach, the word for spirit here. Both prophets name God as Creator so His people know He can keep His promise.

layers.evidence: Bullinger marks the phrase as a reference to the books of Moses, citing Genesis 2:7; the Hebrew verb yatsar, to form, appears in both verses.
layers.text: The verb for forming the spirit of man is the same one used when the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7). Some see this line as pointing back to that account of man's creation.

passages.saying: as great as the wailing of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its link to 12:10; Keil and Delitzsch explain that the comparison shows the depth of grief over the slain Messiah.
layers.text: When the people look on the One they pierced, Jerusalem's grief will be deep and widespread. It is compared to the most famous mourning in Israel's memory, the wailing at Hadad-rimmon near Megiddo.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Clarke, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and Bullinger all take this as the mourning for King Josiah, slain in the plain of Megiddo; Wesley adds that this mourning grew into a proverb for great grief.
layers.text: Hadad-rimmon was a town in the plain of Megiddo, where good King Josiah was fatally wounded in battle. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him, and laments for him were sung for generations (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). That national grief is the measure of Israel's future mourning.

passages.saying: a fountain will be opened to the house of David
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Clarke explains sin and impurity as the guilt of sin and the soul's pollution by it.
layers.text: After the people mourn, God promises a fountain opened for the royal house of David and all who live in Jerusalem. It will wash away both the guilt of sin and the stain of impurity.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the figure is taken partly from the red heifer's sprinkling water, called water of uncleanness, in Numbers 19:9; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) sets that law's water for defilements beside this one ever-open fountain.
layers.text: The two Hebrew words here for sin and impurity, chattat and niddah, appear together in Numbers 19:9, where the red heifer's ashes were kept to make the water of purification. That water removed the uncleanness of touching the dead; this fountain will cleanse from sin itself.

passages.saying: he will not put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Clarke explains that false prophets wore the true prophets' rough garment because they claimed the same gifts.
layers.text: In the day God cleanses His people, false prophets will be ashamed of the visions they claimed. They will stop wearing the rough clothing of a prophet to fool others.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say false prophets put on the hairy garment of the ancient prophets, Elijah for example; Gill says they imitated true prophets, particularly Elijah, called a hairy man in 2 Kings 1:8; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also point to that verse.
layers.text: A hairy cloak was the mark of a true prophet like Elijah, who was known as a hairy man with a leather belt (2 Kings 1:8). False prophets copied his dress to look like men of God. In that day they will give up the disguise.

passages.saying: I am not a prophet; I work the land
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and 13:3-4; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains that the speaker is trying to rid himself of all suspicion of false prophecy.
layers.text: A man who once claimed to prophesy will deny it when challenged. He will insist he has only ever been a farm worker, bought as a servant when young, to clear himself of any suspicion.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) sets the man's plea beside Amos 7:14, where Amos said truly of himself that he was no prophet but a herdsman. The Hebrew for I am not a prophet is the same three words in both verses.
layers.text: His words, ‘I am not a prophet,’ match the Hebrew of Amos 7:14 exactly, lo navi anokhi. Amos said it truthfully, for he was a herdsman before God called him. Some see this man making the same plea falsely, to hide that he once played the prophet.

passages.saying: You will flee as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the valley opened in verse 4, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains.
layers.text: When the LORD comes to save His people, the valley made by splitting the Mount of Olives becomes their way of escape. They will flee through it as their fathers fled from a great earthquake, and then the LORD will come with all His holy ones.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible tie this earthquake to the one in Amos 1:1, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Clarke and Wesley say the same on Amos 1:1. Both verses use the same Hebrew word for the earthquake, ra'ash.
layers.text: Zechariah compares the coming flight to the panic in the great earthquake of King Uzziah's day. Amos dated his own message to "two years before the earthquake," so it was a disaster Israel still remembered long afterward.

passages.saying: living water will flow out from Jerusalem
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, with the two seas identified as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains.
layers.text: On that day fresh, living water will flow out from Jerusalem, half east toward the Dead Sea and half west toward the Mediterranean. Unlike the streams of the land, it will never dry up, but will run in summer and winter alike.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch read this water by Joel 3:18 and Ezekiel 47:1-12; the Companion Bible calls it the waters of Ezekiel 47; Bullinger's Figures of Speech and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also point to Ezekiel 47. Both passages speak of water (mayim) flowing out from where God dwells.
layers.text: This picks up Ezekiel's vision of water flowing out from under the temple and bringing life wherever it goes (Ezekiel 47), and Joel's promise of a spring from the LORD's house. Zechariah adds that this stream will never fail, summer or winter.

passages.saying: HOLY TO THE LORD will be inscribed on the bells of the horses
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, read as E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains it.
layers.text: In that day even ordinary things will belong wholly to God. Horses' bells will carry the words once worn only by the high priest, and the common cooking pots in the temple will be as holy as the bowls used at the altar.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible all tie this inscription to the high priest's gold plate in Exodus 28:36. The Hebrew words are the same in both verses (qodesh, holy).
layers.text: HOLY TO THE LORD was engraved on the gold plate the high priest wore on his turban (Exodus 28:36). Zechariah sees the same words on horses' bells, showing that in that day the most everyday things will be as holy as the plate on the high priest's head.

passages.saying: there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Hosts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, read as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains it.
layers.text: In that day holiness will reach everything, so that every ordinary pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be fit for cooking sacrifices. And no Canaanite will be found in the LORD's house any longer.

layers.evidence: Gill says the word means merchant, as in Hosea 12:7; Clarke says the Canaanite is the merchant; the Companion Bible says it means merchant but also stands for what is unclean; Wesley gives both senses. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown prefers the sense of an unclean person here.
layers.text: The word for Canaanite, kena'ani, could also mean a trader or merchant, and Hosea 12:7 uses Canaan this way. So the promise can mean both no ungodly person and no buying and selling in God's house, like the trade Jesus later drove from the temple.

passages.saying: the burden of the word of the LORD to Israel through Malachi
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the heading of the book, as Gill explains it.
layers.text: This book is a burden, that is, a message the LORD laid on His prophet to carry. It was sent to the people of Israel through Malachi, whom God used to deliver it.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible gives the name as my messenger, as do Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown in their introductions. Keil and Delitzsch, who think it may be short for messenger of the LORD, see an obvious play on the name in 3:1, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Malachi foretold the forerunner under his own name.
layers.text: The name Malachi means my messenger (or it may be short for messenger of the LORD). In 3:1 God says, "Behold, I will send My messenger," with the same Hebrew word, so the prophet's own name points ahead to the one who would prepare the Lord's way.

passages.saying: Yet Jacob I have loved
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, read as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains it.
layers.text: God tells Israel He has loved them. When they ask how, He points to Jacob and Esau. They were brothers with equal standing, yet God chose Jacob and his people, not because they earned it but out of His own free love.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) all explain God's love for Jacob by the word spoken to Rebekah before the twins were born in Genesis 25:23. The Companion Bible notes that Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:13.
layers.text: God reaches back to the twins in Rebekah's womb. Before they were born He told her, "the older will serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). Esau was the firstborn, yet God chose Jacob, so His love was free, not earned. Paul later quotes Malachi's words in Romans 9:13.

passages.saying: They will be called the Land of Wickedness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, read as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains it.
layers.text: Edom, the nation that came from Esau, boasts that it will rebuild its ruins. But the LORD says He will tear down whatever they build. They will be known as a wicked land, a people under the LORD's lasting anger.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) notes the land had its own name, the border of Edom, but would now be known as the border of wickedness, while the border of Israel keeps its name (1:5). Gill says this will be the name Edom goes by among men, as a proverb and reproach. The same word, gevul, stands in both verses.
layers.text: Edom's land had been known as the territory of Edom. Now people will call it by a new name, the Land of Wickedness (literally the territory of wickedness), so its very name will tell its sin. In 1:5, by contrast, Israel's land is still called by its own name.

passages.saying: When you offer blind animals for sacrifice, is it not wrong?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, read as E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) explains it.
layers.text: The priests were offering blind, lame and sick animals to God. The LORD asks whether their governor would accept such gifts. If they would not dare give them to a human ruler, how could they give them to God?

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) and the Companion Bible point to Leviticus 22:22. Pusey and the Companion Bible add Deuteronomy 15:21, which uses the same Hebrew words for blind (ivver) and lame (pisseach) as Malachi does.
layers.text: God's law said no blind, injured or maimed animal could be offered to Him (Leviticus 22:22), and Deuteronomy 15:21 names the lame and the blind too. The priests were bringing the very animals the law ruled out, gifts their governor would not accept.

passages.saying: I will spread dung on your faces, the waste from your feasts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording, which the commentaries read as God throwing the priests' unworthy offerings back at them.
layers.text: God warns the careless priests that He will rebuke their descendants and smear the waste of their festival sacrifices on their faces. Like refuse, they will be carried off with it. He is throwing their unworthy offerings back at them.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says this dung was by the law carried outside the camp and burned with the animal; Bullinger's Companion Bible notes that the word is always sacrificial and occurs seven times. The same Hebrew word names the bull's dung in Exodus 29:14.
layers.text: The word for dung here, peresh, is the Law's term for the waste of sacrificial animals, which had to be carried outside the camp and burned (Exodus 29:14). God threatens to fling this refuse of their own sacrifices in the priests' faces and sweep them away with it.

passages.saying: My covenant with him was one of life and peace
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording, which the commentaries read as God's covenant with the priestly line of Levi.
layers.text: God reminds the priests of His covenant with Levi, the priestly tribe. He gave Levi life and peace, and Levi answered with reverence, standing in awe of God's name.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares Numbers 25:11-13 and Phinehas' zeal, noting that peace is named both here and there; Bullinger's Companion Bible marks a reference to Numbers 25:10-13 and Deuteronomy 33:8-10 and sees a distinct reference to Phinehas.
layers.text: The covenant of life and peace with Levi likely recalls the covenant of peace God granted Aaron's grandson Phinehas, a lasting priesthood given because he was zealous for God (Numbers 25:12-13). The same Hebrew words for covenant and peace appear in both.

passages.saying: do not break faith with the wife of your youth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording and its setting, where men of Judah were divorcing the wives of their youth (Malachi 2:14-16).
layers.text: Malachi reminds the men of Judah that God made husband and wife one and seeks godly children through marriage. So they must guard their hearts and stay faithful to the wives they married when young.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible reads it as making the two one flesh, citing Genesis 2:24; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says God made Adam first to mark the oneness of marriage; Gill and Matthew Henry speak of God making only Adam and Eve. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown prefers another reading. The Hebrew word for one, echad, is the one used in Genesis 2:24.
layers.text: The question "Has not the LORD made them one?" likely looks back to creation, when God made one man and one woman and joined them as one flesh (Genesis 2:24). He could have made more wives for Adam but made only one pair, showing that marriage is meant to be one faithful union.

passages.saying: Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: The people complain, "Where is the God of justice?" God answers that He will send a messenger to clear the way, and then the Lord Himself will come to His temple, "like a refiner’s fire," to purify His people.

layers.evidence: TBESH H4401: Malachi, My messenger. JFB (Fausset) takes it as the name of an office, as the Septuagint of 1:1 (by the hand of his messenger) suggests; the Pulpit Commentary holds it is a proper name.
layers.text: The prophet's name, Malachi, means "My messenger," the very words of this verse. The word recurs: a priest "is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts." Some think Malachi is a title rather than a name; the Greek Old Testament of 1:1 has "his messenger."

layers.evidence: TBESH H4397: messenger, angel; TAHOT tags both messengers in 3:1 H4397. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary: it must mean God Himself, since He comes to His temple.
layers.text: The verse has two messengers. The first prepares the way; the second, the "Messenger of the covenant," is "the Lord whom you seek" and comes "to His temple," His own house. Mal'akh means messenger or angel, and many read the second as God Himself arriving.

layers.evidence: Pulpit, Bengel and Ellicott on Matthew 11:10: Christ applies to Himself a prophecy of God's coming. The Septuagint of Exodus 23:20 and TAGNT of Matthew 11:10 share idou egō apostellō ton angelon mou pro prosōpou sou. NET Bible notes on Mark 1:2. TAHOT: in Hebrew both verses open with sholeach (sending) and mal'akh (messenger or angel).
layers.text: Jesus applies the verse to John the Baptist, changing "before Me" to "before You": the messenger prepares for God, and Jesus takes that place. Matthew's Greek matches Exodus 23:20, "I am sending an angel before you," and so do the Hebrew openings.

layers.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Malachi 4:5: an Elijah in spirit, not the literal Elijah. Keil and Delitzsch: Elijah was sent in the person of John. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes): in denying he was Elijah (John 1:21), John denied only that he was that great prophet himself.
layers.text: Malachi names the messenger: "I will send you Elijah the prophet." John would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah," and Jesus calls him "the Elijah who was to come." Yet asked "Are you Elijah?", John said, "I am not": the role returned, not the man.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry and Keil and Delitzsch on Malachi 4:5: the close of Old Testament prophecy. Orthodox Bibles follow the Septuagint order and end the prophets with Daniel. NET Bible notes on Mark 1:2-3 and 1:6; Benson and Gill on 2 Kings 1:8: John dressed like Elijah.
layers.text: Malachi closes the Old Testament in Protestant and Catholic Bibles, and Mark opens by quoting it with Isaiah's "voice of one calling." Then John appears dressed like Elijah, "with a leather belt around his waist." The story resumes where the prophets left off.

layers.evidence: Bengel on Matthew 17:3 and Ellicott on Malachi 4:5: both are named together in Malachi 4:4-5. The Pulpit Commentary: they represent the Law and the Prophets.
layers.text: Malachi's closing lines name Moses and Elijah together: "Remember the law of My servant Moses" and "I will send you Elijah the prophet." On the mountain of transfiguration those two appear, "talking with Jesus," the Law and the Prophets gathered around Him.

passages.saying: open the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing without measure
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording and its setting, where the people were robbing God of tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:8-9).
layers.text: God calls His people to bring the whole tithe into the temple storehouse so His house has food. He invites them to test Him and promises to open heaven and pour out blessing without measure.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the windows of heaven were opened at the flood to man's destruction, but now God would rain abundantly for His people; Gill contrasts this blessing with the times of Noah, when the windows of heaven were opened and a curse was poured out. Keil and Delitzsch compare the same figure in 2 Kings 7:2.
layers.text: The same Hebrew words, the windows of heaven, describe the floodgates opened in Noah's day to pour out the flood (Genesis 7:11). Here God promises to open them again, not in judgment but to pour out rain and blessing on those who honor Him with the full tithe.

passages.saying: a scroll of remembrance was written before Him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording and its setting after the scoffers' complaints in Malachi 3:13-15.
layers.text: While others scoffed, those who feared the LORD encouraged one another. The LORD listened and heard, and a record was written before Him of all who feared Him and honored His name, so that none would be forgotten.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it an allusion to records kept by kings, citing Esther 6:1; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the kings of Persia kept such records to reward service; Keil and Delitzsch say it recalls this Persian custom. Esther's Book of Records uses the same two Hebrew words, sefer (book) and zikkaron (remembrance).
layers.text: The scroll pictures the record books Persian kings kept of those who served them, so they could be rewarded. In Esther 6:1 the king has his Book of Records read to him, which leads him to find Mordecai's unrewarded service and honor him. God keeps such a record of all who fear Him.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the image is one of the oldest in Scripture, found in the self-same words when the Lord told Moses to write a memorial in a book. Exodus 17:14 and this verse share the Hebrew words katav (write), zikkaron (reminder) and sefer (scroll).
