layers.text: The Hebrew words here for writing, scroll and remembrance also come together when God told Moses, "Write this on a scroll as a reminder" (Exodus 17:14). Some hear that early written memorial in the record God keeps of His faithful people.

passages.saying: I will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording, which follows the scroll of remembrance in Malachi 3:16.
layers.text: God promises that those who fear Him will be His own on the day He acts. In that day of judgment He will spare them with the tender care a father shows a son who serves him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call Exodus 19:5 the original passage, where Israel is to be God's segullah; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives the literal sense my peculiar treasure and cites Exodus 19:5; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says Israel was God's special treasure chosen out of all nations. Both verses say they will be to Me a segullah.
layers.text: My treasured possession translates segullah, the title God gave Israel at Sinai: "you will be My treasured possession" (Exodus 19:5). Malachi applies this covenant title to the faithful who fear the LORD, whom God will claim as His own on His day.

passages.saying: the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's title and on God's promises to Abraham and David.
layers.text: Matthew begins his Gospel with Jesus' family line. It shows that Jesus descends from Abraham, the father of Israel, and from David, its great king, the two men to whom God promised that the Messiah would come from their families.

layers.evidence: Gill says Matthew's opening is the Hebrew way of speaking found in Genesis 5:1, which the Septuagint renders by the same phrase, and draws the line from the first Adam to the second. Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also note that the same expression is used in Genesis 5:1. Rabanus Maurus, in the Catena Aurea, says Matthew began so because he knew Genesis 5:1.
layers.text: Matthew opens with the same Greek phrase that the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 5:1 for the record of Adam's descendants. Some see a deliberate echo: as that record traced the line of the first Adam, this one traces the line of Jesus, the second Adam.

passages.saying: you are to give Him the name Jesus
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's own words to Joseph.
layers.text: The angel tells Joseph that Mary will have a son and that Joseph is to name Him Jesus. The reason is His mission: He will save His people from the guilt and power of their sins.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes, Wesley, Gill and Matthew Henry tie Jesus to the name Joshua, and with Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible they explain it as Saviour, or the LORD who saves. Barnes adds that the angel's promise expresses the same as the name.
layers.text: Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua, which comes from the verb to save and means the LORD saves. The angel gives the reason for the name: He will save His people from their sins. His very name announces what He came to do.

passages.saying: they will call Him Immanuel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Matthew's quotation of Isaiah 7:14.
layers.text: Matthew quotes Isaiah's promise that a virgin would conceive and give birth to a son called Immanuel. He sees it fulfilled when Mary, still a virgin, gives birth to Jesus.

layers.evidence: Gill calls Immanuel a compound of God and with us. Clarke reads the Hebrew as the Strong God with us and takes it to mean God in human nature. Barnes says the Hebrew word literally means God with us. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley say the name describes His nature as God come in the flesh.
layers.text: Immanuel is a Hebrew name joining immanu, with us, and El, God. Matthew translates it for his readers as God with us. The name describes who the child truly is: God Himself come to live among His people as a man.

passages.saying: We saw His star in the east
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wise men's own question in Jerusalem.
layers.text: Wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking where the newborn King of the Jews is. They saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all connect the star with Balaam's prophecy in Numbers 24:17, and say the wise men may have known it. Gill says the expectation of a star at the Messiah's coming is founded on that prophecy. The Companion Bible also points to Numbers 24.
layers.text: The star that marks the birth of the King of the Jews recalls Balaam's prophecy: A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel. The wise men may well have known this promise of a coming King linked with a star.

passages.saying: gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's account of the visit.
layers.text: The wise men find the child with His mother Mary. They bow down and worship Him, then open their treasure chests and give Him costly gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh.

layers.evidence: Gill, writing on Isaiah 60:6, says the nations will bring their gold and incense as the wise men did to Christ, and on Matthew 2:11 notes that some see Isaiah 60:6, with its gold and frankincense, fulfilled here. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points readers to Isaiah 60:3 and 60:6 and Psalm 72:10-11.
layers.text: Wise men from the east bowing before the young King with gifts of gold and frankincense can recall Isaiah 60, where nations come to Jerusalem's light and all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense. Some see their gifts as an echo of that promise.

passages.saying: those seeking the Child’s life are now dead
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's command to Joseph after Herod's death.
layers.text: After Herod dies, an angel tells Joseph in a dream to take the child and His mother back to the land of Israel, because those who were trying to kill the child are dead.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the angel's words are taken from Exodus 4:19, where Moses is told to return to Egypt because the one who sought his life is dead, and that the greater than Moses is now brought back for the same reason.
layers.text: The angel's words echo what God told Moses in Midian: all the men who sought to kill you are dead. Moses could go back once those who wanted him dead had died, and now Jesus, the greater Moses, is brought back from Egypt after Herod's death.

passages.saying: He will be called a Nazarene
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's account of the move to Nazareth.
layers.text: Joseph settles the family in the town of Nazareth in Galilee, where Jesus grows up. Matthew says this fulfilled what the prophets had spoken, that the Messiah would be called a Nazarene.

layers.evidence: Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown link Nazarene with netzer, the Branch of Isaiah 11:1, and Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 11:1 say the humble netzer was a despised Nazarene. Clarke lists Isaiah 11:1 as one likely source. Bullinger's Companion Bible and Figures of Speech reject the netzer link.
layers.text: Nazareth and Nazarene sound like the Hebrew netser, the Branch that Isaiah said would grow from the roots of Jesse. Jesus grew up in a small, looked-down-on town whose name can recall that humble shoot, the promised King from David's family line.

passages.saying: a garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of John's dress and food.
layers.text: John the Baptist wore rough clothing woven from camel's hair, tied with a leather belt, and he ate locusts and wild honey. His plain, self-denying life in the wilderness matched his call to repent.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say John's dress was Elijah's as described in 2 Kings 1:8, and Wesley says his leather belt was like Elijah's. Clarke adds that John took the same habit because he was foretold under Elijah's name in Malachi 4:5.
layers.text: John's camel-hair garment and leather belt match Elijah, a "hairy man" (most take this as a garment of hair) with a leather belt around his waist. His dress marked him as the one who came in Elijah's spirit and power, the Elijah God promised to send before the day of the LORD.

passages.saying: He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of the baptism and John's own testimony in John 1:32-34.
layers.text: As soon as Jesus is baptized and comes up from the water, heaven opens and the Spirit of God comes down on Him like a dove. God publicly marks Jesus out for His work as the Messiah.

layers.evidence: Gill says the Spirit who lights on Christ here is the same who moved on the waters at creation, now coming on Christ as He comes up out of the Jordan.
layers.text: As Jesus comes up out of the water, the Spirit of God comes down on Him. Some see an echo of creation, when the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters: the same Spirit who moved over the first waters now rests on Jesus.

layers.evidence: Gill asks who can read this account without thinking of Noah's dove and its olive leaf, a token of peace and reconciliation.
layers.text: The dove can also call to mind Noah's dove, which returned with a freshly plucked olive leaf after the flood, a token of peace and reconciliation. Now the Spirit comes down like a dove as Jesus rises from the water.

passages.saying: This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the voice from heaven at the baptism, heard again at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:5).
layers.text: While the Spirit rests on Jesus, the Father speaks from heaven. He names Jesus as His own beloved Son and says He is fully pleased with Him, giving open approval to Jesus at the start of His work.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the voice plainly alluded to Isaiah 42:1. Gill says the Father delighted in Him as His servant (Isaiah 42:1). Barnes, on Isaiah 42:1, calls the wording remarkably similar. Bullinger's Companion Bible and Figures of Speech also set the two side by side.
layers.text: The Father's words echo Isaiah, where God says of His Servant, "My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him." At the baptism the Spirit rests on Jesus as God speaks, marking Him as that Servant.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Psalm 2:7, says the decree may be applied to any time Christ is declared to be the Son of God, naming His baptism.
layers.text: Some also connect the Father's words with Psalm 2, where the LORD says to His anointed King, "You are My Son." They see the baptism as one of the times that decree about the Son was openly declared.

passages.saying: After fasting forty days and forty nights, He was hungry
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording and on Luke 4:2, which says He ate nothing in those days.
layers.text: In the wilderness Jesus went without food for forty full days and nights. Only when that time was over did He feel hungry.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley all set this fast beside Moses (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8). Clarke notes Moses received the law, Elijah was chief of the prophets, and Christ is the giver of the New Covenant.
layers.text: This fast matches two great servants of God. Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights when the covenant was written, and Elijah walked forty days and forty nights to Horeb. Jesus begins His own work the same way.

passages.saying: I will make you fishers of men
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jesus' call to Simon Peter and Andrew as they were casting a net into the sea (verse 18).
layers.text: Jesus calls two fishermen to follow Him as His disciples. He promises to turn their old trade into a new one: instead of catching fish, they will bring people to Him through the gospel.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Ezekiel 47:8-10 casts much light on this verse and that the Lord probably alludes to that prophet. Gill, on Ezekiel 47:10, says those fishers are the apostles, whom Christ made fishers of men.
layers.text: Ezekiel saw a river flowing from God's temple that made salt waters fresh and full of fish, with fishermen spreading their nets along the shore. Jesus' promise to make fishermen into fishers of men may point to that picture of a great catch for God.

passages.saying: He went up on the mountain and sat down
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the setting of the Sermon on the Mount and the custom that teachers sat to teach.
layers.text: Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the hillside and sat down, the usual posture of a teacher. His disciples gathered around Him to hear what He would teach.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible note on this verse says the mountain corresponds with the Mount of Olives in the Gospel's structure, and that there is a reference also to Sinai.
layers.text: Some see Jesus going up the mountain to teach as pointing back to Sinai, where Moses went up to God and was given words to tell the house of Jacob. On this reading, Jesus Himself now teaches God's people from the mountain.

passages.saying: Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the second beatitude, read beside the first (verse 3) and Jesus' call to repentance.
layers.text: Jesus calls blessed those who grieve, above all over their sin and their need of God. God will comfort them, in part now and fully when every tear is wiped away.

layers.evidence: Gill says Isaiah 61:1 seems to be referred to in this verse and the one before. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls these mourners the mourners in Zion of Isaiah 61:1-3 and says they receive the oil of joy for mourning.
layers.text: This promise likely echoes Isaiah 61, where the One anointed by God's Spirit is sent to comfort all who mourn and to give God's grieving people joy in place of mourning. Jesus now speaks that comfort over those who mourn.

passages.saying: Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the third beatitude and the meaning of meekness elsewhere in Scripture (Matthew 11:29).
layers.text: Jesus calls blessed the meek, those who are gentle and patient when wronged and leave their cause with God. They will receive the earth as their inheritance from Him.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this promise a repetition of Psalm 37:11. On the psalm, Gill says the Lord seems to refer to it, Barnes says the Saviour probably quoted it, and Keil and Delitzsch note Matthew's words match the Septuagint there. The Companion Bible also compares it.
layers.text: Jesus repeats the promise of Psalm 37: the meek will inherit the land. In the psalm the promise is the land God gave Israel. In Hebrew and Greek the word can mean land or earth, and Jesus gives the promise to all His meek followers.

passages.saying: for it is the city of the great King
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; Barnes explains that swearing by things God owns is really swearing by God.
layers.text: Jesus forbids casual oaths by the earth or by Jerusalem. Both belong to God: the earth is where He rests His feet, and Jerusalem is His royal city. So an oath by them is still an oath by God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Jesus is quoting Isaiah 66:1 here, Gill says He refers to Isaiah 66:1, and Barnes on Isaiah 66:1 says the Saviour probably had that passage in mind in the Sermon on the Mount.
layers.text: Calling the earth God's footstool comes from Isaiah 66:1, where the LORD says, "Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool." Jesus uses the prophet's picture to show that an oath by the earth still calls on God, whose footstool it is.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Jesus is quoting Psalm 48:2 here. Gill says the great King is not David but the King of kings, the Lord of hosts, and points to Psalm 48:2. Barnes also explains the Great King as God and lists Psalm 48:1-2 among verses to compare.
layers.text: Calling Jerusalem the city of the great King repeats Psalm 48:2, which praises Mount Zion as "the city of the great King." That King is God Himself, so an oath by Jerusalem is still an oath that involves God.

passages.saying: they disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; the commentaries explain that the hypocrites made a show of looking unwashed and gloomy.
layers.text: Jesus warns against fasting for show. The hypocrites made themselves look gloomy and unkempt so people would notice they were fasting. The praise of people is all the reward they will get.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible names the figure paronomasia in aphanizousin and phanosin (disfigure and appear). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that the verb for disfigure literally means make unseen.
layers.text: In Matthew's Greek there is a play on words: the hypocrites make their faces disappear (aphanizo) so that they may appear (phaino) to others as fasting. They hide their true faces in order to put on a show.

passages.saying: depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; Barnes explains that I never knew you means Christ never owned them as His.
layers.text: On the day of judgment Jesus will plainly tell those who only claimed Him that He never knew them as His own. He will send them away from Himself because they practiced lawlessness.

layers.evidence: Gill on Psalm 6:8 says these very words will be used by David's antitype, the Lord Jesus Christ, against carnal professors of religion. On Luke 13:27, the parallel saying, he adds that there seems to be a reference to Psalm 6:8.
layers.text: Jesus' sentence may echo David's cry in Psalm 6:8, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity", spoken to his enemies after God heard his prayer. If so, Jesus says it as Judge to those who claimed Him but lived in sin.

passages.saying: Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording and the request in verse 21; Christ's call outranks even a son's duty at his father's burial.
layers.text: A disciple asked to go and bury his father before following Jesus. Jesus told him to follow now and leave the burial to others. Christ's call comes before every other duty.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the word dead is used here in two different senses. The Companion Bible and Figures of Speech call it antanaclasis, one word repeated with two meanings: first the spiritually dead, then those who have died. Gill and Clarke explain it the same way.
layers.text: The word dead is used in two senses. The first dead are the spiritually dead, people alive in body but dead toward God. The second dead are those who have died. Let those without spiritual life bury the bodies of the dead.

passages.saying: like sheep without a shepherd
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; the commentaries explain that the crowds were neglected by their religious teachers.
layers.text: Jesus saw the crowds and was moved with compassion. They were weary and neglected, with no one to care for their souls, like sheep with no shepherd to guide and protect them.

layers.evidence: Gill on Ezekiel 34:5 applies the scattered flock to Christ's time, when the Scribes and Pharisees did not feed the people, so they were as sheep without a shepherd, and cites Matthew 9:36. On Matthew 9:36 he likens those teachers to the shepherds of Israel of old who fed themselves, not the flock.
layers.text: Some hear Ezekiel 34 behind "like sheep without a shepherd." There God's flock was "scattered for lack of a shepherd" because Israel's leaders fed themselves instead of the sheep. Read this way, Jesus finds the crowds neglected in the same way and has compassion on them.

passages.saying: Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; it closes Matthew's list of the twelve apostles.
layers.text: These are the last two names in Matthew's list of the twelve apostles: Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, the one who would betray Jesus.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all say the word is not about Canaan but means Zealot. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible call it the Aramaic term; Clarke derives it from the Hebrew kana, zealous, which Luke renders zelotes.
layers.text: Matthew's Greek calls Simon Kananaios. This does not mean he came from Canaan. The word comes from qana, the Hebrew and Aramaic root for zeal, so it means the Zealot, as Luke 6:15 puts it in plain Greek. Simon was known for his zeal.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains Iscariot as Judas of Kerioth, a town of Judah. Clarke says it is probably from the Hebrew ish kerioth, a man of Kerioth. Barnes agrees, while Gill lists it among several proposed explanations.
layers.text: Iscariot most likely comes from the Hebrew ish Kerioth, man of Kerioth, naming Judas by his hometown, a town in Judah. Other explanations have been suggested, so this meaning is probable rather than certain.

passages.saying: be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; the commentaries explain the pairing of caution with innocence.
layers.text: Jesus sends His disciples out defenseless into a hostile world. They must be wise and careful to avoid needless danger, yet stay innocent and never use wrong means to escape it.

layers.evidence: Clarke and Barnes point to Genesis 3:1 for the serpent's cunning, and Clarke says Jesus corrects that cunning by the simplicity of the dove. Keil and Delitzsch on Genesis 3:1 cite Matthew 10:16 for the serpent's natural shrewdness and note the Septuagint's word there, phronimos, though in Eden the sense is bad craftiness.
layers.text: The shrewd serpent first appears in Eden, where it was more crafty than any beast of the field. The Greek Old Testament there uses the same word Matthew's Greek uses here for shrewd. Jesus likely means the serpent's caution, not its evil cunning, and so pairs it with a dove's innocence.

passages.saying: a man against his father, a daughter against her mother
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain sense of Jesus' warning in its setting of persecution.
layers.text: Jesus warns that following Him will divide even families. When some in a home trust Him and others oppose Him, those closest to a believer may turn against them. This split is a result of His coming, not its aim.

layers.evidence: Gill says these lines are borrowed from Micah 7:6, Barnes says the saying is taken from Micah 7:6, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Bullinger's Companion Bible both say it is quoted from that verse. The family pairs match Micah's list one for one.
layers.text: Jesus takes these words from the prophet Micah, who mourned a faithless age when a son dishonored his father, a daughter rose against her mother, and a man's enemies were in his own house. Jesus says loyalty to Him will bring the same kind of split.

passages.saying: The blind receive sight, the lame walk
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jesus' answer to the question John sent from prison.
layers.text: When John the Baptist asks from prison whether Jesus is the One who was to come, Jesus answers by pointing to what He is doing: healing the blind, the lame, the lepers and the deaf, raising the dead, and bringing good news to the poor.

layers.evidence: Gill says Jesus has reference to the prophecies of the Messiah in Isaiah 35, Barnes ties the good news to the poor to Isaiah 61:1, and Bullinger's Companion Bible says these were the miracles foretold in Isaiah 35:5-6 and 61:1. Wesley also points to Isaiah 35:5.
layers.text: Jesus answers in words that echo Isaiah. Isaiah promised that when God came to save His people, the blind would see, the deaf hear and the lame leap, and that the Lord's anointed would preach good news to the poor. Jesus' works match those promises, showing John who He is.

passages.saying: will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jesus' woe over the towns that saw His miracles and did not repent.
layers.text: Capernaum, the town where Jesus lived and did many miracles, had been honored above other towns. Because it did not repent, it would be brought low. Even wicked Sodom would have repented if it had seen such miracles.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary says our Lord's words are an adaptation of Isaiah's address to the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:13-15). Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown only cross-reference the two verses.
layers.text: Jesus' warning may echo Isaiah's taunt against the proud king of Babylon, who boasted, "I will ascend to the heavens," but was told, "you will be brought down to Sheol," the realm of the dead. Read this way, Capernaum, like that king, would be brought down rather than lifted up.

layers.evidence: Barnes says this was strictly fulfilled, the site hard to fix; Clarke says the prediction was literally fulfilled; Ellicott says the words had an almost literal fulfilment, a few conjectured ruins marking the site. Barnes and Clarke date the ruin to the Roman wars, which the town outlived, so the note gives no date for its fall; 'by the 1800s' reflects the state of the site when these three wrote.
layers.text: Jesus' warning came true in history as well. The prosperous lakeside town later fell into ruin, and by the 1800s so little was left that its very site was hard to identify. Its full reckoning still waits for the day of judgment.

passages.saying: you will find rest for your souls
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the yoke picture Jesus uses in His invitation to the weary.
layers.text: Jesus invites the weary to take on His yoke, that is, to submit to Him and learn from Him. Because He is gentle and humble, not harsh, those who follow Him will find true rest for their souls.

layers.evidence: Gill says the promise of rest unto your souls refers to Jeremiah 6:16. Bullinger's Companion Bible, on Jeremiah 6:16, compares Matthew 11:29-30, where a like invitation and promise is given. In the BSB the two promises are worded the same.
layers.text: Jesus repeats God's promise in Jeremiah. There the LORD told Israel to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way and walk in it, and they would find rest for their souls. Israel refused to walk in it. Jesus now offers that same rest to all who come to Him.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse as a play heard in Syriac, giving nich for meek and n'yacha for rest from the Peshitta. Since it rests on the Syriac translation, any Aramaic form is a reconstruction.
layers.text: In the Syriac translation of Matthew, the word for gentle (nich) and the word for rest (nyacha) sound alike: the gentle One gives rest. Some think Jesus' own Aramaic carried the same echo, though that is a reconstruction.

passages.saying: the birds of the air come and nest in its branches
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast between the tiny seed and the large plant in the parable.
layers.text: A mustard seed is tiny, yet it grows into a plant big enough for birds to nest in. In the same way, the kingdom of heaven starts small and grows far beyond its humble beginning.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Ezekiel 17:23, calls Ezekiel's cedar with its birds the Gospel mustard tree of Matthew 13:32, small at first but at length sheltering all, and on Daniel 4:12 sets the gospel kingdom's tree against the empire tree. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes), on Ezekiel 17:23, says the birds are people flocking to the kingdom and compares Matthew 13:32.
layers.text: The prophets pictured a kingdom as a great tree with birds nesting in its branches. Ezekiel used it for the cedar God Himself would plant, sheltering birds of every kind, and Daniel for a proud king's empire. Jesus' tiny seed growing into such a tree echoes that picture.

passages.saying: the righteous will shine like the sun
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jesus' explanation of the parable of the weeds.
layers.text: At the end of the age, when the wicked are removed, God's righteous people will shine with glory in their Father's kingdom. Jesus closes by urging everyone who can hear to listen and take it to heart.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Daniel 12:3, says our Lord seems to have respect to this passage in Matthew 13:43. Keil and Delitzsch, on the same passage, quote Matthew 13:43 as referring to it.
layers.text: Jesus' promise echoes Daniel's vision of the end, where the wise shine like the brightness of the heavens and those who lead many to righteousness shine like the stars forever. Jesus places that same glory in His Father's kingdom.

passages.saying: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Near Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks, "Who do you say I am?" Simon Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus says this was revealed to him by His Father in heaven, and promises to build His church.

layers.evidence: Tertullian (Prescription Against Heretics 22): Peter; John Chrysostom (Homilies on Matthew 54): the faith Peter confessed; Ellicott lists Peter's faith, the truth he confessed, or Christ. TBESG: petra is a mass of rock, petros a stone, but Ellicott notes the two Greek words differ in gender and were identical in Aramaic.
layers.text: Jesus puns on the name: "you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church." In Matthew's Greek, Peter is Petros and rock is petra; a man's name takes the masculine form. What the rock is has long been debated: Peter, the faith he confessed, or Christ.

layers.evidence: Ellicott: the two words were identical in the Aramaic Jesus probably spoke; the Pulpit Commentary gives the one word, kepha. TBESG: Cephas is the Aramaic kepha, Peter. The Syriac version, a later translation from the Greek, has kepha both times (Bengel). Not all agree: some read the change from petros to petra as meaningful.
layers.text: Jesus probably spoke Aramaic, and John keeps Peter's Aramaic name, Cephas, "which is translated as Peter"; Paul uses it too. Kepha means rock, so if Jesus said kepha both times, as Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary hold, the pun was exact: the same word twice.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary link the keys to Eliakim in Isaiah 22:22, and Ellicott and the continuation of Poole's Annotations to Revelation 3:7. Barnes: to bind was to forbid, to loose to allow, a phrase often used by the Jews, as in the saying that the school of Shammai binds.
layers.text: Jesus gives Peter "the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Isaiah's steward Eliakim was given "the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut," and Revelation gives it to Jesus. Binding and loosing were rabbis' words for forbidding and allowing.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Bengel find the phrase in Hezekiah's song (Isaiah 38:10); Gill cites Job 38:17, where the Septuagint has the same phrase. The NET Bible note: Hades is the Hebrew Sheol. TBESG: in the Greek Old Testament hades chiefly renders Sheol, and pyle (gate) renders sha'ar. The NET Bible note: the gates of Hades may stand for the power of death.
layers.text: "The gates of Hades" is Old Testament language. Facing death, Hezekiah says, "I must go through the gates of Sheol," and God asks Job, "Have the gates of death been revealed to you?" Hades is Greek for Sheol. Death will not overpower what Jesus builds.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott on John 1:42 compare the renamings of Abram, Sarai and Jacob.
layers.text: God renames people at turning points: Abram becomes Abraham, "a father of many nations," and Jacob becomes Israel. On first meeting Simon, Jesus does the same: "You will be called Cephas." Older commentators compare these renamings.

passages.saying: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and on Acts 2 and 10, where Peter first preaches to Jews and then to Gentiles.
layers.text: Jesus promises Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, the authority to open it to others. Peter first opened it by preaching to Jews at Pentecost and later to Gentiles. The same keys were given to all the apostles, and God confirmed in heaven what they bound or loosed on earth.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Clarke, on Isaiah 22:22, say Jesus used the same or a like expression for the apostles' authority in Matthew 16:19 and applied the prophet's words to Himself in Revelation 3:7. Keil and Delitzsch see a resemblance to the keys given to Peter and note that the steward held the key only in the king's stead.
layers.text: The keys recall Isaiah 22:22, where God places the key to the house of David on the shoulder of Eliakim, the king's steward: "What he opens no one can shut." A steward used the key for the king. In Revelation 3:7 the risen Christ holds the key of David Himself.

passages.saying: whoever loses his life for My sake will find it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain contrast in the verse between saving and losing one's life.
layers.text: Whoever tries to keep his life safe by turning away from Jesus will lose it in the end. Whoever gives up his life for Jesus' sake will find it, because what he loses on earth he will receive in heaven.

layers.evidence: Clarke and the Companion Bible both note that one Greek word, psuche, is translated life in verse 25 and soul in verse 26, and say it should be rendered the same way in both verses.
layers.text: In Matthew's Greek one word, psyche, stands behind both life in verse 25 and soul in verse 26. English hides the link, but the two verses speak of the same thing: the life a person tries to save for this world is the very life he loses, and nothing can buy it back.

passages.saying: His face shone like the sun
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the word transfigured, which describes a change of appearance.
layers.text: On the mountain Jesus was transfigured before Peter, James and John. His appearance changed, though He was still the same Jesus: His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light.

layers.evidence: Barnes on this verse compares the radiance of Moses' face in Exodus 34:29-30 and points to Hebrews 1:3, where Christ is the brightness of God's glory. The Companion Bible on Exodus 34:29 says Moses reflected the divine glory and compares Matthew 17:2.
layers.text: Jesus' shining face can recall Moses, whose face became radiant after he spoke with the LORD on Mount Sinai, reflecting God's glory like a mirror. Hebrews calls the Son the radiance of that glory.

passages.saying: This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the cloud as the familiar sign of God's presence and on the words spoken from it.
layers.text: While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud, the sign of God's presence, enveloped them. The Father's voice called Jesus His beloved Son and told the disciples to listen to Him, honoring Him above Moses and Elijah.

layers.evidence: Gill says the command has the very words Moses spoke of the coming prophet in Deuteronomy 18:15; Clarke says the voice refers to that prediction; Keil and Delitzsch, on Deuteronomy 18, say the phrase is used of Christ at the transfiguration word for word.
layers.text: Listen to Him! echoes Moses' promise in Deuteronomy 18:15 that God would raise up a prophet like him: "You must listen to him." With Moses standing by, the Father points to Jesus as that promised Prophet.

layers.evidence: Barnes lists the cloud on Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:15-17) among the clouds that showed God's presence and says the disciples were thus prepared to hear God speak. Gill sets this bright cloud, a sign of the clearness of the gospel, against the thick, dark cloud in which God came down on Sinai to give the law.
layers.text: The cloud and the voice from it recall Mount Sinai, where the cloud covered the mountain and the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud. The same sign of God's presence now surrounds Jesus. At Sinai God gave the law out of thick darkness, but this cloud is bright.

passages.saying: There was a landowner who planted a vineyard
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the parable's details and on the leaders seeing in verse 45 that it was about them.
layers.text: Jesus tells of a landowner who carefully prepared a vineyard and rented it to tenants before going away. The owner stands for God, and the tenants for the leaders of Israel, who were trusted to tend His people and bring Him its fruit.

layers.evidence: Gill says the Lord seems to have taken many ideas of this parable from Isaiah 5, where the vineyard is the house of Israel. Clarke says He takes the parable from Isaiah 5:1. JFB says its details and its basis come from Isaiah 5:1-7.
layers.text: The planted vineyard, the winepress and the tower come from Isaiah's song of the vineyard, where God builds a watchtower and digs a winepress but gets only sour fruit. There the vineyard is the house of Israel. Jesus' hearers would know whom the story was about.

passages.saying: He will bring those wretches to a wretched end
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the hearers' own answer to Jesus' question in verse 40.
layers.text: Asked what the owner will do, the hearers say he will destroy the wicked tenants and rent the vineyard to others who will give him its fruit. Without realizing it, they pass judgment on themselves.

layers.evidence: JFB calls it an emphatic alliteration not easily conveyed in English. The Companion Bible and Figures of Speech name it paronomasia: kakous kakos, the two words side by side.
layers.text: In Matthew's Greek the answer opens with two sound-alike words side by side, kakous kakos: bad men, badly destroyed. The BSB keeps the echo with wretches and a wretched end. The repeated sound may make the verdict ring with force.

passages.saying: There will be famines and earthquakes in various places.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse in Jesus' answer about the signs of the end.
layers.text: Jesus warns His disciples that nations and kingdoms will rise against each other, and that famines and earthquakes will strike in many places.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible note calls famines and pestilences, limoi kai loimoi, the figure Paronomasia, a play on like sounds, and renders it dearths and deaths. His Figures of Speech lists this verse, and Luke 21:11, under the same figure.
layers.text: Many Greek copies of Matthew read famines and pestilences here, limoi and loimoi, two words that sound almost alike. The BSB follows copies without pestilences, but it keeps the same pair in Luke 21:11.

passages.saying: The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which follows the great tribulation Jesus has just described.
layers.text: Jesus says that right after the distress of those days the sun will go dark, the moon will give no light, the stars will fall, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible says these words are quoted from Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4. Clarke points to Isaiah 13:10 for the fall of Babylon told in these pictures, and Barnes names Isaiah 13:10 for Babylon and Isaiah 34:4 for Bozrah and Idumea as the same language.
layers.text: Jesus speaks in Isaiah's words. Isaiah said the sun would be darkened and the moon would not give its light when God judged Babylon, and that the stars would fall when He judged Edom. These are the prophets' pictures of the LORD's day of judgment.

passages.saying: They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which continues Jesus' answer about the sign of His coming.
layers.text: Jesus says the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. All the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see Him coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible says the words are quoted from Daniel 7:13. Barnes on Daniel 7:13 says the Saviour probably meant to refer to this language when He spoke of coming in clouds, and Keil and Delitzsch call Daniel 7:13 the foundation of Christ's words about His coming.
layers.text: Jesus describes His coming with Daniel's vision of "One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven," who approaches the Ancient of Days. By using this title and picture, Jesus shows that He is the one Daniel saw.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible says these words are quoted from Zechariah 12:12 and notes that earth may be read land. Barnes says the wailing will be chiefly because they pierced and rejected the Saviour, citing John 19:37 and Zechariah 12:12.
layers.text: The mourning of all the tribes echoes Zechariah 12, where the people look on "the One they have pierced" and "The land will mourn, each clan on its own." Matthew's Greek word for earth can also mean land.

passages.saying: He will send out His angels with a loud trumpet call
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which follows the coming of the Son of Man.
layers.text: Jesus says He will send His angels with a loud trumpet call to gather His chosen people from every direction, from one end of the heavens to the other.

layers.evidence: Gill on this verse points to Isaiah 27:13 for the great trumpet. Clarke on Isaiah 27:13 asks whether it does not refer to the time our Lord spoke of in Matthew 24:31, when His angels gather His elect with a great sound of a trumpet.
layers.text: The loud trumpet that gathers God's chosen people may echo Isaiah 27:13, where "a great ram’s horn will sound" and the scattered exiles in Assyria and Egypt come home to worship the LORD in Jerusalem.

passages.saying: And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, where Judas makes his bargain with the chief priests.
layers.text: Judas asks the chief priests what they will pay him to hand Jesus over to them, and they set out thirty pieces of silver for him.

layers.evidence: Gill says thirty shekels was the price of a servant (Exodus 21:32) and that Christ was valued at it according to the prophecy in Zechariah 11:12. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) on Zechariah 11:12 says the high priest fixed on the price named by Zechariah, the price of a slave. Wesley and Clarke also call it the price of a slave.
layers.text: The price matches Zechariah 11:12, where the shepherd's wages, "thirty pieces of silver," are weighed out in contempt. The law set thirty shekels of silver as the payment for a servant gored by an ox, so Jesus was valued at the price of a slave.

passages.saying: Jesus went with His disciples to a place called Gethsemane
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and its setting after the Last Supper.
layers.text: After the Last Supper, Jesus went with His disciples to Gethsemane, a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives. He told most of them to sit and wait while He went farther on to pray.

layers.evidence: Gill calls olive press the true meaning of the name and sees in it a picture of Christ about to tread the winepress of His Father's wrath. Clarke derives it from the words for press and oil. Barnes allows either oil press or valley of fatness, the meaning Wesley gives.
layers.text: Gethsemane most likely means oil press, from gat (press) and shemen (oil). Olives from the Mount of Olives were probably pressed there. Some see this place of pressing as fitting, since Jesus was about to tread the winepress of His Father's wrath alone.

passages.saying: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the words of the prayer and the Bible's common use of a cup for an appointed portion of suffering.
layers.text: Jesus fell facedown and prayed to His Father. He asked that, if it were possible, the cup of suffering before Him might pass Him by. Yet He yielded His own will fully to His Father's will.

layers.evidence: Gill calls the cup Jesus faced a cup of fury, cursing and trembling, made up of the curse of the law and the wrath of God borne for His people. Barnes, writing on Isaiah 51:17, explains the cup of the Lord's wrath and sets beside it the cup the Saviour speaks of in Matthew 26:39.
layers.text: In the prophets, a cup from the Lord's hand pictures His wrath. Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem drinking the cup of His fury. The cup Jesus prayed about can be read as this cup of wrath, which He would drink for His people.

passages.saying: Then he went away and hanged himself.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: Judas threw the silver he had been paid back into the temple. Returning the money could not ease his guilty conscience, and he went away and hanged himself.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes the verb occurs only here in the New Testament, and that the Septuagint uses it at 2 Samuel 17:23 of Ahithophel, whom it calls a type of Judas. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Judas resembled Ahithophel in his treason and in his end.
layers.text: Matthew's Greek word for hanged himself appears nowhere else in the New Testament. The Greek Old Testament uses it of Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor who betrayed him and then hanged himself. Judas, the friend who betrayed Jesus, came to the same end.

passages.saying: it has been called the Field of Blood to this day
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse read with the two verses before it.
layers.text: The chief priests used the silver Judas returned to buy a potter's field as a burial ground for foreigners. Because of how it was bought, the field was still called the Field of Blood when Matthew wrote.

layers.evidence: Gill says the people named the field for the money paid for betraying innocent blood, and that Aceldama in Acts 1:19 has the same meaning. Barnes explains the name as the field bought with the price of blood.
layers.text: The field was named for its price. It was bought with blood money, the silver paid for betraying innocent blood, so people called it the Field of Blood. Acts gives the name in the local Aramaic, Akeldama, which means the same thing.

passages.saying: they were holding a notorious prisoner named Barabbas
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse with Mark 15:7 and Luke 23:19, which describe his crimes.
layers.text: Barabbas was a well-known prisoner, a robber who had joined in a rebellion and committed murder. Pilate set him beside Jesus and asked the crowd which of the two they wanted released.

layers.evidence: Gill says the Syriac form of the name means the son of a father, calls this its true sense, and notes such names were common. Clarke reads it as son of Abba and notes old manuscripts that give his name as Jesus Barabbas.
layers.text: Barabbas is an Aramaic name. Bar means son and abba means father, so it means son of a father, or son of a man named Abba. Names like this were common, as with Simon Bar-Jonah, son of Jonah. Some early copies of Matthew give his full name as Jesus Barabbas.

passages.saying: he took water and washed his hands before the crowd
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: Pilate saw that he could not sway the crowd and that a riot was starting. He washed his hands before them, declared himself innocent of Jesus' blood, and put the blame on them. Yet washing could not remove his guilt.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all point to the hand washing of Deuteronomy 21:6 as a known way to declare innocence in a death. Gill and Clarke add that Greeks and Romans had a like custom. All three say the washing did not clear Pilate.
layers.text: Pilate's washing matches a rite in the law of Moses. When a murder went unsolved, the elders of the nearest town washed their hands over a heifer and declared that their hands had not shed the blood. Pilate used the sign, but he had the power to free Jesus and did not.

passages.saying: they twisted together a crown of thorns and set it on His head
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: The soldiers mocked Jesus as a pretend king. They twisted thorny branches into a crown, put a staff in His hand for a scepter, knelt before Him, and hailed Him as King of the Jews in scorn.

layers.evidence: Gill ties the crown to Christ being made a curse for us, since thorns were the curse laid on the earth for man's sin. Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary says that as thorns came in with sin, Christ was crowned with thorns for us. The Companion Bible calls thorns the sign of the curse.
layers.text: Thorns first appear in the Bible in the curse on the ground after Adam sinned. The soldiers meant the crown of thorns as mockery, but it pictured what Jesus came to do. He bore the curse of sin for His people and wore the sign of that curse on His head.

passages.saying: a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in the account of the crucifixion.
layers.text: Jesus was led outside the city to a place called Golgotha to be crucified. Matthew gives the meaning of the name for his readers.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and the Companion Bible all give the meaning skull. Clarke and Barnes think the place was named for the executions held there, and both mention the view that it was shaped like a skull. Gill sets aside the old story that Adam's skull was found there.
layers.text: Golgotha is an Aramaic word for skull, close to the Hebrew gulgoleth. Matthew explains it as The Place of the Skull, and the name Calvary comes from the Latin for skull. It was most likely named as a place of execution, though some think the hill looked like a skull.

passages.saying: they offered Him wine to drink, mixed with gall
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on the custom, described by Barnes and Clarke, of giving the condemned a numbing drink; both say Jesus refused it so as to bear His pain fully.
layers.text: When Jesus reached the place of crucifixion, He was offered wine mixed with gall, a bitter drink often given to the condemned to dull their pain. He tasted it but refused to drink, choosing to bear His suffering fully.

layers.evidence: Gill says this offer fulfilled Psalm 69:21. On Psalm 69:21, Gill, Clarke and the Companion Bible tie the verse to Matthew 27:34, and Wesley says it was fulfilled metaphorically in David but properly in Christ. The psalm's word rosh means a bitter poison, rendered gall.
layers.text: Psalm 69 is the prayer of a righteous sufferer who says his enemies "poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar" for his thirst. When Jesus was offered wine mixed with gall at the cross, He lived out that psalm. Words that fit the psalmist as a figure came true of Jesus in fact.

passages.saying: those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes and Clarke explain the head shaking as a gesture of scorn.
layers.text: As Jesus hung on the cross, people passing by insulted Him and shook their heads at Him in contempt.

layers.evidence: Gill says this was prophesied in Psalm 22:7 and, on the psalm, that it was fulfilled at Matthew 27:39. Barnes and JFB on Psalm 22:7 point to this head shaking at the cross, and Wesley says the verse is applied to Christ.
layers.text: In Psalm 22 the sufferer says, "All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads." The passers-by at the cross did exactly this to Jesus, acting out the scene the psalm had described long before.

passages.saying: He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in verses 41 to 43; Gill explains the taunt as scorn of His claim to trust God.
layers.text: The religious leaders mock Jesus on the cross. Since He claimed to trust God and to be the Son of God, they jeer that God should rescue Him now, if God really wants Him.

layers.evidence: Gill says Psalm 22:8 holds these very words, foretold to be said to Christ. Clarke calls the taunt a quotation of Psalm 22:8 as worded in the Septuagint, where the Greek for wants renders the Hebrew for delights. Barnes on Psalm 22:8 says they fulfilled the prophecy without suspecting it.
layers.text: The taunt echoes Psalm 22:8, where the sufferer's enemies sneer, "He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him." The mockers at the cross used nearly the same words, never realizing they were fulfilling the very psalm that described the Messiah's suffering.

passages.saying: My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Wesley explains the cry as both trust in God and a deep sense of the wrath due to the sins He was bearing.
layers.text: About three in the afternoon Jesus cried out with a loud voice, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" Bearing the sins of others, He felt the full weight of God's judgment, yet He still called God His own God.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Jesus quoted these words from Psalm 22:1, Barnes on the psalm calls them the very words He uttered on the cross, and the Companion Bible notes the quotation. Matthew keeps the Hebrew Eli, the same word for my God that opens the psalm.
layers.text: Jesus' cry is the opening line of Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" Other details of that psalm, its mockers, head shaking and casting of lots, also appear around the cross in this same chapter.

layers.evidence: On verse 47, Gill says the bystanders either misheard because of the nearness of the sound or wilfully mistook Him to mock Him; Barnes says they could pretend Eli meant Elias (Elijah); the Companion Bible says the word was mistaken for the Hebrew or Aramaic name of Elijah.
layers.text: Eli means my God, but to some standing nearby it sounded like the name Elijah. They said He was calling Elijah, either because they misheard Him or because they twisted His words to mock Him. The likeness is in the sound; it was not a pun Jesus intended.

passages.saying: there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and John 19:38; Barnes notes that Joseph had been a disciple who did not follow openly because he feared the Jewish leaders.
layers.text: As evening came, Joseph, a rich man from the town of Arimathea, came forward. He was a disciple of Jesus who had kept quiet for fear of the Jewish leaders, and now he came to see to Jesus' burial.

layers.evidence: Gill says Joseph's wealth is mentioned to show the fulfilling of Isaiah 53:9. Matthew Henry's Concise says the leaders meant Him to be buried with the thieves, but God overruled it so His grave was with the rich. JFB on Isaiah 53:9 points to Matthew 27:57 and the rich men who honored Him at His death.
layers.text: Isaiah said the Servant would be "assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death." Jesus died between two criminals, yet a rich disciple, Joseph, laid Him in his own tomb, just as the prophet foretold.

passages.saying: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the commission that follows; Barnes and Gill explain this as authority given to Christ as Mediator to gather and rule His church.
layers.text: The risen Jesus comes to His disciples and declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Him. On that authority He then sends them out to the nations.

layers.evidence: Clarke on Daniel 7:14 says Jesus applied this verse to Himself after His resurrection in Matthew 28:18. Barnes says the Son of Man received this dominion from the Ancient of Days and points to Matthew 28:18. Both verses speak of rule being given to Him.
layers.text: In Daniel's vision, a figure like a son of man comes before God and "was given dominion, glory, and kingship" over every people. Risen from the dead, Jesus, who often called Himself the Son of Man, now says that all authority has been given to Him.

passages.saying: whom He named Boanerges
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Jesus chose twelve men "to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach." Three of them received new names: Simon was named Peter, and the fishermen brothers James and John, sons of Zebedee, were named Boanerges.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: Boanerges (G0993) and brontes, of thunder (G1027). Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) notes the derivation is debated. Ellicott: an Aramaic compound, b'ne regesh; Hammond, quoted by Benson, takes it as sons of commotion; Gill notes the odd form. Mark translates other Aramaic words the same way (5:41, 7:34).
layers.text: Boanerges is not a Greek word but most likely Aramaic, the language Jesus probably spoke. Mark keeps it and translates it: "Sons of Thunder." Boane- is usually taken as bene, "sons of"; the rest is harder to trace, and its derivation is still debated.

layers.evidence: Luke 9:51-56. Barnes and Ellicott tie the nickname to their fiery zeal, as in this scene; Benson and Gill suggest it honors their forceful preaching. The text itself does not say.
layers.text: The Gospels never say why Jesus gave the name. Many find it fits a later scene: when a Samaritan village turned Jesus away, James and John asked, "do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?" Jesus rebuked them.

passages.saying: Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the sea
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; JFB and Gill note that the sea, which normally stays rough after the wind drops, was calmed at the same moment by His word.
layers.text: Woken in the boat during a violent storm, Jesus rebukes the wind and orders the sea to be still. At once the wind stops and the sea becomes perfectly calm, though waves usually keep heaving long after a storm ends.

layers.evidence: Gill on Psalm 107:29 says Christ did this by a word in Mark 4:39. Barnes on the same verse says only God can calm the storm, so Jesus doing it proves He was divine; on Psalm 89:9 he says Jesus used this very power over the sea of Galilee.
layers.text: Psalm 107 praises the LORD, who "calmed the storm to a whisper" so that the waves of the sea were hushed. When Jesus silences wind and waves with a word, He does what the psalm credits to the LORD, and His disciples ask who He can be.

passages.saying: My name is Legion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and on Luke 8:30, which says many demons had entered the man.
layers.text: Jesus asks the possessed man his name. The answer comes back that his name is Legion, because many demons have taken hold of him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, the Companion Bible and Matthew Henry all explain that a Roman legion was a large body of soldiers, about six thousand at full strength. Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Matthew Henry add that the name points to the great number of demons in the man.
layers.text: A legion was a unit of the Roman army that had about six thousand soldiers at full strength. The name is explained on the spot, “for we are many,” showing that a whole army of demons held this one man.

passages.saying: Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: At night the disciples strain to row against the wind. In the fourth watch Jesus comes to them walking on the sea. They think He is a ghost and cry out, until He speaks, climbs into the boat, and the wind dies down.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) hears Job 9 in Mark 6:48. The Septuagint of Job 9:8 has peripaton epi thalasses, walking on the sea, as Mark has peripaton epi tes thalasses.
layers.text: In the Old Testament it is God who walks on the sea: "He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea." The Greek Old Testament has Him walking on the sea, in the words Mark uses when Jesus comes "walking on the sea."

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) links Exodus 33, 1 Kings 19 and Job 9. The NET Bible note gives both readings and cites Exodus 33:19, 22. The Septuagint has parerchomai, Mark's verb, in all three passages.
layers.text: "He intended to pass by them" recalls God passing by Moses and Elijah: "the LORD is about to pass by." Job says, "Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him." The Greek Old Testament uses Mark's verb in each. Others take it as how it looked to the disciples.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition): ego eimi could better be rendered I am, the language of the LORD's self-revelation. The Septuagint of Isaiah 43 has me phobou (do not fear) in verse 1, meta sou eimi in verse 2 and ego eimi in verse 10.
layers.text: "It is I" is ego eimi, literally "I am." It can be ordinary speech (the healed man says it in John 9:9), but here it may echo Isaiah 43, which pairs the same words in Greek too: "Do not fear," "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you," "I am He."

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (Westminster Theological Seminary, writing in The Gospel Coalition): the miracle anticipates the Transfiguration in Mark 9:2-8.
layers.text: The two men God "passed by" on His mountain were Moses and Elijah, and three chapters later they appear on another mountain, "talking with Jesus." One scholar reads the sea crossing as pointing ahead to that moment of glory.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) reads it as a new exodus led by the incarnate I am, citing Psalm 77:16-20 and Isaiah 43:16.
layers.text: Psalm 77 remembers the exodus: "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found." Isaiah's LORD "makes a way in the sea." Some read the night crossing as a new exodus, led by the "I am" Himself.

passages.saying: For everyone will be salted with fire.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse after the warnings about hell in Mark 9:43-48. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Barnes read it of trials; Gill and Wesley of the fire of judgment.
layers.text: Jesus says that everyone will be salted with fire. It is a hard saying, and Bible teachers read it in two main ways: as the fiery trials that purify His followers, or as the fire of judgment that the lost endure without being consumed.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible tie the saying to the law of salting every sacrifice in Leviticus 2:13, and Barnes explains it from the salt sprinkled on offerings. Gill, on Leviticus 2:13, says our Lord refers to that law here.
layers.text: The picture comes from God's altar. The law said, “you are to add salt to each of your offerings” (Leviticus 2:13), and many manuscripts of Mark here add that every sacrifice will be salted with salt. Salt and fire both belonged to an offering made ready for God.

passages.saying: a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and Jesus' journey up to Jerusalem in Mark 10:32-52.
layers.text: As Jesus leaves Jericho on His way to Jerusalem, with His disciples and a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus is sitting beside the road.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that bar means son in Syriac, that is Aramaic, so the man was named for his father Timaeus. The Companion Bible likewise notes that the name is Aramaic and is explained in the verse.
layers.text: Bar is the Aramaic word for son, so the name Bartimaeus simply means son of Timaeus. Mark gives the meaning right beside the name.

passages.saying: you will find a colt tied there
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the entry into Jerusalem that follows in Mark 11:7-10.
layers.text: Jesus sends two disciples into the village ahead to bring Him a young colt that no one has ever ridden. He will ride it into Jerusalem.

layers.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), Gill and Clarke, on Zechariah 9:9, say the prophecy of the King riding on a colt was fulfilled when Jesus rode into Jerusalem, and Pusey names this verse. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties the colt to the same entry into Jerusalem.
layers.text: By sending for a colt, Jesus sets up the scene Zechariah foretold: “your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt.” He comes to Jerusalem as its promised King, but in humility.

passages.saying: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Jesus ends His parable of the tenants, who kill the owner's beloved son, by quoting Psalm 118. The leaders understand that He told the parable against them.
In the psalm the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner: "This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes." The rejection is not the end; God reverses it.
Days earlier the crowds greeted Jesus with the same psalm: "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!" The week opens with one verse of Psalm 118 and turns on another.

layers.evidence: Gregory Lanier (JETS 56/4, 2013) argues that the parable and its quotation of Psalm 118:22 hinge on the son and stone wordplay, lost in the Greek, as a mark that the quotation goes back to Jesus. Hebrew ben (H1121) and eben (H68).
layers.text: In Hebrew "son" is ben and "stone" is even (eben), a likeness lost in Greek. Some scholars suggest the parable's rejected son and the psalm's rejected stone are tied by this sound.

In Luke, Jesus adds that whoever falls on this stone will be broken and whoever it falls on will be crushed, drawing on Isaiah's "stone of stumbling" and Daniel's stone, cut without hands, that crushes the kingdoms and fills the earth.

The apostles keep building with this stone: Peter quotes it to the rulers and elders in Jerusalem, calls believers "living stones," and joins it to Isaiah's precious cornerstone, and Paul names Christ the cornerstone.

passages.saying: This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: At the Passover meal on His last night, Jesus breaks the bread, saying, "this is My body," then gives the cup: "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many." He explains His death before it happens.

layers.evidence: Gill and Poole on Exodus 24:8 tie Moses' words to Christ's at the Supper, and Ellicott on Matthew 26:28 traces the phrase to Exodus 24:4-8. TBESG: diatheke nearly always renders berit in the Greek Old Testament.
layers.text: Jesus takes up Moses' words at Sinai. Moses sprinkled blood on the people and said, "This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you." The first covenant was sealed in blood, and Hebrews quotes Moses' words as it explains the death of Christ.

layers.evidence: Gill on Exodus 24:11: a feast was common at covenant making; Keil and Delitzsch see the Sinai meal as a type of the marriage supper of the Lamb. On the parallel Matthew 26:29, Ellicott cites Isaiah 25:6 and the Pulpit Commentary reads it as the marriage supper of the Lamb.
layers.text: At Sinai the covenant ended in a meal: the elders "saw the God of Israel," and "they ate and drank." Jesus seals His covenant at a table too, and looks ahead to drinking "anew in the kingdom of God," at Isaiah's feast where God "will swallow up death forever."

layers.evidence: In Mark 14:24 the most reliable manuscripts lack new (kaines), which other copies likely took from Luke 22:20 (NET Bible note; TAGNT). The NET Bible note: Jesus' death established the forgiveness promised in Jeremiah 31:31. Ellicott on Matthew 26:28 points to Jeremiah 31:31-34.
layers.text: Luke and Paul record "the new covenant in My blood," and Matthew adds "for the forgiveness of sins." Jeremiah had promised a new covenant written on the heart: "I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more."

layers.evidence: The Reformation Study Bible note on Mark 14:24: Jesus alludes to Isaiah 53:12. Jeannine K. Brown (JETS 2020) finds allusions to Isaiah 53 in Mark 10:45 and 14:24; Maclaren on Isaiah 53:12 joins it to the ransom for many. The echo of poured out is with the Hebrew, he'erah (TAHOT; TBESH); the Greek Old Testament shares only many.
layers.text: "Poured out for many" echoes Isaiah's suffering servant, who "poured out His life unto death" and "bore the sin of many." Jesus had already said He came "to give His life as a ransom for many."

layers.evidence: The Reformation Study Bible note on Mark 14:24 points to the Passover blood that protected Israel and the covenant blood of Exodus 24:8; the NET Bible note says Jesus is reinterpreting the Passover meal.
layers.text: It is Passover, "when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed." In Egypt the lamb's blood on the doorframes shielded Israel: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." At Sinai blood sealed the covenant. In this cup Jesus gathers both.

passages.saying: you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, Jesus' answer to the high priest's question; Gill reads it as His proof that He is the Son of God.
layers.text: When the high priest asks whether He is the Christ, Jesus answers, I am. He tells His judges that they will see Him, the Son of Man, seated at God's right hand and coming with the clouds of heaven.

layers.evidence: Gill on Mark 14:62 says the words refer to the prophecy in Daniel 7:13. On Daniel 7:13, Barnes lists Mark 14:62 among the places where the Saviour speaks of Himself in this language, and Clarke says Jesus applied Daniel's words to Himself before the high priests.
layers.text: Coming with the clouds of heaven takes up Daniel's vision of One like the Son of Man, who comes before the Ancient of Days and is given an everlasting kingdom. On trial for His life, Jesus applies that vision to Himself.

passages.saying: a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, where Mark gives the local name and its meaning; Matthew Henry's Concise notes that it was the common place of execution.
