layers.text: The soldiers bring Jesus to the place where He will be crucified. Mark gives its local name, Golgotha, and explains it for his readers as The Place of the Skull.

layers.evidence: Mark himself translates the name. Gill explains it as the place of a skull, saying that skulls of men executed and buried there lay scattered about.
layers.text: Golgotha comes from the Aramaic word for skull, and Mark translates it: The Place of the Skull. Why the spot had this name is not certain. One older explanation is that skulls of executed men lay scattered there.

passages.saying: whose wife Elizabeth was a daughter of Aaron
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes notes that John was descended from priests on both his father's and his mother's side.
layers.text: Luke sets the scene in the days of King Herod. Zechariah is a priest from the division of Abijah, and his wife Elizabeth also comes from Aaron's priestly family, so John will be born to priests on both sides.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that Elizabeth is the same name as Elisheba, Aaron's wife in Exodus 6:23, which the Septuagint spells Elisabeth as Luke does, and thinks it was likely a common name among Aaron's descendants; the Companion Bible makes the same link. Gill links the two again in his note on Exodus 6:23.
layers.text: Elizabeth bears the same name as Elisheba, the wife of Aaron, Israel's first high priest. The Greek Old Testament spells that name Elisabeth, just as Luke does. It was likely a common name among Aaron's descendants, and this daughter of Aaron carries it.

passages.saying: Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes explains their age as one that left no prospect of children.
layers.text: Zechariah and Elizabeth had no children. Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and both of them were now old, so by nature they had no hope of a child.

layers.evidence: Gill says the phrase for their age is a Hebrew way of speaking that matches Genesis 18:11, where the Septuagint uses the same phrase. Clarke calls the case an exact parallel to Sarah and Abraham, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown names Abraham and Sarah first among the once-childless couples it recalls.
layers.text: A barren wife and a couple well along in years recall Abraham and Sarah before Isaac was born. Genesis uses the same phrase of them, and the Greek Old Testament there words it much as Luke does. As with Isaac, God is about to give a son where nature offered no hope.

passages.saying: you are to give him the name John
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes takes the prayer to be Zechariah's prayer for a child.
layers.text: The angel calms Zechariah's fear and tells him that God has heard his prayer. Elizabeth will have a son, and Zechariah is to name him John.

layers.evidence: Gill gives the Hebrew as Jochanan, meaning gracious; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives Jehovah's gracious gift; Wesley gives the grace or favour of Jehovah; the Companion Bible gives Jehovah sheweth favour. Gill and Wesley call it a fitting name for the forerunner of the Messiah's reign of grace.
layers.text: John is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yohanan, which means the LORD is gracious, or the LORD has shown favor. God chose the name through the angel, and it suits the one who would go before the Messiah and open the way for His grace.

passages.saying: He shall never take wine or strong drink
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes explains being filled with the Holy Spirit as being set apart and fitted by God for John's office.
layers.text: John will be great in the sight of the Lord. He must never touch wine or any strong drink, and the Holy Spirit will fill him even before he is born.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes both point to Numbers 6:3, where wine and strong drink are forbidden to the Nazirite, and Barnes says John abstained because he bore that character. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains the words as making John a Nazirite, a separated one.
layers.text: Giving up wine and strong drink was the rule for a Nazirite, a person set apart to God under the law of Numbers 6. John is to keep that rule all his life, marking him as wholly separated to the Lord for his work.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that the Nazirite vow was usually temporary and voluntary, and that only Samson, Samuel and John the Baptist were Nazirites from the womb.
layers.text: Most Nazirite vows lasted for a set time, but a few people were given to God before birth. Samson was to be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and Samuel was vowed to the LORD by his mother. Some see John, filled with the Holy Spirit before his birth, standing in that line.

passages.saying: in the spirit and power of Elijah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes explains making ready a people as preparing them for the Messiah by calling them to repentance.
layers.text: John will go ahead of the Lord with the same spirit and power that marked Elijah. He will call people back to God, turning the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, so that a people is ready when the Lord comes.

layers.evidence: Gill says Malachi 4:6 is the prophecy referred to; Clarke says Malachi had likened John to Elijah and points to Malachi 4:5-6; the Companion Bible marks the words as a reference to Malachi 3:1 with 4:5-6.
layers.text: The angel takes up the closing promise of the Old Testament. Malachi foretold that God would send Elijah the prophet, who would turn the hearts of the fathers to their children. The angel says John will fulfill that promise, coming in Elijah's spirit and power.

passages.saying: The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes explains the throne as the kingdom and calls David His father because Jesus descended from him.
layers.text: The angel tells Mary that her Son will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. God will give Him the throne of His father David, for He comes from David's royal line.

layers.evidence: Barnes sees an undoubted reference to Isaiah 9:6-7, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the verse an echo of that prophecy, and Gill says Isaiah 9:6 is referred to here. Clarke also points to Isaiah 9:7.
layers.text: The angel's words echo Isaiah's promise of a child to be born and a son to be given, who would reign on the throne of David with no end to the growth of His rule. Mary's Son is that promised King.

layers.evidence: On 2 Samuel 7:13, Gill says the promise is fulfilled more fully in Christ, given the throne of His father David; Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) says the angel's words in Luke 1:31-33 plainly refer to it; Keil and Delitzsch say Christ was born to raise up the throne of His father David again.
layers.text: Through the prophet Nathan, God promised David a son whose throne He would establish forever. The angel announces that this promise reaches its full meaning in Jesus, the Son of David whose reign has no end.

passages.saying: For no word from God will ever fail.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's closing answer to Mary's question of how she could bear a son.
layers.text: The angel assures Mary that nothing God has spoken will fail. Whatever He has said or promised He is able to do, including a virgin bearing a Son. Older English Bibles word it as nothing being impossible with God.

layers.evidence: Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown both say the angel points Mary back to God's promise of Isaac in Genesis 18:14. Clarke adds that Luke's Greek follows the Septuagint wording of that verse almost exactly, as a statement instead of a question.
layers.text: The angel's words echo the LORD's question to Abraham when He promised old Sarah a son: "Is anything too difficult for the LORD?" In the Greek Old Testament that verse reads almost word for word like Luke's Greek here, only turned from a question into a firm promise.

passages.saying: My soul magnifies the Lord
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the meaning of the verb magnify, which here means to praise or extol.
layers.text: Mary answers Elizabeth's greeting with a song of praise. To magnify the Lord does not mean to make Him greater than He is, but to declare His greatness and praise Him with all her heart.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke on this verse, and Gill and Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Samuel 2:1, all tie Mary's song to Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2:1-10. Keil and Delitzsch say the songs of both Mary and Zechariah rest on Hannah's ode.
layers.text: Mary's song closely follows the song Hannah sang when God gave her, once childless, a son. Hannah began, "My heart rejoices in the LORD"; Mary begins by magnifying the Lord. Both women praise God for bringing down the proud and lifting up the lowly.

passages.saying: He has raised up a horn of salvation for us
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Old Testament picture of an animal's horn as a sign of strength.
layers.text: Zechariah praises God for raising up a mighty Savior from the royal family of David. An animal's strength is in its horn, so a horn of salvation means a strong Savior, the promised Messiah.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls the phrase a quotation from Psalm 18:2, and the Companion Bible note there says it is quoted in Luke 1:69. Gill on Psalm 132:17 and Keil and Delitzsch on Psalm 132:14-18 tie that psalm's horn for David to Zechariah's song, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to both psalms.
layers.text: In Psalm 18 David calls the LORD "the horn of my salvation," and in Psalm 132 God says, "There I will make a horn grow for David." Zechariah's song echoes this language: God has now raised up that mighty Savior from David's own house.

layers.evidence: Clarke on 1 Samuel 2:1 quotes with approval the observation that Zechariah alludes to Hannah's song when he calls Christ a horn of salvation. Keil and Delitzsch say the songs of Mary and Zechariah rest on Hannah's ode.
layers.text: Hannah's song opens with her horn lifted high in the LORD and her joy in His salvation, and it closes with God lifting up the horn of His anointed king. Zechariah echoes her song when he praises God for raising up a horn of salvation.

passages.saying: the Dawn will visit us from on high
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the word for Dawn, the rising of the sun, used here of the coming Savior.
layers.text: Zechariah says all this flows from God's tender mercy. Because of that mercy the Dawn from heaven, the promised Savior, is coming to His people like the morning sun breaking over the night.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on this verse takes the Dawn as Christ, the Sun of righteousness of Malachi 4:2. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) on Malachi 4:2 sets Zechariah's Dayspring from on high beside that Sun, after noting that Zechariah speaks of John's work in Malachi's words. Gill there says Christ the Sun has risen as the dayspring from on high.
layers.text: Calling Christ the Dawn from on high recalls Malachi's promise that "the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings," for those who fear God. John would prepare the way, and Christ Himself is that rising Sun, shining on a world sitting in darkness.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that anatole is the Septuagint word for tsemach, the Branch, in Jeremiah 23 and Zechariah 3:8, and says both meanings, branch and light, are combined here. Gill also notes it is the Septuagint word for the Branch in Jeremiah 23:5.
layers.text: The word for Dawn, anatole in Luke's Greek, means a rising, like sunrise. The Greek Old Testament uses the same word for the Branch, tsemach in Hebrew, the King God promised to make sprout from David's line. So one word shows Christ as both the rising light and the Branch.

passages.saying: For my eyes have seen Your salvation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Simeon's words as he holds the infant Jesus in the temple.
layers.text: Holding the infant Jesus, Simeon says he has now seen God's salvation. The Child Himself is the Savior God promised, so Simeon is ready to depart in peace.

layers.evidence: Gill on Isaiah 49:6 says Simeon has this passage in mind; the Companion Bible says it is quoted in Simeon's song; Keil and Delitzsch link it to Luke 2:32; and Bullinger's Figures of Speech pairs Luke 2:30 with Isaiah 49:6.
layers.text: Simeon's song echoes God's word to His Servant: "I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth." Simeon says he has seen that salvation in the Child, and in the next breath calls Him a light for the Gentiles.

passages.saying: this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Simeon's words in the verse; Wesley explains the fall and rising as death to unbelievers and life to believers.
layers.text: Simeon blesses Joseph and Mary and tells Mary that her Child will divide Israel. Many will fall because they reject Him, and many will rise because they believe in Him. He will be a sign from God that people speak against.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls the phrase an allusion to Isaiah 8:14-15; Barnes sees a plain reference to the stone of stumbling there; the Companion Bible explains the fall as stumbling and points to Isaiah 8:14. Gill likewise speaks of the Child as the stone of stumbling and rock of offence.
layers.text: Simeon's words about the rise and fall of many echo Isaiah, where the LORD is a sanctuary to some but "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense" to others, and many stumble and fall. Jesus is that stone: some fall over Him in unbelief, while others rise through faith.

passages.saying: Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words; Gill explains that His human soul grew in wisdom as His body grew in stature.
layers.text: Jesus truly grew up as a man. His wisdom increased along with His body, and both God and the people around Him looked on Him with growing favor.

layers.evidence: Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes), on 1 Samuel 2:26, says Luke's account of Jesus' growth is very similar to what is said of Samuel; Keil and Delitzsch, on the same verse, point to Luke 2:52.
layers.text: Luke's words closely match what was said of the boy Samuel, who "continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man." Luke seems to describe Jesus' boyhood in the language used of an earlier child raised in God's service.

passages.saying: spoke about His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; the Companion Bible notes that His death did not merely happen but that He Himself accomplished it, fulfilling the Scriptures.
layers.text: On the mountain, Moses and Elijah appeared in heavenly glory and talked with Jesus about His coming death at Jerusalem. His death would not simply happen to Him; He would carry it out Himself, fulfilling what the Scriptures foretold.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that the word rendered decease is Exodus, the name of Moses' second book, the word used for Israel's departure in Hebrews 11:22, and says the allusion is to that departure from Egypt; Barnes says the word may allude to Israel's departure from Egypt.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek, the word for His departure is exodos, the same word used for Israel's going out of Egypt. Moses, who led that first exodus, speaks with Jesus about the exodus He would accomplish at Jerusalem, which some read as a greater rescue of God's people.

passages.saying: Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes explains that Jesus determined to go to Jerusalem and set out resolutely, knowing what awaited Him.
layers.text: As the time drew near for Jesus to be taken up to heaven, He firmly resolved to go to Jerusalem, knowing that suffering and death awaited Him there. He went willingly, by His own choice.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call the phrase His own prophetic language from Isaiah 50:7; the Companion Bible, on Isaiah 50:7, sees its fulfilment in Jesus setting His face; Keil and Delitzsch connect the Greek wording of Isaiah's phrase with Luke 9:51. Gill also reads it as setting His face like a flint.
layers.text: Luke's Greek says literally that Jesus set His face to go to Jerusalem. This echoes the Servant in Isaiah, who trusts God amid insult and says, "I have set My face like flint," sure he will not be put to shame. Jesus walked toward His suffering with that same settled resolve.

passages.saying: but first let me bid farewell to my family
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and Jesus' reply in Luke 9:62; Barnes explains the request and why Jesus did not allow it.
layers.text: Another man offers to follow Jesus but first wants to go home and say goodbye to his family. Jesus answers that following Him calls for an undivided heart, with no turning back to what was left behind.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all tie this request to Elisha's in 1 Kings 19:19-20. Wesley says Jesus' answer seems to allude to Elisha's call from the plow, Clarke on Luke 9:62 sees a plain reference to that call, and George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) on 1 Kings 19:20 points to Luke 9:61-62.
layers.text: This request echoes Elisha, who was plowing when Elijah called him. Elisha asked, "Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye," before following him. Jesus' reply about a hand on the plow draws on the same scene: following Him leaves no room for looking back.

passages.saying: the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and its setting in Luke 10.
layers.text: Besides the Twelve, Jesus chose a larger group of followers and sent them out in pairs. They went ahead of Him into every town and place He planned to visit, to prepare the people for His coming.

layers.evidence: Gill says Jesus chose them in allusion to the seventy elders of Numbers 11:16. Clarke says He appointed seventy as Moses did the seventy elders who helped him govern. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown sees a probable allusion to the elders on whom the Spirit came (Numbers 11:24-25). Barnes thinks Jesus likely followed Moses' example.
layers.text: The number recalls the seventy elders God told Moses to gather to share his load, on whom God put His Spirit. Many copies read seventy here and others seventy-two. As the Twelve match Israel's twelve tribes, these helpers match the elders who served with Moses.

passages.saying: I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: Jesus gave His messengers authority over snakes, scorpions and all the power of the enemy, Satan. He promised that nothing would harm them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the promise of Psalm 91:13 calls to mind Mark 16:18 but still more Luke 10:19. Gill on Psalm 91:13 links the psalm's promise with the power Jesus gave His disciples to tread on serpents and scorpions.
layers.text: Treading on snakes and scorpions recalls Psalm 91:13: "You will tread on the lion and cobra." The psalm promises this safety to the one who trusts in God. Jesus now gives His followers that authority Himself, over every danger and over the enemy.

passages.saying: But when a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, he looked at him and had compassion.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: An expert in the law, "wanting to justify himself," asks Jesus, "And who is my neighbor?" Jesus tells of a man beaten on the road down to Jericho. A priest and a Levite pass by; a Samaritan stops, binds his wounds and pays for his care. "Go and do likewise."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Leviticus 19:34: the command to love your neighbor as yourself is here enacted for the stranger. Both verses use ve'ahavta (you shall love) and kamokha (as yourself) (TAHOT); a ger is a foreigner living in Israel (TBESH).
layers.text: The lawyer quotes Leviticus: "Love your neighbor as yourself," said there of "any of your people." Sixteen verses on it says of the foreigner living in Israel, "love him as yourself," in the same Hebrew. The law's love already reached past Israel's own people.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on 2 Chronicles 28:15: some have supposed our Lord had this passage in mind, and the likenesses between the two stories are curious. Gill: these men of Samaria acted the part of the good Samaritan.
layers.text: Some commentators hear an older story. In 2 Chronicles 28 men of Samaria, rebuked by a prophet, clothed their captives from Judah, "anointed their wounds, and put all the feeble on donkeys," and brought them to Jericho.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Luke 10:33: the Samaritans were the Jews' most inveterate foes, with no dealings between them (compare John 4:9). Gill: above all men hated by the Jews.
layers.text: Jews and Samaritans were bitter neighbors: "Jews do not associate with Samaritans." A chapter earlier a Samaritan village refused Jesus, and James and John wanted to "call down fire from heaven." Jesus rebuked them, then made a Samaritan the hero of His story.

layers.evidence: Strong's: to have the bowels yearn, to feel sympathy, to pity. TAGNT has it in 12 verses, all in the first three Gospels: 8 of Jesus, 1 in a plea to Him (Mark 9:22), and 3 in parables. Benson: the Samaritan's bowels yearned; Matthew Henry's Concise turns from his compassion to the compassion of Jesus.
layers.text: "Had compassion" is splanchnizomai, to be moved in one's inmost parts. The Gospels use it for Jesus, in a plea to Him, and in parables for the forgiving master, the father who runs to his lost son, and this Samaritan. The outsider feels what Jesus feels.

layers.evidence: Augustine, Tractates on John 43: Samaritan means keeper, and the Samaritan of the parable is our Keeper. TBESH: shamar, to keep or guard; Samaria, watch mountain.
layers.text: Opponents once called Jesus "a Samaritan," and He denied only the demon. An early Christian reading took Samaritan to mean keeper (from shamar, to keep) and saw the Lord in the Samaritan: "The LORD is your keeper," who "will neither slumber nor sleep."

passages.saying: if I drive out demons by the finger of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the charge in Luke 11:15 that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul.
layers.text: Some claimed Jesus drove out demons by the power of Satan. Jesus answered that He drives them out by God's own power, and if so, the kingdom of God has already come among them.

layers.evidence: Gill says the finger of God in Luke 11:20 means the power of God, referring to Exodus 8:19. Clarke and the Companion Bible also send readers to Exodus 8:19 for the phrase.
layers.text: The finger of God is the phrase Pharaoh's magicians used when they could not copy the plague of gnats: "This is the finger of God." Some hear an echo here: the same power of God that the magicians had to admit may now be at work as Jesus drives out demons.

passages.saying: a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its contrast with the rich man of Luke 16:19.
layers.text: In Jesus' story, a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, was laid at the gate of a rich man who lived in luxury every day.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Lazarus is a contraction of Eleazar, meaning the help or assistance of God, fitting a man with no help but from heaven. Gill says it is a contraction of Eleazar and signifies that the Lord was his helper. The Companion Bible and Wesley also read it as Eleazar. Barnes instead explains it as one destitute of help.
layers.text: Unlike the rich man, the poor man is given a name. Lazarus is a short form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, meaning God's help. It suits a man who had no help on earth except the help that came from God.

passages.saying: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the story of Zacchaeus in Luke 19:1-9.
layers.text: Jesus explains why He went to the home of Zacchaeus, a tax collector the crowd called a sinner. He came to search out people lost in sin and to rescue them.

layers.evidence: Gill on Ezekiel 34:16 applies God's promise to seek the lost to Christ, who he says has been sent to seek and to save them, the wording of Luke 19:10. Keil and Delitzsch see the chapter's shepherd promises fulfilled in Jesus, who came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). On Luke 19:10 Gill adds that the lost sheep of Israel are meant.
layers.text: Jesus' words likely echo God's promise in Ezekiel 34:16: "I will seek the lost." Facing Israel's careless shepherds, God said He would search for His lost sheep Himself. Jesus, the Son of Man, came to do that very work.

passages.saying: if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes reads the saying as strong proverbial language: the Messiah's coming was too joyful to be silenced.
layers.text: When the Pharisees tell Jesus to rebuke His disciples for praising Him as King, He answers that if they kept silent, the very stones would cry out. His coming was too great a thing to pass without praise.

layers.evidence: Ellicott says the startling imagery had a precedent in the language of Habakkuk 2:11, and the Pulpit Commentary says the Lord was recalling Habakkuk's prophecy. JFB cross-references the two verses both ways, and E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) on Habakkuk 2:11 points to Luke 19:40.
layers.text: Shouting stones recall Habakkuk, where "the stones will cry out from the wall" against a man whose house was built by plunder. There the stones accuse a wicked builder; here they would cry out in praise of the King if His people were silenced.

passages.saying: If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Luke 19:41-42: had the city repented and received the Messiah, it would have been spared.
layers.text: As Jesus comes near Jerusalem He weeps over it. If only the city had known, on this day of His coming, what would bring it peace. But now that peace is hidden from its eyes, and judgment will follow.

layers.evidence: Clarke on Luke 19:42 thinks it very likely that Jesus alludes to the meaning of the name Jerusalem, which he links with shalom, peace. JFB says Jesus was thinking perhaps of the name of the city, and cites Hebrews 7:2.
layers.text: Jerusalem's name was long understood to hold shalom, the Hebrew word for peace, and Hebrews 7:2 says that Salem means peace. Jesus' grief may echo the name: the city named for peace did not know what would bring it peace.

passages.saying: Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill: those who stumble at Christ in unbelief hurt themselves, and those on whom He falls in judgment are ruined.
layers.text: Jesus ends the parable of the tenants with a warning about Himself, the rejected stone. Whoever stumbles over Him will be broken, and whoever the stone falls on in judgment will be crushed.

layers.evidence: JFB on Luke 20:17-18 ties falling and being broken to Isaiah 8:15, and the stone that falls and grinds to powder to Daniel 2:34-35. Gill on Isaiah 8:15 says those who stumble at Christ are broken in pieces by this stone, citing the same saying in Matthew 21:44.
layers.text: The saying joins two prophecies. In Isaiah the LORD becomes a stone of stumbling, and many "will fall and be broken." In Daniel a stone cut out without human hands strikes the great statue and crushes it. Stumbling over Jesus brings harm; when that stone falls in judgment, the ruin is complete.

passages.saying: There will be great earthquakes, famines, and pestilences in various places
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill relates the fearful sights and signs to those reported before Jerusalem fell, as Josephus records.
layers.text: Jesus warns His disciples that great earthquakes, famines and plagues will come in many places, along with fearful sights and great signs from heaven.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible calls limoi kai loimoi a paronomasia used for emphasis, like English dearths and deaths, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the same pair as a play on sound.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek, famines and pestilences are limoi and loimoi, two words only one letter apart. Some hear the sound pair as making the warning ring, much like saying dearths and deaths in English.

passages.saying: This cup is the new covenant in My blood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke: the cup signifies the blood of the new covenant, soon to be ratified by the shedding of Christ's blood.
layers.text: After supper Jesus takes the cup and tells His disciples it is the new covenant in His blood, poured out for them. The wine stands for His blood, soon to be shed to seal that covenant.

layers.evidence: Gill on Jeremiah 31:31 says this new covenant is ratified by the blood of Christ. On Exodus 24:8 Gill says our Lord may have this rite in mind in His words at the Supper (Matthew 26:28), and JFB compares 1 Corinthians 11:25, whose wording matches Luke 22:20.
layers.text: Jesus' words recall God's promise in Jeremiah, "I will make a new covenant" with Israel and Judah. Covenant and blood together may also recall Sinai, where Moses sprinkled the people and said, "This is the blood of the covenant." The new covenant is sealed with Jesus' own blood.

passages.saying: Satan has asked to sift each of you like wheat
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: Satan wanted to shake Peter with trials to see whether any faith would remain.
layers.text: Jesus warns Simon Peter that Satan has asked to sift all the disciples like wheat, shaking them hard to test their faith. In the next verse Jesus tells Peter He has prayed that his faith will not fail.

layers.evidence: JFB on Luke 22:31 says the verb means asked and obtained, alluding to Job 1 and 2. Gill and Barnes both compare Satan's leave to afflict Job, and Matthew Henry's Concise on Job 1 says God let Job be tried as He let Peter be sifted.
layers.text: Satan's request recalls Job, where Satan came before the LORD and was allowed to test Job, but only within the limits God set. Satan cannot touch Jesus' disciples without leave either, and Jesus answers his demand by praying for Peter.

layers.evidence: Gill on Luke 22:31 refers to Amos 9:9 for being tossed like wheat in a sieve, and on Amos 9:9 applies God's sifting to Satan's temptations and Christ's intercession in Luke 22:31. JFB on Amos 9:9 says the solid grains are kept safe, citing Luke 22:32.
layers.text: The sifting picture can also recall Amos, where God shakes Israel "as grain is sifted in a sieve," yet keeps what is His. Satan sifts to destroy, but none of God's own is lost, and Jesus prays that Peter's faith will hold.

passages.saying: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: the prayer was for those guilty of putting Jesus to death, perhaps both the Jews and the Roman soldiers.
layers.text: As He is crucified, Jesus prays for the people putting Him to death, asking His Father to forgive them because they do not understand what they are doing. Meanwhile the soldiers divide His clothes by casting lots.

layers.evidence: Clarke and Barnes on Luke 23:34 both say this prayer fulfilled Isaiah 53:12, He made intercession for the transgressors. The Companion Bible also compares Isaiah 53:12.
layers.text: Isaiah says the suffering Servant was numbered with the transgressors, yet "bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors." Jesus does exactly this on the cross, praying for the very men who crucify Him.

passages.saying: today you will be with Me in Paradise
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes: the plain meaning is that the man would be received into blessedness with Christ at death, that same day.
layers.text: One of the criminals crucified with Jesus asks Him to remember him when He comes into His kingdom. Jesus promises more than he asked: that very day he will be with Jesus in Paradise.

layers.evidence: Clarke notes that the Septuagint calls the garden of Genesis 2:8 a paradise, and Barnes points to the same verse. Gill explains that heaven is called Paradise because, like Eden's garden, it is of God's planting.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek, Paradise is paradeisos, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the garden God planted in Eden, where man first lived with God. Jesus promises the dying man the blessing that garden pictured: to be with Him that very day.

passages.saying: In the beginning was the Word
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's three short clauses, read with verse 14, which shows that the Word is the Son who became man.
layers.text: Before anything was created, the Word already existed. The Word was with God as a distinct person, and the Word was Himself fully God. Verse 14 shows that this Word is Jesus, who became a man.

layers.evidence: Clarke and Barnes both say John alludes to Genesis 1:1 here, and Wesley and the Companion Bible point to the same verse. Gill links the title Word to the repeated words And God said in the creation account.
layers.text: John opens his Gospel with the same words that open the Bible: In the beginning. Genesis tells how God created the world by speaking, and John calls the Son the Word, through whom all things were made. When creation began, the Word already was.

passages.saying: the world did not recognize Him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between the world being made through Him and the world failing to know Him.
layers.text: Jesus was present in the very world He had made, yet the people of that world did not recognize Him as their Creator.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse as a word repeated in a different sense: the created world, then unbelieving men. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes the world resounding in all three clauses, first as the created world, then as mankind.
layers.text: In John's Greek, as in English, the word world comes three times in one sentence. At first it means the created world that came into being through Him. At the end it means the people of the world, who did not know their own Maker. The repeated word sharpens the irony.

passages.saying: He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the setting: Jesus came to Israel, the people chosen as God's own, and the nation rejected Him.
layers.text: Jesus came to His own land and to Israel, His own chosen people, but as a nation they did not welcome Him as their Messiah.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes the first his own is neuter (His land, city, temple) and the second masculine (the Jews). Barnes says the distinction is lost in translation. Clarke, Wesley and Bullinger draw the same line between possessions and people.
layers.text: In John's Greek the same word, His own, appears twice in two forms. The first (ta idia) means His own things: His land, city and temple. The second (hoi idioi) means His own people. He came to His own land, and His own people would not take Him in.

passages.saying: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the word flesh, used for full human nature, and on the eyewitness claim that the disciples saw His glory.
layers.text: The eternal Word became a real human being and lived among people. His disciples saw His divine glory, the glory of God's one and only Son, full of grace and truth.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke all read made His dwelling as tabernacled and tie it to the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt; Wesley says the same. JFB adds that the next words, we beheld his glory, put this almost beyond doubt.
layers.text: In John's Greek, made His dwelling is literally pitched His tent. It recalls the tabernacle, the tent where the glory of the LORD came down to live among Israel. So John adds at once, "We have seen His glory." In Jesus, God came to dwell with His people in a human body.

passages.saying: He who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Baptist's contrast between Jesus' later public ministry and His existence before John.
layers.text: John the Baptist testifies that Jesus, though He began His work after John, is far greater than John, because He existed long before John was born.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this an enigmatic play upon the senses of before and after: after in public appearing, before in rank, before in existence. Wesley likewise splits the two befores into office and nature.
layers.text: The Baptist speaks in a riddle about after and before. Jesus comes after John in time and ministry, yet ranks ahead of him, because He was before John in existence. The riddle only makes sense if Jesus lived before He was born as a man.

passages.saying: Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the sacrificial meaning of a lamb in Israel's worship and on the phrase takes away the sin.
layers.text: John the Baptist points to Jesus as the sacrifice God Himself provides. Jesus bears the guilt of sin and carries it away, and He does this for the whole world, not for Israel alone.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the words allude to Isaiah 53:7. Barnes, Wesley and the Companion Bible also tie the title to the lamb led to the slaughter there.
layers.text: Isaiah foretold a suffering Servant who was "led like a lamb to the slaughter" and stayed silent while He suffered for the sins of others. By calling Jesus the Lamb who takes away sin, the Baptist points to Him as that Servant.

layers.evidence: Barnes points to the Passover lamb of Exodus 12. Clarke calls the paschal lamb a type of this Lamb, and Matthew Henry's Concise and Wesley say the same. Paul later calls Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).
layers.text: At the first Passover each household in Israel killed a lamb and put its blood on the doorframe, and death passed over them. The title points to Jesus as the true Passover lamb, whose blood shelters His people from judgment.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible glosses of God as provided by God and points to Genesis 22:8. On Genesis 22:8, Gill, Clarke and Matthew Henry say Abraham's words look ahead to the Lamb of God, and Wesley says Christ the great sacrifice was of God's providing.
layers.text: The Lamb of God can also mean the lamb God provides. On the mountain Abraham told Isaac, "God Himself will provide the lamb." Earlier sacrifices were brought by people, but the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb that God Himself has now provided.

passages.saying: We have found the Messiah
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Andrew's words to Simon and on the evangelist's note translating the title.
layers.text: After spending time with Jesus, Andrew first goes to his own brother Simon and tells him that the long-promised Messiah has come.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Bullinger's Figures of Speech all state that the Hebrew Messiah and the Greek Christ both mean anointed. Wesley notes that the translation is the evangelist's own addition.
layers.text: Messiah comes from the Hebrew word for anointed. Christ is the Greek word with the same meaning, so John translates the title for his readers. Both name Jesus as God's Anointed One, the One the prophets promised.

passages.saying: You are Simon son of John. You will be called Cephas
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says this directly; Gill explains Andrew bringing Simon to Jesus.
layers.text: Andrew brings his brother Simon to Jesus. Jesus looks at him, calls him by his own name and his father's name, and tells him he will be given a new name, Cephas, which John explains means Peter.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Gill, Wesley and the Companion Bible say Cephas is the Aramaic (Syriac) word for a stone or rock, matching the Greek Petros; Clarke notes that Petros means a stone. Barnes and Gill see in the name the firmness and steadfastness Peter would later show.
layers.text: Jesus gives Simon a new name, Cephas, the Aramaic word for a rock or stone. John translates it for Greek readers as Peter (Petros), which means the same thing. The name looks ahead to the firm, steady follower Simon would become.

passages.saying: angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says this directly; Clarke explains it as heaven and earth opened to each other through Christ.
layers.text: Jesus tells Nathanael and the other disciples that they will see heaven opened and God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man, His name for Himself. Through Him, heaven and earth are joined.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all hear Jacob's ladder in Genesis 28:12 here. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown see Christ Himself as the real ladder between heaven and earth; Barnes reads the angels as God's help given to Him. Clarke doubts a direct reference and reads the words as heaven opened through Christ the Mediator.
layers.text: These words recall Jacob's dream at Bethel, where God's angels went up and down a ladder that reached from earth to heaven. Now the angels go up and down on the Son of Man. Read this way, Jesus Himself is the true ladder that joins heaven and earth.

passages.saying: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Asked for a sign in the temple courts, Jesus answers with a riddle. His hearers take Him to mean the temple building, which had taken 46 years to build.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) cites this passage for both senses of egeiro
layers.text: John explains: "Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body." The verb egeiro means both to raise a building and to raise the dead. The disciples understood only after the resurrection.

The misunderstood saying returns as a charge at His trial and a taunt at the cross: "You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days." The mockers are watching the first half come true.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG): in the Greek Old Testament this verb chiefly stands for shakan
layers.text: John has said the Word "made His dwelling among us." The verb comes from the word for a tent, and in the Greek Old Testament it chiefly stands for shakan, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt. Jesus' body is where God lives among His people.
The temple thread keeps widening: believers' bodies become "a temple of the Holy Spirit," and the new Jerusalem has no temple, "because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple."

passages.saying: many people saw the signs He was doing and believed in His name
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse and the next one say this directly; Clarke explains the shallow faith described.
layers.text: During the Passover in Jerusalem, many people saw the miracles Jesus did and believed in Him. But their faith rested on the signs they saw, and Jesus, who knew every heart, did not trust Himself to them.

layers.evidence: Barnes, the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech all point out that believed in verse 23 and entrust in verse 24 translate the same Greek verb, pisteuo. Bullinger lists it as a figure where a repeated word carries a new sense.
layers.text: In John's Greek, one verb (pisteuo) is used twice. Many believed in Jesus when they saw His signs, but Jesus did not believe in them, that is, He did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all.

passages.saying: Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born again, and Nicodemus asks how a grown man could enter his mother's womb a second time.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: anothen means both again and from above, mainly from above here; Abbott-Smith (TBESG) reads again, as most do. In John, TAGNT has it only at 3:3, 3:7, 3:31, 19:11 and 19:23. Barnes: the language Jesus used probably lacked the Greek ambiguity. Ellicott: His word almost certainly had one sense, and the early Syriac version reads anew.
layers.text: In John's Greek, "born again" is anothen, which also means "from above," as in "The One who comes from above." Nicodemus hears only a second birth. Jesus likely spoke Aramaic, and many think His word had one sense, so the play on both may be John's.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on John 3:8 points out the wordplay on wind and spirit. TBESG: pneuma is wind, breath or spirit. TBESH: Aramaic ruach (rucha with the article) is wind or spirit; TAHOT has it as wind in Daniel 2:35 and 7:2 and as spirit in Daniel 5:12 and 7:15.
layers.text: "The wind blows where it wishes," and "So it is with everyone born of the Spirit." Wind and Spirit are one word in John's Greek, pneuma, and in Hebrew and Aramaic, so the saying is not a pun of the Greek alone.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Ezekiel's promise of clean water and God's Spirit (Ezekiel 36:25-27). On the water, Barnes and Bengel see baptism, the continuation of Poole's Annotations the Spirit's cleansing of the soul, and Gill a figure of God's grace.
layers.text: "Born of water and the Spirit" joins two promises God made through Ezekiel: "I will also sprinkle clean water on you" and "I will put My Spirit within you." So Jesus expects Israel's teacher to understand. Commentators still differ on what the water means.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on John 3:5 points to Ezekiel 37:9-10. TBESH: ruach is wind, breath, mind or spirit; TAHOT has it four times in Ezekiel 37:9.
layers.text: Hebrew has the same double word, ruach. In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones it is breath, wind and Spirit at once: "Come from the four winds, O breath," and "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 3:2: the night visit is recalled in the description of Nicodemus at 19:39. Matthew Henry's Concise: though he came by night, afterward he owned Christ publicly. Some, after Augustine, read the night as a symbol of his darkness; the Pulpit Commentary calls that far-fetched.
layers.text: Nicodemus came "at night," and John recalls it when he brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial. The man who first came to Jesus by night later honors Him openly.

passages.saying: The wind blows where it wishes
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says this directly; Wesley explains that the fact is plain though the manner is hidden.
layers.text: Jesus tells Nicodemus that the new birth is like the wind. No one can see the wind or say where it comes from, yet its sound and effects are plain. The Spirit's work in giving new birth is just as real, though hidden.

layers.evidence: Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that one word means both wind and spirit in Hebrew and in Greek. The Companion Bible also notes that pneuma opens and closes the verse, though it would render both as Spirit.
layers.text: In John's Greek, the word for wind at the start of this verse, pneuma, is the same word translated Spirit at its end. The Hebrew word ruach also means both wind and spirit. So the wind that blows where it wishes is a living picture of the Spirit who gives new birth.

passages.saying: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Jesus tells Nicodemus that, like the bronze snake Moses raised in the wilderness, He must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.
In Numbers the people speak against God, venomous snakes bite them, and God tells Moses to make a snake and set it on a pole. Moses makes it of bronze, and whoever is bitten and looks at it lives.

layers.evidence: Adam Clarke on Numbers 21:9: the word for brass comes from the same root as nachash, serpent. Ellicott on 2 Kings 18:4 hears both words in the name Nehushtan.
layers.text: In Hebrew, snake is nachash and bronze is nechoshet, so the "bronze snake" is a nechash nechoshet: the two words sound almost alike.

layers.evidence: TBESG (Abbott-Smith): hypsoo is to lift up (John 3:14, 12:32) and to exalt (Acts 2:33). The Aramaic behind it is debated; some propose a pun on zeqaph, used of a man lifted onto a beam in Ezra 6:11 (TAHOT).
layers.text: In John's Greek, "lifted up" (hypsoo) means raised up and also exalted. When Jesus says it again, John adds that it showed "the kind of death He was going to die," and Acts uses the verb for His exaltation to God's right hand. The cross is His lifting up.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Isaiah 52:13: the phrase impressed itself, through the Greek Old Testament, on Christ's mind in reference to His crucifixion, citing John 3:14, 8:28 and 12:32.
layers.text: Isaiah's suffering servant "will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted," just before the description of His suffering. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb there, and many scholars think John's "lifted up" draws on this verse.

layers.evidence: Meaning of nechoshet from TBESH
layers.text: Centuries later Israel was burning incense to that same bronze snake, now called Nehushtan, a name built on nechoshet, "bronze," and King Hezekiah smashed it. The sign had become an idol; the healing never lay in the bronze.

passages.saying: The One who comes from above is above all
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says this directly; Barnes explains the contrast between Christ and human teachers.
layers.text: Christ comes from heaven and is above all. Every merely human messenger, John the Baptist included, comes from the earth and speaks as an earthly man. So the One from heaven stands above every other teacher.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under Ploce, where a repeated word gains a fuller sense, and explains the three uses as birth and origin, nature, and speech.
layers.text: In John's Greek, the phrase from the earth (ek tes ges) comes three times in a row, and some see each use saying more: a man from the earth by birth is earthly in nature and speaks in an earthly way. On this reading the repetition sets him far below the One who comes from heaven.

passages.saying: near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says this directly; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown identifies Sychar with Shechem.
layers.text: On His way from Judea to Galilee, Jesus came to Sychar, a town of Samaria in the area of ancient Shechem, close to the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and the Companion Bible all tie this field to Jacob's gift to Joseph in Genesis 48:22. Clarke, Barnes and the Companion Bible add Joseph's burial there in Joshua 24:32, and the purchase in Genesis 33:19.
layers.text: John points back to Genesis. Jacob bought land near Shechem, and before he died he gave Joseph a portion above his brothers. Later Joseph's bones, carried up from Egypt, were buried there. Jesus comes to the very land of Jacob and Joseph.

layers.evidence: Gill and Clarke both suggest Sychar was a name meaning drunken, pointing to Isaiah 28:1 and the drunkenness of Ephraim. Both offer it as a likely guess, not a certainty, and the Companion Bible places Sychar at the village now called Askar.
layers.text: Some older interpreters think Sychar was a mocking nickname for the town, meaning drunken, sounding like the Hebrew word for drunkard (shikkor). They link it with Isaiah's woe on Ephraim's drunkards, since the town lay in the land of Ephraim.

passages.saying: you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Mishnah named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Weary from His journey, Jesus sits by Jacob's well in Samaria and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. She asks how a Jew can ask her. He offers her living water instead, "a fount of water springing up to eternal life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the word translated living is used in Greek of flowing water. Abbott-Smith (TBESG): springing as opposed to still water. Barnes and Benson: living water meant spring or running water.
layers.text: In Greek, "living water" meant flowing water, from a spring rather than a cistern. So she asks how He will draw it, since "the well is deep." She hears spring water; Jesus means water that wells up to eternal life.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: mayim chayyim in Genesis 26:19 and Jeremiah 2:13, and the same chayyim in the cleansing law of Leviticus 14:5 (BSB fresh water there too). TBESH: chay is living, and of water, flowing or fresh. The Pulpit Commentary on John 4:10 cites Genesis 26:19 and Jeremiah 2:13.
layers.text: Hebrew says the same, mayim chayyim. Isaac's servants find "a well of fresh water" (literally living water), and Jeremiah gives the phrase to God: "They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns."

layers.evidence: Carissa Quinn (BibleProject): when the biblical authors portray a man meeting his future bride, the setting is often a well (Rebekah, Rachel, Zipporah); calling it Jacob's well links the scene with Jacob and Rachel, and Jesus is called the groom in the chapter before.
layers.text: A man meets a woman at a well, and a marriage follows: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah, Jacob meets Rachel, Moses meets Zipporah. This is "Jacob’s well," a chapter after John the Baptist calls Jesus "the bridegroom." This time many in her town believe.

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 describes water drawn from the Siloam pool in a golden jug and poured at the altar. The NET Bible note on John 7:38: Jesus takes up the water of the ceremony and uses it figuratively.
layers.text: At the Feast of Tabernacles, when by Jewish tradition water from Siloam was poured at the altar, Jesus promises "streams of living water," meaning the Spirit. Zechariah's vision of living water from Jerusalem ends with the nations keeping that feast.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: a question opened with me in Greek expects the answer no; Ellicott renders it "Thou surely art not greater." Bengel compares John 8:53; the Pulpit Commentary finds her words possibly ironic.
layers.text: She asks, "Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well?" In Greek the question expects the answer no, but John's readers know better. Jesus meets the same question about Abraham, and the Samaritans end up calling Him "the Savior of the world."

passages.saying: Meanwhile the disciples urged Him, “Rabbi, eat something.”
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill on John 4:31: the disciples saw He was weary from the journey and that it was time He had some food.
layers.text: While the Samaritan woman has gone back to her town, the disciples, back from buying food, urge Jesus to eat. They know He is weary from the journey and that it is time He had a meal.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists John 4:31-32 among examples of Antanaclasis or Ploce, one word repeated in a different sense: eat is used naturally of food the first time and spiritually of doing the Father's will the second. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on 4:32 notes the disciples still thought of a meal.
layers.text: The disciples mean ordinary food when they say eat. In John's Greek, Jesus' reply uses the same word in another sense: He has food to eat that they know nothing about. They wonder who brought Him a meal, so He explains that His food is to do the will of the One who sent Him.

passages.saying: a pool with five covered colonnades, which in Hebrew is called Bethesda
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes on John 5:2 takes the Sheep Gate as the gate Nehemiah names, through which sheep were brought into the city for sacrifice.
layers.text: John describes a pool in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate, where sheep were brought in for the temple sacrifices. It had five covered colonnades, and its Hebrew name was Bethesda.

layers.evidence: Clarke on John 5:2 gives the Hebrew as Bethchasdah, house of mercy, named from the cures there. Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley give the same meaning, and Gill finds it in the Syriac and Arabic versions. Clarke lists other spellings, such as Bethzatha, which some Greek editions print, but judges Bethesda genuine.
layers.text: Bethesda is explained as beth (house) and chesed (mercy): house of mercy, a name probably given for the healings there. At this pool Jesus healed a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. Some manuscripts spell the name Bethzatha.

passages.saying: Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill on John 6:14: the five thousand who had been fed drew this conclusion from the miracle.
layers.text: After Jesus feeds the five thousand with five barley loaves and two small fish, the people who saw the sign say that He is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.

layers.evidence: Gill and Clarke on John 6:14 both identify the Prophet as the one Moses foretold in Deuteronomy 18:15, that is, the Messiah. Gill adds that in the miracle Jesus appeared like Moses and greater, and on Deuteronomy 18:15 he points to John 6:14 as this expectation.
layers.text: The Prophet who is to come points back to Moses' promise that God would raise up a prophet like him from among Israel, one they must listen to. Having seen the sign, the crowd takes Jesus to be that promised Prophet.

passages.saying: What must we do to perform the works of God?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 6:28: the works of God are such works as God will approve.
layers.text: Jesus has told the crowd to work for the food that lasts to eternal life. They ask what they must do to perform the works of God, meaning the deeds God approves.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists John 6:28-29 under Synœceiosis (Cohabitation), a word repeated with an extended meaning: the crowd uses works in its usual sense, and Christ repeats it with another meaning altogether. His Companion Bible marks work the works in 6:28 as Polyptoton. Bengel and Ellicott note that Jesus answers their plural works with the singular work.
layers.text: In John's Greek the crowd asks how to work (ergazomai) the works (erga) of God, meaning deeds they must do. Some see the answer repeating the same word with a new meaning: the work (ergon) of God is to believe in the One He has sent.

passages.saying: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: The day after feeding five thousand, Jesus tells the crowd that He Himself is the bread that satisfies: whoever comes to Him will never hunger.

The crowd asks for a sign like the manna and quotes Scripture: "He gave them bread from heaven to eat," words close to Exodus 16:4 and Psalm 78:24. Jesus answers that the true bread from heaven comes from His Father, and unlike the manna, whoever eats it will not die.
Manna is named after a question. When Israel first saw it they asked one another, "What is it?" (man hu), and they called it man. Moses answered, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat."

Moses said the manna taught Israel that "man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD." Jesus quotes this in the wilderness, and in John the Word made flesh is Himself the bread.
John notes that Passover was near. The bread Jesus will give "for the life of the world" is His flesh, which many readers connect with the Last Supper: "This is My body, given for you."

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH
layers.text: Jesus was born in Bethlehem, whose name means "house of bread," and was laid in a manger, a feeding trough. Christians have long noticed the Bread of Life coming from the House of Bread; the Gospels do not point it out.

passages.saying: Streams of living water will flow from within him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke on John 7:38 takes from within him as the believer's heart and soul, where the Spirit dwells.
layers.text: On the last day of the feast Jesus promises that whoever believes in Him will have streams of living water flowing from deep within. The next verse explains that He meant the Spirit, given to believers after Jesus was glorified.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes, Wesley and Gill on John 7:38 agree no single verse is quoted. JFB names Isaiah 58:11, Joel 3:18, Zechariah 14:8 and Ezekiel 47:1-12; Barnes leans to Isaiah 58:11; Wesley names Zechariah 14:8. Bullinger's Companion Bible lists the same verses.
layers.text: No single verse says these exact words. The phrase as the Scripture has said gathers several promises: “living water will flow out from Jerusalem” (Zechariah), water flowing from under the temple (Ezekiel), and “a spring whose waters never fail” (Isaiah).

passages.saying: He was a murderer from the beginning
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes on John 8:44: they share the devil's temper and imitate him, so they may rightly be called his children.
layers.text: Jesus tells those trying to kill Him that they belong to their father, the devil, and want to do what he desires. The devil was a murderer from the beginning and has no truth in him. Lying is his native language, for he is a liar and the father of lies.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 8:44 all read murderer from the beginning as the devil bringing death on Adam and Eve by deceit. Barnes adds that this shows the tempter of Genesis 3 was Satan, and Clarke that the devil deceived Eve by his lies.
layers.text: Murderer from the beginning points back to Eden. The serpent told Eve, “You will not surely die,” and through that lie death came on Adam and all his descendants. From the start the devil has killed by lying.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes on John 8:44 add that the devil stirred up Cain to kill his brother, Barnes citing 1 John 3:12. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown disagrees: the reference is to Adam, not Cain.
layers.text: Some also think of Cain, who killed his brother Abel. John later writes that Cain “belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother.” Others hold that Jesus is speaking of Eden alone.

passages.saying: before Abraham was born, I am!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 8:58: was and am are different words; Abraham came into being, while Christ simply exists.
layers.text: When the crowd scoffs that He is not yet fifty years old and has seen Abraham, Jesus answers that before Abraham was born, He is. He does not say I was but I am, claiming a life that never had a beginning.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes on John 8:58 and Matthew Henry's Concise on 8:54-59 all tie I am to the name God gave at the bush in Exodus 3:14. Barnes calls the likeness remarkable, and Matthew Henry's Concise says the Jews were about to stone Him for blasphemy. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adds that the stones show how they understood Him.
layers.text: I am echoes the name God gave Moses at the burning bush: “I AM WHO I AM.” It speaks of a life without beginning, as God alone lives. His hearers picked up stones to throw at Him, treating His words as blasphemy.

passages.saying: Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Mishnah named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused it; Jesus says neither: it happened "so that the works of God would be displayed in him." He makes mud, puts it on the man's eyes and sends him to wash. He comes back seeing.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the Hebrew name shiloah comes from the verb to send. Augustine, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary see Jesus as the one Sent; Gill only reports that reading, and Barnes rejects it. John's word for Sent is a form of apostello, the verb of John 17:3 and 20:21 (TAGNT).
layers.text: John stops to translate the pool's name: Siloam, Isaiah's "Shiloah," means "Sent." In John, Jesus is the Sent One, doing "the works of Him who sent Me." So a man sent to the pool called Sent is healed by the One sent from God.

layers.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.15.2: the clay points to how man was first fashioned and shows the hand of God that formed him from the dust. The Greek pelos (clay) occurs in the New Testament only in John 9 and Romans 9:21 (TAGNT).
layers.text: Only here in the Gospels does Jesus make mud to heal. An early Christian reading sees the Creator's hand: as God formed man "from the dust of the ground," so Jesus used clay on the eyes, showing how humanity was first made. John himself does not say this.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Isaiah 42:7: the Messiah would cure blindness of body and of spirit. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 11:5 hear the prophets' promises in Jesus' answer. Isaiah 35:5 and 42:7 share the verb paqach (open) and the noun ivver (blind) (TAHOT).
layers.text: "Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind." Yet Isaiah promised that "the eyes of the blind will be opened," and that God's servant would open them. Asked by John the Baptist, Jesus points to such signs: "The blind receive sight."

layers.evidence: Gill on John 9:39 cites Isaiah 6:9, which John quotes in 12:40, and Ellicott points ahead to John 12:37-50. The NET Bible note calls the man's worship the climax of the story.
layers.text: The sign becomes a two-edged saying: "so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind." The man goes from "The man they call Jesus" to "a prophet" to worship, while leaders who "claim you can see" stay blind. John later ties this to Isaiah.

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 (water from Siloam poured at the altar) and 5:3 (every courtyard in Jerusalem lit), written down later. Ellicott and Gill on John 9:7 link Siloam's water to the feast; Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 8:12 describe its great lamps.
layers.text: This follows the Feast of Tabernacles, where Jesus said, "I am the light of the world." Later Jewish writings say that feast drew water from Siloam for the altar and lit every courtyard in Jerusalem. Now the Light of the world sends a blind man there.

passages.saying: Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in John 9:18-24, where the leaders refuse to accept that the man was healed.
layers.text: The leaders call the healed man back a second time and charge him to tell the truth before God. They insist that Jesus is a sinner, and they want the man to admit that his story of being healed is a fraud.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes and the Companion Bible all link the phrase to Joshua 7:19 as a form of oath or solemn charge to confess. Barnes adds that the Septuagint of Joshua 7:19 has the very wording John records.
layers.text: “Give glory to God” was a solemn charge to tell the whole truth before God. Joshua used the same charge when he urged Achan to confess the sin he had hidden. The leaders use it to press the healed man to confess, as though his account of being healed were a lie.

passages.saying: I am the good shepherd.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which Clarke reads as Christ giving His life as a sacrifice for His people.
layers.text: Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd, the true and faithful Shepherd of God's people. A good shepherd gives up his own life to save the sheep, and Jesus is pointing ahead to His death for His people.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Jesus calls Himself the Good Shepherd with obvious reference to Ezekiel's promise, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Lord refers to this prophecy. Gill and Wesley also read Ezekiel 34:23 of Christ the good Shepherd, and the Companion Bible links it to John 10:11.
layers.text: In Ezekiel 34 God condemns Israel's selfish shepherds and promises to appoint one shepherd over His flock, whom He calls My servant David. By calling Himself the good shepherd, Jesus presents Himself as that promised Shepherd who truly cares for the sheep.

passages.saying: Then there will be one flock and one shepherd.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Wesley, Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agree that the other sheep are Gentiles.
layers.text: Jesus says He has other sheep who are not of this fold, meaning Gentiles who will believe. He must bring them in too. They will listen to His voice, and together with His Jewish followers they will become one flock under one shepherd.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Ezekiel 34:23, says Christ is called the one Shepherd with respect to Jew and Gentile and points to John 10:16. On John 10:16 he points back to Ezekiel 34:23.
layers.text: Through Ezekiel God promised to appoint one shepherd over His scattered flock. Some hear Jesus' words “one flock and one shepherd” as an echo of that promise, widened so that believing Jews and Gentiles are gathered together under Him as their one Shepherd.

passages.saying: Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on John 11:14, where Jesus says plainly that Lazarus is dead.
layers.text: Jesus tells His disciples that their friend Lazarus has fallen asleep and that He is going to wake him. No one had told Him, yet He knows that Lazarus has died, and He means to raise him.

layers.evidence: Gill says Lazarus sleeping means he was dead, and reads the waking as raising him from the dead. Barnes says Scripture calls death sleep to show that death will not be final and that there will be an awaking, a resurrection. Wesley calls this the death of good men in the language of heaven and notes the disciples did not yet understand it, as verse 13 says.
layers.text: Jesus speaks of death as sleep. He means that Lazarus has died and that He will raise him, but the disciples take Him to mean ordinary sleep and think Lazarus will get better. Calling death sleep also hints that for God's people death is not final, since Jesus can wake the dead.

passages.saying: Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on John 11:8, where the disciples remind Jesus that the Jews had just tried to stone Him.
layers.text: When Jesus decides to return to Judea, where His enemies had just tried to stone Him, Thomas urges the other disciples to go with Him, even if it means dying with Him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and the Companion Bible all say both names mean twin, one Hebrew and one Greek. Clarke notes the Hebrew word is used of the twins Esau and Jacob in Genesis 25:24.
layers.text: Thomas comes from the Hebrew and Aramaic word for twin, and Didymus is the Greek word for twin. So John gives the same name twice, once in its Hebrew form and once translated into Greek.

passages.saying: Lazarus, come out!
