passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Greek text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with Genesis Rabbah named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: When His friend Lazarus falls sick, Jesus waits two days, saying the sickness is "for the glory of God." He arrives when Lazarus has been four days in the tomb, tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life," and calls the dead man out.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (TBESG): a colloquial short form of Eleazar; TBESH: Eleazar means God has helped. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Luke 16:20 derive it from Eleazar; Ellicott and Barnes think the name may picture the beggar's helplessness.
layers.text: Lazarus is a short form of Eleazar, a Hebrew name meaning "God has helped." John never comments on the name. For Luke's beggar, some commentators think it may picture a man who had no other help; others see no symbolism.

layers.evidence: Bengel, Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Luke 16:31 note the match with the raising of Lazarus.
layers.text: In a parable in Luke, Jesus names a beggar Lazarus, and the story ends, "they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead." In John a man named Lazarus rises, and the chief priests plan "to kill Lazarus as well." The Gospels never link the two.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: Caiaphas meant political expediency, and John reads his words in a sense Caiaphas could not have imagined.
layers.text: Caiaphas argues, "it is better for you that one man die for the people." He means politics, but John says that as high priest he "was prophesying" that Jesus would die for the nation and for "the scattered children of God." One sentence, two meanings.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 11:43 point to John 5:25 and 5:28-29. The same noun, phone (voice), is in John 11:43 and 5:28 (TAGNT).
layers.text: Jesus had said that "all who are in their graves will hear His voice" and come out. At Bethany one grave hears that voice early: "The man who had been dead came out." It is a near, partial fulfillment of a far promise.

layers.evidence: Genesis Rabbah 100:7; Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on John 11:39 cite the tradition. Barnes: the four days rule out deception or a mere swoon.
layers.text: John mentions the four days twice, and Martha warns, "by now he stinks." A rabbinic saying, written down later, held that the soul stays near the grave for three days. After four days, commentators note, no one could say Lazarus had only seemed dead.

passages.saying: And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on John 12:33, which says Jesus was showing the kind of death He would die.
layers.text: Jesus says that when He is lifted up from the earth, He will draw people of every kind to Himself. John explains in the next verse that this pointed to the way He would die, raised up on a cross.

layers.evidence: Gill says Christ's death is signified by being lifted up from the earth, in allusion to the bronze serpent lifted up on the pole. Bullinger's Figures of Speech links the serpent of Numbers 21:5-9 and John 3:14 with the lifting up of John 12:32.
layers.text: Being lifted up recalls the bronze snake that Moses set on a pole in the wilderness. Anyone who had been bitten and looked at it would live. In the same way Jesus, raised up on the cross, draws people of every kind to Himself for life.

passages.saying: I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the picture that follows in John 15:2-5, as Barnes explains.
layers.text: Jesus calls Himself the true vine, the real source of life for His people, and His Father the keeper of the vineyard who tends it. As branches draw all their life from the vine, so His disciples draw all their strength from Him.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the Jewish people are compared to a vine God planted (Isaiah 5:1-7, Psalm 80:8-16). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this a figure familiar to Jewish ears (Isaiah 5:1). The Companion Bible says Israel's vine failed and Christ is the true vine.
layers.text: Israel was pictured as God's vine. Isaiah sang of a vineyard God tended that gave only sour grapes, and said the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel. Jesus calls Himself the true vine, which some read as the genuine vine where Israel's vine had failed.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes both suggest Jesus alludes to Jeremiah 2:21. Gill notes that the Septuagint there calls Israel a fruitful vine, wholly true, and sets Christ, the noble vine, against the wild and degenerate one.
layers.text: Through Jeremiah God said He had planted Israel like a choice vine, yet it turned into a rotten, wild vine. The Greek Old Testament calls that vine wholly true, with the same word John's Greek uses here. Jesus may be echoing this: He is the true vine, the genuine stock that never turned wild.

passages.saying: He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the vine picture, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains it.
layers.text: The Father, the keeper of the vineyard, cuts off every branch in Jesus that bears no fruit. Every branch that does bear fruit He prunes, so that it bears even more.

layers.evidence: Clarke sets airei (takes away) beside kathairei (prunes) to show the contrast; Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the pair as a figure of like-sounding words (Paregmenon); Bullinger's Companion Bible ties katharos, clean, in verse 3 to the verb kathairo in verse 2.
layers.text: In John's Greek the two verbs sound alike: the Father airei, takes away, the fruitless branch, and kathairei, prunes or cleanses, the fruitful one. Verse 3 carries the sound on: the disciples are already katharoi, clean, a word from the same family as prunes.

passages.saying: He went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown describes the place.
layers.text: After speaking these words, Jesus leaves the city with His disciples, crosses the Kidron Valley on the east side of Jerusalem, and enters a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives.

layers.evidence: Clarke says John names the brook to call to mind David driven out by Absalom, a figure of the second David betrayed by His own disciple. Wesley calls David here a type of Christ. Gill on 2 Samuel 15:23 says the Messiah, David's antitype, crossed the same brook just before His sufferings.
layers.text: Jesus crosses the Kidron Valley on the night He is betrayed. King David crossed the same valley, with the people weeping, when he fled Jerusalem from his rebel son Absalom. The Kidron recalls that day: the greater Son of David goes out the same way, betrayed by one of His own.

passages.saying: a place called the Stone Pavement, which in Hebrew is Gabbatha
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, as Barnes explains the judgment seat.
layers.text: After the leaders warn him that releasing Jesus would make him no friend of Caesar, Pilate brings Jesus out and sits down on the judgment seat to pass sentence, at a place called the Stone Pavement.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes, Wesley, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill all explain Gabbatha as a raised or high place, and Clarke notes it is not a translation of the Greek name. Bullinger's Companion Bible is more cautious and calls its meaning uncertain.
layers.text: John gives the place two names. In Greek it is Lithostroton, the Stone Pavement. Its local Hebrew (Aramaic) name, Gabbatha, is not a translation of that; it is usually explained as a raised place or height, fitting the raised seat where Pilate sat to judge.

passages.saying: Carrying His own cross, He went out to The Place of the Skull
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, as Clarke explains it alongside the other Gospels.
layers.text: Jesus carries His own cross out of the city to the place of execution, called The Place of the Skull. The other Gospels add that Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it.

layers.evidence: Gill, on both verses, calls Isaac carrying the wood for the burnt offering a type of Christ bearing His cross. Wesley says the same on Genesis 22:6, and Bullinger's Companion Bible there points to John 19:17 and to the Father and the Son as the antitype.
layers.text: Jesus carries His own cross to the place where He will die. Long before, Abraham laid the wood for the burnt offering on his son Isaac, and Isaac carried it up the mountain where he was to be offered. Isaac bearing the wood is a picture of the Son bearing His cross.

layers.evidence: Gill says Golgotha signifies a man's skull and that the name comes from the Syriac (Aramaic) the Jews then spoke; Bullinger's Companion Bible marks Golgotha as Aramaic.
layers.text: John gives the place's meaning and its local name. Golgotha is the Aramaic word for a skull, from the language the Jews then spoke, which John calls Hebrew. So both names say the same thing: The Place of the Skull.

passages.saying: What I have written, I have written.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of Pilate's answer, as Clarke explains it.
layers.text: The chief priests want the sign over the cross changed so it no longer calls Jesus the King of the Jews. Pilate refuses: he will not change what he wrote.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this among words repeated in a different sense: first the act of writing, then the writing that stands written. Gill and Wesley explain the doubled words as meaning the writing stands and is not to be undone.
layers.text: In John's Greek Pilate uses one word twice: gegrapha, I have written. Some read the repeat as shifting the sense: the first speaks of the act of writing the sign; the second means the writing now stands as written and is not to be undone.

passages.saying: When He had said this, He breathed on them
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, read as a sign of the Spirit to be given at Pentecost.
layers.text: On the evening of His resurrection, Jesus breathed on His disciples and told them to receive the Holy Spirit. The act was a sign and a pledge of the fuller gift of the Spirit that came at Pentecost.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes and Bullinger's Companion Bible all tie this act to God breathing life into Adam in Genesis 2:7, and Gill mentions it too. The Companion Bible notes the verb, emphusao, occurs only here in the New Testament and is the word the Septuagint uses in Genesis 2:7.
layers.text: Jesus breathing on His disciples recalls creation, when God breathed the breath of life into the first man. In John's Greek the verb is rare, found only here in the New Testament but also in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 2:7. The Lord who gave Adam life now gives new life by His Spirit.

passages.saying: they called that field in their own language Akeldama
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in Acts 1:18, which tells of Judas's field and his death.
layers.text: Everyone in Jerusalem heard how Judas died and how the field was bought with his betrayal money. So the people gave the field a name that remembered it, and Luke translates that name for his readers.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Clarke and Gill all explain Akeldama as two words in the Aramaic of Jerusalem (they call it Syro-Chaldaic, Chaldee or Syriac) meaning field of blood, and Gill and Clarke tie the name to the price of Christ's blood. Wesley notes that Luke added the translation for Greek readers.
layers.text: Akeldama is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jerusalem at the time. It joins two words meaning field and blood, so it means Field of Blood. The name kept alive the memory that the field was bought with the price paid for Jesus' blood.

passages.saying: each one heard them speaking his own language
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and on Acts 2:7, where the crowd marvels that the speakers are Galileans.
layers.text: When this sound rang out, a crowd gathered in bewilderment, because each person heard these Galileans speaking in his own native language.

layers.evidence: Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, commenting on Babel at Genesis 11:7, both set the gift of tongues at Pentecost against the confusion of tongues there: the one scattered the nations, the other began gathering them to God.
layers.text: A crowd from many nations hearing one message in their own languages recalls Babel, where God confused human language and scattered the nations. There new languages divided people; at Pentecost the gift of languages began gathering people of every nation to God.

passages.saying: God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: At Pentecost Peter tells the crowd that Jesus died "by God’s set plan and foreknowledge," but God raised Him. Death had seized Him but could not keep Him: "it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches."

layers.evidence: Ellicott: literally travail-pangs, from a Greek rendering of the Hebrew for cords of death. TBESH lists chevel, a cord, and chevel, pain or travail; Gill: the word signifies both cords and sorrows. The Septuagint of Psalm 18:4 has odines thanatou, as in Acts 2:24.
layers.text: The word behind "agony" is odines, labor pains. It echoes the Psalms: "The cords of death encompassed me." In Hebrew chevel means a cord, and a word with the same letters means a labor pain. The Greek Old Testament took it the second way, in Luke's very words.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary and Gill: loosed applies better to cords than to pangs. Ellicott reads the resurrection as a new birth from the womb of the grave. The Septuagint of Psalm 18:5 renders the cords of Sheol as odines hadou.
layers.text: Both senses fit. The verb for "releasing" is lyo, to untie, which suits cords better than pains: God loosed "the cords of Sheol." Some also hear a birth: death went into labor and could not hold what it bore.

layers.evidence: G. G. Findlay (Pulpit Commentary) on Colossians 1:18 likens the grave Christ rose from to a womb. Ellicott calls the resurrection His second birth, and the continuation of Poole's Annotations a kind of new birth. Barnes reads firstborn as rank, and TBESG files it under priority.
layers.text: Many hear the same picture in a title Paul and John both give Jesus: "firstborn from among the dead" and "the firstborn from the dead." Older commentators call the resurrection His second birth, coming out of the grave as a child comes from the womb.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 16:21: the figure was often used by the prophets (Isaiah 21:3, 26:17-18, 66:7-8). Isaiah 26:17 has chevel, pain (TAHOT); in 26:19 the verb for bring forth can mean give birth (NET Bible note).
layers.text: Jesus pictured the grief of His death and the joy of Easter as childbirth: the mother "forgets her anguish," and "I will see you again." Isaiah 26 uses the same picture: labor pains give way to "Your dead will live" and "the earth will bring forth her dead."

passages.saying: to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on Peter's offer in Acts 2:38 of forgiveness and the gift of the Holy Spirit.
layers.text: Peter tells his hearers that God's promise of forgiveness and the Holy Spirit is for them and their children, and also for people far away, both Jews scattered abroad and the Gentile nations, everyone the Lord calls to Himself.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, commenting on Joel 2:31-32, note that Peter quoted Joel's prophecy at Pentecost (Acts 2:17-21) without its closing words, and that in Acts 2:39 he even adds those closing words of Joel 2:32 about the ones the Lord calls.
layers.text: Earlier in this sermon Peter quoted Joel's prophecy of the Spirit but stopped before its last words about the remnant called by the LORD. Some see him picking up that ending here: the promise is for all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke, on Isaiah 57:19, read Isaiah's near and far off as Israel and the Gentiles and point to Acts 2:39 (and Ephesians 2:13, 17) where those terms are taken up.
layers.text: Peter's words to all who are far off echo Isaiah's promise of peace to those far and near. Paul applies Isaiah's far and near to Gentiles and Jews (Ephesians 2:17), and so the promise here reaches past Israel to the nations God calls.

passages.saying: has glorified His servant Jesus
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on Peter's explanation that the lame man was healed by God's power in Jesus' name (Acts 3:12, 16).
layers.text: Peter tells the crowd that the God of their fathers has honored Jesus by this healing. They had handed Jesus over and rejected Him before Pilate, even though Pilate had decided to release Him.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the word here should be read Servant, in the high sense in which Isaiah always applies it to the Messiah, and lists Isaiah 42:1, 49:6, 52:13 and 53:11. The Companion Bible also reads Servant here and compares Isaiah 42:1 and 49:6.
layers.text: Peter calls Jesus God's Servant, the title Isaiah gives the coming Messiah. Of that Servant Isaiah says that He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted. The people had rejected Jesus, but God has glorified Him as that Servant.

passages.saying: whom the apostles called Barnabas
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the next one, where Joseph sells a field and brings the money to the apostles.
layers.text: Luke introduces Joseph, a Levite born on Cyprus, whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas. He is held up as a fine example of the generous spirit in the early church, for he sold a field and gave the money to the apostles.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all explain Barnabas as bar, son, joined to a word for prophecy (Clarke gives Bar naba), and note that Luke's Greek word paraklesis means exhortation as well as comfort. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley say the name came from the character of his ministry.
layers.text: Bar is the Aramaic word for son. The rest of the name is usually traced to a word for prophecy, Spirit-given speaking that exhorts and comforts. Luke renders it Son of Encouragement, a fitting name for a man who later encouraged the believers at Antioch to stay true to the Lord.

passages.saying: he kept back some of the proceeds for himself
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and its setting in Acts 4:36-5:11.
layers.text: Ananias sold a piece of land and, with his wife's full knowledge, secretly kept some of the money for himself. He laid only part of it at the apostles' feet while pretending it was the whole amount.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible on Joshua 7:1 notes that the Septuagint uses the same verb there as Acts 5:1-2. T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) on Joshua 7:1 says Achan's taking of devoted things was the same sin of sacrilege as that of Ananias and Sapphira.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek, Ananias kept back part of the price. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb in the story of Achan, who took for himself some of the things devoted to God at Jericho. Both men secretly held back part of what was meant for God.

passages.saying: whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the apostles' answer to the council.
layers.text: Peter and the apostles tell the council that the God of their fathers raised up Jesus, the very One the council had put to death on a cross, which they call a tree.

layers.evidence: Gill and Wesley on Deuteronomy 21:23 say this law about one hanged on a tree pointed ahead to Christ, who was made a curse for His people; Paul quotes it in Galatians 3:13. Barnes on Acts 5:30 explains the tree as the cross and points to Galatians 3:13.
layers.text: Calling the cross a tree can recall the law of Moses, which said that anyone hung on a tree was under God's curse. Those words looked ahead to Jesus, who was hanged on a tree and bore the curse for His people. Yet God raised Him up.

passages.saying: You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse as the close of Stephen's speech.
layers.text: Stephen ends his defense by charging the council with stubbornness. Like their fathers, they will not listen to God and keep resisting the Holy Spirit.

layers.evidence: Gill calls stiff-necked a name often given to Israel (Exodus 32:9). The Companion Bible notes the Greek word is the Septuagint's in Exodus 33:3 and 33:5. Clarke calls uncircumcised in heart and ears a manner of speech often used by the prophets.
layers.text: Stephen's charge is made of Old Testament words. God called Israel a stiff-necked people in the days of Moses, and the prophets spoke of uncircumcised hearts and ears that would not listen. Stephen says the council is acting just as their fathers did.

passages.saying: Do you understand what you are reading?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: An Ethiopian official, treasurer to his queen, is riding home from worship in Jerusalem, reading Isaiah aloud. Philip runs up beside the chariot. The passage is about one "led like a sheep to the slaughter," and Philip tells him about Jesus.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: ginoskeis (G1097) and anaginoskeis (G0314) side by side. Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) gives know again as the first sense of anaginosko and lists Acts 8:30 under read. Philip and the official may well have spoken Greek, but the wording we have is Luke's. Ellicott and Bullinger both point out the play.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek, Philip's question is a pun: ginoskeis ha anaginoskeis? Ginosko means "to know," and the verb for read is the same word with ana- in front, "to know again." Reading the words is not yet knowing what they mean.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: sarisim, eunuchs (H5631), in Isaiah 56:4; TAGNT: eunouchos (G2135) in Acts 8:27. Ellicott, Barnes and the continuation of Poole's Annotations note that eunouchos may be only an official's title. Ellicott, the continuation of Poole's Annotations and Gill link the scene with Isaiah 56:3-5.
layers.text: Luke calls the reader a eunuch, a castrated man; the law kept such men out of the assembly. Soon after the passage he was reading, Isaiah promises faithful eunuchs "a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters." Many see that promise come true here.

passages.saying: the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: As soon as the official was baptized, the Spirit of the Lord took Philip away. The official never saw him again, but he went on his way full of joy.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the wording repeats what is told of the ancient prophets in 1 Kings 18:12 and 2 Kings 2:16. Wesley says the same had happened to several of the prophets.
layers.text: The Old Testament spoke the same way of Elijah. Obadiah feared that the Spirit of the LORD would carry Elijah off, and the sons of the prophets wondered whether the Spirit had set him down on some mountain. Luke tells of Philip being taken away just as the prophets of old were.

passages.saying: In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: In the port town of Joppa lived a disciple named Tabitha, also called Dorcas. She spent her life doing good and giving to the poor.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Wesley, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all say Tabitha (Aramaic or Syriac) and Dorcas (Greek) mean the same thing, a gazelle, roe or antelope. Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown add that the animal's beauty made it a name for women.
layers.text: Tabitha is an Aramaic name, and Dorcas is the Greek word with the same meaning: gazelle, a graceful animal like a small deer. Its beauty made it a fitting name for a woman. Luke gives her name in both languages.

passages.saying: opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and the account in Acts 13:6-12.
layers.text: On Cyprus a sorcerer called Elymas stood against Barnabas and Saul. He tried to keep the Roman governor from believing the message about Jesus.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible trace Elymas to an Arabic word for wise or learned, and Barnes says it is an Arabic word meaning the same as magus. Gill instead takes it as a rendering of Bar-Jesus.
layers.text: This man was also called Bar-Jesus, but he went by Elymas, and Luke says the name means sorcerer. It likely comes from an Arabic word for a wise or learned man, like magos, Luke's Greek word here, which can mean a wise man or a sorcerer. His name was really his trade.

passages.saying: Then Saul, who was also called Paul
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse's own wording, read with the account in Acts 13:6-12.
layers.text: Saul, from here on called Paul, is filled with the Holy Spirit and fixes his eyes on Elymas, the sorcerer who was trying to turn the governor away from the faith.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes and JFB all say the Latin Paulus means little; Clarke and Barnes give Saul as asked or desired. Barnes notes the change of a single letter, and Clarke and JFB connect the name with his small stature (2 Corinthians 10:10).
layers.text: From this point Luke calls him Paul, his Roman name, instead of his Hebrew name Saul. Saul means asked for, while the Latin name Paulus means little. The two names differ by one letter, and some think the new name suited his small, unimpressive presence (2 Corinthians 10:10).

passages.saying: O child of the devil and enemy of all righteousness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse's own wording; the commentaries read it as exposing the sorcerer's deceit.
layers.text: Filled with the Spirit, Paul exposes Elymas as full of deceit and trickery, a child of the devil and enemy of all righteousness who keeps twisting the straight ways of the Lord.

layers.evidence: Gill on this verse says Paul is perhaps alluding to the name: instead of Bar-Jesus, son of a saviour, he should be called son of Satan. Clarke and Barnes on Acts 13:6 explain Bar-Jesus as son of Jesus or Joshua.
layers.text: The sorcerer was named Bar-Jesus, son of Jesus (the same name as Joshua). In Luke's Greek, Paul's rebuke is literally son of the devil, and it may play on that name: far from living up to a name that points to a savior, he was acting as a son of the devil.

passages.saying: Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul they called Hermes
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse itself gives the reason for the name Hermes.
layers.text: After Paul healed a lame man at Lystra, the crowd took the two missionaries for gods. They called Barnabas Zeus and called Paul Hermes, because Paul was the one doing the speaking.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, JFB and the Companion Bible all explain Hermes (Mercury) as the messenger of the gods or the god of eloquence. Clarke adds that the phrase used of Paul here, leader of the discourse, was a title applied to Hermes by ancient writers.
layers.text: In Greek belief Hermes was the messenger of the gods and the god of eloquence, so the crowd gave his name to Paul, the speaker, and gave Zeus, the chief god, to Barnabas. Luke's phrase for Paul, leader of the word, closely matches a title ancient writers gave Hermes.

passages.saying: what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse's own wording; the commentaries agree Paul takes the altar as the starting point of his speech.
layers.text: Paul tells the Athenians he found an altar inscribed to an unknown god, and he uses it to announce the true God, the One they had been honoring without knowing Him.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls this a fine paronomasia, or play on the words, linking the altar's word unknown with Paul's word for worshiping unknowingly. JFB likewise renders the clause knowing Him not and says it alludes to the Unknown God.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek the altar's word agnosto (unknown) is picked up by agnoountes (not knowing) in Paul's next sentence. The shared root ties the inscription to his message: the God they honored without knowing is the God he now makes known.

passages.saying: does not live in temples made by human hands
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse's own wording, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Paul tells the Athenians that the God who made the world and everything in it is Lord of heaven and earth, so He cannot be housed in shrines that people build.

layers.evidence: JFB on this verse calls the thought familiar to Jewish ears and cites 1 Kings 8:27 and Isaiah 66:1-2. Barnes on Isaiah 66:1 links that verse with Solomon's prayer and says the same thought is found in Paul's address at Athens.
layers.text: Paul's point that God does not live in buildings made by people echoes Solomon's prayer that even the highest heaven cannot contain God, and the Lord's question through Isaiah, "What kind of house will you build for Me?"

passages.saying: He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse's own wording; the Giver of all cannot depend on those He gives to.
layers.text: God is not served by human hands as if He lacked anything, because He is the One who gives every creature its life, its breath and everything else.

layers.evidence: Barnes says it is highly probable that Paul had Genesis 2:7 in mind here. Gill likewise explains the words by God breathing into man at first, so that he became a living soul.
layers.text: God giving everyone life and breath recalls the creation of man, when the LORD God breathed the breath of life into his nostrils (Genesis 2:7). The One who gave the first breath still gives every breath.

passages.saying: Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Greek en oligo, which can mean almost, in a little time, or with little effort.
layers.text: After Paul presses King Agrippa about believing the prophets, Agrippa answers that Paul is trying to persuade him, in a little, to become a Christian. Older English Bibles read this as almost persuaded; others read it as so quickly.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible notes that verse 29 reads literally in little and in great, and that Paul takes up Agrippa's words with a higher meaning. His Figures of Speech says Paul repeats Agrippa's word with a far higher and more extended meaning.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek, Agrippa's question turns on en oligo, "in a little," rendered "in such a short time." Paul picks up the same phrase and widens it: in little or in great, he wishes to God that Agrippa and all who hear him would become what he is, except for his chains.

passages.saying: exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verb exchanged, which describes a change in the worshippers, not in God.
layers.text: People who knew about God traded the worship of the undying God for idols shaped like mortal humans, birds, animals and reptiles. God's glory did not change; the change was in them, as they put lifeless images in His place.

layers.evidence: Clarke on Psalm 106:20 points to the use Paul makes of that verse in Romans 1:23, and Barnes compares the two passages. The Septuagint of the psalm uses the same Greek words for exchanged, glory and likeness that Paul uses.
layers.text: Paul's wording echoes Psalm 106:20, where Israel at Horeb exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox. Paul uses the same language for the nations, who likewise traded the glorious God for images of His creatures.

passages.saying: since they did not see fit to acknowledge God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the link between refusing to keep God in mind and being given up by Him.
layers.text: People had some knowledge of God but chose not to keep Him in mind. So God handed them over to a corrupt way of thinking that leads them to do what ought not to be done.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the same Greek word appears in two forms and Paul meant to keep the link; Clarke says it is the same word in both places; Bullinger's Companion Bible calls it a play upon two words, dokimazo and adokimos, hard to express in English.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek one word root appears twice. They did not see fit (edokimasan, to test and approve) to acknowledge God, so God gave them up to an adokimos mind, one that fails the test. Because they would not approve of God, they were left with a mind He could not approve.

passages.saying: They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the phrase filled with, meaning these sins abounded among them.
layers.text: Paul lists the sins that filled the lives of people who turned away from God, from wickedness, greed and depravity to envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice and gossip.

layers.evidence: Gill notes an elegant paronomasia in the Greek here and says envy and murder are put together because murder sometimes arises from envy. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes the paronomasia phthonos, phonos, and his Figures of Speech lists the pair under Paronomasia.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, envy (phthonos) and murder (phonos) stand side by side and differ by just one letter. Some see them paired because envy can grow into murder.

passages.saying: They are senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the meaning of each word in the list.
layers.text: Paul ends his list by describing people who are foolish, who break their promises and agreements, who lack natural love for their own families, and who show no mercy.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible notes the paronomasia of asunetos with the next word, and his Figures of Speech lists asunetous and asunthetous under Paronomasia.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the first two words nearly rhyme: asunetous, senseless, and asunthetous, faithless or covenant breaking. They differ by a single letter, and some hear a deliberate sound-play as the pair rings together in the ear.

passages.saying: For on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the judge doing the same things he condemns in others.
layers.text: Paul turns to anyone who condemns others for the sins just listed. Such a person has no excuse, because he does the same things, so in judging others he passes sentence on himself.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible says the three uses of krino and one of katakrino form the figure Paregmenon, words from one root; his Figures of Speech lists this verse under the same figure.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the verb to judge (krino) comes three times, and once it is sharpened to katakrino, to condemn. The same root runs through the verse's warning: on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself.

passages.saying: All who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the law meaning God's written revelation given to Israel.
layers.text: God judges fairly. Those who sinned without having God's written law will still perish for their sin, and those who sinned while having that law will be judged by it.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse as a repeated word used in two senses: the first without law means not under the Law, the second means without the judgment of the Law.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the same word, anomōs (without law), is used twice in two senses. Those who sinned without having the law will perish without the law being used to judge them.

passages.saying: will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verb regarded, meaning reckoned or counted by God.
layers.text: Paul asks whether a Gentile who is not circumcised but keeps what the law requires will not be counted by God as though he were circumcised. The outward sign alone does not decide a person's standing with God.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse as one word repeated in two senses: first uncircumcision means the Gentiles, then it means their condition as people who fulfil what the Law requires.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the word uncircumcision (akrobustia) appears twice. Some see its sense shift: first it stands for the uncircumcised man himself, a Gentile; then it may mean his condition as one who keeps the law, which God will count as circumcision.

passages.saying: Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between outward and inward, letter and Spirit.
layers.text: A true Jew is one inwardly. Real circumcision is a work of the Spirit on the heart, not an outward mark under the written code. Such a person looks for praise from God, not from people.

layers.evidence: Gill says Paul here alludes to the name Judah, which comes from a word meaning to praise. Clarke calls this a highly probable reading, tracing Judah (Yehudah) to yadah, to praise. Genesis 29:35 gives the name's origin.
layers.text: The name Jew comes from Judah, a name tied to the Hebrew word for praise. At his birth Leah said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Paul seems to play on this: the true Jew, changed in heart, receives his praise not from men but from God.

passages.saying: no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain statement about the law and sin.
layers.text: No one will be declared righteous before God by keeping the law. The law cannot save anyone; it only makes people aware of their sin.

layers.evidence: Gill on Psalm 143:2 says the apostle explains that verse in Romans 3:20. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Psalm 143:2 at the words in his sight. Barnes and the Companion Bible also link the two verses.
layers.text: Paul's words echo David's prayer: “Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You.” Paul adds that works of the law cannot change this, because the law only makes people aware of sin.

passages.saying: apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between law-keeping and the witness of Scripture.
layers.text: Now God has made known a righteousness that comes apart from keeping the law. It is not new, for the Law and the Prophets, the Old Testament Scriptures, already bore witness to it.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse as one word repeated in two senses: law without the article means law as a moral rule of works, the Law with the article means the Law of Moses. Barnes likewise reads the second as the five books of Moses.
layers.text: Paul uses the word law twice with two meanings. Righteousness comes apart from the law, that is, apart from keeping its commands. Yet it is attested by the Law and the Prophets, meaning the books of Scripture. Law-keeping cannot earn it, but the Law foretold it.

passages.saying: God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording about the atoning sacrifice and God's forbearance.
layers.text: God put Christ forward as the atoning sacrifice, received through faith in His blood. This shows that God is righteous, because in His patience He had passed over sins committed beforehand without yet punishing them.

layers.evidence: Gill says the word alludes to the mercy seat, a type of Christ, and is the Septuagint's word for it. Clarke renders it the mercy seat, where the sacrifice's blood was sprinkled. The Companion Bible notes the Septuagint's use for the ark's cover in Exodus 25:17. Barnes ties it to the blood sprinkled on the mercy seat in Leviticus 16:14-15.
layers.text: Paul's word for atoning sacrifice, hilasterion, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the mercy seat, the gold lid of the ark where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement. Christ, by His own blood, fulfills what that cover pictured.

passages.saying: Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's question and answer about boasting, works and faith.
layers.text: No one can boast before God. Boasting is ruled out, not by a way of earning through works, but by the way of faith, which receives salvation as a gift.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse as one word in two senses: first God's law, then not law at all but faith itself. Gill likewise says the law of faith is not a new law but a doctrine or instruction, a sense the Hebrew word for law can carry.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the word law (nomos) is in both the question and the answer, though here it is translated principle. Boasting is shut out, not by a law of works, but by a law of faith. Paul stretches the word so that the answer is not law-keeping at all but trusting God.

passages.saying: I see another law at work in my body
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of warfare and captivity within.
layers.text: Paul sees a pull toward sin at work in his body. It fights against what his mind approves and takes him captive, like a prisoner of war.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse as one word in different senses: the first and third laws are indwelling sin, the second the new nature. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says law here means an inward principle of action, two of which Paul found within him.
layers.text: Just after saying he delights in God's law, Paul uses the same word for a steady force inside him. He sees “another law at work in my body” at war with the law of his mind. One word now names two rival powers, sin's pull and the mind that loves God.

passages.saying: God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between what the law could not do and what God did by sending His Son.
layers.text: The law could show what is right, but it could not set sinners free, because our sinful nature left it powerless. God did what the law could not do. He sent His own Son as a real man, yet without sin, as an offering for sin, and so condemned sin in the flesh.

layers.evidence: Clarke reads the phrase as a sacrifice for sin, its sense in many places; Gill says it means an offering for sin, as the word is used in Hebrews 10:6; Barnes agrees, and Bullinger calls Christ the sin offering personified. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown grants the Septuagint usage but prefers a broader sense.
layers.text: Paul's Greek for "as an offering for sin" is peri hamartias, literally concerning sin. The Greek Old Testament uses this phrase for the sin offering of the Law, and Hebrews 10:6 uses it the same way. So Paul pictures God's Son Himself as the sin offering.

passages.saying: if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two conditions: living by the flesh, or putting sin to death by the Spirit.
layers.text: A life ruled by the sinful nature ends in death. But those who, by the power of the Holy Spirit, keep putting to death the sinful deeds of the body will live. The Spirit gives the strength, and the believer takes part in the fight against sin.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Paul uses mortify, put to death, as a kind of play upon the word die just before: if ye do not kill sin, it will kill you. Barnes states the same turn: either your sins must die, or you must.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, put to death (thanatoute) answers die (apothneskein) earlier in the verse, and both words come from the Greek word family for death. The turn is pointed: either the believer puts sin to death, or sin will bring death to him.

passages.saying: For the creation was subjected to futility
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words subjected, futility and in hope.
layers.text: Creation was made subject to futility, a state of frustration, decay and misery that it did not choose. This happened because of the One who subjected it, and it was done in hope, looking ahead to the day when creation will be set free.

layers.evidence: Wesley names Genesis 3:17 as where God subjected creation, and on that verse says the ground by man's sin is made subject to vanity. Keil and Delitzsch tie Romans 8:20-21 to the curse on the earth for Adam's sin, and the Concise Commentary, abridging John Evans's continuation of Matthew Henry, traces creation's misery to the fall. Gill, Clarke and Barnes read creature here more narrowly.
layers.text: The futility Paul speaks of goes back to Genesis 3. After Adam sinned, God said, "cursed is the ground because of you," and the ground began to bring forth thorns and thistles. Creation has carried the effects of that curse ever since, waiting in hope for its release.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that the Septuagint often uses this Greek word for the Hebrew hebel, as in Ecclesiastes. W. T. Bullock (Barnes' Notes), on Ecclesiastes 1:2, says the place of vanity is explained by Paul in Romans 8, where its origin is traced to the fall of man.
layers.text: Paul's Greek word for futility (mataiotes) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the futility of Ecclesiastes, the Hebrew hevel, a breath. The Teacher saw that everything under the sun is futile. Read this way, Paul shows where that futility came from and that it will not have the last word.

passages.saying: He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's argument from the greater gift to the lesser.
layers.text: God has already given the greatest gift there could be: His own Son, handed over to death for all His people. Since He gave that, He will surely give them, along with Christ, everything else they need.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that the Septuagint of Genesis 22:12 renders not withheld as not spared. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the phrase and the whole thought are suggested by Genesis 22:12, and Clarke draws the same parallel with Abraham, who did not withhold his only son Isaac.
layers.text: Paul's words echo God's praise of Abraham, who did not withhold his only son Isaac. The Greek Old Testament there uses the same verb, did not spare. Abraham was stopped before Isaac died, but God the Father did not spare His own Son. He truly gave Him up for us.

passages.saying: Who will bring any charge against God’s elect?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the courtroom picture of the verse, where God is the Judge who justifies.
layers.text: No accusation can stand against the people God has chosen, because God Himself, the Judge of all, has declared them righteous. If the Judge has acquitted them, no one can bring a charge that will hold.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Isaiah 50:9, says Paul seems to have some reference to that passage in Romans 8:33. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Isaiah 50:8, says the believer, by his oneness with Christ, uses the same language, pointing to Romans 8:32-34.
layers.text: Paul's courtroom questions echo the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 50, who says that the One who vindicates Him is near and asks who will contend with Him or condemn Him. Joined to Christ, believers can now speak the same confident words.

passages.saying: Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's chain of Christ's death, resurrection, place at God's right hand and intercession.
layers.text: No one can condemn those who belong to Christ. He died for them, He was raised to life, He now sits at God's right hand, and He prays for them. Each step makes their safety more certain.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Christ's sitting at the right hand of God was predicted in Psalm 110:1 and signifies the glory and ruling power of the exalted Son of Man.
layers.text: Some see Christ at the right hand of God as fulfilling Psalm 110:1, where the LORD says to David's Lord, "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet." The risen Christ now holds that place of royal honor and power.

passages.saying: I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's stated grief for Israel in Romans 9:2-3.
layers.text: Paul loves his fellow Israelites so much that he says he could wish to be cursed and cut off from Christ for their sake, if that could save them. It shows how deep his sorrow is over their unbelief.

layers.evidence: Barnes, on Romans 9:3, gives Exodus 32:32 as a similar case, and Samuel Clark (Barnes' Notes) on Exodus 32 says the same thought is in Romans 9:3. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the verse recalls the similar idea Moses expressed in Exodus 32:32, and Keil and Delitzsch call Moses' words just as deep and true as Paul's wish.
layers.text: Paul's wish recalls Moses after the golden calf. Moses asked God to forgive Israel's sin, and if not, "please blot me out of the book that You have written." Like Moses, Paul loved his people so much that he would give himself up for their sake.

passages.saying: For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's answer to the charge that God's word had failed.
layers.text: Israel's unbelief does not mean God's promise has failed. God never promised that every physical descendant of Jacob would belong to His true people. Within the nation there was always a true Israel, the children of His promise.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under antanaclasis, one word used twice in different senses: the true spiritual seed, and Israel according to the flesh. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill explain the two senses the same way, the natural seed and the Israel of God's choice.
layers.text: Paul uses the one name Israel in two senses in one sentence. Those descended from Israel are the natural children of Jacob, whose God-given name was Israel. The second Israel is the true Israel, the people of God's promise. Birth into the nation did not by itself make anyone part of that Israel.

passages.saying: Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between man and God, the thing formed and its Maker.
layers.text: Paul answers the objector by reminding him who he is: a created man talking back to his Creator. Something that has been made has no right to demand that its Maker explain why He made it as He did.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says the words are quoted from Isaiah 45:9. Barnes says the sentiment is found in Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9, and Clarke, on Isaiah 45:9, says Paul borrowed the image there. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also points to Isaiah 45:9.
layers.text: Paul borrows Isaiah's picture of clay questioning the potter who shapes it, "Does the clay ask the potter, ‘What are you making?’" Isaiah 29:16 asks almost the same question in almost Paul's own words. A creature has no standing to put its Maker on trial.

passages.saying: Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the potter's right over his clay as a picture of God's right over what He has made.
layers.text: A potter may shape one part of a lump of clay into a vessel for special occasions and another into one for common use. In the same way God, the Maker, has the right to do as He wills with what He has made.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the same sentiment is found in Jeremiah 18:6. Clarke says Paul points to the parable of the potter in Jeremiah 18. The Companion Bible compares Isaiah 45:9, Isaiah 64:8 and Jeremiah 18:1-6, and Wesley also cites Jeremiah 18:6.
layers.text: The potter and the clay recall Jeremiah 18, where Jeremiah watched a potter at the wheel and the LORD told Israel, "Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand." Isaiah 64:8 also calls God the potter and His people the clay.

passages.saying: If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's two pictures, the first part of the dough and the root, as Clarke explains them.
layers.text: Paul gives two pictures of one truth. When the first part of the dough was offered to God, the whole batch was counted holy; when a tree's root is holy, its branches are too. Israel's holy beginnings are a pledge that God has not finished with the nation.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown both tie the first part of the dough and the whole batch (the lump) to the dough offering commanded in Numbers 15:19-21.
layers.text: Paul draws on the law of the dough offering: "From the first of your dough, you are to lift up a cake as a contribution". Once that first portion was given to God, the whole batch was counted holy and could be eaten. A small offering hallowed the whole.

layers.evidence: Barnes suggests, with a perhaps, that the root and branches recall Jeremiah 11:16, where the nation is pictured as an olive tree.
layers.text: The root and branches may also recall Jeremiah's word to Judah: "The LORD once called you a flourishing olive tree". In the very next verses Paul pictures Israel as an olive tree, with some natural branches broken off and wild ones grafted in.

passages.saying: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's plain warning against pride, as Barnes explains it.
layers.text: Speaking with an apostle's authority, Paul tells every believer not to rate himself too highly. Instead each should judge himself soberly and honestly, by the measure of faith God has given him.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it a paronomasia, a play upon words; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says each word plays upon another; Bullinger names the figure Paregmenon, several words of one origin in one sentence.
layers.text: Paul's Greek repeats one root four times: not to hyperphronein (think too highly) beyond what one ought to phronein (think), but to phronein (think) so as to sōphronein (think soberly). The repeated phron sound drives the point home: right thinking about yourself is sober thinking.

passages.saying: Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain command to answer persecution with blessing, as Clarke explains it.
layers.text: Christians are to answer those who persecute them with blessing, asking God's good for them and never calling down harm on them, whatever the provocation.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the command is taken from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:44); Gill calls it the order Christ gave to His disciples there.
layers.text: Paul echoes Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount: "love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you". The apostle hands on his Lord's own teaching to the believers in Rome.

passages.saying: Do not be proud, but enjoy the company of the lowly. Do not be conceited.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's call to humble unity, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains it.
layers.text: Paul calls believers to live in harmony, to set aside proud ambitions, to be glad to keep company with humble people, and not to think themselves wiser than everyone else.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes on Proverbs 3:7 say that verse is quoted in Romans 11:25 and Romans 12:16.
layers.text: Some hear behind "Do not be conceited" Solomon's warning, "Be not wise in your own eyes". Paul's Greek says, do not be wise in yourselves. He gave Rome the same warning in 11:25, telling Gentile believers not to be conceited about Israel's hardening.

passages.saying: Carefully consider what is right in the eyes of everybody.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain command against revenge, as the Concise Commentary, abridging John Evans's continuation of Matthew Henry, explains it.
layers.text: Believers must never pay back evil with evil. Instead they should think ahead about doing what is honorable, so that everyone watching can see that their conduct is good.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the idea is from Proverbs 3:4; Barnes says the expression in the sight of all men is taken from Proverbs 3:4.
layers.text: Paul's call to do "what is right in the eyes of everybody" draws on Proverbs, where the one who holds on to loving devotion and faithfulness will find "favor and high regard in the sight of God and man".

passages.saying: Therefore let us stop judging one another.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's call to stop condemning one another over disputed matters, as Gill explains it.
layers.text: Since all will stand before God's judgment seat, believers must stop condemning one another over disputed matters like food and holy days. Instead each should resolve never to put anything in a brother's path that would make him stumble.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it a beautiful play upon the word judge; Barnes calls it a happy turn: whoever is eager to judge should judge his own conduct.
layers.text: Paul plays on one Greek verb, krinō, to judge. Let us stop judging one another, he says, but judge this instead: never to trip up a brother. In this verse the second judge is translated make up your mind. The urge to judge is turned on oneself.

passages.saying: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the promise as victory over those sowing discord in the church.
layers.text: Paul assures the believers in Rome that God, who gives peace, will soon give them victory over Satan, who was stirring up division through false teachers. He closes with a prayer that the grace of Jesus Christ be with them.

layers.evidence: Gill calls this a manifest allusion to Genesis 3:15, Barnes says the language refers to that prediction, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it a reproduction of the first great promise, that the Seed of the woman would bruise the serpent's head.
layers.text: Paul's promise that God will soon crush Satan under believers' feet echoes the first promise in Eden, where God told the serpent that the woman's offspring would crush its head. Christ won that victory, and God will let His people share in it.

passages.saying: Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Wesley explains that God has shown the world's wisdom to be foolishness.
layers.text: Paul asks where the wise man, the scholar and the clever debater of this age now stand. Through the message of the cross, God has shown that the world's wisdom cannot save anyone.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley all connect Paul's questions with Isaiah 33:18. Barnes and Wesley note that Isaiah was celebrating Jerusalem's rescue from Sennacherib. Gill notes the sense there differs, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Paul applies it in a higher sense.
layers.text: Paul's run of Where is...? questions echoes Isaiah 33:18. There Isaiah pictures Jerusalem, rescued from Assyria, asking where the enemy officials who had tallied, weighed and counted the towers had gone. Paul turns the same taunt on the world's wise men, left baffled by the cross.

passages.saying: If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The Concise Commentary, abridging Simon Browne's continuation of Matthew Henry, explains that those who corrupt the church bring destruction on themselves.
layers.text: Paul tells the church that together they are God's temple, and that temple is holy. Anyone who ruins it, for example by false teaching or division, will himself be destroyed by God.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all note that one Greek verb stands in both clauses. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it God repaying in kind, and the Companion Bible suggests the word mar for both.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the same verb, phtheiro (to ruin or destroy), is used twice: if anyone ruins God's temple, God will ruin him. The repeated word shows the punishment exactly matching the crime.

passages.saying: For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Wesley explains the old leaven as both sinners and sin, which the church must put away.
layers.text: Paul tells the church to clear out the old leaven of sin, including the unrepentant man among them, so they can be a new, pure batch. The reason is that Christ, their Passover lamb, has already been sacrificed.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown trace the image to the careful search for leaven before Passover, and Clarke points to his notes on Exodus 12. Barnes says the paschal lamb was a type of the Messiah, and Wesley calls the Jewish Passover only a type of Christ.
layers.text: Paul sets the church in the Passover story. Israel had to remove all leaven from their houses and slaughter the Passover lamb. Christ is the true Passover lamb, already sacrificed, so His people must now clear out the leaven of sin.

passages.saying: how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Wesley explains the unjust as the heathen judges and the saints as fellow believers.
layers.text: Paul rebukes believers who take their disputes with one another to pagan courts. He says such matters should be settled among fellow believers instead.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls this a paronomasia: heathen judges were termed dikastai for their supposed justice, and Paul calls them adikoi, unrighteous. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the word was chosen to fit a case about justice.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the pagan judges are called adikoi, the unrighteous or unjust. Judges in Greek courts were called dikastai, a title built on dike, justice. So the word stings: believers were seeking justice from men Paul calls unjust.

passages.saying: Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that the verse shows Christians are able to settle their own disputes.
layers.text: Paul reminds the believers that God's people will one day judge the world. If they are to have such a role, they are surely able to settle small disputes among themselves.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Paul refers to Daniel 7:18 and 7:27, where the kingdoms of the earth are promised to the saints. Gill says the teaching might be drawn from Daniel 7:18 and applies the words of Daniel 7:27 to it, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares Daniel 7:27. Barnes instead reads the verse of the final judgment.
layers.text: Paul's question seems to draw on Daniel 7, where the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom and are given dominion under all of heaven. If God's people will share in that rule, Paul reasons, they are fit to settle small disputes now.

passages.saying: but I will not be mastered by anything
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two answers to the saying it quotes, as Wesley explains them.
layers.text: Paul quotes a saying used at Corinth, "Everything is permissible for me," and answers it twice: not everything does any good, and a Christian must not let any appetite or habit become his master.

layers.evidence: JFB notes that the Greek words for lawful (exestin) and brought under the power (exousiasthesomai) are from the same root, and calls it a play on the words.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, permissible (exestin) and mastered (exousiasthesomai) come from the same root, which has to do with right or power. Some hear a play here: all things may be within Paul's rights, yet he will let nothing gain rights over him.

passages.saying: they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Paul warns the Corinthians not to presume on their privileges: Israel was rescued, fed and given water in the wilderness, and still most of them fell.
Twice God gave water from a rock. At Horeb Moses was told to strike it; years later he was told to speak to it, struck it twice instead, and was barred from the land.

Moses named the place Massah (testing) and Meribah (quarreling) because the people asked, "Is the LORD among us or not?" Psalm 95 keeps the names as a warning, and Hebrews, quoting the psalm in Greek, gives their meanings: "in the rebellion, in the day of testing."

In the Song of Moses, Rock is a name for God: "He is the Rock, His work is perfect." Paul echoes that song twice in this chapter (sacrifices to demons, provoking God to jealousy), so "that rock was Christ" puts Christ in the place of Israel's God.
Paul names his way of reading: these things happened "as examples" and "were written down as warnings for us." The Greek words are typoi and typikos, where the word "type" comes from.
Jesus calls out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink." Some readers also connect the struck rock with Christ pierced on the cross, when "blood and water flowed out" from His side.

passages.saying: the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's conclusion about idol sacrifices, as Clarke explains it.
layers.text: Paul says that what pagans sacrifice is not offered to God but to demons, and he does not want the Corinthians to become partners with demons by sharing in idol feasts.

layers.evidence: Gill says reference is had to Deuteronomy 32:17, and the Companion Bible marks the same reference. Clarke on Deuteronomy 32:17 gives the Septuagint wording there as they sacrificed to demons; Paul uses the same Greek verb (thuo) and noun (daimonion) here.
layers.text: Paul's words echo the Song of Moses, which says Israel sacrificed to demons, not to God. Paul brings the same charge against pagan sacrifice at Corinth: an idol is nothing, but the worship offered to it goes to demons.

passages.saying: Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two questions, which Wesley explains as warnings against courting God's rivals.
layers.text: Paul asks whether the Corinthians, by joining in idol feasts, mean to stir up the Lord's jealousy, and whether they think they are stronger than He is. Both questions expect the answer no.

layers.evidence: JFB says Deuteronomy 32:21 is before the apostle's mind here. Paul quotes that verse in Romans 10:19 with the same Greek verb for provoking to jealousy, and verse 20 has just drawn on the same Song (Deuteronomy 32:17).
layers.text: Paul's question may look back to the Song of Moses, where the Lord says His people provoked His jealousy with what is not God. On this reading, sharing in idol feasts would repeat Israel's old sin and stir the same jealousy.

passages.saying: he is the image and glory of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the reason Paul gives for a man's uncovered head in public worship.
layers.text: Paul says a man should not cover his head in worship, because he is the image and glory of God, while the woman is the glory of man.

layers.evidence: Barnes, JFB and Gill all tie the phrase to the creation of man in Genesis 1. JFB adds that the woman too is created in God's image (Genesis 1:26-27). Paul's word for image, eikon, stands for the Hebrew tselem of Genesis 1:27.
layers.text: Calling man the image and glory of God looks back to creation, when God created man in His own image. Genesis says male and female alike bear that image; Paul's point here concerns order, since the man was made first and the woman from him.

passages.saying: eats and drinks judgment on himself
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on Paul's explanation in verses 30 to 32.
layers.text: Anyone who eats and drinks at the Lord's Supper carelessly, without recognizing the body, brings judgment on himself. The verses that follow show this judgment was the Lord's discipline, such as sickness, and not final condemnation.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Greek marks the sin (not distinguishing in judgment) and its punishment (judgment) as corresponding. The Companion Bible names the figure here Paregmenon, a repeat of words that grow from one root.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, judgment (krima) and recognizing (diakrinon) both grow from the verb to judge (krino). The one who fails to judge rightly about the body eats judgment on himself, so the sin and its penalty are tied together by the same root.

passages.saying: if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and the one after it.
layers.text: If believers examine themselves honestly and deal with their own sin, the Lord will not need to judge them. When He does judge them, it is a father's discipline that keeps them from being condemned with the world.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says the figure Paregmenon, a run of words from one root, occurs again in verses 31 and 32, and that judge in verse 31 is the same word as discern in verse 29. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown renders it: if we duly judged ourselves, we should not be judged.
layers.text: Paul's Greek keeps returning to words built on the verb to judge (krino). If we judged (diekrinomen) ourselves, we would not be judged (ekrinometha). When the Lord judges us (krinomenoi), it is discipline, so that we are not condemned (katakrithomen) with the world.

passages.saying: then we shall see face to face
