passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between now and then.
layers.text: In this life believers see and know God only in part, like a dim reflection in a mirror. In the life to come they will see Him directly, face to face, and know Him fully, just as God already knows them fully.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Paul alludes to Numbers 12:8, where the Septuagint has not in enigmas. Gill sees a reference to what the Lord says of Moses there, speaking with him plainly and not in dark speeches.
layers.text: Paul's Greek says we now see in a riddle (ainigma), the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Numbers 12:8, where God speaks with Moses face to face, clearly and not in riddles. Paul takes that picture of Moses to describe the clear sight all believers will one day have.

passages.saying: So he will fall facedown and worship God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and Paul's argument in verses 23 to 25.
layers.text: When an unbeliever hears God's word spoken plainly, the hidden things of his heart are brought to light. He is humbled, worships God, and openly confesses that God is truly present among the believers.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Isaiah 45:14, say there can be no doubt Paul had that passage in mind, setting his word truly (ontos) beside the Hebrew akh (indeed). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Zechariah 8:23, links the nations' words God is with you to 1 Corinthians 14:25.
layers.text: The outsider's confession echoes Isaiah 45:14, where the nations bow down to God's people and say, "God is indeed with you." Zechariah 8:23 pictures the nations saying the same. Paul shows an unbeliever making that very confession in the church.

passages.saying: the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and Paul's argument in verses 12 to 23.
layers.text: Christ really has been raised from the dead. His resurrection is the first part of the harvest and the pledge that all who have died trusting in Him will also be raised.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to the sheaf of firstfruits waved by the priest. Barnes says Paul uses the word in allusion to the first sheaf of Leviticus 23, the pledge of the whole harvest. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Leviticus 23:10-11 and notes that the offering fell on the day of Christ's resurrection.
layers.text: Firstfruits recalls Leviticus 23, where the first sheaf of the harvest was waved before the LORD on the day after the Sabbath as a pledge of the whole harvest. Christ rose on that very day, the first sheaf of the great harvest of the resurrection.

passages.saying: He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the one after it.
layers.text: Christ reigns now, and His reign must go on until every one of His enemies has been brought under His feet. Even death will finally be defeated.

layers.evidence: Gill says reference is had to Psalm 110:1, Christ's sitting at God's right hand being explained as His reigning. Barnes says Paul doubtless had this passage in his eye. The Companion Bible calls it the fifth quotation of Psalm 110:1. Clarke and Wesley also point to the psalm.
layers.text: Paul takes up Psalm 110:1, where the LORD says to David's Lord, "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet." Paul reads it as God's promise that Christ will reign until every enemy is put down.

passages.saying: The first man was of the dust of the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast between the two men in verses 45 to 49.
layers.text: Adam, the first man, was made from the earth and shares its weakness and decay. Christ, the second man, came from heaven, and those who belong to Him will bear His heavenly likeness.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Paul calls Adam choikos, of the dust, because his body was made of dust from the ground in Genesis 2:7. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Genesis 2:7 and 3:19, dust thou art. Barnes cites the same two verses, and Gill cites Genesis 2:7.
layers.text: Paul's word for Adam, made of dust, looks back to Genesis 2:7, where the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground, and to Genesis 3:19, where Adam is told that he is dust and will return to dust.

passages.saying: Death has been swallowed up in victory.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Paul ends his chapter on the resurrection with a mystery: "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed." At the last trumpet the dead will rise imperishable, and then the saying will come true: "Death has been swallowed up in victory."

layers.evidence: NET Bible note on Isaiah 25:8: in Canaanite thought death was a hungry enemy swallowing its victims. The Pulpit Commentary calls Paul's words a free citation from the Hebrew; Bengel gives the Septuagint's wording, in which death prevails and swallows. TBESG: katapino renders bala.
layers.text: Paul quotes Isaiah's promise of a banquet "for all the peoples," where "He will swallow up death forever." Death was pictured as a hungry enemy swallowing its victims; here God swallows death. The common Greek version reversed it, so Paul follows the Hebrew.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 25:8: a kindred Aramaic (Chaldee) verb means to conquer, so the word may denote victory; Barnes adds that the Syriac unites victory and perpetuity. TBESG lists Septuagint renderings of netsach as eis nikos, including 2 Samuel 2:26.
layers.text: Isaiah's "forever" is netsach, which in Hebrew means perpetuity. A related Aramaic word means victory, so Greek translators often wrote "to victory," even in "Must the sword devour forever?" With that echo, one word holds both promises: forever, and victory.

layers.evidence: Readers differ. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read a promise that God will not go back on; Ellicott reports that reading but prefers to hear death summoned against Ephraim, and the Pulpit Commentary sets out both. Where the Septuagint of Hosea has dike (penalty), Paul has nikos, victory (TBESG).
layers.text: Paul echoes Hosea: "Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?" Readers differ on Hosea's tone: a promise of rescue, or God calling death against Israel, for the verse ends "Compassion is hidden from My eyes." Paul makes it a taunt.

layers.evidence: Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Isaiah 25:8 point ahead to Revelation 21:4, and Ellicott to Revelation 7:17, which repeats the promise.
layers.text: Isaiah's verse goes on: "The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face." Paul takes the first half and John the second: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes," and "there will be no more death." One promise ends both death and tears.

layers.evidence: TBESG: katapino is the Septuagint's usual word for bala, swallow, as in Isaiah 25:8. Ellicott and Barnes on 2 Corinthians 5:4 compare 1 Corinthians 15:54.
layers.text: Paul uses the picture again: in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed, "so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life." The Greek verb is the same, katapino. Death used to do the swallowing. Now life does.

passages.saying: If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Greek text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The Greek text spells out the Aramaic marana tha (NET Bible note).
layers.text: Paul takes the pen to write the closing greeting in his own hand. Then come a warning and a prayer: "If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!" The prayer is in Aramaic, not Greek: marana tha.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note gives both readings; David Capes: an acclamation, Our Lord comes, or an invocation, Come, our Lord. TAGNT: NA28, NA27 and SBL print marana tha; Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text print maran atha.
layers.text: The Aramaic divides two ways. Marana tha (Our Lord, come!) is a prayer; maran atha (our Lord has come, or is coming) is a confession. Printed Greek texts divide it both ways. Both are true of Jesus: He came, and He is coming.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Barnes call the words Syriac. David Capes: Qumran texts show the Aramaic Mareh (TBESH mare') could be a divine title, as Larry Hurtado argued. Michael Bird: the earliest churches of Judea and Syria called Jesus Lord in Aramaic and made Him the object of prayer in worship.
layers.text: Why Aramaic in a letter to Greeks? No one knows for sure, but many scholars hear a prayer of the first church in Judea, which called Jesus maran, our Lord, a title that could also be used of God. In their worship, Jesus was the one they prayed to.

layers.evidence: Didache 10.6, in J. B. Lightfoot's translation; New Advent's reads: Let grace come, and let this world pass away, and later Maran atha. Michael Bird notes the same language in Revelation and the Didache and reads the prayer as looking to Jesus' return. Walter Riggans (Themelios) ties it to 1 Corinthians 11:26.
layers.text: The Didache, an early Christian writing, ends its prayer after the Lord's Supper the same way, asking for grace to come and this world to pass away, then maran atha. Paul ties the Supper to the same hope: "you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes."

layers.evidence: David Capes and Michael Bird compare Revelation 22:20. Barnes: John answers in the precise language the Savior had used.
layers.text: If Paul's words are the prayer marana tha, the Bible's last book closes with the same prayer in Greek. Jesus says, "Yes, I am coming soon," and John answers in His own words, "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!" Both ask the Lord to come.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Galatians 4:6: Christ's own cry becomes the believers' cry. TBESG: abba is Aramaic for father.
layers.text: Paul's Greek letters keep another Aramaic prayer word, Abba. Jesus prayed "Abba, Father" in Gethsemane, and the Spirit of the Son in our hearts cries "Abba, Father!" The Son's own cry becomes the cry of God's children.

passages.saying: anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's defense of his sincerity in 1:12-14.
layers.text: Paul answers those who doubted his honesty. He writes nothing beyond what the Corinthians read and already know to be true of him from his life among them, and he hopes they will understand him fully to the end.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Greek words for read and acknowledge are kindred in sound and root; on 3:2 it points back to this verse for the same kind of pairing.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, read is anaginoskete and understand is epiginoskete. Both verbs grow from the same root for knowing (ginosko), so the two words sound alike. Some see a play here: what the Corinthians read, they can also recognize as true.

passages.saying: You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture of the church as Paul's letter of recommendation (3:1-2).
layers.text: Paul needs no letter of recommendation. The Corinthian believers themselves are his letter, written on his heart. Their changed lives are a testimony that everyone can see and read.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls known and read words akin in root, sound, and sense, pointing back to 1:13; the Companion Bible marks a paronomasia (a play on similar-sounding words) here.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, known is ginoskomene and read is anaginoskomene. The second word is the first with a prefix added, so the phrase rings like an echo: known and read by everyone. Paul makes a similar play in 1:13, pairing read with understand.

passages.saying: not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's picture of Christ as the author, Paul as the pen, and the Spirit as the ink.
layers.text: The Corinthians are a letter from Christ himself, delivered through Paul's ministry. This letter was written not with ink but by the Spirit of the living God, and not on stone but on human hearts.

layers.evidence: Barnes says it is generally admitted that Paul refers to the law engraved on tablets of stone; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Exodus 31:18; Clarke, Gill and Wesley also point to the Ten Commandments written on stone at Sinai.
layers.text: The tablets of stone recall the two stone tablets of the law that God gave Moses on Mount Sinai, inscribed by the finger of God. Paul sets that writing on stone beside the Spirit's writing on living hearts.

layers.evidence: Gill says Paul is alluding to Ezekiel 36:26; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley explain the phrase as God taking away the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh; the Concise Commentary, abridging Daniel Mayo's continuation of Matthew Henry, also cites Ezekiel 36:26.
layers.text: Stone and flesh also echo God's promise in Ezekiel: "I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh." Paul's word for human hearts means hearts made of flesh, the soft new hearts the Spirit writes on.

layers.evidence: Gill on Jeremiah 31:33 says the law is written not on tables of stone but on the fleshly tables of the heart, citing 2 Corinthians 3:3; Keil and Delitzsch on Jeremiah 31:31-34 set writing on the heart against the stone tablets and cite the same verse.
layers.text: Writing on hearts also recalls the new covenant promise in Jeremiah, where God says He will put His law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. Paul sees that promise at work as the Spirit writes in believers.

passages.saying: ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's contrast between the law written on stone and the Spirit's work in the heart.
layers.text: God has made Paul fit to serve a new covenant. It is not a covenant of the written letter, which exposes sin and brings death, but of the Spirit, who gives life.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says plainly that this is the covenant of Jeremiah 31:31 and compares Hebrews 8:6-13.
layers.text: The words new covenant may point back to God's promise in Jeremiah that days are coming when He will make a new covenant with Israel and Judah. Read this way, Paul presents himself as a servant of that promised covenant.

passages.saying: whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's account of the veil over the heart in 3:13-18.
layers.text: The veil that keeps hearts from seeing the meaning of the old covenant does not have to stay. Whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away and the truth is seen clearly.

layers.evidence: Clarke sees an evident allusion to Moses in Exodus 34:34; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Exodus 34:34 is the allusion; Gill on Exodus 34:34 applies Moses' removing the veil to those who turn to the Lord, citing 2 Corinthians 3:16.
layers.text: Paul words this after Moses, who removed his veil whenever he went in before the LORD to speak with Him. In the same way, anyone who turns to the Lord has the veil lifted and comes before Him with an uncovered face.

layers.evidence: Barnes says there may be an allusion to Isaiah 25:7; Gill on Isaiah 25:7 suggests the veil there may include the veil on Israel that is taken off when it turns to the Lord.
layers.text: Some also hear an echo of Isaiah's promise that on God's mountain He will swallow up the shroud that enfolds all peoples, the sheet that covers all nations. In both passages the covering that keeps people from seeing is taken away.

passages.saying: we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Paul compares two ministries. At Sinai the Israelites "could not gaze at the face of Moses," and he veiled it. In Christ the veil is gone: believers "with unveiled faces" reflect the Lord's glory and are being changed into His image.

layers.evidence: Barnes: Moses has not himself declared the design of the veil; Ellicott, Bengel and the Pulpit Commentary say Paul gives the account his own turn. The Hebrew for this veil, masveh, occurs only in Exodus 34:33-35 (TAHOT).
layers.text: Paul is retelling Exodus 34. Moses came down Sinai "unaware that his face had become radiant," and after speaking to the people "he put a veil over his face." Exodus never says the glow faded; that detail is Paul's own reading.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: qaran comes from qeren in the sense of a ray of light; Aquila's Greek and the Vulgate give horns. Gill: the Septuagint says his face was glorified. On Exodus 34:29, Samuel Clark (Barnes' Notes) and George Rawlinson (Ellicott): the Latin rendering of the word is why Moses came to be shown with horns.
layers.text: The word for "radiant," qaran, comes from qeren, a horn or a ray (Habakkuk 3:4). The Greek Old Testament says his face was glorified, and Paul calls it glory. The Latin Bible said horned, and Michelangelo's Moses has horns, though the history is complex.

layers.evidence: Bengel calls the verse a paraphrase on Exodus 34:34, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown hears the same allusion. The Septuagint of Exodus 34:34 and Paul's verse share henika (whenever), periaireo (remove) and kalymma (veil).
layers.text: Exodus says that whenever Moses went in before the LORD, "he would remove the veil." Paul reworks it, keeping its Greek words for whenever, remove and veil: "whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away." What Moses alone did, anyone may now do.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and MacLaren: the same verb as the Transfiguration. It occurs only in Matthew 17:2, Mark 9:2, Romans 12:2 and here (TAGNT; TBESG).
layers.text: The word for "transformed" is metamorphoo, used when Jesus "was transfigured" and "His face shone like the sun." Its only other use is "be transformed by the renewing of your mind." Moses' face shone, Jesus' face shone, and now believers are being changed.

layers.evidence: TBESG: to reflect as a mirror; TAGNT: beholding as in a mirror. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary read beholding; Ellicott and MacLaren weigh both senses of the verb.
layers.text: The verb for "reflect," katoptrizomai, comes from the word for a mirror. It can mean to reflect like a mirror or to look as into a mirror, and commentators split between the two. Moses did both: he met the LORD face to face, and his face shone.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Gill hear the creation of light (Genesis 1:3) in these words; Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown link the face of Jesus to the face of Moses.
layers.text: Paul goes back to creation: the God who said "Let light shine out of darkness" now gives "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." The face that shone at Sinai pointed to this face: Christ, "the image of God."

passages.saying: made His light shine in our hearts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul linking God's creating word with His work of shining into the heart.
layers.text: The God who first commanded light to shine in the dark has shone into believers' hearts. He gives them the light of knowing His glory, which is seen in the face of Jesus Christ.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the apostle refers to Genesis 1:3; Gill, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible point to the same creation word, and the Concise Commentary, abridging Daniel Mayo's continuation of Matthew Henry, compares the light of the first creation with the new creation.
layers.text: "Let light shine out of darkness" recalls the first day of creation, when God said, "Let there be light." The God who spoke light into a dark world now shines into dark hearts, so coming to know Christ is like a new creation.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the allusion is still to the brightness on Moses' face; Barnes sees an undoubted allusion to the glory reflected on Moses' face (3:13); Wesley says Christ's face reflects God's glory in another manner than the face of Moses did.
layers.text: The face of Jesus Christ also looks back to Moses, whose face shone after he spoke with the LORD. God's glory is now seen fully in the face of Christ, in a different way than it once shone from Moses.

passages.saying: perplexed, but not in despair
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrasts Paul draws in 4:7-9 between weak clay jars and God's surpassing power.
layers.text: Paul describes the hardships of his ministry. He is pressed on every side but not crushed, often at a loss about what to do, yet never in despair, because God's power carries him through.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under Paregmenon, words from the same root set side by side, and renders it at a loss but not utterly at a loss; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown renders the second word not utterly perplexed.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, perplexed is aporoumenoi and despair is exaporoumenoi, the same verb with a prefix meaning utterly. The sense is that Paul is at a loss, but never utterly at a loss.

passages.saying: an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's contrast between brief, light affliction now and eternal, weighty glory to come.
layers.text: Paul says the troubles believers suffer now are light and last only a moment. They are working out for them a glory that is eternal and greater than anything they could measure.

layers.evidence: Clarke quotes with approval Blackwall's note that Hebrew kabad means both to be heavy and to be glorious, and that Paul unites the two senses in his Greek. Gill says Paul has respect to the Hebrew word meaning both weight and glory. Barnes says kabod denotes weight as well as glory and Paul perhaps had it in mind.
layers.text: Paul's Greek speaks of a weight (baros) of glory. In Hebrew the word for glory, kabod, comes from a root meaning heavy, so Paul carries over the Hebrew idea that glory is weighty. Present trouble is light, but the glory to come is heavy and eternal.

passages.saying: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the phrase new creation (kainē ktisis) for the change in everyone joined to Christ.
layers.text: Anyone united to Christ is not merely improved but made new by God. The old life has gone, and a new one has begun.

layers.evidence: JFB says the word behold implies an allusion to Isaiah 43:19 and 65:17. Gill links the new creation to Isaiah's new heavens and new earth, and on Isaiah 43:19 describes the new thing in Paul's own words: old things passed away and all things became new.
layers.text: Paul's words "Behold, the new has come!" echo Isaiah, where God says, "Behold, I am about to do something new," and promises new heavens and a new earth. The new creation God foretold has already begun in everyone who is in Christ.

passages.saying: God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the exchange between Christ, who knew no sin, and believers, made righteous in Him.
layers.text: Christ never sinned, yet God laid our sin on Him in our place. In exchange, those joined to Christ receive the righteousness of God.

layers.evidence: Clarke says hamartia occurs twice here, first meaning sin and then a sin offering, like Hebrew chattath, which means both. Gill says the Hebrew word signifies both sin and a sin offering. Bullinger's Figures of Speech reads the second as a sin offering. JFB instead takes it as Christ the Sin-bearer.
layers.text: Paul uses the same Greek word for sin twice. Christ knew no sin, yet God made Him sin for us. The Hebrew word for sin, chattath, also means the sin offering, so many read the second use as meaning that Christ was made the offering for our sin.

passages.saying: What harmony is there between Christ and Belial?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's paired questions setting Christ against Belial and believer against unbeliever.
layers.text: Christ and Belial have nothing in common, and neither do a believer and an unbeliever. Paul asks these questions to warn the church against close partnership with unbelief.

layers.evidence: Barnes, JFB and the Companion Bible all say Belial is a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness. Barnes says Paul applies it here to Satan, and Gill notes that most interpreters understand the devil by it. JFB sets Belial against Christ as Satan is set against God.
layers.text: Belial is a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness, used in the Old Testament for wicked, good-for-nothing people. Paul uses it here as a name for Satan, so the question sets the worthless one against Christ.

passages.saying: For God loves a cheerful giver.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast of willing giving with giving out of regret or compulsion; Barnes explains it.
layers.text: Each believer should give what he has freely decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under pressure. God delights in the person who gives gladly.

layers.evidence: Gill says Paul refers to the line the Septuagint has at Proverbs 22:8, God blesses a cheerful man, and a giver. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes give the same Septuagint line, placing it at 22:9.
layers.text: "God loves a cheerful giver" echoes the old Greek translation of Proverbs 22:8, which adds a line saying that God blesses a cheerful man who gives. The Hebrew text does not have that line. Paul backs his rule for giving with words drawn from that proverb, saying loves where it says blesses.

passages.saying: God is able to make all grace abound to you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise of God's power to supply and its aim of good works; Barnes explains it.
layers.text: Those who give generously need not fear running short. God can pour out every kind of grace, so that they always have what they need and plenty left over for every good work.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible notes count the four alls with every as Polyptoton and call panti pantote pasan a Paronomasia; his Figures of Speech lists this verse under both figures.
layers.text: Paul's Greek piles up words for all: all grace, in all things (panti), at all times (pantote), all you need (pasan), every (pan) good work. Some hear the run of matching sounds driving home that God's supply leaves nothing out.

passages.saying: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's farming picture applied to giving; Barnes explains it.
layers.text: The God who gives the farmer seed to plant and bread to eat will also supply and multiply what the Corinthians sow by giving, and He will make their generous righteousness yield a growing harvest.

layers.evidence: Gill says the words refer to Isaiah 55:10 and describe God by a roundabout title; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown translates the phrase as in Isaiah 55:10.
layers.text: Paul describes God in words drawn from Isaiah 55:10, where rain and snow water the earth, "providing seed to sow and food to eat." The God who gives seed and bread in nature will also supply and multiply the store of those who give.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that the Septuagint renders the rain of righteousness in Hosea 10:12 as fruits of righteousness, the same phrase as here, and judges that Paul seems to take it from there.
layers.text: Paul's phrase "the harvest of your righteousness" may echo Hosea 10:12, which begins "Sow for yourselves righteousness" and ends with the Lord sending righteousness like rain. The old Greek translation of Hosea renders that ending as fruits of righteousness, the same Greek words Paul uses here.

passages.saying: your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparison of the church with Eve; Barnes explains it.
layers.text: Paul fears that, just as the serpent's cunning deceived Eve, false teachers may lure the church away from its sincere and undivided devotion to Christ.

layers.evidence: Barnes points to Genesis 3:1-11 for the serpent beguiling Eve and to Genesis 3:1 for its subtlety; Gill describes the serpent as the most subtle creature of the field.
layers.text: Paul points back to Genesis 3, where the serpent was "more crafty than any beast of the field" and deceived Eve by questioning what God had said. He fears the false teachers will use the same kind of cunning to turn the church from Christ.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse under Homoeoptoton (like inflections), splitting haplotetos and hagnotetos to show their shared ending, and says the critical Greek texts read and purity. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that the oldest manuscripts add purity after simplicity.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, the words translated simple and pure are two nouns with the same rhyming ending: haplotetos (simplicity) and hagnotetos (purity). Both describe the devotion to Christ that Paul fears they may be led astray from.

passages.saying: God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, read with Paul's defense of his calling in Galatians 1.
layers.text: Paul says his calling was God's work from the start. Before he was born God had set him apart, and in His grace God called him, so Paul's apostleship came from God and not from men.

layers.evidence: Gill says reference seems to be had to Jeremiah 1:5. Clarke on Jeremiah 1:5 says Paul speaks of his own call in similar terms. Barnes on Isaiah 49:1 sets the Servant's call from the womb beside Galatians 1:15. Wesley and the Companion Bible make the same comparison.
layers.text: Paul tells of his call in words that echo earlier callings. God set Jeremiah apart before birth as a prophet to the nations, and the Servant in Isaiah says the LORD called Him from the womb. Paul too was set apart before birth and sent to the nations.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggests, with a perhaps, a contrast with the derivation of Pharisee from the Hebrew pharash, separated.
layers.text: Paul's Greek word for set apart (aphorizo) may glance at his past. The name Pharisee is traced to a Hebrew word meaning separated. Paul had once been a Pharisee, a separated one, but God had separated him for something far better.

passages.saying: God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and Paul's argument about heirs in Galatians 4:1-7.
layers.text: When the time God had appointed fully came, He sent His own Son into the world as a true man, born of a woman and born under the law of Moses.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the Son was made of a woman according to the promise of Genesis 3:15. Gill says He was the woman's seed from the beginning, and on Genesis 3:15 says Christ is fitly called her seed because He was made of a woman.
layers.text: Paul's phrase born of a woman can recall the first promise of a Savior. After the fall God said that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head. Read this way, Jesus, sent by God and born of a woman, is that promised offspring.

passages.saying: Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in Paul's illustration of the two covenants in Galatians 4:21-31.
layers.text: Paul is reading Hagar's story as a picture. Hagar the slave woman stands for the covenant given at Mount Sinai, and she matches the Jerusalem of Paul's day, which was in slavery to the law along with her children.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, following Chrysostom, reads the verse as saying the word Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in the Arabian tongue, and cites a traveller who says Arabs still call Sinai Hadschar, meaning a rock or stone. Gill says the Arabic word means stone or rock but prefers to take Hagar as the woman herself. Barnes doubts the Arabic link, so this is a possible play, not a certainty.
layers.text: An old explanation notes that in Arabic a word that sounds like Hagar means a rock or stone, and some reported that Arabs called rocky Sinai by that name. If so, the slave woman's very name pointed to the mountain where the law was given.

passages.saying: the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse read with Galatians 4:22-28, where the two sons stand for the two covenants.
layers.text: Ishmael, born in the ordinary way, mistreated Isaac, who was born by God's promise and power. Paul says the same thing is happening now, as those who trust in the law persecute those born of the Spirit.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke all tie the persecution to Ishmael's mocking in Genesis 21:9. Gill adds that the Hebrew word there alludes to Isaac's name, laughter.
layers.text: Paul points back to Genesis, where Sarah saw Ishmael mocking Isaac. The Hebrew word for mocking comes from the same root as Isaac's name, which speaks of laughter. Paul treats that mockery as persecution and says the children of promise still meet it.

passages.saying: Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse read with Galatians 5:2-7 and 1:6, where God is the One who called them.
layers.text: The teaching that had won the Galatians over, that they must keep the law of Moses to be saved, did not come from God, who had called them by His grace.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it a play on words: persuasion is akin to obey in verse 7. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists verses 7-10 as three forms from one root, peitho.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, obeying the truth in verse 7 is literally being persuaded by it (peithesthai), and persuasion here is peismone, from the same root. Verse 10 uses it again for his confidence (pepoitha). They had traded the truth for a persuasion God never gave.

passages.saying: I wish they would proceed to emasculate themselves
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verb, which means to cut off; several early church fathers and the BSB read it as self-mutilation, others as excommunication.
layers.text: Paul is so troubled by the men unsettling the Galatians that he wishes they would be cut off. This translation takes it as a wish that they would go beyond circumcision and emasculate themselves; many older commentators took it as a wish that they be removed from the church.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the wish to the teachers' demand for circumcision: as they would have your foreskin cut off, so may they be cut off. It also notes the early fathers' reading, that if circumcision was not enough for them they should have excision too.
layers.text: Many see Paul turning the false teachers' own knife back on them. They wanted the Galatians' foreskins cut off, so Paul wishes the cutting would go further and fall on them. His verb (apokopto) means to cut off, whether by mutilation, as this translation has it, or by removal from the church.

passages.saying: who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of Paul's opening praise to God.
layers.text: Paul opens his letter with praise. God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is worthy of praise, because in Christ He has already given believers every spiritual blessing, the riches of heaven itself.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse as one word repeated in different forms and says 'blessed' is used in two senses, since we do not bless God as He blesses us. Wesley's Notes likewise set God's blessing us beside our blessing God as two different acts.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek one word family runs through the verse: God is eulogetos (blessed), He has blessed (eulogesas) us, and He gives every blessing (eulogia). The word works both ways. We bless God by praising Him, and He blesses us by giving us every spiritual blessing in Christ.

passages.saying: God put everything under His feet
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse about the risen Christ's rule.
layers.text: God the Father has placed all things under the authority of the risen Christ, and He has given Christ to the church as its head, ruling over everything for her good.

layers.evidence: Gill says these words are taken out of Psalm 8:6, and on the psalm he applies its dominion to Christ as head over all things to the church. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Psalm 8:6 for the phrase put in subjection under.
layers.text: Paul borrows the words of Psalm 8, which praises God for placing everything under man's feet. Paul applies them to the risen Christ, whom God made head over everything for the church.

passages.saying: He came and preached peace to you who were far away
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast of those far off and those near.
layers.text: Christ brought the good news of peace with God both to Gentiles, who had been far from God, and to Jews, who had been near. Both now hear the same message of peace through Him.

layers.evidence: Gill says the apostle seems to have respect to Isaiah 57:19, and Barnes, on Isaiah, says Paul evidently alludes to that passage. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties the repeated word peace to Isaiah 57:19. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch also link the two verses.
layers.text: Paul echoes Isaiah, where the LORD says, "Peace, peace to those far and near." Paul shows the fullest meaning of that promise in Christ. Gentiles who were far off and Jews who were near hear the same message, and Paul even repeats the word peace as Isaiah does.

passages.saying: with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of the church as a building.
layers.text: Believers are built like a temple on the teaching of the apostles and prophets, and Christ Jesus Himself is the cornerstone who holds the whole building together.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Isaiah 28:16 was present to Paul's mind here. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes that the Greek word for cornerstone occurs only here and in 1 Peter 2:6 and points to the Septuagint of Isaiah 28:16. Clarke quotes Isaiah 28:16 on this verse.
layers.text: Calling Christ the cornerstone recalls God's promise in Isaiah to lay in Zion "a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation." Paul's Greek word for cornerstone is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in that verse. Jesus is the stone God promised.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown speaks of the apostle's plain reference here to Psalm 118:22. On the psalm, Barnes and Wesley both point to Ephesians 2:20 as Christ taking the place of the rejected stone.
layers.text: Christ as the cornerstone also echoes the psalm: "The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone." Jesus applied that psalm to Himself. The One His own people's leaders rejected is the stone on which God builds His church of Jews and Gentiles.

passages.saying: I bow my knees before the Father
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of Paul kneeling in prayer.
layers.text: Paul kneels in humble prayer before God the Father for the believers, asking that the great work God has begun among them would go on and that they would not lose heart.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the word for family (patria) is akin in sound and etymology to the word for Father (pater). Bullinger's Companion Bible explains patria as a group of families claiming descent from one pater, or father.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the word for family, patria, is built on the word for father, pater. Paul kneels before the Father (pater), from whom every family (patria) in heaven and on earth gets its name. The very word for family points back to Him.

passages.saying: do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain warning and the sins named around it.
layers.text: Believers must not bring sorrow to the Holy Spirit by sinful words and ways. He lives in them and has marked them as God's own until the day their redemption is complete.

layers.evidence: Clarke says it is very likely the apostle had Isaiah 63:10 in view, and the Reformation Study Bible calls Paul's words a quotation of Isaiah 63:10, showing the idea is not new to the New Testament. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Barnes only compare the two verses, so they are not cited.
layers.text: Paul's warning echoes Isaiah's memory of Israel after the exodus: "But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit." Grieving God's Spirit is not a new idea. His people did it long before, and believers can still do it today.

passages.saying: Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to love as Christ loved.
layers.text: Believers are to live a life of love, following Christ, who loved them and gave Himself up to death for them as an offering that fully pleased God.

layers.evidence: Clarke notes that Paul's Greek words here are the very words the Septuagint uses in Genesis 8:21. Gill says Paul refers to that passage, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls Noah's sacrifice a type of Christ's offering.
layers.text: Paul's words for a fragrant offering are the very words the Greek Old Testament uses when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma of Noah's sacrifice after the flood. That sacrifice was followed by God's promise of mercy, and it pointed ahead to Christ's offering of Himself.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Paul evidently had Leviticus 1:9 in view, using the same terms as the Septuagint. Gill calls the burnt offering of that verse typical of Christ's sacrifice, citing this verse.
layers.text: The same phrase runs through the law of the burnt offering, which was burned whole on the altar as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD." Those offerings were pictures of Christ, who gave Himself wholly to God for His people.

passages.saying: crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on verse 3, which calls for what is proper among the saints.
layers.text: Paul tells believers to put away filthy talk, foolish chatter and crude joking. Such speech does not fit God's holy people. Their words should turn instead to giving thanks to God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls eucharistia set against eutrapelia a happy play on sounds in Greek. Clarke and Barnes trace eutrapelia to eu, well or easily, and trepo, to turn; Clarke says it means words easily turned to other meanings.
layers.text: Many hear a play on sound in Paul's Greek. Crude joking is eutrapelia, witty talk that turns easily to double meanings, and thanksgiving is eucharistia. The two words begin alike, but only the second fits God's people: a quick tongue should turn to thanks.

passages.saying: with the belt of truth buckled around your waist
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the call in verses 11 and 13 to put on the full armor of God and stand.
layers.text: Paul pictures the believer as a soldier holding his ground against evil. Truth is the belt that holds the rest of the armor in place, and righteousness is the breastplate that guards the heart.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the belt to Isaiah 11:5 and the breastplate to Isaiah 59:17, both the Messiah's. The Companion Bible compares Messiah's panoply in both verses, Gill hears Isaiah 59:17 in the breastplate, and Wesley says our Lord is described in both. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes the Septuagint has truth in Isaiah 11:5.
layers.text: Paul's armor echoes the armor worn in Isaiah. There the Messiah wears faithfulness as the sash around His waist (truth, in the Greek Old Testament), and the LORD "put on righteousness like a breastplate." Believers now stand in that same armor.

passages.saying: take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, which itself names the sword as the word of God.
layers.text: Paul finishes the armor of God. Salvation, received as God's gift, guards the head like a helmet, and the word of God, given by the Spirit, is the believer's sword.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to Isaiah 59:17, and the Companion Bible compares Isaiah 59:17. Both also point to 1 Thessalonians 5:8, where the helmet is the hope of salvation.
layers.text: The helmet of salvation likely recalls Isaiah, where God arms Himself to rescue His people and puts "the helmet of salvation on His head." Paul tells believers to receive the helmet of salvation as God's gift.

passages.saying: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: To teach humility, Paul tells Christ's story. Existing "in the form of God," He "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant," and became obedient to death on a cross. So God gave Him "the name above all names," before which every knee will bow.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Pulpit Commentary hear Isaiah 45:23, which the Pulpit Commentary notes are the words of Jehovah.
layers.text: Paul's words come from Isaiah 45, where the LORD swears by Himself: "Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance." He has just said, "I am God, and there is no other." Paul applies the LORD's own oath to Jesus.

layers.evidence: TBESG: kampto (bow) and exomologeo (confess) in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10-11, from the Septuagint of Isaiah 45:23, whose printed editions vary between confess and swear. Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Pulpit Commentary note Romans 14:11.
layers.text: In Romans Paul quotes the same verse about God's judgment: "every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God." In Philippians the same bowing and confessing, in the same Greek verbs, happen at the name of Jesus, "to the glory of God the Father."

layers.evidence: TBESG: kyrios chiefly renders YHWH in the Septuagint. Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary (Lord, or Jehovah) read God's own name; MacLaren and Benson take it as the name Jesus, and Gill and Bengel as His dignity.
layers.text: Which is "the name above all names"? Many older commentators answer: Lord, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God's own name, YHWH. Others disagree. Isaiah's speaker is "I, the LORD," and now every tongue confesses "that Jesus Christ is Lord."

layers.evidence: Ellicott: the Lord in Joel means Jehovah, and here it is applied to our Lord; Barnes, Richard Mayo (Poole's Annotations) and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also apply it to Christ.
layers.text: Paul does the same with Joel. Joel's promise, "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved," uses God's own name, YHWH. Romans quotes it soon after "if you confess with your mouth" that "Jesus is Lord," so the Lord to call on is Jesus.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary: Isaiah prophesied of Christ as the Servant of Jehovah (Isaiah 49 and 52). Gill: He was often prophesied of as a servant (Isaiah 42:1).
layers.text: The story follows Isaiah's suffering Servant. Christ takes "the form of a servant," is "obedient to death," and God exalts Him to the highest place. The Servant "will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted," because "He has poured out His life unto death."

layers.evidence: The continuation of Poole's Annotations and Gill contrast the sin of Adam and Eve; Bengel cites Genesis 3:5. Harpagmos (grasped) comes from harpazo, to seize, and its exact sense is disputed (TBESG).
layers.text: Some readers also hear Adam. The serpent promised, "you will be like God," and our first parents reached for it. Christ, though "in the form of God," "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped." It is an echo, not a quotation.

passages.saying: children of God without fault in a crooked and perverse generation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the call in verse 14 to do everything without complaining or arguing.
layers.text: Paul wants the believers to live blameless, pure lives as God's children. They live among twisted and crooked people, and against that darkness they shine like lights.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the whole verse tacitly refers by contrast to Deuteronomy 32:5, and Barnes says Moses used this language there. The Septuagint of Deuteronomy 32:5 has blemished children and the same Greek words for a crooked and perverse generation.
layers.text: Paul turns Moses' words around. Moses sang that Israel's spot showed they were not acting as God's children, but as "a perverse and crooked generation." Paul wants believers to be "children of God without fault" while living in just such a generation.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Paul's Greek means luminaries like the sun and moon, and that the Septuagint uses the very same word in Genesis 1:14 and 1:16. Clarke also says Paul refers to the sun and moon.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, the word for lights is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for the sun and moon at creation, when "God made two great lights." As those lights shine on the earth, God's children shine in a dark world.

passages.saying: even if I am being poured out like a drink offering
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, read with Paul's words on living and dying in chapter 1.
layers.text: Paul knows he may be put to death for Christ. He pictures the Philippians' faith as an offering to God and his own life poured out with it. Even so, he is glad and rejoices with them.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley explain the verb as being poured out like the wine of a drink offering at a sacrifice, and Barnes compares Numbers 15:5 and 28:7. Paul uses the same verb of his coming death in 2 Timothy 4:6.
layers.text: Paul's picture likely comes from the law's sacrifices, where wine was poured out to the LORD as a drink offering with each lamb. The Philippians' faith is the sacrifice, and Paul's blood, if he is killed, is the drink offering poured out with it.

passages.saying: those mutilators of the flesh
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: "Dogs" was a sharp insult. Ellicott, Benson, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary say Paul turns back on these teachers a word Jews used for Gentiles, though the text does not say so. His target is these teachers and their teaching, not the Jewish people; he was a Jew himself.
layers.text: Paul warns the church, in harsh words, against teachers who most likely insisted that non-Jewish believers be circumcised to belong to God's people. Paul was himself a Jew, "circumcised on the eighth day"; he objects to making it a requirement.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: katatomen (G2699) in 3:2, peritome (G4061) in 3:3. Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) says katatome is used here in sarcasm, by paronomasia (wordplay), in contrast to true peritome. Katatome occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.
layers.text: Paul's Greek has a sharp pun. Circumcision is peritome, "a cutting around." He calls these teachers the katatome, "a cutting up," in English "mutilators of the flesh." Then: "it is we who are the circumcision," meaning all who trust Christ, Jew or Gentile.
The idea of an inner circumcision is older than Paul. Moses promised, "The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts," and Paul writes that "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit."

passages.saying: my true yokefellow, to help these women who have labored with me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and verse 2, where Paul urges Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord.
layers.text: Paul asks a trusted coworker at Philippi to help the women who struggled at his side for the gospel, most likely Euodia and Syntyche of verse 2. With Clement and his other fellow workers, their names are written in the Book of Life.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares Exodus 32:32, Psalm 69:28 and Daniel 12:1, beside the citizen rolls of free cities. Clarke sends readers to his note on Exodus 32:32-33 on the writing in and blotting out of the book of life. Wesley instead hears the rolls of the Olympic games.
layers.text: The Book of Life is an Old Testament picture. Moses offered to be blotted out of God's book for Israel's sake, and a psalm prays that the wicked "be blotted out of the Book of Life." Paul's faithful coworkers are written there.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown offers Synzygus as a proper name, so that he is truly what his name means. Gill reports the same view but thinks a fellow laborer such as Epaphroditus is meant. Barnes rejects the name reading.
layers.text: Some think yokefellow (syzygos) was this man's real name, Syzygus. Then Paul would be calling him a man who truly lives up to his name, pulling in the same yoke with Paul. Others read it simply as a description, and no one knows for sure who he was.

passages.saying: The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and the next verse, which says all things were created through the Son.
layers.text: Paul says the Son makes the unseen God known, because He is the exact image of the Father. As firstborn He holds first place over everything created, for all things were created through Him.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown sets this title beside Genesis 1:27, where Adam was made in God's image, and calls Christ the second Adam, who perfectly shows the invisible God whose glories Adam showed only in part.
layers.text: Calling the Son the image of God may recall Genesis 1:27, where God created man in His own image. On this reading, Adam showed that image only in part, but Christ, the second Adam, shows the invisible God perfectly.

layers.evidence: Gill, in one of his readings, takes firstborn as Christ the King, Lord and Governor of all creatures, higher than the kings of the earth, and points to Psalm 89:27; on that psalm he applies the firstborn promise to Christ with Colossians 1:15. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says priority and highest dignity are implied, citing Psalm 89:27.
layers.text: Firstborn here can be read as a title of rank, as in Psalm 89:27, where God promises to make David His firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth. Read this way, Christ holds the highest place over all creation, not as a created being but as its Lord and heir.

passages.saying: being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording about a new self that is still being renewed.
layers.text: Believers have put on a new self, and God keeps renewing it, so that they grow in true knowledge of Him and come more and more to bear the likeness of the One who created it.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the apostle is interpreting the words of Moses about man made in God's image (Genesis 1:26); Jamieson-Fausset-Brown quotes Genesis 1:26 and calls the new creation analogous to the first; Barnes says the renewed soul is made as man was when first created.
layers.text: The wording recalls Genesis 1:26, where God said, "Let Us make man in Our image." In the new creation God remakes His people in that image, restoring the true knowledge of Himself that the first man was given.

passages.saying: you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own reason for not writing: God has already taught them.
layers.text: Paul says he does not need to write to them about loving fellow believers, because God Himself has taught them to love one another.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Isaiah 54:13, say Zion's children will carry within them the teaching of heaven, as those taught of God, and point to John 6:45 and to Paul's word theodidaktoi in 1 Thessalonians 4:9.
layers.text: Paul's word for taught by God (theodidaktoi) may recall Isaiah 54:13, which promises that all of Zion's children will be taught by the LORD. Taught within by God Himself, the Thessalonians need no letter to tell them to love one another.

passages.saying: the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a soldier's armor.
layers.text: Since believers belong to the day, Paul calls them to stay alert and self-controlled, guarding heart and head with faith, love, and the hope of salvation, as a soldier wears a breastplate and helmet.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Isaiah 59:17 says believers' armor is like the Messiah's, except that for salvation, which is God's alone, they wear the hope of salvation (1 Thessalonians 5:8); on this verse it adds that our Head first wore the breastplate and helmet so we might receive both.
layers.text: Some hear in this armor an echo of Isaiah 59:17, where the LORD put on righteousness like a breastplate and the helmet of salvation. On this reading believers wear armor like His, but because salvation belongs to God alone, their helmet is the hope of salvation.

passages.saying: He will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own description of the man of lawlessness named in verse 3.
layers.text: Paul says the man of lawlessness will set himself against and above everything called god or worshiped, and will take his seat in God's temple, declaring that he himself is God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Daniel 11:36-37 is here referred to, its words about Antiochus Epiphanes fitting the man of sin even better; Gill on Daniel 11:36 says the apostle has manifestly a reference to that passage; Keil and Delitzsch say Daniel's words are expressly referred to Antichrist in this verse.
layers.text: This picture draws on Daniel 11:36, where a coming king will exalt and magnify himself above every god and speak monstrous things against the God of gods. Paul applies those words to the final man of lawlessness.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Isaiah 14:14 notes a remarkable resemblance to 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and says Paul probably had Isaiah's passage in his eye; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the verse tallies with 2 Thessalonians 2:4, sitting in God's temple answering to being like the Most High.
layers.text: The claim also echoes the king of Babylon's boast in Isaiah 14:14: "I will make myself like the Most High." In the same way, the man of lawlessness will take his seat in God's temple and declare himself to be God.

layers.evidence: Gill on Ezekiel 28:2 calls the prince of Tyre an emblem of antichrist and sets his sitting in the seat of God beside antichrist sitting in the temple of God; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the language has a fuller accomplishment in Antichrist, citing 2 Thessalonians 2:4.
layers.text: The same pride is heard from the ruler of Tyre in Ezekiel 28:2, who said, "I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods," though he was only a man. His boast is read as a picture of this final enemy, who will sit in God's temple claiming to be God.

passages.saying: whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of His mouth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Wesley explains the breath of His mouth as Christ's immediate power and the overthrow as coming with the first appearance of His glory.
layers.text: When the lawless one is revealed, the Lord Jesus will destroy him with the breath of His mouth and bring him to nothing by the splendor of His coming. Christ needs no long battle; His word and His appearing are enough.

layers.evidence: Gill calls this a manifest reference to Isaiah 11:4, and Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to the same verse. Keil and Delitzsch, on Isaiah 11:4, say the breath of His lips is enough to destroy and cite this verse. The Companion Bible and Wesley also link the two.
layers.text: Paul says the Lord Jesus will slay the lawless one "with the breath of His mouth." This echoes Isaiah's promise that the coming King from Jesse's line would "slay the wicked with the breath of His lips." Paul applies that promise about the Messiah to Christ.

passages.saying: accomplishing nothing but being busybodies
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting of idleness; Barnes explains that those with nothing of their own to do tend to meddle in the affairs of others.
layers.text: Paul has heard that some believers in Thessalonica are living idle, disorderly lives. Instead of doing their own work, they busy themselves with other people's affairs.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls this a fine paronomasia evidently intended by the apostle. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the similar sound marks the contrast. Bullinger's Figures of Speech gives it as a beautiful example of the figure: not busy with their bodies, but busybodies.
layers.text: Paul's Greek plays on the word for work. These people are not ergazomenous (working) but periergazomenous (overdoing, meddling). In English one might say they are not busy but busybodies, doing none of their own work and too much of everyone else's.

passages.saying: These men regard godliness as a means of gain
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains that they regard piety as a means of gain, a way of advancing their worldly interests.
layers.text: Paul describes false teachers whose corrupt minds stir up constant friction. They have lost hold of the truth and treat religion as a way to make money.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech notes that porismos is used in two opposite senses in verses 5 and 6: what false teaching supposes godliness to be, and what it really is. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown likewise says that in another sense piety is a great means of gain.
layers.text: Paul uses one Greek word, porismos (gain), twice in a row. The false teachers regard "godliness as a means of gain," a way to get rich. Paul takes up their word and turns it: "godliness with contentment is great gain," a far better profit than money.

passages.saying: we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words; Barnes notes that we bring no property into the world and plainly take nothing with us when we leave it.
layers.text: Paul gives a reason to be content: we come into the world with nothing and leave it with nothing. Since wealth cannot go with us, it should not rule us.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the apostle probably had Job 1:21 in his eye. Gill, on Job 1:21, calls Paul's words a proper comment on Job's and says Paul perhaps refers to them; on this verse he also points to Job 1:21.
layers.text: Paul's words likely echo Job after he lost everything: "Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return." Paul draws a similar lesson: since we bring nothing into life and take nothing out, we can be content with what God gives.

passages.saying: Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words; Barnes explains that the wish to be rich tempts people to do wrong to reach their goal.
layers.text: Paul warns that the desire to be rich is a trap. Those set on wealth fall into temptation and many harmful cravings that drag them down to ruin.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Greek words for temptation and gain make a play on sounds. Bullinger's Figures of Speech connects porismos, gain, in verses 5 and 6 with peirasmos, temptation, in verse 9.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, temptation (peirasmos) sounds much like gain (porismos), the word used just before in verses 5 and 6. The likeness in sound links the two: those who chase gain fall into temptation.

passages.saying: Fight the good fight of the faith
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words; Barnes explains the fight as the noble conflict in the cause of religion and eternal life as the crown of victory held out to Timothy.
layers.text: Paul urges Timothy to keep up the hard struggle of faith and to take hold of eternal life. God called him to that life, and he made the good confession of his faith before many witnesses.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks a paronomasia in the verb agonizomai and the noun agon here. Clarke renders the phrase literally as agonize the good agony and says the language alludes to the public Greek games.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek the command and its object share one root, agōnizou and agōna, so it reads literally agonize the good agony. These were words for athletes in a contest, picturing Timothy's life of faith as a hard struggle for a prize.

passages.saying: The Lord knows those who are His
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the seal's two inscriptions as Wesley explains them.
layers.text: Even when some fall away from the faith, the foundation God has laid stands firm. It carries a seal with two sayings: the Lord knows His own people, and everyone who calls on His name must turn away from evil.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible each tie the first saying to Numbers 16:5, which in the Septuagint reads God knew those who are His. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible add Numbers 16:26 for the call to depart, and Gill compares the false teachers to Korah and his company. Bullinger's Figures of Speech also points to Numbers 16:5.
layers.text: The seal's first line echoes the rebellion of Korah, and the second likely does too. Moses told the rebels that the LORD would reveal who belongs to Him, then warned the people, "Move away now from the tents of these wicked men." God still knows His own, and His people must step away from evil.

passages.saying: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Barnes's explanation of how the two men resisted Moses.
layers.text: Paul compares the false teachers to two men who opposed Moses. These teachers resist the truth, their minds are corrupt, and they have failed the test of true faith.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and the Companion Bible all identify Jannes and Jambres as Pharaoh's magicians of Exodus 7:11. Gill and Barnes note the names were kept in Jewish tradition, and they appear in the Targum of Jonathan on Exodus 7:11.
layers.text: Paul names two of Pharaoh's magicians, who are not named in Exodus. When Aaron's staff became a serpent, they did the same things by their magic arts. The false teachers likewise oppose the truth by imitating it.

passages.saying: I am already being poured out like a drink offering
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Paul's words about his departure, as the Concise Commentary, abridging Benjamin Andrews Atkinson's continuation of Matthew Henry, explains them.
layers.text: Paul knows that his death is near. He speaks of his life as already being poured out, and of his death as a departure from this world.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all read the Greek verb as being poured out like a libation or drink offering on a sacrifice. Gill adds that this offering was not to atone for sin. Matthew Henry, on Numbers 28, calls that drink offering a figure of the blood of the martyrs.
layers.text: Paul pictures his coming death as a drink offering. In Israel's worship wine was poured out to the LORD with each lamb offered. His blood would be poured out for Christ's sake, not to pay for sin, which only Christ's sacrifice does, but as an offering of his life to God.

passages.saying: He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words about Christ's self-giving, as Wesley explains them.
layers.text: Christ gave His own life in place of ours. He did it to set us free from all sin and to make us clean, a people who belong to Him and are eager to do good.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the word means peculiarly His own, as Israel was of old. The Companion Bible notes that the Greek word periousios occurs in the Septuagint at Exodus 19:5. Keil and Delitzsch, on Exodus 19:5, say the Septuagint renders it laos periousios, and that Titus 2:14 takes that phrase.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, "a people for His own possession" is the phrase the Greek Old Testament uses at Sinai, when God calls Israel His treasured possession. Those Christ has redeemed are His own special treasure, just as God called Israel His own.

passages.saying: Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Readers differ on what Paul is asking: that Philemon free Onesimus (Paul expects him to "do even more than I ask," Philemon 1:21), or that he welcome him as a brother while he stays a slave. The letter does not say. In later centuries both defenders and opponents of slavery appealed to it.
layers.text: Onesimus, a slave, had left his master Philemon, a Christian, and met Paul while Paul was in prison; there he came to faith. Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to receive him "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother."

layers.evidence: TAGNT: Onesimos (G3682) in 1:10; achreston (G0890) and euchreston (G2173) in 1:11. Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG): Onesimus means profitable, from onesis, profit, and was a common name among slaves. Achrestos occurs only here in the New Testament.
layers.text: Onesimus was a common slave name meaning "useful" or "profitable." Paul plays on it: he was achrestos, "useless," but now he is euchrestos, "useful," to you and to me. Since meeting Christ, he has begun to live up to his name.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: onaimen (G3685), the only New Testament use of oninemi, to benefit, the verb behind onesis, the word Abbott-Smith (in TBESG) derives the name from. Ellicott, Bengel, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Pulpit Commentary hear the name in it; in 1:13 Paul says he would have liked to keep Onesimus with him.
layers.text: Near the end Paul does it again: "let me have some benefit from you in the Lord." Benefit is onaimen, from the verb behind the name Onesimus. Many read it as a gentle hint: the benefit Paul hopes for may be Onesimus himself.

passages.saying: let me have some benefit from you in the Lord
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes reads the request as Paul asking Philemon for the favor of receiving Onesimus as Paul has asked.
layers.text: Paul presses his request warmly. He asks Philemon to do him this favor by welcoming Onesimus back, and so to refresh Paul's heart in Christ.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls the verb an evident play on the name of Onesimus and ties it to verse 11. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it refers to the name Onesimus, profitable. The Companion Bible notes that oninemi is the root word from which Onesimus comes.
layers.text: In Paul's Greek, the verb behind "let me have some benefit" (onaimen) comes from the same root as the name Onesimus, which means profitable. Paul is sending back Onesimus, the profitable one, and now gently asks that he in turn may have profit from Philemon.

passages.saying: He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high
