passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains that the Majesty is God the Father and that the Son's sitting down marks His exaltation after His sufferings, death and resurrection.
layers.text: The Son shows God's glory perfectly and holds all things together by His word. After His sacrifice made cleansing for sins, He took His seat beside God the Father in heaven, the place of highest honor.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says His sitting down at the right hand fulfills Psalm 110:1. Barnes on Psalm 110:1 lists Hebrews 1:3 among the passages that use this phrase and applies it to the Messiah exalted at God's right hand.
layers.text: Sitting down at God's right hand echoes Psalm 110:1, where the LORD says to David's Lord, "Sit at My right hand." Hebrews quotes that psalm outright later in this chapter, showing that Jesus now holds the seat of honor God promised to the Messiah.

passages.saying: so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that the devil's defeat was to come through Christ's own dying, which required Him to become a man.
layers.text: Because God's children are flesh and blood, the Son became fully human too. As a man He could die, and by dying He defeated the devil, who held the power of death.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech says the first death stands for the atoning results of Christ's death and the second for natural death, one word in two senses. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Christ overcame death by His death, as David cut off Goliath's head with the giant's own sword.
layers.text: The word death is used twice in two senses. First it means Christ's own death, which atoned for sin. Then it means natural death, which the devil held power over. Jesus defeated the devil by means of death itself, much as David cut off Goliath's head with the giant's own sword.

passages.saying: Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Clarke explains that Moses was faithful as a servant and steward of God's house, not its framer, and that everything under the law bore witness to Christ.
layers.text: Moses served God faithfully among all God's people, but he served as a servant, not as the builder or owner of the house. His work bore witness to things God would make known later, things fulfilled in Christ.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, discussing Numbers 12:7, note that the Greek Old Testament renders faithful there as pistos and servant as therapon, the same words Hebrews 3:5 uses, and they compare Hebrews 3:6 on God's house.
layers.text: This line echoes God's own praise of Moses in Numbers 12:7: "My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house." The Greek Old Testament there uses the same words for servant and faithful found here. Hebrews honors Moses with God's words, then shows Christ is faithful as the Son over that house.

passages.saying: if Joshua had given them rest
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains that if Canaan were God's rest, God would not have spoken of another day of entering it after Israel was already in the land.
layers.text: Joshua led Israel into Canaan, but that was not the final rest God promised. If it had been, God would not have spoken long afterward, through David, of another day of rest still to come.

layers.evidence: Gill says Hosheah, Joshua and Jesus are one and the same name. Clarke notes that the Septuagint everywhere renders Yehoshua as Iesous and that the writer follows it. Barnes says Jesus is the Greek way of writing Joshua.
layers.text: In the Greek of Hebrews, Joshua is written Iesous, which is exactly the name Jesus. The Greek Old Testament spells Joshua's Hebrew name, Yehoshua, the same way, and Hebrews follows it. Some older English Bibles printed Jesus here, though Joshua son of Nun is meant.

layers.evidence: Gill calls Joshua an eminent type of Christ, noting that both names signify a saviour, Joshua a temporal one and Christ a spiritual one. He adds that Joshua gave Israel only a typical rest, not the true spiritual rest.
layers.text: The names Joshua and Jesus are the same, and some see in their shared meaning, saviour, a picture of Jesus in Joshua. Joshua gave Israel rest from their enemies for a time in Canaan, but not the true rest; read this way, Jesus gives the lasting rest that Joshua did not.

passages.saying: He learned obedience from what He suffered.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every way yet without sin. Christians explain how the sinless Son could learn obedience in somewhat different ways; most say He learned it by experience, not by correction.
layers.text: Hebrews says the Son of God did not escape suffering. He prayed "with loud cries and tears," and through what He suffered He learned obedience. This does not mean He had ever disobeyed: the same letter says He "was without sin."

layers.evidence: TAGNT: emathen (G3129) and epathen (G3958). Bengel and the NET Bible notes call it a play on words, and Figures of Speech lists it under paronomasia. Bengel and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite the Greek adage pathemata mathemata, sufferings are the means of learning. Aeschylus has a like phrase, pathei mathos (learning by suffering), in his Agamemnon.
layers.text: The Greek rhymes: emathen, "He learned," and epathen, "He suffered," differ by a single letter. Learning and suffering, mathein and pathein, were a famous pair in Greek wisdom. Hebrews applies the old saying to the Son of God.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary, Bengel, the continuation of Poole's Annotations and Benson take Hebrews 5:7 to refer to Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42); Barnes says Gethsemane or the cross, and Ellicott and Gill think of the cross.
layers.text: Many hear Gethsemane in the "loud cries and tears" of the verse before. There Jesus prayed, "Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will." On this reading, that is the obedience He learned in suffering.

passages.saying: But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the farming picture of Hebrews 6:7-8, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Land that soaks up the rain but grows only thorns and thistles is useless to its owner. It is close to being cursed and ends up burned. The writer warns that those who receive much from God yet bear no good fruit are in grave danger.

layers.evidence: Ellicott says the words are partly a quotation from Genesis 3:18, and the Pulpit Commentary says the thorns and thistles, joined with a curse on the ground, seem suggested by Genesis 3:17-18. Hebrews uses the same Greek pair for thorns and thistles that the Septuagint uses in Genesis 3:18.
layers.text: Thorns, thistles and a curse may recall the ground God cursed after Adam sinned, which would yield thorns and thistles (Genesis 3:18). Read this way, land that drinks in the rain yet bears only thorns is like that cursed ground, and its own curse is near.

passages.saying: We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the anchor picture in the verse, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Christian hope holds the soul steady the way an anchor holds a ship in a storm. This hope is firm and secure because it is fastened in heaven itself, in the very presence of God.

layers.evidence: Gill calls the phrase an allusion to the veil that divided the holy place from the holy of holies. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown pictures heaven as the Holy of Holies and Christ as the High Priest going before us within the veil. Leviticus 16 is the law for entering behind that veil.
layers.text: The phrase "behind the curtain" points to the veil before the Most Holy Place. God told Aaron not to go behind it whenever he pleased (Leviticus 16:2); the high priest entered only once a year. Our hope is anchored there, in heaven, where Jesus has gone in for us as High Priest.

passages.saying: First, his name means “king of righteousness.” Then also, “king of Salem” means “king of peace.”
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: Hebrews argues that Jesus is a priest of a different and permanent kind, not from Levi's family but "in the order of Melchizedek," who "always lives to intercede."

Genesis gives Melchizedek three verses: king of Salem and "priest of God Most High," he brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth from him. The only other Old Testament verse to name him is Psalm 110:4.
Later, in Psalm 110, God swears to David's Lord: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." Hebrews builds its argument on this oath.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from TBESH. The Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 14:18 identifies Salem with Jerusalem. Josephus, Jewish War 6.10.1: the city Melchizedek built, formerly called Salem, was Jerusalem.
layers.text: Hebrews reads the names. Melchizedek joins melek (king) and tsedeq (righteousness), and Salem means peace. The Old Testament names Salem only once more, in Psalm 76:2, in parallel with Zion, so it is usually taken to be Jerusalem.
Jesus Himself raised Psalm 110 in the temple: David calls the Messiah "my Lord." The psalm that seats the Messiah at God's right hand also makes Him a priest forever.
Genesis records no father, mother, birth or death for Melchizedek, and Hebrews makes the silence part of the picture: "like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time."
Many Christian writers link Melchizedek's bread and wine to the bread and cup of the Last Supper. Hebrews does not mention it.

passages.saying: Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the word guarantee, or surety, a person who pledges himself for another, as the commentaries explain.
layers.text: Because God confirmed His priesthood with an oath, Jesus stands as the guarantee of a better covenant. Like someone who pledges himself for another, He makes Himself responsible that the covenant's promises will hold for His people.

layers.evidence: A note in Barnes's commentary reports the view that the writer chose the rare word enguos (surety) to echo engizomen (we draw near) in verse 19, a play on sound, and calls that account probable enough.
layers.text: Verse 19 says a better hope lets us draw near (engizomen) to God. Here Jesus is the guarantee (enguos), a rare word that sounds much like it in the Greek of Hebrews. The echo may be deliberate: the One who brings us near is Himself our pledge.

passages.saying: In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Greek text and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: Hebrews explains why Christ had to die. He is "the mediator of a new covenant," so that the called may receive "the promised eternal inheritance." And an inheritance comes through a death: "a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died."

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (TBESG): diatheke nearly always renders berit in the Septuagint, but in classical Greek means a will. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill and Benson read will in 9:16-17 while keeping covenant in view; Ellicott reads covenant throughout.
layers.text: One Greek word, diatheke, is "covenant" in verse 15 and "a will" in verses 16-17. In the Greek Old Testament it nearly always stands for berit, covenant, but in everyday Greek it meant a will. Many hear a play on both senses; some read "covenant" throughout.

layers.evidence: Easton's Bible Dictionary: the Vulgate renders diatheke by testamentum, whence the names Old and New Testament; so the Pulpit Commentary on 1 Corinthians 11:25. Clarke on Matthew 26:28: the two covenants named the two sets of books. Barnes: the only place Scripture calls the Jewish books the Old Testament; Gill: the books read in the synagogue; the Pulpit Commentary: Moses being read.
layers.text: This double word named the Bible's two halves. Latin rendered diatheke as testamentum, a will, even where it meant covenant, so the covenants became the Old and New Testaments. Paul once says "the old covenant," for the books of Moses read in the synagogue.

layers.evidence: Bequest: Bengel, who calls it a word fit for one dying and cites Hebrews 9:16. Covenant: Ellicott and Barnes. Abbott-Smith (TBESG) glosses Luke's diatithemi as to assign, and says diatheke is a will in classical Greek but in the Septuagint nearly always stands for berit, covenant.
layers.text: At the Last Supper Jesus says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood," and "I bestow on you a kingdom." Luke's verb for bestow is kin to diatheke. Some hear Jesus making His will; others hear covenant. The will sense is Greek: Hebrew berit is a covenant.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary: the expression comes from Isaiah 63:11, where the Septuagint has ton poimena ton probaton, and the covenant blood from Zechariah 9:11. Also Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ellicott and MacLaren.
layers.text: Hebrews closes by naming the God who, "through the blood of the eternal covenant," raised "that great Shepherd of the sheep." The Greek of Isaiah 63:11 gives Moses, brought up from the sea, the same title, and Zechariah speaks of "the blood of My covenant."

passages.saying: Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast the verse draws between Christ's first coming and His second, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Christ died once, and in that one offering He carried the sins of many. When He appears a second time it will not be to deal with sin again, but to bring full salvation to those who are waiting for Him.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says to bear the sins refers to Isaiah 53:12, and the Pulpit Commentary says the words are taken from Isaiah 53:12. Keil and Delitzsch, on Isaiah 53:12, point to Hebrews 9:28, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the two verses together.
layers.text: The words "to bear the sins of many" echo what Isaiah said of the suffering Servant: "He bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). Read this way, Jesus is that Servant, whose one offering of Himself carried the sins of many people.

passages.saying: knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the reason the verse gives for their joy, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: These believers stood by those in prison and even accepted with joy the seizing of their property. They could do this because they knew they owned something better and lasting that no one could take from them.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible says this verse contains the figure Paregmenon, and his Figures of Speech lists it under that figure, which repeats words from the same root, pairing huparchonton (goods) with huparxin (substance).
layers.text: In the Greek of Hebrews, they lost their possessions (hyparchonton) yet had a better possession (hyparxis). The two words come from the same root, and some see a deliberate pairing: goods that could be plundered set beside a better and permanent possession that no one can seize.

passages.saying: they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's summary of the patriarchs' faith, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Jacob kept trusting God's promises until they died, though they never saw them fulfilled. They saw them from far off, welcomed them, and openly admitted that this earth was not their true home.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown names Abraham's words to the sons of Heth (Genesis 23:4) and Jacob's words to Pharaoh (Genesis 47:9). Barnes quotes Genesis 23:4, and Gill cites Genesis 47:9 as their confession. The Companion Bible also points to Genesis 23:4.
layers.text: This confession comes from Genesis. Abraham told the Hittites, "I am a foreigner and an outsider among you" (Genesis 23:4), and Jacob spoke to Pharaoh of his years as a traveler (Genesis 47:9). They lived as people passing through, looking for a better home.

passages.saying: who shut the mouths of lions
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the list of faith's victories in Hebrews 11:32-34, as the commentaries explain it.
layers.text: The writer lists what God's people did through faith. Some conquered kingdoms, some ruled with justice, some received what God had promised, and some were kept safe from lions.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Gill, Wesley and Barnes all name Daniel in the lions' den here, and Wesley points to Daniel 6:22. Gill and Barnes add that Samson and David also overcame lions.
layers.text: This points above all to Daniel. Thrown into the lions' den, he told the king, "My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions" (Daniel 6:22). He came out without a wound, because he trusted God.

passages.saying: Women received back their dead, raised to life again.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's place in the roll call of faith, where it turns from those who did great deeds to those who suffered.
layers.text: Among those who trusted God, some women saw their dead children raised back to life. Others were tortured and refused to be set free on terms that denied their faith, because they looked for a better resurrection, to a life that never ends.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all name the widow of Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised, and the Shunammite woman, whose son Elisha raised. Wesley cites both stories.
layers.text: This looks back to two mothers. Elijah raised the son of the widow of Zarephath and told her, "Look, your son is alive." Elisha raised the son of the Shunammite woman and told her, "Pick up your son." Each woman received her dead child back alive.

passages.saying: They went around in sheepskins and goatskins
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's list of what faithful people of the Old Testament era suffered.
layers.text: Other believers were stoned, sawed in two, or killed with the sword. Some had to wander from place to place dressed only in the skins of sheep and goats, poor, hunted and badly treated, yet they held on to God.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all point to Zechariah son of Jehoiada in 2 Chronicles 24:21; Gill, Clarke and the Companion Bible also name Naboth.
layers.text: Being stoned recalls Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He warned Judah that they had forsaken the LORD, and by order of the king "they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD." Naboth, falsely accused, was stoned to death too.

layers.evidence: Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that the Septuagint calls Elijah's cloak a melote, the word Hebrews uses for sheepskins. Clarke quotes 2 Kings 2:8-13; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites 1 Kings 19:13. Gill also names Elijah and Elisha.
layers.text: In the Greek of Hebrews, the word for sheepskins is melote, the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for Elijah's cloak, which he wrapped around his face at the cave and which later fell to Elisha. So these wanderers likely dressed as Elijah did when he fled from Jezebel.

passages.saying: The world was not worthy of them.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between the world that drove these believers out and their true worth.
layers.text: The world treated these believers as outcasts, but it was the world that was not worthy of them. Driven from their homes, they wandered in deserts and mountains and hid in caves and holes in the ground.

layers.evidence: Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to the prophets Obadiah hid in caves in 1 Kings 18:4 and to Elijah; Gill also names Elijah and cites 1 Kings 18:4.
layers.text: Hiding in caves recalls the days of Ahab and Jezebel. While Jezebel was killing the LORD's prophets, Obadiah hid a hundred of them, "fifty men per cave," and kept them fed. Elijah too fled for his life and spent the night in a cave at Horeb.

passages.saying: Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's link with the teaching on God's fatherly discipline just before it.
layers.text: Since hardship is God's loving discipline, believers worn out by it should not give up. Hands that hang limp and knees that shake are to be made strong again, and each believer is to help the others keep going.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all say the words come from Isaiah 35:3, and Wesley gives the same reference.
layers.text: These words come from Isaiah: "Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!" There the fearful are told, "Be strong, do not fear!" because God will come to save them. Hebrews passes the same comfort on to tired believers.

passages.saying: no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to watch over one another and its picture of a poisonous root.
layers.text: Believers are to watch over one another so that no one drifts away from God's grace. One bitter person or false teaching left to grow can spread like a poisonous root, troubling the church and spoiling many.

layers.evidence: Gill says the phrase is taken from Deuteronomy 29:18, and Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the same. The Septuagint of that verse already speaks of a root springing up in gall and bitterness.
layers.text: This echoes Moses' warning to Israel: "Make sure there is no root among you that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit." He meant anyone whose heart turns from the LORD to other gods. One such person can poison a whole people.

passages.saying: the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's place at the end of the list of what believers have come to under the new covenant.
layers.text: Believers have come to Jesus, who stands between God and His people in a new covenant, and to His blood, which is sprinkled to make them clean. That blood "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel."

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Clarke and Barnes read this as Abel's sacrifice, and Gill, after setting out other readings, prefers it too. Wesley takes the blood Cain shed.
layers.text: Many read "the blood of Abel" as Abel's sacrifice: the firstborn of his flock, the first animal sacrifice the Bible records, which God accepted. By faith Abel "still speaks, even though he is dead." Read this way, Jesus' blood is the true sacrifice Abel's pointed to, so it speaks a better word.

layers.evidence: Wesley says Abel's blood cried for vengeance. Gill also sets out this reading, that Abel's blood cried for vengeance while Christ's cries for peace and pardon, though he finally prefers Abel's sacrifice.
layers.text: Others hear the scene after Abel's murder, when God told Cain, "The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground." Abel's blood cried out for justice against his killer, but the blood of Jesus pleads for pardon and peace.

passages.saying: some people have entertained angels without knowing it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's command to welcome strangers and the reason it gives.
layers.text: Christians are to keep opening their homes to strangers and travelers. Some who did this in the past found that their guests were angels, so no stranger should be turned away lightly.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and the Companion Bible all name Abraham and Lot; the Companion Bible adds Manoah and Gideon.
layers.text: This looks back to Abraham, who ran from his tent to welcome three travelers and served them a meal, and to Lot, who begged two visitors to stay in his house in Sodom. They took their guests for men, but they were angels: Abraham's brought the promise of a son, and Lot's rescued him.

passages.saying: the bodies are burned outside the camp
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the law of the sin offering, which the next verse applies to Jesus.
layers.text: On the Day of Atonement the high priest carried the blood of the sin offering into the Most Holy Place, but the bodies of the animals were not eaten. They were burned up outside the camp.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes cite Leviticus 16:27, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown names the Day of Atonement. All three tie the burning outside the camp to Jesus' death outside Jerusalem.
layers.text: This takes up the Day of Atonement law: the bull and goat "whose blood was brought into the Most Holy Place" were taken outside the camp and burned. Jesus, the true sin offering, likewise "suffered outside the city gate" of Jerusalem.

passages.saying: a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call to offer praise through Jesus in place of the old animal sacrifices.
layers.text: Through Jesus, believers are to keep offering God a sacrifice of praise. The offering is no longer an animal on an altar but spoken thanks, from lips that openly confess God's name.

layers.evidence: Gill says Hosea 14:2 is thought to be referred to here; Clarke says the phrase is probably borrowed from Hosea 14:2 as the Septuagint renders it (fruit of lips); the Companion Bible calls it a reference to Hosea 14:2. Hosea's Hebrew has parim, bulls.
layers.text: The fruit of lips likely echoes Hosea 14:2, where repentant Israel asks God to receive them, "that we may present the fruit of our lips." Hosea's Hebrew says bulls of our lips, meaning praise given in place of sacrificed animals. The Greek Old Testament reads fruit there, as Hebrews does.

layers.evidence: Gill suggests the phrase may rather be borrowed from Isaiah 57:19, where the Hebrew has niv sephatayim, fruit of the lips; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible also point to that verse.
layers.text: The same phrase appears in the Hebrew of Isaiah 57:19, where God speaks of bringing praise to their lips, literally creating the fruit of the lips, as He proclaims peace to those far and near. Some think Hebrews borrows the phrase from this verse rather than from Hosea.

passages.saying: brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's prayer to the God who raised Jesus and its title for Him, the great Shepherd.
layers.text: The writer begins a closing prayer to the God of peace, who raised the Lord Jesus from the dead. Jesus is the great Shepherd who cares for God's people, and His blood sealed the eternal covenant.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the title shepherd of the sheep comes from Isaiah 63:11 in the Septuagint, first of Moses and then of Christ, and notes the Greek verb means brought up; the Companion Bible also points to the Septuagint of Isaiah 63:11.
layers.text: God brought Jesus up from the dead as the great Shepherd of the sheep. This recalls Isaiah 63:11, which remembers how God brought His people up out of the sea with the shepherds of His flock, Moses above all. The Greek Old Testament there uses the same words, shepherd of the sheep.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Zechariah 9:11 is seemingly referred to here, and the Companion Bible on Zechariah 9:11 compares Hebrews 13:20.
layers.text: The blood of the eternal covenant may echo Zechariah 9:11, where God tells Zion, "because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit." By that blood God raised Jesus, and on this reading He will raise His people too.

passages.saying: he will pass away like a flower of the field
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call for the rich to remember how brief their wealth and life are.
layers.text: A rich believer should take pride in being humbled, because wealth and life itself are brief. Like a wild flower, the rich man will soon pass away.

layers.evidence: Barnes says James probably had his eye on Isaiah 40:6-8, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on James 1:11 says the picture is taken from Isaiah 40:6-8. James's Greek for flower of the grass is the wording of the Greek Old Testament in Isaiah 40:6, which 1 Peter 1:24 also quotes.
layers.text: James likely draws his picture from Isaiah 40:6 to 8, where all flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field. In both passages the grass dries up and its flower drops. In Isaiah only the word of God lasts.

passages.saying: For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain denial that God is the source of temptation to sin.
layers.text: When people feel pulled toward sin, they must not blame God. God cannot be tempted by evil, and He never entices anyone to do wrong.

layers.evidence: Gill says the apostle uses tempted here in another sense than before; Clarke says the word has two grand meanings, trial and solicitation to sin; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the earlier temptation meant testing by afflictions. The Greek words are peirasmos and peirazo.
layers.text: In James's Greek one word family means both trial and temptation. In verses 2 and 12 it means hard testing, which believers can meet with joy and which ends in blessing. Here James turns the same word to mean enticement to sin, which never comes from God.

passages.saying: have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's rebuke of favoring the rich visitor over the poor one in verses 2 and 3.
layers.text: Giving the rich visitor the best seat and pushing the poor one aside is favoritism. Those who do it have made themselves judges of others, and their judging comes from wrong motives.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Greek words for judges and partial are akin in sound and meaning, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech says diekrithete and kritai come from the same root.
layers.text: In James's Greek the verb for making distinctions, diekrithete, and the noun for judges, kritai, come from the same root. By sorting people into rich and poor, the believers had turned themselves into judges, and judges with evil thoughts.

passages.saying: with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between blessing God and cursing people made like Him.
layers.text: The same tongue that praises God the Father also curses people. That makes no sense, because every person is made in God's likeness.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes both tie the phrase to man's creation in Genesis 1:26, and the Companion Bible notes that homoiosis, the Greek for likeness, is used in the Septuagint of Genesis 1:26. The Hebrew there is demuth.
layers.text: James points back to creation, when God said, "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness." His Greek word for likeness is the one the Greek Old Testament uses there. To curse a person is to curse someone who bears God's likeness.

passages.saying: The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's charge of withheld wages and its warning that God has heard.
layers.text: The rich had cheated the workers who harvested their fields out of their pay. Those unpaid wages and the workers' cries have reached God, the Lord of Hosts, who will act for them.

layers.evidence: Gill says the reference is to Deuteronomy 24:15, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says James refers to Deuteronomy 24:14-15, where the unpaid worker cries to the Lord against his employer.
layers.text: James draws on the law in Deuteronomy 24:15, which told employers to pay a hired man before sunset, or "he may cry out to the LORD against you." These rich men had broken that law, and the workers' cry had reached God just as the law warned.

passages.saying: You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of animals fattened for slaughter.
layers.text: The rich lived in luxury and pleasure at the expense of others. Like cattle fattened for slaughter, they kept feeding themselves while their day of judgment drew near.

layers.evidence: Gill on Jeremiah 12:3 says the riches of the wicked fattened them like sheep for slaughter and points to James 5:5; the Companion Bible on James 5:5 compares Jeremiah 12:3. Jeremiah's Hebrew is yom haregah, day of slaughter.
layers.text: The day of slaughter may recall Jeremiah 12:3, where the prophet asks God to drag away the wicked like sheep to the slaughter and set them apart for the day of carnage, literally the day of slaughter. Read this way, the rich who fatten themselves are only being readied for judgment.

passages.saying: See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of a patient farmer, as Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains it.
layers.text: James tells suffering believers to be patient until the Lord comes. He points to a farmer, who cannot hurry his crop but waits through the autumn and spring rains for the harvest he hopes for.

layers.evidence: Clarke on this verse quotes Deuteronomy 11:14 as God's promise of the first and latter rain. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Deuteronomy 11:14 lists James 5:7 among the passages about these two rains.
layers.text: The fall and spring rains James mentions are the two rains God promised Israel in Deuteronomy 11:14, sent in their season so the land would yield its harvest. Some see the farmer as waiting patiently on that promise, as believers are to wait for the Lord's coming.

passages.saying: He prayed earnestly that it would not rain
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on James's point that Elijah was an ordinary man, as Barnes explains it.
layers.text: James reminds his readers that Elijah was an ordinary man like them. Yet when he prayed earnestly, God held back the rain for three and a half years. So God also hears the earnest prayers of ordinary believers.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all read the Greek as he prayed with prayer and call it a Hebraism for earnest prayer. Bullinger's Figures of Speech and Companion Bible name it as a figure of speech.
layers.text: In James's Greek, Elijah literally prayed with prayer, setting the noun and the verb of the same word side by side (proseuche, proseuxato). This copies a Hebrew way of repeating a word for emphasis, so it means he prayed earnestly, with his whole heart.

passages.saying: Therefore prepare your minds for action.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of tying up a long robe for work, as Barnes explains it.
layers.text: Peter tells believers to get their minds ready for action, to stay clear-headed, and to set their hope fully on the grace they will receive when Jesus Christ is revealed.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the image is taken from Israel eating the Passover with robes girded up, ready for a journey. Gill likewise points to Israel at the first Passover, ready to march out of Egypt.
layers.text: Peter's Greek literally pictures tying up a long robe around the waist, here the waist of the mind. Israel ate the first Passover dressed this way, ready to leave Egypt at a moment's notice. Believers are to be just as ready.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the command refers to Christ's own words in Luke 12:35. Gill also points to Luke 12:35 when he speaks of waiting for the Lord's coming.
layers.text: The same picture echoes Jesus' words to His disciples, "Be dressed for service," spoken about servants waiting for their master to return. Peter applies it to believers, who are to be ready in mind for the day Jesus Christ is revealed.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggests a possible link between teleios (fully) here and telos, the end of faith, in verse 9.
layers.text: Peter's word for fully (teleios) comes from telos, end, the word behind the goal of your faith in verse 9. Some see a link: believers are to hope fully, all the way to that goal.

passages.saying: not with perishable things such as silver or gold
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the meaning of redeem, paying a price to free a captive, as Clarke explains it.
layers.text: Peter reminds believers that they were set free from the empty way of life handed down to them. The price paid was not money, which perishes, but the precious blood of Christ.

layers.evidence: Gill on Isaiah 52:3 compares that promise with redemption not by silver and gold in 1 Peter 1:18. The Companion Bible renders without money there as not with silver and compares 1 Peter 1:18.
layers.text: Through Isaiah the LORD told His people, "You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed." The Hebrew says literally not with silver. Peter may be echoing this: God's people were bought back, but not with silver or gold.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to Israel's redemption by shekels in Exodus 30:12. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that each Israelite was ransomed with half a shekel and contrasts this with Christ's precious blood.
layers.text: Under the Law, each man counted in Israel's census paid the LORD a ransom for his life, a half shekel of silver. Peter's readers were ransomed at a far greater price, not with silver or gold but with Christ's own blood.

passages.saying: the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Peter's contrast between perishable silver and gold and Christ's blood, as Barnes explains it.
layers.text: The price of the believer's redemption was the precious blood of Christ. He is pictured as a sacrificial lamb with no flaw at all, worth far more than silver or gold.

layers.evidence: Gill likens Christ particularly to the Passover lamb, which had to be without spot and blemish. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares Israel's redemption by the paschal lamb's blood. The Companion Bible sets without blemish beside Exodus 12:5.
layers.text: Calling Christ a lamb with no blemish recalls the Passover, when each household had to choose an unblemished lamb. That lamb's blood marked Israel's rescue from Egypt, and Christ's blood rescues His people from sin.

passages.saying: you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own list of titles, which the commentaries read as Israel's titles now given to all who believe in Christ.
layers.text: Peter tells those who believe in Christ who they now are: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation and God's own possession. God made them His so that they would proclaim the virtues of the One who called them out of darkness into His marvelous light.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all say royal priesthood and holy nation are taken from Exodus 19:6, and Gill and Barnes link God's own possession to the treasured possession of Exodus 19:5. Keil and Delitzsch, on Exodus 19:5-6, say Peter took up this promise in its Septuagint wording.
layers.text: God's words to Israel at Sinai lie behind this verse: "unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Peter gives these titles, along with being God's treasured possession, to everyone who believes in Christ, Jew and Gentile alike.

layers.evidence: Gill says Peter refers to Isaiah 43:20-21: the Septuagint of verse 20 has the same phrase Peter uses for a chosen people, and verse 21 uses the same Greek word that Peter uses for God's virtues or praises.
layers.text: Peter may also echo Isaiah 43, where God calls Israel My chosen people and says, "The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise." Believers in Christ are chosen for the same purpose: to proclaim the virtues of the God who called them.

passages.saying: Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between once and now, which the commentaries read as the change God's mercy made in these believers.
layers.text: Peter reminds his readers that they once stood outside God's people and had not received His mercy. Now, through Christ, they belong to God as His people and have received His mercy.

layers.evidence: Gill traces the verse to Hosea 1:6 and 1:9 and names the two children, Lo-ammi and Lo-ruhamah. Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown trace it to Hosea 1:9-10 and 2:23 and see in it the calling of the Gentiles. Barnes calls it an allusion to Hosea 2:23, and the Companion Bible compares Hosea 2:23.
layers.text: This verse echoes Hosea, whose children were named Lo-ammi, meaning Not My People, and Lo-ruhamah, meaning No Compassion. God promised to have compassion on No Compassion and to call Not My People His own. Peter applies that promise to believers, many of them once Gentiles.

passages.saying: He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, which the commentaries read as Christ bearing the punishment our sins deserved.
layers.text: Christ Himself took the punishment for our sins in His own body on the cross, so that we would be done with sin and live for what is right. Peter ends with Isaiah's words, "By His stripes you are healed."

layers.evidence: Barnes says the verse undoubtedly alludes to Isaiah 53:4 and 53:12, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Isaiah 53:11-12, and Gill says this sin-bearing was foretold by Isaiah. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also note that the verb is a sacrificial one for carrying up or offering up, and the Companion Bible says it is the same word as offer up earlier in this chapter.
layers.text: Peter's words echo Isaiah's Servant, who "bore the sin of many." Peter's Greek verb for bore is also used for carrying a sacrifice up to the altar, so Christ is shown both carrying our sins and offering Himself for them on the cross.

passages.saying: refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording, which the commentaries read as wives winning unbelieving husbands by their conduct.
layers.text: Christian wives are to submit to their husbands, so that a husband who rejects the gospel may be won to Christ without words, by the godly way his wife lives.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse as one word used twice in different senses: the first logos means the Gospel, the second means speaking or talking. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also mention the reading without word, meaning without the wives' direct gospel talk.
layers.text: In Peter's Greek one word, logos, is used twice, and some read it in two senses. Husbands who "refuse to believe the word," meaning the gospel message, may be "won over without words," meaning without talk from their wives, simply by how their wives live.

passages.saying: But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording, which the oldest texts give as sanctify Christ as Lord.
layers.text: Believers are to honor Christ in their hearts as the holy Lord, and to be ready to explain gently and respectfully the reason for their hope whenever anyone asks.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and the Companion Bible all trace the command to Isaiah 8:12-13. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the oldest manuscripts read Christ as Lord, the Companion Bible says the texts read so, and Gill says Christ is the One meant in Isaiah 8:13.
layers.text: Peter is using Isaiah's words: "The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy." Where Isaiah names the LORD of Hosts, Peter puts Christ, telling believers to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts instead of fearing those who threaten them.

passages.saying: love covers over a multitude of sins
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording, which the commentaries read as love passing over the faults of others.
layers.text: Above everything else, believers are to love one another deeply, because love is ready to forgive and to overlook the faults of others instead of exposing them.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Peter quotes or refers to Proverbs 10:12, and the Companion Bible compares it. Gill, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown add that love covers the faults of others and is not a way of earning pardon for one's own sins.
layers.text: Peter's reason comes from Proverbs: "Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions." Love covers other people's sins by forgiving them and not stirring them up again. It does not earn pardon for the one who loves.

passages.saying: the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording, which the commentaries read as the Holy Spirit abiding with persecuted believers.
layers.text: Believers who are insulted because they belong to Christ are blessed, because God's own glorious Spirit rests on them and stays with them in their suffering.

layers.evidence: Gill says the words allude to Isaiah 11:2. Clarke, Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the same Spirit that rested on Jesus now rests on His persecuted followers.
layers.text: Isaiah said of the Branch from Jesse's roots, "The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him." Peter likely uses the same picture for believers: the Spirit who rested on Christ now rests on those who are insulted for His name.

passages.saying: Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own commands to the elders Peter addresses in verse 1.
layers.text: Peter tells the church elders to care for God's people as shepherds care for a flock. They are to watch over them willingly, as God wants, not because they are forced and not for money, but with eager hearts.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Albert Barnes and John Gill each say Peter is recalling the charge Jesus gave him in John 21, and Bullinger's Companion Bible also points to John 21:16. Both verses use the same Greek verb for shepherding (poimaino).
layers.text: Peter tells the elders to shepherd God's flock. After His resurrection, Jesus had given Peter himself that same charge: "Shepherd My sheep." Now Peter passes it on to his fellow elders. The verb for shepherding in John's Greek is the same one Peter uses here.

passages.saying: Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain command and the reason it gives for it.
layers.text: Peter tells believers to hand all their worries over to God, because God truly cares for them.

layers.evidence: John Gill says the words are taken from Psalm 55:22 and notes the Septuagint there reads cast thy care upon the Lord. Adam Clarke calls it a plain reference to that psalm, Albert Barnes says the passage was probably taken from it, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agrees.
layers.text: Peter's command echoes Psalm 55:22: "Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you." The old Greek translation of that psalm uses the same words for casting and for care that Peter uses, so Peter is handing on the psalm's promise to his readers.

passages.saying: Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own warning and its picture of a hungry lion.
layers.text: Peter urges believers to stay clear-headed and alert, because their enemy the devil roams about like a hungry, roaring lion, looking for someone to devour.

layers.evidence: Adam Clarke calls Peter's phrase about the devil walking about a plain reference to Job 2:2, and John Gill ties it to Satan going to and fro in the earth in Job 1:7. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also lists both Job verses here.
layers.text: When Peter says the devil prowls around, he echoes Job, where Satan tells the LORD he has been "roaming through the earth" and "walking back and forth in it." The same enemy who roamed the earth in Job's day still prowls, looking for someone to devour.

passages.saying: I know that this tent will soon be laid aside
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of the body as a tent and Peter's stated knowledge.
layers.text: Peter knows his death is near. He pictures his body as a tent that will soon be taken down, just as the Lord Jesus had made clear to him.

layers.evidence: Adam Clarke says Peter plainly refers to his conversation with the Lord in John 21:18-19. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Albert Barnes agree, and John Gill, John Wesley and Bullinger's notes also point to John 21:18. Barnes adds that Peter's old age told him the foretold death was near.
layers.text: Peter is recalling what Jesus told him by the Sea of Galilee: "when you are old, you will stretch out your hands," and someone else will lead you. John explains that this pointed to how Peter would die. Now that Peter is old, he knows that time is near.

passages.saying: after my departure, you will be able to recall these things
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain promise, which Peter keeps by writing this letter.
layers.text: Peter promises to do all he can so that after his death his readers will always be able to remember what he has taught them.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that exodos is the very word used at the Transfiguration, and on Luke 9:31 says Peter's use of it recalled that scene, leading to his account of it in 2 Peter 1:16-18. It adds that tent appears in both places. Bullinger's notes also point to Luke 9:31.
layers.text: Peter calls his coming death his departure, exodos in Peter's Greek. Luke's Greek uses that same word for the departure Moses and Elijah discussed with Jesus at the Transfiguration. Many see the word as recalling that scene; Peter was there, and in the very next verses he describes it.

passages.saying: the earth was formed out of water and by water
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words about creation by God's word.
layers.text: Peter says the scoffers deliberately ignore that long ago God's word brought the heavens into being and formed the earth out of water and by means of water.

layers.evidence: Albert Barnes says Peter doubtless refers to the creation account in Genesis 1. John Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain the earth standing out of the water by the gathering of the waters in Genesis 1:9, and Adam Clarke calls this the teaching of Moses.
layers.text: Peter points back to the creation account in Genesis. There the Spirit of God hovered over the waters, and God gathered the waters so that the dry land appeared. Peter's point seems to be that the waters God used in making the world are the same waters He later used to judge it in the flood.

passages.saying: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, read with the scoffers' complaint about delay in verse 4.
layers.text: Peter asks believers not to miss one thing: the Lord does not measure time as we do. A day is like a thousand years to Him, and a thousand years like a day. So the seeming delay of His coming is no reason to doubt His promise.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls the words a quotation from Psalm 90:4. JFB and Gill point to the same verse, Wesley says Peter applies what Moses had said there, and Barnes notes a similar thought in Psalm 90:4.
layers.text: Peter draws on Moses' prayer in Psalm 90, which says that in God's sight a thousand years are but a day that passes. Peter repeats the thought and also turns it around: one day is like a thousand years with the Lord.

passages.saying: we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting after the burning of the present heavens and earth in verses 10 to 12.
layers.text: The present heavens and earth will pass away in fire, but believers look ahead in hope. Trusting God's promise, they wait for a new heaven and a new earth, a world where righteousness is at home.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the allusion is beyond a doubt to Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. Clarke and Gill name Isaiah 65:17 as the promise meant, and JFB lists both Isaiah passages.
layers.text: The promise Peter means is the one God gave through Isaiah: “I will create new heavens and a new earth.” Isaiah repeats it in chapter 66. Believers wait for God to keep that very promise.

passages.saying: That which was from the beginning
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's string of senses: heard, seen, gazed upon and touched.
layers.text: John writes as an eyewitness. The Word of life, who was from the beginning, came in the flesh, and the apostles heard Him, saw Him with their own eyes, gazed on Him and touched Him with their hands.

layers.evidence: JFB sets the opening beside John's Gospel, In the beginning was the Word. Wesley says from the beginning here is equivalent to in the beginning, and that He is termed the Word as in John 1:1. Gill takes it of Christ's eternal existence and points to John 1:1.
layers.text: In his Gospel John wrote, “In the beginning was the Word,” and he opens this letter the same way. He writes of what was from the beginning and calls Jesus the Word of life, the eternal Word whom the apostles heard, saw and touched.

passages.saying: You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its contrast with those who went out from the church in verse 19.
layers.text: Unlike those who left the church, John's readers have received an anointing, the Holy Spirit, from the Holy One. Because of it they know the truth and can stand firm against those who deny Christ.

layers.evidence: JFB says the Greek chrism, anointing, is a play upon similar sounds with the antichrists of verse 18. Wesley says the anointing is perhaps so named in opposition to the name antichrist.
layers.text: In John's Greek the word for anointing is chrisma, close in sound to Christ, the Anointed One. John sets it against the antichrists of verse 18: those who oppose Christ are antichrists, but believers have the chrism, the Spirit's anointing.

passages.saying: God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and verse 19; commentators read it either as warning or as comfort.
layers.text: Our conscience may condemn us, but God is greater than our hearts and knows everything. Some read this as a warning, since God sees even more than our conscience does. Others read it as comfort, since God knows our love for Him even when our hearts accuse us.

layers.evidence: JFB notes that the Greek for condemn means to know something against us, and that God is said to know (ginoskei), not to condemn (kataginoskei).
layers.text: In John's Greek, the heart condemns with kataginōskō, which is literally to know against, while God simply knows (ginōskō) all things. Some see the shared root as setting the heart's verdict beside God's complete knowledge.

passages.saying: This is the One who came by water and blood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; most take the water as Jesus' baptism and the blood as His death.
layers.text: Jesus came by water and blood. Most understand the water as His baptism, where the Father declared Him His Son, and the blood as His death on the cross. The Spirit also testifies to Him, because the Spirit is the truth.

layers.evidence: Gill says there may be an allusion here to the water and blood from Jesus' pierced side, which John saw. Wesley ties Jesus' coming by blood to the cross, where blood and water came out of His side.
layers.text: John saw a soldier pierce Jesus' side, and blood and water flowed out (John 19:34). When he writes here that Jesus came by water and blood, he may also be recalling that sight, to which he had borne witness.

passages.saying: But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its contrast with the slanderers of verses 8 and 10.
layers.text: Even Michael, the chief of the angels, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous charge against him. He left the judgment to God and said, “The Lord rebuke you!”

layers.evidence: JFB notes the same rebuke was spoken against Satan on behalf of Joshua in Zechariah 3:2. Gill says the latter part of the verse shows reference to Zechariah 3. Clarke favors a reading that ties the dispute to that vision. Barnes grants the shared words but doubts the events are the same.
layers.text: Michael's words, “The Lord rebuke you!”, repeat the rebuke the LORD spoke to Satan in Zechariah's vision, when Satan stood ready to accuse Joshua the high priest. Michael does not judge the devil on his own authority but leaves the rebuke to the Lord.

layers.evidence: JFB says the name means Who is like God? Gill says it signifies who is as God, and Clarke breaks it into mi (who), ke (like) and El (God).
layers.text: The archangel's name, Michael, is Hebrew for a question: Who is like God? It is formed from mi (who), ke (like) and El (God).

passages.saying: shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jude's own pictures, which the commentaries read as false teachers who use the church to serve their own appetites.
layers.text: Jude warns that false teachers sit at the church's love feasts like hidden reefs. They feast without shame and care only for themselves. Like rainless clouds and dead, uprooted trees, they promise much and give nothing.

layers.evidence: Gill likens them to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock. The Companion Bible notes the Greek means pasturing themselves, as a shepherd does his flock, and points to Ezekiel 34:2.
layers.text: In Jude's Greek they shepherd only themselves. This may echo God's charge in Ezekiel: "Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves!" Like those faithless shepherds, these men feed their own appetites instead of caring for the flock.

passages.saying: They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jude's pictures of the sea and the sky, which the commentaries apply to loud but empty false teachers.
layers.text: Jude compares false teachers to wild sea waves that throw up nothing but foam, which shows their shame. They are like wandering stars that keep no steady course, and the deepest darkness is reserved for them forever.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it the same metaphor as Isaiah 57:20, where the troubled sea casts up mire and dirt. JFB says Jude has Isaiah 57:20 in mind.
layers.text: The waves foaming up shame recall Isaiah 57:20: "the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea," and "its waves churn up mire and muck." Like that restless sea, these teachers are never still, and all they stir up is filth.

passages.saying: save others by snatching them from the fire
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jude's picture of pulling people out of a fire, which the commentaries read as urgent rescue from sin and judgment.
layers.text: Jude tells believers to rescue some people with urgent effort, like pulling them out of a fire. To others they should show mercy, but with fear of being drawn into sin, hating even what sin has stained.

layers.evidence: JFB compares snatching them out of the fire with Amos 4:11 and Zechariah 3:2, said of a very narrow escape, and in its note on Zechariah 3:2 points back to Jude 1:23. It adds that Jude 1:9 already drew on the same chapter of Zechariah.
layers.text: Snatching people from the fire may echo Zechariah 3:2, where the LORD calls Joshua the high priest "a firebrand snatched from the fire" (compare Amos 4:11). Like a burning stick pulled out just in time, some can only be rescued at the last moment.

passages.saying: from Him who is and was and is to come
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the greeting itself, which the commentaries read as a blessing from the Father, the Spirit and the Son.
layers.text: John greets the seven churches in Asia with grace and peace. The blessing comes from the eternal God, from the seven Spirits before His throne, understood as the Holy Spirit in His fullness, and, in the next verse, from Jesus Christ.

layers.evidence: Gill calls the title a periphrasis and explanation of the name Jehovah, which includes all tenses, past, present and to come. JFB calls it a periphrasis for the name JEHOVAH, the self-existing One. Wesley calls it a translation of that great name. Clarke, William Tong (Matthew Henry's Commentary) and the Companion Bible say the same.
layers.text: God is named "Him who is and was and is to come." This unfolds His covenant name, the LORD, which He explained to Moses at the burning bush with "I AM WHO I AM." He is the same unchanging God in the past, the present and the future.

passages.saying: Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.text: John greets the seven churches with grace and peace from God, from the seven Spirits, and from Jesus, named three ways: witness, firstborn, ruler. Then he breaks into praise: "To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood."

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale, as reported by Peter Leithart (Theopolis Institute, 2011): all three phrases are in Psalm 89:27 and 37. The Septuagint of 89:37 has martys and pistos, witness and faithful; Ellicott also cites the psalm.
layers.text: All three titles come from Psalm 89, God's oath to David's heir: "I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth," and his throne will last like the moon, "a faithful witness in the sky."

layers.evidence: Peter Leithart (Theopolis Institute, 2011): the psalm asks but never answers, and Revelation is about the faithfulness of Israel's God to Israel's King.
layers.text: Psalm 89 then turns to grief: "You have renounced the covenant with Your servant," and "Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old?" The psalm never answers. Some read Revelation as the answer: David's heir is alive and reigning.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the word can mean both witness and martyr. Easton's Bible Dictionary: a martyr bears witness and suffers death for Christ, and the Greek word is elsewhere rendered witness. Abbott-Smith (TBESG): the sense martyr belongs to later Christian writing. The Pulpit Commentary: the same Greek phrase is used of Antipas and of Christ.
layers.text: The Greek for "witness," martys, later came to mean martyr, and gave English that word. Jesus gives His own title to a believer who died for Him: "My faithful witness Antipas was killed among you." Antipas shares his Lord's title, and his Lord's death.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the two oldest manuscripts read freed; the NET Bible note gives it better manuscript support. TAGNT: lousanti in the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text. MacLaren: washed pictures sin as a stain, loosed as a chain.
layers.text: Copies differ here by one letter. The oldest read lysanti, "released"; others read lousanti, "washed." One pictures sin as a chain, the other as a stain. Revelation knows both: the saints "have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."

layers.evidence: MacLaren calls Exodus 19:6 the charter of Israel's national life, given right after the exodus. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes and Gill on Revelation 1:6 cite Exodus 19:6, and the Pulpit Commentary notes that Peter's royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9) follows the Septuagint of that verse.
layers.text: The words "a kingdom, priests" come from Sinai, just after the exodus: "you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." John keeps Israel's order: first freed, then made priests. Heaven sings, "You have made them to be a kingdom and priests."

passages.saying: who has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain words of John's praise to Christ, which the commentaries explain as believers' royal and priestly standing.
layers.text: John praises Jesus, who loves us and freed us from our sins by His blood. He has made His people a kingdom and priests who serve His God and Father. To Him belong glory and power forever.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, JFB and the Companion Bible all trace these words to Exodus 19:6, a kingdom of priests. Barnes adds that Peter quotes the same verse when he calls believers a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), and JFB sets the two side by side.
layers.text: John's words, "a kingdom, priests to His God and Father," take up God's call to Israel at Sinai: you shall be "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Through Christ's blood, all His people now share that calling to belong to God and serve Him.

passages.saying: Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, which most of the works read as Christ's visible return.
layers.text: John announces that Jesus is coming with the clouds. Everyone will see Him, even those who pierced Him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him. John seals it: "So shall it be! Amen."

layers.evidence: Gill says He will come with clouds as Daniel prophesied (Daniel 7:13). Keil and Delitzsch, on Daniel 7:13, call that verse the foundation for Christ's words about His coming on the clouds and cite Revelation 1:7. JFB, on Daniel 7:13, points to Revelation 1:7, and Barnes there compares the two as well.
layers.text: Coming with the clouds recalls Daniel's vision of "One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven" to the Ancient of Days. Jesus, who went up into a cloud at His ascension, will return as that Son of Man.

layers.evidence: Barnes sees an allusion to Zechariah 12:10, as do the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech. Gill and JFB, on Zechariah 12:10, say Revelation 1:7 refers to it, and JFB adds John 19:37, where John applies it to the spear wound.
layers.text: Those who pierced Him and the mourning tribes echo Zechariah 12:10: "they will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn for Him." The Gospel of John quotes this verse at the spear thrust into Jesus' side (John 19:34-37); here it is applied to His return.

passages.saying: I saw seven golden lampstands
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the vision itself and on verse 20, which says the lampstands are the seven churches.
layers.text: John turns to see who is speaking to him and sees seven golden lampstands. Verse 20 explains that they are the seven churches, each meant to hold out light in a dark world.

layers.evidence: Gill sees an allusion to the seven lamps of the sanctuary lampstand (Exodus 25:37). Clarke calls it a reference to the seven-branched lampstand of Exodus 25:31-37. JFB compares Exodus 25 and Zechariah 4:2. Barnes stresses that the scene itself is not set in the temple.
layers.text: The seven golden lampstands recall the golden lampstand with seven lamps that lit the holy place of the tabernacle. There one stand held all seven lamps; here seven stand apart, one for each church. Like that lampstand, they hold out a light that is the Lord's, not their own.

passages.saying: among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the vision itself, which verse 18 shows is the risen Jesus standing among His churches.
layers.text: Among the lampstands, which are the churches, John sees One like the Son of Man, the risen Jesus. He wears a long robe and a golden sash around His chest. He is present with His churches and watches over them.

layers.evidence: Gill says there is a reference here to Daniel 7:13. Clarke calls it a reference to Daniel 7:13. Barnes sees an allusion to Daniel 7:13 in the New Testament use of the phrase.
layers.text: "One like the Son of Man" are the words of Daniel 7:13, where Daniel sees this heavenly figure coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days. John now sees Him in glory and soon learns that He is Jesus, who was dead and is alive forever.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls the robe a description of the high priest in his robes (Exodus 28:4). JFB sees the robe and girdle as emblems of His priesthood. Wesley says the Jewish high priests wore such, adding that they also mark royal dignity. Gill calls Him the antitype of Aaron. Barnes reads the dress as royal instead.
layers.text: The long robe and the sash around the chest recall the holy garments God commanded for Aaron the high priest, which included a robe and a sash. Jesus walks among His churches as their great High Priest, and His dress also shows His royal dignity.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Daniel 10:5, takes the man in linen to be the Son of God, not Gabriel, and points to Revelation 1:13, where Christ wears a golden girdle, saying such a one was this.
layers.text: The golden sash may also recall Daniel 10:5, where Daniel sees "a certain man dressed in linen, with a belt of fine gold" around his waist. Some see that glorious man as the Son of God Himself, the same Lord John now sees.

passages.saying: The hair of His head was white like wool, as white as snow
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on John's description of the risen Jesus in Revelation 1:13-16.
layers.text: John sees the risen Jesus with hair as white as wool and snow and eyes like a blazing fire. The picture shows His majesty and purity, and eyes that see through everything.

layers.evidence: Gill says the description is the same as that of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9 and shows Christ's true deity. Barnes thinks John probably had Daniel's vision in mind. Wesley: like the Ancient of Days in Daniel's vision. The Companion Bible also compares Daniel 7:9.
layers.text: In Daniel's vision the Ancient of Days, God on His throne, has clothing white as snow and hair like pure wool. John sees the risen Jesus with the same white hair, so He bears the look of God Himself.

passages.saying: His voice was like the roar of many waters
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on John's description of the risen Jesus in Revelation 1:13-16.
layers.text: John sees the risen Jesus with feet glowing like bronze refined in a furnace and a voice like the roar of many waters. The picture speaks of His strength, majesty and authority.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the same description is found in Ezekiel 43:2; Barnes quotes Ezekiel 43:2 as the parallel; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Ezekiel 43:2 for the phrase. The Companion Bible lists it too.
layers.text: In Ezekiel the glory of the God of Israel comes from the east, and "His voice was like the roar of many waters." John now hears that same sound, which Ezekiel heard from the glory of God, in the voice of the risen Jesus.
