layers.evidence: Barnes on Daniel 10:6 notes a very striking resemblance to the Saviour as John saw Him on Patmos, matching the bronze feet with Revelation 1:15. Keil and Delitzsch say the comparison with Revelation 1:13-15 shows the figure Daniel saw was a manifestation of the Lord.
layers.text: His feet like polished bronze recall the glorious man Daniel saw by the great river, whose arms and legs gleamed like polished bronze and whose eyes were like flaming torches. John's picture of the risen Jesus closely matches Daniel's vision.

passages.saying: a sharp double-edged sword came from His mouth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on Hebrews 4:12, where God's word is sharper than a two-edged sword.
layers.text: John sees the risen Jesus holding seven stars in His right hand, with a sharp double-edged sword coming from His mouth and a face shining like the sun. The sword pictures the power of His word.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the same person is described in Isaiah 49:2, whose mouth is made like a sharp sword. The Companion Bible says the meaning is seen in Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2.
layers.text: In Isaiah the Servant of the LORD says, "He made My mouth like a sharp sword." The sword coming from Jesus' mouth takes up that picture: His word cuts deep, both to judge and to pierce the heart.

passages.saying: I am the First and the Last
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on the same title in Revelation 1:8.
layers.text: John falls at the feet of the risen Jesus as though dead. Jesus lays His right hand on him and tells him not to be afraid, because He is the First and the Last, the eternal One.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech calls the words an allusion to Isaiah 41:4 and 44:6; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12; the Companion Bible compares the same Isaiah verses. Wesley explains the title as the one eternal God, citing Isaiah 41:4.
layers.text: In Isaiah the LORD says, "I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me." The risen Jesus takes this title of the one true God as His own.

layers.evidence: Wesley says John was prepared for the prophecy like Daniel of old, whom he peculiarly resembles. Barnes compares Daniel 8:18, where the messenger touched Daniel and set him upright, and on Daniel 8:17 he points back to Revelation 1:17. Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the touch gave John strength.
layers.text: John's experience matches Daniel's. Daniel fell with his face to the ground before a heavenly messenger, who touched him and helped him to his feet. John too falls as though dead and is strengthened by the touch of Jesus' right hand, ready to receive visions as Daniel did.

passages.saying: I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the promise to the overcomer and on Revelation 22:2, where the tree of life stands in the new Jerusalem.
layers.text: Jesus promises the believer who overcomes that he will eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God. It is a promise of everlasting life in God's presence.

layers.evidence: Gill says the tree of life is named in allusion to the tree in the garden of Eden; Clarke sees an allusion to Genesis 2:9; Barnes says the phrase refers undoubtedly to Eden, Genesis 2:9 and 3:22. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the tree lost by the fall is restored by the Redeemer.
layers.text: In Eden the tree of life stood in the middle of the garden, and after Adam sinned he was sent away so he could not eat from it and live forever. Jesus promises the one who overcomes the right to eat from that tree again, in the Paradise of God.

passages.saying: I will give the hidden manna
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the promise to the overcomer at Pergamum and the contrast with idol food in Revelation 2:14.
layers.text: Jesus promises the believer who overcomes the hidden manna, the true food of the soul, and a white stone with a new name on it, known only to the one who receives it.

layers.evidence: Barnes sees an allusion to the manna laid up in the pot before the ark of the testimony; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the pot of manna laid up before the testimony is the allusion; Wesley notes that the Jewish manna was kept in the ark of the covenant. The Companion Bible compares Exodus 16:32-34.
layers.text: Moses told Aaron to keep a jar of manna before the LORD, and it was laid up in front of the Testimony, hidden away in the sanctuary. Jesus promises the one who overcomes this hidden manna, heavenly food instead of the food sacrificed to idols at Pergamum.

passages.saying: You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the letter to Thyatira and the same sins named at Pergamum in Revelation 2:14.
layers.text: Jesus rebukes the church at Thyatira for tolerating a woman who called herself a prophetess. By her teaching she was leading His servants into sexual immorality and into eating food sacrificed to idols.

layers.evidence: Clarke sees an allusion to the history of Ahab and Jezebel; Barnes thinks the name was given to express her character and influence; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says she was to Thyatira what Jezebel was to Ahab. Wesley says she is fitly called by the name from the likeness of their works.
layers.text: Jezebel was the wife of King Ahab. She drew him and Israel into Baal worship, and her idolatry and witchcraft were notorious. Jesus calls the false prophetess at Thyatira by her name because she does the same work, leading God's servants into idolatry and immorality.

passages.saying: I am the One who searches minds and hearts
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, read as Christ's claim to know every heart.
layers.text: Jesus warns that He will judge those in Thyatira who follow the false prophetess, so that every church will know He sees into each person's thoughts and desires and repays each one according to their deeds.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says Jeremiah 17:10 is quoted in Revelation 2:23. Gill on Jeremiah says that since Christ searches the reins and heart, He must be Jehovah. Barnes calls heart-searching God's special prerogative and lists Jeremiah 17:10.
layers.text: Jesus takes up the LORD's words in Jeremiah 17:10: "I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way." What God claims there as His own right, Jesus claims here as His own.

passages.saying: He will rule them with an iron scepter
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on this verse together with verse 26, which promises authority over the nations.
layers.text: Jesus promises the believer who overcomes a share in His own rule over the nations, a rule as unbending as iron that breaks all opposition, just as He Himself received that authority from His Father.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls it an allusion to Psalm 2:9. JFB traces it to Psalm 2:8-9 and notes the Septuagint, reading the Hebrew vowels differently, has rule as a shepherd, as here. Gill on Psalm 2:9 says the verse is cited in Revelation 2:27.
layers.text: The promise comes from Psalm 2:9, where God tells His anointed King, "You will break them with an iron scepter; You will shatter them like pottery." John's Greek word for rule means to shepherd, as in the old Greek translation of the Psalm. The King now shares His rule with those who overcome.

passages.saying: I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's three promises to the one who overcomes.
layers.text: Jesus promises the believer who overcomes three things: white clothing, a name that will never be erased from the Book of Life, and His own open acknowledgment of that person before the Father and His angels.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Exodus 32 say the book Moses names is the book of life, which reappears in Revelation 3:5. JFB lists Exodus 32:32 first among the Old Testament passages on the book of life.
layers.text: This Book of Life is likely the book Moses spoke of when he pleaded for sinful Israel, "please blot me out of the book that You have written." The LORD replied that He would blot out whoever sinned against Him. Jesus promises the one who overcomes that his name will never be blotted out.

passages.saying: who holds the key of David
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's titles of Christ and the key as a sign of authority.
layers.text: Jesus speaks to the church in Philadelphia as the Holy and True One who holds full authority in God's kingdom. When He opens a door, no one can shut it, and when He shuts one, no one can open it.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it an allusion to Isaiah 22:22 and says the words applied to Christ show His authority is absolute. Barnes says the phrase is manifestly taken from Isaiah 22:22. Wesley ties the key to the one given to Eliakim.
layers.text: The words come from Isaiah 22:22, where God gives Eliakim, steward of the royal palace, the key to the house of David: "What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open." Eliakim held that key for a king; Jesus holds it as His own.

passages.saying: I will make them come and bow down at your feet
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's promise to the church in Philadelphia.
layers.text: Jesus tells the faithful church in Philadelphia that those who claim to be Jews but are not will one day come and bow at their feet, and will know that He loves this church.

layers.evidence: Gill on Isaiah 60:14 says what Isaiah foretells there is what is promised to the church in Philadelphia, citing Revelation 3:9. Barnes on Isaiah 60:14 points to Revelation 3:9 for the bowing at Zion's feet.
layers.text: The promise echoes Isaiah 60:14, where God tells Zion, "The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you." Jesus gives that promise to His faithful church: those who opposed it will bow at its feet and see that He loves it.

passages.saying: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true Witness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's three titles of Christ.
layers.text: Jesus speaks to the church in Laodicea as the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, and the Originator of God's creation. Every word He is about to say to them is wholly true and carries His full authority.

layers.evidence: Clarke derives Amen from the Hebrew aman and says the verse interprets it as the faithful and true witness. Barnes says Amen means true, certain, faithful. JFB points to Isaiah 65:16, where the Hebrew reads the God of Amen.
layers.text: Jesus calls Himself the Amen. The word comes from the Hebrew aman, to be true and faithful, and the verse explains it at once: the faithful and true Witness. In Isaiah 65:16 the LORD is twice called "the God of truth," which in Hebrew is the God of Amen.

passages.saying: Those I love, I rebuke and discipline
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's link between Christ's love and His correction.
layers.text: Jesus tells the lukewarm church in Laodicea that His sharp rebuke and discipline come from love, not rejection. Because He corrects those He loves, they should turn from their indifference in earnest and repent.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the language is taken from Proverbs 3:12. JFB heads its comment with Proverbs 3:11-12 and its use in Hebrews 12:5-6.
layers.text: Jesus' words echo Proverbs 3:12: "the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights." What Proverbs says of the LORD, Jesus says of Himself, so His hard words to Laodicea are a father's loving correction.

layers.evidence: JFB notes the alliteration of hot (zestos) and be zealous (zeleue) and traces both to zeo, to boil; the sound link is plain in the Greek, though the shared root is that commentary's view.
layers.text: In John's Greek, the call to be earnest, zeleue, sounds like zestos, the word for hot in verse 15. The church that was neither hot nor cold is called to burn with zeal.

passages.saying: I stand at the door and knock
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jesus' own words to the church in Laodicea (Revelation 3:14) and the everyday picture of a visitor knocking.
layers.text: Speaking to the church in Laodicea, Jesus says He stands at the door and knocks. Whoever hears His voice and opens the door, He will come in and dine with him, and that person with Him, a picture of warm and close fellowship.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Song 5:2 on this verse and says Song 5:4-6 is plainly alluded to, likening the drowsy bride to lukewarm Laodicea. Matthew Henry's Concise, on Song 5:2, ties the Beloved's knocking to Revelation 3:20.
layers.text: This echoes the Song of Solomon, where the bride, half asleep, hears, "My beloved is knocking," and he calls, "Open to me." Jesus' words to lukewarm Laodicea picture the same loving knock, waiting for His people to open the door.

passages.saying: a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own description of the One on the throne and the rainbow around it.
layers.text: John sees God seated on His throne, shining like jasper and carnelian, with a rainbow like an emerald all around the throne. God is pictured by His brilliant glory, not by any shape or form.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley all read the rainbow around the throne as the covenant sign God gave Noah after the flood (Genesis 9:9-13). William Tong (Matthew Henry's Commentary) also calls it an emblem of the covenant.
layers.text: After the flood God said, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds," as the sign of His covenant. The rainbow circling His throne in heaven recalls that promise, showing God's covenant mercy surrounding His rule.

layers.evidence: Gill on Ezekiel 1:28 says this part of the vision agrees with Revelation 4:3. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible also link Ezekiel's bow in the cloud to Revelation 4:3, and Wesley's note on Ezekiel 1:28 does the same.
layers.text: Ezekiel also saw the Lord on His throne with brilliant light all around Him, like "a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day." John's vision of the throne with a rainbow around it recalls that scene.

passages.saying: From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings, and peals of thunder
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which also names the seven torches as the seven Spirits of God.
layers.text: Lightning, rumblings and thunder come out from God's throne, showing His majesty and power. Before the throne burn seven torches of fire, which are the seven Spirits of God.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to the giving of the law on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:16). Barnes says the scene at once recalls Sinai, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares the giving of the law on Sinai.
layers.text: When God came down on Mount Sinai to give the law, "there was thunder and lightning," and all the people trembled. Lightning and thunder now come from His throne in heaven, recalling that scene and showing His majesty.

passages.saying: four living creatures, covered with eyes in front and back
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of the scene before and around the throne.
layers.text: Before God's throne John sees what looks like a sea of glass, clear as crystal. In the center, around the throne, stand four living creatures covered with eyes in front and back.

layers.evidence: Barnes on this verse points to the wheels full of eyes in Ezekiel 1:18 as emblems of the same thing. The Companion Bible identifies the living creatures as Ezekiel's cherubim and cites Ezekiel 10:12 for their eyes.
layers.text: In Ezekiel's vision the living creatures, which he calls cherubim, were full of eyes all around, and so were the rims of their wheels. The eye-covered creatures at God's throne recall that scene, picturing a God who sees everything.

passages.saying: The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's list of the four creatures; the Greek word for calf can mean a young bull.
layers.text: John describes the four living creatures around God's throne. The first was like a lion, the second like a calf or young ox, the third had a face like a man, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight.

layers.evidence: Gill says the calf, which the Greek can call an ox, agrees with Ezekiel 1:10. Wesley says the four cherubim in Ezekiel, who supported the moving throne of God, were just such.
layers.text: Ezekiel saw four living creatures, each with the face of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. John sees the same four likenesses around God's throne, though here each creature bears one of them.

passages.saying: Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of the creatures and the words of their unending song.
layers.text: Each of the four living creatures has six wings and is covered with eyes. Day and night they never stop praising God as holy, the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes and Wesley all compare the six wings and the threefold Holy with the seraphim of Isaiah 6:2-3. The Companion Bible also points to Isaiah 6:3.
layers.text: Isaiah saw six-winged seraphim above the Lord's throne, calling, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts." In heaven John hears six-winged creatures give the same threefold cry before God's throne, without ceasing.

passages.saying: It had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of the scroll and its seals.
layers.text: John sees a scroll in the right hand of God on the throne. It has writing on both sides, so it is full, and it is sealed shut with seven seals, so no one can read it until the seals are opened.

layers.evidence: Gill says this scroll was very much like Ezekiel's roll, written within and without, and on Ezekiel 2:10 he says the book John saw was of the same kind. The Companion Bible on Ezekiel 2:10 also compares Revelation 5:1.
layers.text: When God called Ezekiel, He unrolled before him a scroll with writing on the front and back, full of lament and woe. The scroll in God's hand, with writing on both sides, recalls that full scroll Ezekiel was given.

passages.saying: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the elder's words in the verse and on Jesus' descent from Judah and David.
layers.text: One of the elders tells John not to weep. Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Root of David, has won the victory, so He is able to open the scroll and its seven seals.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all say the title alludes to Jacob's prophecy over Judah in Genesis 49:9. Wesley and the Companion Bible point to the same blessing.
layers.text: Jacob blessed his son by saying, "Judah is a young lion." Jesus, born from Judah's tribe, is called the Lion of that tribe, the strong and royal One to whom that blessing pointed.

layers.evidence: Gill links the title to the Root of Jesse in Isaiah 11:10. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley point to Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10, and Clarke to Isaiah 11:1; Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley explain that Christ is both David's offspring and, as God, David's source.
layers.text: Isaiah foretold that "the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples." Jesse was David's father. Calling Jesus the Root of David points to that promise: He is David's descendant and also the source from whom David came.

passages.saying: Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Wesley reads the wounds as the marks of Christ's death and the horns and eyes as perfect strength and wisdom.
layers.text: John sees Jesus as a Lamb standing alive yet bearing the marks of having been slain. His seven horns picture complete power, and His seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth, picture complete knowledge and watchful care.

layers.evidence: Wesley points to Zechariah 3:9 and 4:10, where the seven eyes of the Lord go forth over all the earth. Gill also sends readers to Zechariah 3:9 for the Lamb's seven eyes.
layers.text: The Lamb's seven eyes, sent out into all the earth, echo Zechariah's vision of the seven eyes of the LORD, which scan the whole earth. Here they picture the Lamb's perfect knowledge.

passages.saying: golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which explains the incense as the saints' prayers.
layers.text: When the Lamb takes the scroll, the living creatures and elders fall down and worship Him. They hold harps for praise and golden bowls full of incense, and John explains that the incense is the prayers of God's people.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all point to Psalm 141:2, where prayer is compared to incense offered before God.
layers.text: The incense that stands for the prayers of the saints recalls David's prayer in Psalm 141, "May my prayer be set before You like incense." The prayers of God's people rise before His throne like sweet incense.

passages.saying: their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which describes the angels encircling the throne.
layers.text: Around the throne John hears a vast host of angels, too many to count, joining the living creatures and the elders in praising the Lamb.

layers.evidence: Clarke says this is in reference to Daniel 7:10, Barnes that the language seems taken from it, and Gill that it seems to refer to the like number there. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes also point to Daniel 7:10.
layers.text: The angels numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands echo Daniel's vision of God's throne, where thousands upon thousands attended Him and myriads upon myriads stood before Him. Such a countless host now gathers to honor the Lamb.

passages.saying: So I looked and saw a white horse
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Wesley reads the white color and the bow as signs of victory.
layers.text: When the Lamb opens the first seal, John sees a white horse whose rider holds a bow and is given a crown, and he rides out to conquer. Christians have understood this rider in different ways, but the white horse, bow and crown all speak of victory.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown tells readers to compare Zechariah 1:7-17 and 6:1-8 and the colors of the four horses. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), on Zechariah 6:6, explains the red, black and white horses there alongside the horses of Revelation 6.
layers.text: The four horses of the seals, white, red, black and pale green, recall Zechariah's visions of red, black, white and dappled horses that the LORD sent out to patrol the earth. As in Zechariah, these riders go out over the earth, acting by the authority they are given.

passages.saying: to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Clarke reads the four means of death as war, famine, pestilence and wild beasts.
layers.text: The fourth seal brings a pale green horse whose rider is Death, with Hades following behind. They are given power over a fourth of the earth to kill by war, famine, plague and wild beasts.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes and Gill each tie these four judgments to Ezekiel 14:21. Barnes notes that the Septuagint renders Ezekiel's word for plague with thanatos, death, as here.
layers.text: Death's four weapons, sword, famine, plague and wild beasts, are the same four dire judgments God named against Jerusalem in Ezekiel 14:21. In John's Greek the word for plague is simply death, just as in the old Greek translation of Ezekiel.

passages.saying: How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Wesley explains that God's holiness and truth require Him to judge.
layers.text: The souls of those killed for God's word cry out to their Master, holy and true, asking how long until He judges the people of the earth and avenges their blood. They do not doubt that He will act; they ask when.

layers.evidence: Clarke says their blood, like Abel's, cried for vengeance, and Bullinger's Companion Bible notes compare the cry with Abel's blood in Genesis 4:10.
layers.text: The slain saints asking God to avenge their blood recalls Abel, whose blood cried out to God from the ground after Cain killed him. God heard Abel's blood, and He will answer for the blood of His servants too.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Zechariah 1:12, says Messiah's people pray as their Head did there and points to this verse's cry of how long.
layers.text: The martyrs' cry of how long is like that of the angel of the LORD in Zechariah, who asked the LORD of Hosts how long He would withhold mercy from Jerusalem. Some see that angel as Christ, and His people here praying as He did for God to act.

passages.saying: the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; the Concise Commentary, abridging William Tong's continuation of Matthew Henry, calls these signs prophetic emblems of the day of judgment.
layers.text: When the Lamb opens the sixth seal, a great earthquake strikes, the sun turns black like sackcloth and the whole moon turns blood red. These are signs of the great day of God's wrath that the rest of the chapter describes.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties the blood red moon to Joel 2:31. Barnes, on Isaiah 13:10, sets this verse beside the prophets' pictures of a darkened sun, moon and stars as figures of God's judgment.
layers.text: The black sun and blood red moon use the prophets' language for the Day of the LORD. Joel foretold that the sun would be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before that great day, and Isaiah pictured sun, moon and stars going dark when God judges.

passages.saying: The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown pictures the sky rolled up and laid aside like an open scroll.
layers.text: As the sixth seal goes on, the sky is pulled back like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island is moved from its place. The whole created world is shaken as God's judgment comes.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Isaiah 34:4, says the language of Revelation 6:14 seems borrowed from it and that the fig picture recurs in Revelation 6:13. Barnes sends readers to Isaiah 34:4 for the rolled up sky, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites it for the falling figs.
layers.text: The sky rolling up like a scroll echoes Isaiah 34:4, where the skies will be rolled up like a scroll when God judges the nations. The verse before, with stars falling like figs from a tree in the wind, draws on the same verse in Isaiah.

passages.saying: hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's list of every class of people, which shows the terror reaching all alike.
layers.text: When the sixth seal is opened, people of every rank, from kings, nobles and commanders to slaves and free men, run to hide in caves and among the rocks. No rank, wealth or strength can shelter anyone from the judgment of God and the Lamb.

layers.evidence: Barnes, on this passage, says the cry of Revelation 6:16 is found substantially in Hosea 10:8 and was used by Jesus in Luke 23:30. Keil and Delitzsch, on Hosea 10:8, say Christ applied these words to the fall of Jerusalem in Luke 23:30, and Revelation 6:16 to the last judgment. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown there points to both passages.
layers.text: In the next verse they cry to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us." Hosea foretold that Israel under judgment would say this, and Jesus repeated it on the way to the cross, warning of the days coming on Jerusalem.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Isaiah 2:19, say Revelation 6:15 borrows this description and that it shows the prophet is describing the last judgment.
layers.text: Hiding in caves and among the rocks borrows Isaiah's picture of the day of the LORD: "Men will flee to caves in the rocks and holes in the ground, away from the terror of the LORD" when He rises to shake the earth.

passages.saying: until we have sealed the foreheads of the servants of our God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the order to hold back all harm until the sealing is done.
layers.text: An angel tells the four angels who hold back the winds not to harm land, sea or trees until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads. God marks and protects His own before judgment falls.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it manifestly an allusion to Ezekiel 9:4. Gill likens the seal to the mark on the foreheads of those who sighed and cried in Jerusalem. Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also point to Ezekiel 9.
layers.text: The sealing recalls Ezekiel's vision, where a mark was put "on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning" over Jerusalem's sins before judgment began, and the executioners were told not to touch anyone with the mark.

passages.saying: wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the crowd's cry in the next verse, read as the redeemed gathered before God.
layers.text: John sees a crowd too large to count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and the Lamb in white robes and holding palm branches. They cry out that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the palm branch was used at the Feast of Tabernacles in thanksgiving for the gathered harvest. Gill links the palms to Leviticus 23:40 and to God's tabernacle among them. Bullinger's Companion Bible compares the great hosanna of Tabernacles.
layers.text: The palm branches recall the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel took "the branches of palm trees" and rejoiced before the LORD after the harvest. Here a great harvest from every nation rejoices before the throne, and God spreads His tabernacle over them.

passages.saying: Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 14 to 17, which describe the lasting comfort of the redeemed before God's throne.
layers.text: Those who came out of the great tribulation will never again suffer hunger, thirst or burning heat. The Lamb will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes both say the words are taken from Isaiah 49:10, and Barnes adds that the wiping away of tears is taken from Isaiah 25:8. Bullinger's Companion Bible says the two verses refer to Isaiah 49:8-10 and 25:8.
layers.text: These lines take up Isaiah's promise to God's returning people: "They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them," for He will lead them beside springs of water. The wiping away of tears comes from Isaiah 25:8.

passages.saying: hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on the pattern of the first four trumpets, which strike land, sea, rivers and sky.
layers.text: When the first angel blows his trumpet, hail and fire mixed with blood are thrown down on the earth, burning up a third of the land and of the trees and all the green grass. The first four trumpets strike the natural world.

layers.evidence: Gill likens it to the plague of hail mingled with fire in Exodus 9:23. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the language is evidently drawn from the plagues of Egypt, naming the hail and fire of Exodus 9:24. Wesley and Clarke note the same.
layers.text: This echoes the seventh plague on Egypt, when the LORD sent hail with lightning (in Hebrew, fire) flashing through it, and it "beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree." Here too hail and fire fall on trees and grass.

passages.saying: The name of the star is Wormwood
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 10 and 11, read as a picture of bitter calamity.
layers.text: At the third trumpet a great star, burning like a torch, falls on a third of the rivers and springs. Its name is Wormwood. The waters turn bitter, and many people die from drinking them.

layers.evidence: Gill says there seems to be an allusion to Exodus 15:23. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown draws the contrast with Marah, where bitter water was made sweet.
layers.text: Waters made so bitter that people die recall Marah, whose name means bitter, where Israel could not drink the water because it was bitter. There the LORD made the bitter water sweet for His people; here, in judgment, the waters are made bitter.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the star is so called from its bitter effects. Barnes says the name describes its qualities and that wormwood is the emblem of bitterness, comparing Jeremiah 9:15 and 23:15. Gill likens it to Naomi calling herself Mara.
layers.text: Wormwood is a plant with a very bitter taste, and the star's name tells what it does. In John's Greek the same word, apsinthos, names the star and what the waters become. The prophets use wormwood for bitter judgment, as in Jeremiah 9:15.

passages.saying: the locusts looked like horses prepared for battle
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 7 to 9, which describe the locusts in the terms of an armed host.
layers.text: At the fifth trumpet, locusts come out of the smoke of the Abyss. John describes them as an army: like horses ready for battle, with what looked like gold crowns, human faces, lions' teeth, iron breastplates, and wings that roar like chariots.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the description appears to be taken from Joel 2:4 and calls the sound of the wings a simile borrowed from Joel 2:5-7. Gill compares Joel 2:4 for the horses and Joel 1:6 for the lions' teeth. Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also point to Joel 2.
layers.text: John's locusts recall Joel's locust army, whose appearance is "like that of horses," with "the teeth of a lion" and a sound "like that of chariots." Joel tied that plague to the day of the LORD, and John uses the same picture for this judgment.

passages.saying: His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself: the locusts are led and ruled by one king, the angel of the Abyss.
layers.text: The locusts that come up from the Abyss have a king over them, the angel of the Abyss. John gives this king's name twice, first in Hebrew and then in Greek.

layers.evidence: Clarke derives Abaddon from the Hebrew abad, he destroyed, and Apollyon from the Greek for destroy, with the same meaning in both. Barnes, Gill and Wesley agree that both names mean destroyer. The Companion Bible ties Abaddon to the destruction of Job 26:6 and Proverbs 15:11, here personified as the Destroyer.
layers.text: Abaddon is Hebrew for destruction, and Apollyon is Greek for destroyer. John gives the name in both languages, and both say the same thing: this king is the Destroyer. In Job, Abaddon is the place of destruction, named beside Sheol, the realm of the dead.

passages.saying: which cannot see or hear or walk
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself: the judgments did not bring the survivors to repentance.
layers.text: Even after these plagues, the rest of mankind did not repent. They kept worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, things that cannot see or hear or walk.

layers.evidence: Gill, describing idols that neither see, hear nor walk, points to Psalm 115:4, and in his note on that psalm he points back to Revelation 9:20. The Companion Bible: compare Psalm 115:4-8.
layers.text: The list echoes Psalm 115, which mocks idols of silver and gold made by human hands. They have eyes but cannot see, ears but cannot hear, and feet but cannot walk. People in John's vision still worship things that can do nothing for them.

passages.saying: lifted up his right hand to heaven
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the oath that follows in verse 6; raising the hand to heaven was the usual way of swearing.
layers.text: The mighty angel standing on the sea and the land raises his right hand toward heaven. This is the gesture of someone taking an oath, and in the next verse he swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call this an allusion to Daniel 12 and set Revelation 10:5-6 beside Daniel 12:7, noting the contrast between Daniel's time, times and a half and the angel's oath of no more delay. Gill and Wesley both note that the man in Daniel lifted up both hands; Gill takes him to be the same angel, and Wesley thinks it likely. Barnes also points to Daniel 12:7.
layers.text: Daniel saw a man dressed in linen above the river raise both hands toward heaven and swear by Him who lives forever that the end would come after a time, and times, and half a time. John's angel raises his right hand and swears by the same eternal God that there will be no more delay.

passages.saying: in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; eating the scroll is a picture of fully taking in and understanding its message.
layers.text: John asks the angel for the small scroll and is told to eat it. It will taste as sweet as honey but turn his stomach bitter. Eating the scroll pictures taking God's message fully into himself.

layers.evidence: Gill: the scroll was to John as Ezekiel's roll was to him when he ate it. Wesley: the like was commanded to Ezekiel. Barnes points to the same command in Ezekiel 3:1. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Ezekiel 3:3, note that in both books the sweetness is followed by bitterness (Ezekiel 3:14).
layers.text: Ezekiel was also handed a scroll and told to eat it, and it was as sweet as honey in his mouth. Afterward he went away in bitterness. John's scroll works the same way: God's word is sweet to receive, but the suffering it foretells is bitter.

passages.saying: Go and measure the temple of God and the altar
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; the Concise Commentary, abridging William Tong's continuation of Matthew Henry, reads the measuring as God's care for His church in times of danger.
layers.text: John is given a measuring rod like a staff and told to measure God's temple and its altar, and to count those who worship there.

layers.evidence: The Concise Commentary, abridging William Tong's continuation of Matthew Henry, says the measuring of the temple seems to refer to Ezekiel's vision. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to Ezekiel 40:3 and 5, where the temple is also measured with the measuring reed. Clarke and Gill also cite Ezekiel 40:3.
layers.text: In Ezekiel's vision of a new temple, a man with a linen cord and a measuring rod stood in the gateway and then measured the temple part by part. John's vision likely takes up the same scene, but now John himself is handed the rod and told to measure.

passages.saying: the two olive trees and the two lampstands
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; the trees and lampstands are pictures of the two witnesses.
layers.text: The two witnesses of verse 3 are pictured as two olive trees and two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth, serving in His presence.

layers.evidence: Barnes: there can be little doubt of an allusion to Zechariah 4:3, 11 and 14, with the imagery changed. Clarke: the whole account seems taken from Zechariah 4, where the olive trees stand for Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill, Wesley and the Companion Bible agree.
layers.text: In Zechariah's vision two olive trees stand beside a golden lampstand and supply its oil. They are the two anointed ones standing beside the Lord of all the earth, Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor. Zechariah saw one lampstand; John sees two.

passages.saying: power to shut the sky so that no rain will fall
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; to shut the sky means to hold back the rain.
layers.text: During their time of prophesying, the two witnesses can hold back the rain, turn water into blood, and strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.

layers.evidence: Clarke: power to shut heaven, as Elijah did, and to turn the waters to blood, as Moses did. Barnes sees an allusion to Elijah in 1 Kings 17:1 and to Egypt in Exodus 7:17. Gill sees the same two allusions, to Elijah's drought in 1 Kings 17:1 and to Moses and Aaron turning the waters of Egypt into blood in Exodus 7:20. Wesley: as Moses did those in Egypt.
layers.text: These are the signs of two great prophets. Elijah told King Ahab there would be neither dew nor rain except at his word, and through Moses and Aaron the water of the Nile was turned to blood. The two witnesses are given the power of both.

passages.saying: figuratively called Sodom and Egypt
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; the Greek word for figuratively marks Sodom and Egypt as symbolic names, not the city's literal name.
layers.text: The bodies of the two witnesses lie in the street of the great city. That city is given the figurative names Sodom and Egypt, and it is the place where their Lord was also crucified.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Sodom is the very term Isaiah 1:10 applied to apostate Jerusalem, compare Ezekiel 16:48. Wesley also points to Isaiah 1:9, and the Companion Bible to Isaiah 1:9-10 and Ezekiel 16:46.
layers.text: Calling a city Sodom was already the prophets' language. Isaiah addressed the leaders of Jerusalem as "you rulers of Sodom," and Ezekiel told Jerusalem that her sister Sodom never did as she had done. The name says the city has become as wicked as Sodom.

passages.saying: the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says this directly; the commentaries explain it as God bringing His silenced witnesses back to life.
layers.text: After three and a half days, God breathes life back into the two witnesses whom the beast had killed. They stand up on their feet, and everyone watching is struck with great fear at seeing God raise them.

layers.evidence: Gill says the phrase is in allusion to the breathing on the dry bones in Ezekiel's vision; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that 'stood upon their feet' are the very words of Ezekiel 37:10.
layers.text: This echoes Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where breath entered the dead and "they came to life and stood on their feet." As God raised that lifeless army, so He raises His slain witnesses by His own breath.

layers.evidence: Barnes says there is evidently an allusion to Genesis 2:7, where God is the Author of life; the Companion Bible renders the phrase 'breath of life' and points to Genesis 2:7.
layers.text: The words breath of life may also recall creation, when the LORD God breathed the breath of life into the first man and he became a living being. The God who first gave life gives it again to His witnesses.

passages.saying: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The heavenly voices state it outright; the commentaries take it as the final victory of God's kingdom.
layers.text: When the seventh angel blows his trumpet, loud voices in heaven announce that rule over the whole world now belongs to God and to His Christ. His reign will never end.

layers.evidence: Gill points to Psalm 2:2, 'where the same distinction is' between the Lord and His Anointed; Wesley says the world's kings have risen 'against the Lord and against his Anointed' and that God now ends this rebellion.
layers.text: Pairing the Lord with His Christ, His Anointed, recalls Psalm 2, where earthly kings rise up "against the LORD and against His Anointed One." Here that rebellion is over, and the world's kingdom belongs to the Lord and His Anointed.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the verse parallel to Daniel 2:44; Barnes points to his notes on Daniel 2:44-45 and 7:13-14 for the same everlasting kingdom.
layers.text: The never-ending reign echoes Daniel's prophecy that the God of heaven would set up "a kingdom that will never be destroyed," one that would shatter the kingdoms before it and itself stand forever.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the title Christ, the Anointed, is equivalent to King; Wesley notes that kings especially were anointed, so the Messiah's kingdom is always implied; Barnes explains it as His anointed, the Messiah.
layers.text: Christ means the Anointed One, the same title as the Hebrew Messiah. Prophets and priests were anointed, but the title belonged above all to kings, so it fits the moment when the world's kingdom becomes His.

passages.saying: to destroy those who destroy the earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse lists these events itself; the commentaries read it as God's final judgment and reward.
layers.text: The elders say the nations raged, but now God's wrath has come. It is time to judge the dead, to reward His prophets, saints and all who fear Him, small and great, and to destroy those who ruin the earth.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the words allude to Psalm 99:1 as the Septuagint renders it, 'The Lord is become King: let the peoples become angry'; Gill also points to Psalm 99:1 in the Septuagint.
layers.text: The raging nations echo Psalm 99, which begins, "The LORD reigns; let the nations tremble!" In the old Greek translation of that psalm, the peoples are told to be angry instead. Here too, as God begins to reign, the nations rage.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says to translate the two anger words alike 'as the Greek is the same' and calls the destroying of the destroyers retribution in kind; Wesley likewise speaks of God destroying the destroyers.
layers.text: In John's Greek, judgment echoes the sin in the very words used. The nations were angry (orgizo), and now God's anger (orge) has come. God will destroy (diaphtheiro) those who destroy (diaphtheiro) the earth. They reap exactly what they sowed.

passages.saying: a woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries agree the woman is a symbol of God's people rather than a single person.
layers.text: John sees a great sign in heaven: a woman dressed in the sun, standing on the moon, with a crown of twelve stars on her head. She pictures God's people, Israel and the church that grew from it.

layers.evidence: Wesley notes that in Joseph's dream the sun meant his father, the moon his mother and the stars their children, sees some such resemblance here, and takes the twelve stars as the twelve tribes of Israel.
layers.text: The sun, moon and stars likely recall Joseph's dream of "the sun and moon and eleven stars" bowing to him, which stood for his father, mother and brothers. Read this way, the woman's crown of twelve stars points to the twelve tribes of Israel.

layers.evidence: Barnes says Song of Solomon 6:10 was very possibly in the writer's mind when he penned this description.
layers.text: Her shining look may also echo the Song of Solomon, which praises one who shines like the dawn, "as fair as the moon, as bright as the sun."

passages.saying: His tail swept a third of the stars from the sky
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse describes the scene; the commentaries see in it a picture of the dragon's power.
layers.text: The dragon's tail drags a third of the stars out of the sky and flings them to the earth, showing his great power. Then he stands before the woman in labor, waiting to devour her child the moment it is born.

layers.evidence: Gill says this is said in allusion to Daniel 8:10; Barnes sets beside it Daniel's words about the little horn that cast down some of the host and of the stars to the ground.
layers.text: The picture echoes Daniel's vision of a proud horn that "grew as high as the host of heaven" and threw some of the stars down to the earth. In both, an enemy of God's people strikes even at the lights of heaven.

layers.evidence: Gill compares the dragon to Pharaoh, the dragon of the Nile, slaying Israel's male children as soon as born, and to Herod; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the dragon, through Pharaoh, was ready to devour Israel's males, and through Herod sought the infant Jesus.
layers.text: The dragon waiting to devour the newborn recalls Pharaoh ordering every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile. Herod later tried the same against the infant Jesus.

passages.saying: who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse says this directly; the commentaries note the child is taken entirely out of the dragon's reach.
layers.text: The woman gives birth to a son, a male child destined to rule all the nations with an iron scepter. Her child is snatched up to God and to His throne, out of the dragon's reach.

layers.evidence: Gill calls it a manifest reference to Psalm 2:9; Barnes says the language is derived from Psalm 2:9 and the verb from its Septuagint, meaning to rule as a shepherd; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the verb means to tend as a shepherd and that Psalm 2:9 proves the Lord Jesus is meant.
layers.text: The iron scepter comes from Psalm 2, where God tells His anointed King, "You will break them with an iron scepter." In John's Greek, as in the old Greek of the psalm, the word for rule is a shepherd's word: this King both tends and subdues the nations.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, commenting on Isaiah 66:7, say that Zion the mother is no other than the woman clothed with the sun in Revelation 12, while the child born of her there is the shepherd of the nations.
layers.text: Isaiah pictured Zion as a mother who gave birth to a boy before her labor pains came. Some see John's woman as that same mother Zion, though the son she bears here is the Messiah, the shepherd of the nations.

passages.saying: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse describes the battle; the commentaries explain it as faithful angels meeting the rebel angels and their leader.
layers.text: John sees war break out in heaven. Michael and his angels fight against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fight back. Rebel angels began the revolt, and faithful angels led by their archangel meet them.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the reference to Michael is probably derived from Daniel 10:13 and 12:1, where he guards God's people; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the battle to Daniel 10:13 and calls Michael the prince of the Jewish nation.
layers.text: Michael comes from Daniel, where he is "the great prince who stands watch over your people" and fights against hostile powers on Israel's behalf. Here he leads heaven's armies against the dragon.

layers.evidence: Wesley says Michael signifies 'Who is like God?' and that the name rebukes Satan, who would be like God; Gill gives the same meaning, 'who is as God,' though he takes Michael to be Christ.
layers.text: The name Michael is Hebrew for Who is like God? Some see in it a fitting answer to the dragon's pride: no one, not even Satan, is like God.

passages.saying: that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse names the dragon itself; the commentaries explain his casting down to the earth.
layers.text: The great dragon, Satan, the deceiver of the whole world, is thrown out of heaven and hurled down to the earth together with his angels. There he wages war against God's people for a time.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the phrase alludes to Genesis 3:1; Wesley calls it an allusion to his deceiving Eve in that form; Barnes says it doubtless refers to the serpent that deceived Eve, showing the tempter was the devil.
layers.text: Calling the dragon "that ancient serpent" points back to Eden, where the serpent deceived Eve. The same old enemy who deceived the first woman is "the deceiver of the whole world," and now he is thrown down.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Isaiah 27:1, says hostile powers are described the same way in Revelation 12:3 and that antitypically and ultimately Satan is intended; Gill, on the same verse, says Satan, called the dragon, the old serpent and devil, must be taken into the account.
layers.text: The dragon and serpent also recall Isaiah's promise that the LORD will punish Leviathan the coiling serpent and "slay the dragon of the sea." Some see Satan as the final enemy behind that picture, here thrown down and later destroyed for good.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives devil as Greek for accuser or slanderer and Satan as Hebrew for adversary; Gill gives the same meanings and points to Job and Joshua the high priest; Wesley notes one name is Greek and the other Hebrew; the Companion Bible renders them slanderer and adversary.
layers.text: Devil is a Greek word meaning slanderer or accuser, and Satan is a Hebrew word meaning adversary. The next verse fits both names, calling him "the accuser of our brothers," as when he accused Job before God and stood to accuse Joshua the high priest.

passages.saying: the woman was given two wings of a great eagle
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, read with verse 6, where God prepares a place for the woman in the wilderness.
layers.text: When the dragon hunts the woman, who stands for God's people, she is given the wings of a great eagle to fly to her place in the wilderness. There God keeps her safe from the serpent and feeds her for a set time.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to God bearing Israel out of Egypt as on eagles' wings and through the wilderness (Exodus 19:4). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also says the verse alludes to Exodus 19:4 and calls it an eagle flight from Egypt into the wilderness.
layers.text: The eagle's wings recall the Exodus. At Sinai God reminded Israel that He had carried them on eagles' wings out of Egypt and brought them to Himself. Here God again carries His people out of danger into the wilderness and feeds them there.

layers.evidence: Barnes says there is plainly an allusion to Daniel and reckons the phrase as forty-two months. Gill explains the period by comparing Daniel 7:25 and 12:7. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties the Greek word for times (kairous) to Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, and on Daniel 7:25 equates the phrase with the 1,260 days of Revelation 12:6 and 12:14.
layers.text: The phrase “a time, and times, and half a time” comes from Daniel, where it is the span during which the saints are handed over to a proud persecutor before God ends his rule. One time, two times and half a time make three and a half, matching the 1,260 days of verse 6.

passages.saying: like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own description of the beast and the dragon's gift of power.
layers.text: The beast from the sea looks like a leopard, with a bear's feet and a lion's mouth, a picture of speed, strength and ferocity. The dragon, Satan, hands it his own power, his throne and great authority, so the beast acts as his agent.

layers.evidence: Barnes says John combined in one monster the beasts Daniel saw one after another. Gill matches the leopard, bear and lion to Daniel 7:6, 7:5 and 7:4. Clarke calls the leopard an allusion to Daniel's third beast. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agrees.
layers.text: In Daniel's vision a lion, a bear and a leopard rise from the sea one after another, standing for empires that follow each other. John sees one beast with the leopard's body, the bear's feet and the lion's mouth, as if all those empires were joined into a single power set against God.

passages.saying: Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's report of the world's worship and its words of praise.
layers.text: The world worships the dragon for giving the beast its authority, and worships the beast too. They praise it as beyond compare and unbeatable, giving a creature honor that belongs to God alone.

layers.evidence: Gill says the worshipers use expressions used of God Himself and points to Exodus 15:11. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it the very language belonging to God in Exodus 15:11, given blasphemously to the beast.
layers.text: The cry “Who is like the beast?” borrows the words of Israel's praise. After the Red Sea, Moses and Israel sang, “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” The beast's worshipers give a creature the very praise that belongs to God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the cry a parody of the name Michael, meaning Who is like God? Wesley, on Revelation 12:7, explains that Michael's name asks that question and contrasts it with Satan's wish to be like God.
layers.text: Michael, the angel who led the war against the dragon in the chapter before, has a Hebrew name meaning who is like God? (mi, ka, el). Some read the cry “Who is like the beast?” as a twist on that question, one that gives the beast the honor Michael's very name keeps for God.

passages.saying: The beast was given a mouth to speak arrogant and blasphemous words
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the word given, used twice in John's Greek, which shows the beast's power is allowed and limited.
layers.text: The beast is allowed to speak proud words and blasphemies against God and to act for 42 months. Its voice and power are stirred up by Satan, yet they are given, so they exist only by God's permission and only for a set time.

layers.evidence: Gill says the little horn of Daniel 7:8 likewise has a mouth speaking great things. Barnes says the language is the same as in Daniel 7:8 and that the matching period of 42 months shows the same power is meant as in Daniel.
layers.text: This echoes the little horn of Daniel's vision, which had a mouth that spoke words of arrogance and would speak out against the Most High. Daniel limits its rule to a time, and times, and half a time, which matches these 42 months.

passages.saying: the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, which say the beast was permitted to do this.
layers.text: God permits the beast to make war on His people and to conquer them, which means putting them to death, not making them give up their faith. The beast is also given authority over every tribe, people, tongue and nation.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls Daniel 7:21 the parallel passage and says the language is the same. The Companion Bible, on Daniel 7:21, says the phrase connects the little horn with Revelation 13:7. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Daniel 7:21, links it to Revelation 13:7 and notes the limit set by until in Daniel 7:22.
layers.text: These are nearly the words of Daniel's vision, where the horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them. Daniel adds that this lasted only until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints, who then received the kingdom.

passages.saying: to cause even fire from heaven to come down to earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on verse 14, which says these signs deceived the people of the earth.
layers.text: The second beast performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people. The next verse shows the purpose: by these signs it deceives the people of the earth and wins them over to the first beast.

layers.evidence: Gill says the beast does this in imitation of Elijah (2 Kings 1). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says this is the very miracle Elijah performed long ago, which the beast mimics. Barnes also compares Elijah bringing fire down on the sacrifice (1 Kings 18:37-38).
layers.text: Fire from heaven was the sign of the prophet Elijah, once on Mount Carmel to prove the LORD is God, and again on the soldiers sent to seize him. The second beast copies Elijah's sign: a false prophet imitating a true one in order to deceive.

passages.saying: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's call for wisdom and insight.
layers.text: John calls for wisdom: the one with insight should work out the number of the beast. It is the number of a man, and the number is 666. Believers need God-given wisdom so that they are not fooled by the beast.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the verse gives the beast's name under the number 666, since letters served as numbers. Barnes says 666 is expressed by his name by a known way of counting and works out Lateinos. Gill reports Irenaeus' early proposal Lateinos. The Companion Bible calls the method gematria.
layers.text: In Greek, as in Hebrew, letters also served as numbers, so the letters of a name could be added up. To calculate the beast's number most likely means adding up a name this way to reach 666. One very early guess was Lateinos, the Latin man, but the name remains uncertain.

passages.saying: And no lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of the 144,000 who stand with the Lamb.
layers.text: The 144,000 who stand with the Lamb are truthful: no lie or deceit is found in what they say, and they are truly what they profess to be. They stand blameless before God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Zephaniah 3:13, calls the remnant's refusal to speak lies the characteristic of the 144,000 sealed of Israel.
layers.text: Some hear an echo here of Zephaniah's promise that the faithful remnant of Israel will not speak lies, nor will a deceitful tongue be found in their mouths. The truthful remnant the prophet foresaw may be pictured here standing with the Lamb.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the allusion seems to be to Psalm 15:1-2 and points to the 144,000 standing on Mount Zion in Revelation 14:1.
layers.text: Psalm 15 asks, “Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?” It answers, “He who walks with integrity” and “who speaks the truth from his heart.” The truthful, blameless company standing with the Lamb on Mount Zion may echo that answer.

passages.saying: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's words in the verse; Clarke notes that fornication in Scripture often stands for idolatry and false worship.
layers.text: A second angel announces the fall of Babylon the great. She had led all the nations to drink the intoxicating wine of her immorality, a common Bible picture of idolatry and false worship.

layers.evidence: Gill says the very words are taken from the announcement of Babylon's fall in Isaiah 21:9, and makes the same link in his note there; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this the final fulfilment of Isaiah 21:9; the Companion Bible compares the two.
layers.text: The cry repeats Isaiah 21:9, where ancient Babylon's fall is announced with the words "Fallen, fallen is Babylon!" John hears the same announcement over a later Babylon, the great enemy of God's people, and her fall is just as certain.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Jeremiah 51:7, explains Babylon as the cup in God's hand that made the nations drunk, and points to Revelation 14:8 for spiritual Babylon.
layers.text: The picture of the nations drinking Babylon's wine also likely echoes Jeremiah, who called Babylon "a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk." Revelation uses the same picture for a later Babylon that intoxicates the nations.

layers.evidence: Gill notes on this verse that the name Babylon signifies confusion. The link rests on Genesis 11:9, where the Hebrew name Babel (the same name as Babylon) is tied to God confusing the languages.
layers.text: In Hebrew, Babylon and Babel are the same name. Genesis 11:9 links Babel with balal, a Hebrew word for confuse, because there "the LORD confused the language of the whole world." Some see that meaning, confusion, still fitting the Babylon named here.

passages.saying: he too will drink the wine of God’s anger
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words; Barnes explains that the undiluted wine means punishment at full strength, with no mitigation.
layers.text: Anyone who worships the beast will drink the wine of God's anger, poured out at full strength with nothing to soften it. He will be tormented in fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Psalm 75:8, says Revelation 14:10 refers to that passage; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Psalm 75:8 on this verse; the Companion Bible's note on Psalm 75:8 compares Revelation 14:10. Barnes also links the two.
layers.text: The cup of God's wrath likely draws on Psalm 75:8, where "a cup is in the hand of the LORD, full of foaming wine" and "all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." Here that wine is poured undiluted, with no water to weaken it.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all say the fire and brimstone allude to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Barnes cites Genesis 19:24.
layers.text: Fire and sulfur recall the judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah, when "the LORD rained down sulfur and fire" from heaven. That judgment becomes a picture of the punishment awaiting all who worship the beast.

layers.evidence: Gill and Clarke both say that those who drank the wine of Babylon's fornication in verse 8 will now drink the wine of God's wrath. The same Greek words, oinos and thumos, stand behind both verses (BSB passion in verse 8, anger here).
layers.text: In John's Greek the same phrase, the wine of thumos, appears in verse 8 and here. There it is the wine of Babylon's passion; here it is the wine of God's anger. Those who drank her wine must now drink His.

passages.saying: the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's words; Barnes explains that day and night means always, so they never have any rest.
layers.text: The punishment of those who worship the beast and receive its mark does not end. The smoke of their torment rises forever, and they have no rest day or night.

layers.evidence: Barnes, on Isaiah 34:10, says John copied this image to describe the woes of the wicked in Revelation 14:11; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cross-refers Isaiah 34:10 to this verse; the Companion Bible compares Isaiah 34:10 here. Gill links them as well.
layers.text: Isaiah described God's judgment on Edom as a fire never quenched day or night, adding, "Its smoke will ascend forever." John likely takes up the same picture of endless smoke for the final judgment on those who worship the beast.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls this still an allusion to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Barnes says the language is probably drawn from Genesis 19:28.
layers.text: The rising smoke also recalls the morning after Sodom's destruction, when Abraham "saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace." That ruin stands as a warning of the judgment to come.

passages.saying: seated on the cloud was One like the Son of Man
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on John's description; Gill and Barnes take the figure to be the Lord Jesus Christ.
layers.text: John sees One like the Son of Man, the title Jesus used for Himself, seated on a white cloud. He wears a golden crown and holds a sharp sickle, ready to reap the harvest of the earth.

layers.evidence: Gill says Daniel 7:13 holds a like vision of Christ referring to the same time; Barnes thinks there is probably a designed reference to Daniel here.
layers.text: The scene likely draws on Daniel's vision of "One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven," who was brought before the Ancient of Days. Here that same figure sits on a cloud, wearing a golden crown and holding a sickle for the harvest.

passages.saying: Swing Your sickle and reap
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Barnes explains the call is not the angel's own command but one from God the Father to the Son.
layers.text: An angel comes out of the temple with a message for the One seated on the cloud: the time to harvest has come, for the crop of the earth is ripe. The angel carries God's word; he gives no orders of his own.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Joel 3:13, reads the ripe harvest as ripeness for judgment and points to Revelation 14:15; the Companion Bible's note on Joel 3:13 compares Revelation 14:15 and 14:18; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Joel 3:13 cites Revelation 14:15-19.
layers.text: The call likely echoes Joel's summons to judgment: "Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe." Joel goes straight on to the winepress, and Revelation likewise moves from this harvest to the vintage and the winepress in verses 17 to 20.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the call alludes to Mark 4:29, where the sickle is likewise sent in as soon as the harvest is ready.
layers.text: The words may also recall Jesus' parable of the growing seed: "as soon as the grain is ripe, he swings the sickle, because the harvest has come." If so, here that moment arrives for the harvest of the whole earth.

passages.saying: they sang the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the words of the song; Clarke explains that God's ways are just and true because He keeps all His threats and promises.
layers.text: Those who have overcome the beast sing a song of praise. They call God's works great and wonderful and His ways just and true, and they hail Him as King of the nations.

layers.evidence: Gill identifies it as the song of Exodus 15:1, not Deuteronomy 32, and says they sang a song like it on a like occasion; Clarke says it is the song Moses sang after Israel crossed the Red Sea; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the song of the Lamb the antitype of the Red Sea song.
layers.text: The song of Moses was first sung beside the Red Sea, after God threw Pharaoh's horse and rider into the sea. Now the victors stand beside a sea of glass and praise God the same way for their own deliverance, joining Moses' song with the song of the Lamb.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls these words part of Moses' last song (Deuteronomy 32:3-4); Wesley says the song is named for Moses partly because it agrees with the song he taught Israel shortly before his death.
layers.text: The line "Just and true are Your ways" also echoes Moses' last song, which says of God, "all His ways are just." The redeemed praise God in words close to those Moses had used.

layers.evidence: Gill notes the reading King of nations and says this title and the opening of the next verse seem to be taken from Jeremiah 10:7; he makes the same link in his note on Jeremiah 10:7.
