layers.text: The title King of the nations, with the question about fearing God that follows, may echo Jeremiah's praise: "Who would not fear You, O King of nations?"

passages.saying: All nations will come and worship before You
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the song's words; Barnes explains that God's judgments on the beast would teach people to reverence and adore Him.
layers.text: The song asks who could fail to fear the Lord and glorify His name, for He alone is holy. It looks ahead to all nations coming to worship Him, because He has shown His righteous judgments openly.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Psalm 86:9, applies the psalm to the turning of the nations to God and points to Revelation 15:4, and on this verse says the words seem taken from Psalm 86. The Companion Bible, on the song of the Lamb in verse 3, says to compare Psalm 86:9-12.
layers.text: The promise likely takes up Psalm 86:9: "All the nations You have made will come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name." The psalm's hope that every nation will worship God is sung here as sure to come.

passages.saying: the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains that no one could enter because of God's presence in His glory and power while the judgments were carried out.
layers.text: Smoke from God's glory and power filled the temple in heaven, and no one could enter it until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the account is partly copied from the filling of Moses' tabernacle and Solomon's temple, and points to Isaiah 6:4; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Isaiah 6:4, Exodus 40:34 and 2 Chronicles 5:14; Wesley points to the cloud of glory in the tabernacle and temple.
layers.text: This recalls the day the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle and "Moses was unable to enter," and Solomon's temple, where "the priests could not stand there to minister." Isaiah too saw that "the temple was filled with smoke."

passages.saying: loathsome, malignant sores broke out on those who had the mark of the beast
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Wesley notes that the sores strike all who bear the beast's mark, and only them.
layers.text: The first angel pours his bowl out on the earth, and painful, festering sores break out on everyone who bears the mark of the beast and worships its image.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls this a reference to the sixth Egyptian plague of boils; Gill says it alludes to the plague of boils in Egypt; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it the antitype of that plague. Barnes notes that the Septuagint uses the same Greek word, helkos, for the boils of Exodus 9.
layers.text: The sores repeat the sixth plague on Egypt, when "festering boils broke out on man and beast" and even Pharaoh's magicians "could not stand before Moses." God judges the beast's followers as He once judged Egypt.

passages.saying: it turned to blood like that of the dead
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, which Wesley explains as the sea turned to thick, putrid blood.
layers.text: The second angel pours out his bowl of God's wrath into the sea. The sea turns to blood like the blood of a dead body, and every living creature in it dies.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the sea becoming blood answers to another Egyptian plague. Gill, on Exodus 7:21, says the Nile turned to blood looks ahead to the second and third bowls and cites Revelation 16:3.
layers.text: This bowl echoes the first plague on Egypt, when the Nile was turned to blood and the fish in it died. What God once did to Pharaoh's river He now does to the sea, showing that the God who judged Egypt will judge the enemies of His people at the end.

passages.saying: its kingdom was plunged into darkness
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Barnes explains the darkness as a picture of confusion and distress.
layers.text: The fifth angel pours out his bowl on the throne of the beast. Darkness falls over the beast's whole kingdom, and its people gnaw their tongues in anguish.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to the plague of darkness in Egypt (Exodus 10:21). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it parallel to the Egyptian plague of darkness, with Pharaoh as a type of the Antichrist.
layers.text: The darkness over the beast's kingdom recalls the ninth plague, when God sent a darkness over Egypt so thick it could be felt. As Pharaoh's land was darkened when he set himself against God, so is the kingdom of the beast.

passages.saying: its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Barnes explains the Euphrates as a barrier in the path of the kings of the East that is now removed.
layers.text: The sixth angel pours out his bowl on the great river Euphrates. Its water dries up, so the river no longer blocks the way for kings coming from the east.

layers.evidence: Clarke sees an allusion to the ruin of Babylon by Cyrus as Jeremiah foretold. Gill, on Jeremiah 50:38, says Cyrus drained the Euphrates to march into Babylon and applies this to the sixth bowl; on this verse he also points to Isaiah 44:27.
layers.text: Ancient Babylon stood on the Euphrates. Jeremiah foretold that her waters would dry up, and Cyrus took the city by turning the river aside and marching in along its bed. The drying of the same river here can be read as pointing to the fall of the later Babylon of the chapters that follow.

layers.evidence: Barnes says there is undoubtedly an allusion to the dividing of the Red Sea so Israel could pass, and points to Isaiah 11:15. Keil and Delitzsch, on Isaiah 11:15, liken God's stroke on the Egyptian sea there to the bowl poured out in Revelation 16:12.
layers.text: Drying up a river to open a road recalls the Red Sea, which God parted so Israel could cross. Isaiah promised a second such wonder, when God would strike the Euphrates and split it into streams that people could cross with dry sandals. Here the Euphrates is dried up again.

passages.saying: three unclean spirits that looked like frogs
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse read with verse 14; Barnes explains the frog-like spirits as evil powers, the spirits of devils.
layers.text: John sees three unclean spirits that look like frogs. They come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet, and the next verse says they are demonic spirits sent to gather the kings of the world for battle.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to the plague of frogs in Egypt (Exodus 8:5). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls these spirits the antitype to the plague of frogs sent on Egypt.
layers.text: Spirits that look like frogs recall the second plague on Egypt, when frogs came up from the rivers and ponds and covered the land. Like that plague, these unclean spirits spread over the earth, this time sent out by God's enemies to draw the kings into war.

passages.saying: the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse read with verse 14; Barnes explains it as a gathering of forces from the whole world to one battlefield.
layers.text: The kings of the whole world are gathered to one place, which John says is called Armageddon in Hebrew. They are assembled there for the battle on the great day of God the Almighty.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley all recall the defeat of the kings of Canaan at Megiddo (Judges 5:19), and Gill says it suggests the same fate for the powers gathered here. Clarke also notes Josiah's death there (2 Kings 23:29).
layers.text: Megiddo was a famous battlefield, where in the days of Deborah and Barak God routed the kings of Canaan by its waters, and where King Josiah later fell. Gathering the kings of the world at Armageddon hints that they will meet the same defeat as those Canaanite kings.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and the Companion Bible read the name as Hebrew har, mountain, joined to Megiddo, the town of Judges 5:19. Gill and Clarke give the same reading as the likely or a possible one.
layers.text: John says the place is called Armageddon in Hebrew. The name is most often read as Har Megiddo, meaning the mountain of Megiddo. Megiddo was a fortified town in northern Israel beside a wide plain where many battles were fought.

passages.saying: the great prostitute, who sits on many waters
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the angel's explanation in verse 15; Barnes takes the judgment as the condemnation coming upon her.
layers.text: One of the seven angels who had the bowls invites John to come and see God's judgment on the great prostitute who sits on many waters. Later in the chapter the angel explains that the waters stand for peoples, crowds, nations and languages.

layers.evidence: Gill says the phrase refers to Babylon on the Euphrates, said to dwell upon many waters in Jeremiah 51:13. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Jeremiah 51:13 for the many waters.
layers.text: The prostitute who sits on many waters echoes Jeremiah's words to ancient Babylon, the city on the Euphrates: 'You who dwell by many waters.' John's vision describes this new Babylon in the words once spoken of the old one, whose end had come.

passages.saying: She held in her hand a golden cup full of abominations
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Barnes explains the cup as held out to entice lovers.
layers.text: The woman is dressed in royal purple and scarlet and covered with gold, jewels and pearls. In her hand she holds a golden cup, but it is full of abominations and the filth of her sexual immorality.

layers.evidence: Gill says the golden cup is in allusion to Babylon in Jeremiah 51:7. Wesley writes that it is like the ancient Babylon, citing the same verse, and the Companion Bible also compares Jeremiah 51:7.
layers.text: The golden cup echoes Jeremiah's picture of ancient Babylon: 'Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk.' Like the old city, this woman holds out a splendid cup that makes the nations drunk, but what is inside is corrupt.

passages.saying: The ten horns you saw are ten kings
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's own explanation; Barnes reads one hour as a brief and temporary rule.
layers.text: The angel explains that the ten horns on the beast are ten kings who have not yet begun to reign. When they do, they will rule along with the beast for only one hour, a short time.

layers.evidence: Gill identifies these kings with the ten horns of the fourth beast in Daniel. Barnes sends readers to his notes on Daniel 7:24, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Daniel 7:24, links those horns to Revelation 17:12.
layers.text: The angel's explanation repeats what Daniel was told about the fourth beast in his vision: 'the ten horns are ten kings.' John's beast with ten horns takes up Daniel's picture of the last great world kingdom and the kings who rise from it.

passages.saying: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's announcement and the picture of a ruined city left to wild and unclean things.
layers.text: An angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen. The once proud city becomes a home for demons, unclean spirits, and unclean birds and beasts, a picture of complete and lasting ruin.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls the cry a quotation from Isaiah 21:9. Bullinger's Figures of Speech treats the doubled 'is fallen, is fallen' of Isaiah 21:9 as stressing the certainty and completeness of Babylon's fall and points to this verse, and the Companion Bible and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown refer the phrase to Isaiah 21:9.
layers.text: The angel's cry repeats Isaiah's announcement over ancient Babylon: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon!” (Isaiah 21:9). Saying the word twice stresses that the fall is certain and complete.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the language is taken from the description of Babylon in Isaiah 13:20-22, noting Isaiah's creatures dwelling there. Gill compares the demons here with the hairy creatures of ruined old Babylon in Isaiah 13:21.
layers.text: Isaiah foretold that ruined Babylon would be left to desert creatures, howling creatures, ostriches and wild goats (Isaiah 13:21-22). John uses the same picture: the fallen city becomes a haunt for demons, unclean spirits, and unclean birds and beasts.

passages.saying: Come out of her, My people
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the two reasons the verse itself gives for leaving the city.
layers.text: A voice from heaven calls God's people to leave Babylon. They must come out so that they do not share in her sins and are not caught in the punishment about to fall on her.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the words appear to be taken from Jeremiah 51:6 and 51:45, among others. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says they are quoted from Jeremiah 51:6 and 51:45. Barnes says the language is derived from such passages and quotes Jeremiah 51:45 in full.
layers.text: The call repeats God's word through Jeremiah to His people living in ancient Babylon: “Come out of her, My people! Save your lives” (Jeremiah 51:45). As God called Israel out of Babylon before its fall, He calls His people out of this Babylon before her judgment.

passages.saying: her sins are piled up to heaven
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture of sins heaped as high as heaven and God remembering them.
layers.text: Babylon's sins have grown so great that they reach as high as heaven. God, who seemed to be patient with her, now remembers her wrongs and acts in judgment.

layers.evidence: Barnes sets this verse beside Jeremiah 51:9, where the judgment of Babylon reaches unto heaven. Bullinger's Figures of Speech reads Jeremiah 51:9 as showing the size of Babylon's sin that called for such a judgment, and links it to this verse.
layers.text: Jeremiah said of ancient Babylon that “her judgment extends to the sky and reaches to the clouds” (Jeremiah 51:9). John echoes that picture. Babylon's sins are so great that they reach heaven and call for a judgment just as great.

passages.saying: Give back to her as she has done to others
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the command to repay Babylon and the Hebrew way of speaking of double as full payment.
layers.text: Those who carry out God's judgment are told to repay Babylon for the harm she did to others. The double portion mixed in her own cup means that her punishment will be full and fitting.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Jeremiah 50:15, says those words seem to be referred to and much the same are used of mystical Babylon in this verse, and on Jeremiah 50:29 he again compares this verse. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Jeremiah 50:15, calls it just retribution in kind and applies it to spiritual Babylon here.
layers.text: The command repeats Jeremiah's word against ancient Babylon: “as she has done, do the same to her” (Jeremiah 50:15). The just repayment once promised against the first Babylon now falls on this later Babylon.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that the verb for repaying her and for what she rendered to others is the same word, and glosses both the cup she filled and the filling for her as mixing. Gill reads the verse as vengeance by way of retaliation for what she had done.
layers.text: In John's Greek the same verb is used for what Babylon gave out and what she must be given back (apedoken and apodote). She is also served from the cup she mixed, with the same verb for mixing (ekerasen and kerasate). The echoing words show the punishment matching the crime.

passages.saying: I sit as queen; I am not a widow
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Babylon's own boast, which shows her pride and false sense of safety.
layers.text: Babylon is to suffer torment in proportion to her pride and luxury. In her heart she boasts that she rules as a queen, will never be left alone like a widow, and will never mourn.

layers.evidence: Gill says the queen boast refers to Isaiah 47 and points to Isaiah 47:8 for both no widow and no sorrow. Wesley says she speaks in her heart as ancient Babylon did in Isaiah 47:8-9. The Companion Bible refers the words to Isaiah 47:8.
layers.text: Her boast repeats the boast of ancient Babylon in Isaiah, who said, “I will never be a widow or know the loss of children” (Isaiah 47:8). Both cities trusted in their power and thought sorrow could never reach them, and both are brought down.

passages.saying: What city was ever like this great city?
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the sailors' cry as they watch the city burn.
layers.text: Sailors and traders who grew rich from Babylon watch the smoke of her burning from far away. They cry out that no city was ever like this great city, mourning both her greatness and the size of her ruin.

layers.evidence: Gill says the sailors here speak as the sailors did of Tyre in Ezekiel 27, and that this and other expressions in the lament are borrowed from there, including the dust on their heads. Wesley says most of the expressions about Babylon's downfall are taken from Ezekiel's description of the downfall of Tyre.
layers.text: The sailors' cry borrows from Ezekiel's lament over the sea trading city of Tyre, where seamen mourned, “Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?” and put dust on their heads (Ezekiel 27:30-32). Babylon falls as the great merchant city of old fell.

passages.saying: Rejoice over her, O heaven
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast between the world's mourning and heaven's call to rejoice at God's justice.
layers.text: While kings, merchants and sailors mourn, heaven and God's people are told to rejoice. Babylon had persecuted the saints, and now God has judged her on their behalf.

layers.evidence: Gill, on Jeremiah 51:48, explains heaven and earth singing at Babylon's destruction and says the like will be done at the fall of mystical Babylon in this verse. Bullinger's Figures of Speech pairs Jeremiah 51:48 with this verse as part of the same judgment on Babylon.
layers.text: The call echoes Jeremiah's word about the first Babylon: “heaven and earth and all that is in them will shout for joy over Babylon” (Jeremiah 51:48). The joy promised at ancient Babylon's fall is called for again at the fall of this Babylon.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says the Greek literally reads judged your judgment and names it the figure polyptoton, a word repeated in another form. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives the same literal rendering of the Greek.
layers.text: John's Greek says literally that God judged your judgment on her, pairing a verb and a noun from the same root (ekrinen and krima). The doubled wording stresses that God has fully settled His people's case against Babylon.

passages.saying: a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's act and his own explanation of it.
layers.text: A mighty angel hurls a huge millstone into the sea. Like the stone vanishing beneath the waves, Babylon will be thrown down with sudden violence and never be found again.

layers.evidence: Gill compares the stone cast into the Euphrates as a sign of old Babylon's destruction in Jeremiah 51:63. Barnes says the origin of the image is probably Jeremiah 51:63-64. Wesley says Jeremiah foreshowed the fall of Chaldean Babylon by a like emblem, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also points to Jeremiah 51:63-64.
layers.text: The angel's act echoes a sign in Jeremiah. Seraiah was told to tie a stone to Jeremiah's scroll of judgment against Babylon, throw it into the Euphrates, and say that Babylon would sink and never rise again (Jeremiah 51:63-64). Here the angel hurls a stone like a great millstone into the sea.

passages.saying: nor the sound of a millstone be heard in you again
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's list of a city's everyday sounds that will never be heard again.
layers.text: The angel describes Babylon's ruin by what will never be heard there again: no music, no craftsmen at work, no millstone grinding grain. Everything that makes a city alive, from its pleasures to its daily bread, will be gone for good.

layers.evidence: Gill on Jeremiah 25:10 says John seems to have borrowed phrases from it in Revelation 18:22, following the Hebrew text, and on this verse he points to Jeremiah 25:10 for the millstone. The Companion Bible says Jeremiah 25:10 is quoted in Revelation 18:23.
layers.text: This list borrows phrases from Jeremiah 25:10, where God says He will banish from Judah "the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp." In this verse and the next, the same signs of ordinary life vanish from Babylon.

layers.evidence: Gill says the words about the harpers seem to be taken from Isaiah 24:8, and in his note on Isaiah 24:8 he sets the two passages side by side.
layers.text: The silenced music may also echo Isaiah 24:8, where God's judgment on the earth means "the joyful harp is silent." Babylon's harpists and musicians fall silent in the same way.

passages.saying: a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of the rider's robe and His name.
layers.text: The rider on the white horse, who is Christ, wears a robe dipped in blood, a picture of judgment and battle. His name is The Word of God, a title that belongs to Him alone.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Isaiah 63:2 is alluded to here and that the blood there is that of His foes. Barnes calls Isaiah 63:2-3 the probable original of the image, and Wesley explains the blood as that of the enemies He has conquered, pointing to Isaiah 63:1.
layers.text: The blood-dipped robe recalls Isaiah 63:1-3. There the mighty Savior comes from Edom in crimson-stained garments and is asked why His clothes are red. He answers that He trod the winepress of judgment alone, and His enemies' blood stained His clothes.

layers.evidence: Gill says this name of Christ is often used by John in his Gospel, his letters and this book, pointing to John 1:1. Barnes notes that the title Logos for the Son is found in the New Testament only in John's writings.
layers.text: His name, The Word of God, echoes the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." In the New Testament, only John's writings call Jesus the Word.

passages.saying: He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's three pictures of the rider's judgment: sword, scepter and winepress.
layers.text: Christ comes as judge and king. A sharp sword comes from His mouth to strike down the nations, He rules them with an iron scepter, and He crushes His enemies like grapes in the winepress of God's fierce anger.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says there is allusion here to Isaiah 11:4. The Companion Bible lists Isaiah 11:4 among this verse's references, and Gill on Isaiah 11:4 applies the smiting of the earth to Revelation 19:15.
layers.text: The sword from His mouth "with which to strike down the nations" recalls Isaiah 11:4, where the promised King from Jesse's line "will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth." His spoken word is the weapon that defeats the wicked.

layers.evidence: Gill says the phrase is taken out of Psalm 2:9, a prophecy of Christ, and notes there that the Septuagint renders it shall feed or rule them. The Companion Bible lists Psalm 2:9 among this verse's references and says the Greek word for rule is literally shepherd.
layers.text: "He will rule them with an iron scepter" comes from Psalm 2:9, God's promise to His anointed King: "You will break them with an iron scepter." John's Greek uses the word for shepherding, as the old Greek translation of the psalm does, but this shepherd's rod is iron.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion seems to be to Isaiah 63:3 and ties the winepress to the blood-dipped robe. Barnes says the language is probably derived from Isaiah 63:1-4, and the Companion Bible lists Isaiah 63:3 among the verse's references.
layers.text: "He treads the winepress" of God's fury, just as in Isaiah 63:3 the Lord says, "I have trodden the winepress alone." His enemies are crushed like grapes, which is why His robe is already stained red in verse 13.

passages.saying: Come, gather together for the great supper of God
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's call to the birds and the next verse's list of the fallen.
layers.text: An angel standing in the sun calls all the birds to the great supper of God. It is a grim picture of a battle so great that the bodies of the fallen will be left for the birds to eat.

layers.evidence: Wesley says the great supper of God is a figure taken from Ezekiel 39:17. Gill on Ezekiel 39:17 says a like invitation is given in Revelation 19:17, with an angel calling instead of the prophet, and that respect is had to Ezekiel's passage.
layers.text: The call echoes Ezekiel 39:17, where God tells the prophet, "Call out to every kind of bird and to every beast of the field," to come to a great feast on the fallen army of Gog. Here an angel summons the birds to the same kind of feast on the armies Christ is about to defeat.

passages.saying: those seated on them had been given authority to judge
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on what John says he saw in the verse.
layers.text: John sees thrones, and those seated on them are given authority to judge. He also sees those killed for their witness to Jesus and those who refused the beast and its mark. They come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years.

layers.evidence: Wesley names the saints as the ones seated on the thrones and points to Daniel 7:22. Gill ties the thrones and the judgment to Daniel 7:9 and 7:22. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Daniel 7:22, and its note there links the saints' judgment and kingdom to Revelation 20:4. Barnes also notes the likeness to Daniel 7:9.
layers.text: The scene echoes Daniel 7, where Daniel saw thrones set up and the Ancient of Days "pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom." Read this way, those seated here are those saints, now given authority to judge.

passages.saying: Gog and Magog
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in Revelation 20:7-9.
layers.text: When Satan is released after the thousand years, he goes out to deceive the nations in every part of the earth, called Gog and Magog, and gathers them for war. Their army is too large to count, like the sand of the seashore.

layers.evidence: Gill says these are not the same as Ezekiel's Gog and Magog, though the names are taken from there with an allusion to them. Wesley says Ezekiel also calls the prince Gog and that Revelation is brief because Ezekiel described it so fully. Barnes traces both names to Ezekiel 38 and 39.
layers.text: Gog and Magog are names taken from Ezekiel 38 and 39, where God speaks against "Gog of the land of Magog," who leads a vast army against God's people in the last days. Interpreters differ on whether it is the same battle, but John borrows Ezekiel's names for this last rebellion.

passages.saying: And there were open books, and one of them was the Book of Life
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the opened books as the record of human deeds, brought out at the final judgment.
layers.text: John sees the dead, great and small, standing before God's throne. Books recording their deeds are opened, along with the Book of Life, and the dead are judged according to what they have done.

layers.evidence: Clarke says John evidently alludes to Daniel 7:10, Gill says reference seems to be had to it, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to the same verse for the opened books. Both scenes show books opened before God's throne.
layers.text: The opened books likely echo Daniel's vision of God's judgment, where 'The court was convened, and the books were opened' (Daniel 7:10). Here books are opened again as the dead stand before the throne to be judged.

passages.saying: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Wesley places this vision after the resurrection and general judgment, as a new and eternal state of all things.
layers.text: After the final judgment John sees a new heaven and a new earth. The first heaven and earth have passed away, and there is no longer any sea.

layers.evidence: Gill on Isaiah 65:17 says its new heavens and new earth are what John saw in vision. Barnes notes the New Testament uses Isaiah's phrase for the future state of the righteous, citing this verse, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the two passages.
layers.text: John sees what God promised through Isaiah: 'For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth' (Isaiah 65:17). The promise the prophet announced is shown fulfilled after the final judgment.

passages.saying: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that God will dwell with the redeemed as if in a tabernacle prepared for His home among them.
layers.text: A loud voice from the throne announces that God will now live among His people. They will be His people, and He Himself will be with them as their God.

layers.evidence: Gill calls this an allusion to the tabernacle among the Israelites and the fulfilment of the promise in Ezekiel 37:27. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and G. Currey (Barnes' Notes), commenting on Ezekiel 37:27, both see that promise reaching its fullness here in Revelation 21.
layers.text: This fulfills Ezekiel 37:27: 'My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people.' In John's Greek the word for dwelling place means a tent, recalling the tabernacle where God lived among Israel in the wilderness.

layers.evidence: Gill calls this the Immanuel, God with us; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it realizes fully His name Immanuel; Bullinger's Companion Bible calls it the final fulfilment of the promise in Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23.
layers.text: The words 'God Himself will be with them' fully realize the name Immanuel, which means God with us. Isaiah 7:14 promised it as a sign, and Matthew applies it to Jesus in the account of His birth. What began then is complete here.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes it is the same Greek word used of the Son tabernacling among us, first in weakness and at last in glory. Bullinger's Companion Bible gives the verb skenoo and points to John 1:14.
layers.text: In John's Greek, the verb for dwell means to live in a tent, the same verb John used in his Gospel: 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us' (John 1:14). He who once lived among people in humble flesh will then live with them in open glory.

passages.saying: there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Wesley explains that death, sorrow, crying and pain belonged to the former heaven and earth and are now gone for the saints.
layers.text: God will wipe every tear from His people's eyes. Death, mourning, crying and pain will be gone forever, because the old order of things has passed away.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the line about wiping away tears is quoted here from Isaiah 25:8. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains swallowing up death as abolishing it for ever, citing this verse, and Gill ties the same verse of Isaiah, with its end of death and tears, to this one.
layers.text: The wiping of tears comes from Isaiah 25:8, a verse that also promises the end of death: 'He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face.' What Isaiah promised is pictured here as done.

layers.evidence: Gill says Isaiah 65:19 will be fully accomplished when the tabernacle of God is with men, citing this verse. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the promise was foretold first of Jerusalem and then of all the redeemed, citing this verse.
layers.text: The end of mourning and crying also echoes God's promise for Jerusalem in Isaiah 65:19: 'The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her.' What was foretold of Jerusalem is here true of all the redeemed.

passages.saying: To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the spring of the water of life as a common Bible picture of salvation, flowing freely for all who thirst.
layers.text: God declares that His work is complete. He is the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, and He promises to give the water of life freely to everyone who is thirsty.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains freely with Isaiah's words, without money and without price, and refers to Isaiah 55:1. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown lists Isaiah 55:1 among the passages behind this promise of water for the thirsty.
layers.text: The free gift of water to the thirsty may recall Isaiah 55:1, where God calls, 'Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters' and offers wine and milk 'without money and without cost.' The life God gives is a gift, never a purchase.

layers.evidence: Gill says there seems to be an allusion here to the old creation, when God spoke and it was done, and cites Psalm 33:9.
layers.text: Some hear in the cry 'It is done!' an echo of creation, when God spoke and the world came to be, as in Psalm 33:9: 'For He spoke, and it came to be.' The God who made the first world by His word now declares the new one finished.

passages.saying: I will be his God, and he will be My son
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that the overcomer will stand to God in the relation of a son and be honored as a child of God.
layers.text: Everyone who overcomes will inherit all things. God promises to be that person's God, and that person will be His son.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says this is the fullest realization of the promise made in type to Solomon, son of David, and to Christ, the divine Son of David. That promise is the word of 2 Samuel 7:14.
layers.text: Some hear in the promise 'I will be his God, and he will be My son' an echo of God's word about David's son in 2 Samuel 7:14: 'I will be his Father, and he will be My son.' On this reading, what was promised to David's royal line is now given to every believer who overcomes.

passages.saying: he carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that the high mountain gave John an open view of the city in its glory.
layers.text: The angel carries John in the Spirit to a great, high mountain. From there he shows John the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God.

layers.evidence: Gill says Ezekiel was brought to such a mountain in the visions of God and shown a city with its dimensions, as John is here. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares Ezekiel 40:2, where a similar vision is given from a high mountain.
layers.text: John's vision follows the pattern of Ezekiel 40:2, where Ezekiel was taken in visions of God, set on a very high mountain and shown a structure like a city. As Ezekiel then watched the temple being measured, John watches the city being measured.

passages.saying: twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the verse's own description of the wall, gates, names and angels.
layers.text: The city has a great, high wall with twelve gates. Each gate bears the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel, and an angel stands at each gate as a guard.

layers.evidence: Barnes says John seems to have had Ezekiel's city in his eye; Clarke says the description is partly taken from Ezekiel 48:30-35; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note the similar description there. Gill on verse 13 and Keil and Delitzsch on Ezekiel 48 make the same link.
layers.text: Ezekiel's vision of the restored city ends with twelve gates named for the tribes of Israel, three on each side. John's city follows the same pattern: twelve gates bearing the tribes' names, three facing each direction.

passages.saying: all its dimensions were equal—12,000 stadia in length and width and height.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note, with the Septuagint named as an ancient witness.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: a stade was about 607 feet (185 m).
layers.text: An angel shows John "the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God" and measures it with a golden rod. Its length, width and height are equal, 12,000 stadia each: a cube about 1,400 miles (2,200 km) on a side.

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale (Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48, 2005): the city is cubic because only the Holy of Holies was a cube (1 Kings 6:20). The Pulpit Commentary on Revelation 21:16 says the same.
layers.text: The shape points to one room, the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple: "twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high," overlaid with pure gold. The city is pure gold too. The holiest room has become the whole city.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: dwelling place, traditionally tabernacle, literally tent. The Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott and Gill link Ezekiel 37:27 and Leviticus 26:11-12, given on Mount Sinai (Leviticus 26:46).
layers.text: The voice from the throne explains: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them." The word is skene, a tent or tabernacle. It fulfills God's promise at Sinai, "I will make My dwelling place among you," repeated in Ezekiel.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) and Benson on Ezekiel 48:35 point ahead to Revelation 21:2-3; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the reality will be best expressed by this descriptive title.
layers.text: Ezekiel's vision of the restored city ends with its name: "from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE," in Hebrew YHWH shammah. The new Jerusalem is the city whose very name is God's presence.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ellicott, Barnes, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary compare Ezekiel 48:30-35; the Geneva notes give the gates to the Old Testament and the foundations to the New. Gill on Revelation 21:14 cites Hebrews 11:10.
layers.text: Like Ezekiel's city, its gates bear "the names of the twelve tribes of Israel," and its foundations "the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb": one people of God. It is "the city with foundations" Abraham awaited, "whose architect and builder is God."

layers.evidence: The Septuagint of Exodus 28:17-20 shares eight names with Revelation 21:19-20: jasper, sapphire, emerald, sardius, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, amethyst. Ellicott notes the order differs; Gill and Benson see an allusion. The Concise Commentary, abridging William Tong's continuation of Matthew Henry, warns that we are only to take general ideas from the description.
layers.text: The foundations are "adorned with every kind of precious stone," as Isaiah promised. The high priest wore twelve stones for the tribes, and eight of John's twelve are on the Greek Old Testament's list, in another order. Some warn against pressing the details.

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale (Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48, 2005): all God's people will have become high priests. MacLaren and Gill also see the high priest's plate here.
layers.text: Only the high priest wore God's name on his forehead, on a gold plate engraved "HOLY TO THE LORD." In the city every servant of God bears it: "His name will be on their foreheads." What one man wore before the LORD, all His people now wear.

passages.saying: The foundations of the city walls were adorned with every kind of precious stone
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the verse's own list of the foundation stones.
layers.text: The foundations of the city wall are made of precious stones, one kind for each foundation. The first four are jasper, sapphire, chalcedony and emerald, and the next verse names eight more.

layers.evidence: Gill sees some allusion to the breastplate stones that bore the tribes' names; Wesley compares the breastplate with these foundations; Clarke on verse 20 says the stones are nearly the same as in Exodus 28:17. The Companion Bible notes also compare them with Aaron's breastplate.
layers.text: The high priest's breastplate held twelve precious stones, each engraved with the name of one of Israel's tribes. The twelve foundation stones of the new city echo it, and several of the same stones appear in both lists, such as jasper, sapphire, emerald and amethyst.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Isaiah 54:11 says John possibly had that passage in his eye; Keil and Delitzsch say the Apocalypse works out in detail the picture of the new Jerusalem that Isaiah sketches there; Gill on this verse points to Isaiah 54:11, and Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Isaiah 54:11 compare Revelation 21:18-21.
layers.text: Isaiah promised the afflicted city that God would lay its foundations with sapphires and make all its walls of precious stones. John's new city seems to fill out that picture: its foundations are adorned with every kind of jewel, the second of them sapphire.

passages.saying: And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: The city needs no sun or moon to light it. God's own glory shines on it, and the Lamb, Jesus Christ, is its lamp.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Isaiah 60:19 says John's words are probably derived from it; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Isaiah 60:19-20 on this verse, and the Companion Bible notes compare the two. Gill also points to Isaiah 60:19.
layers.text: Isaiah promised Zion: "No longer will the sun be your light by day," for "the LORD will be your everlasting light." John's words likely draw on that promise. The city needs no sun or moon, because the glory of God lights it and the Lamb is its lamp.

passages.saying: By its light the nations will walk
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: The nations will live by the light that shines from the city, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it as an offering to God.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the imagery and language are doubtless derived from Isaiah 60:3-14; Wesley says the whole verse is taken from Isaiah 60:3; Gill on Isaiah 60:3 says Revelation 21:24 applies it to the nations of the saved. Clarke calls the verse an allusion to the promise that the Gentiles would bring their riches and glory to Jerusalem.
layers.text: Isaiah told Zion: "Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn." He also saw the wealth of the nations brought into the city, with their kings led in procession. John sees this in the new city, where the nations walk by its light and kings bring their glory into it.

passages.saying: a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: The angel shows John a river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. All the life and joy of the city come from God.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls it doubtless an allusion to the river of Eden and adds Ezekiel 47; Clarke calls it evidently a reference to the river of paradise and to Ezekiel 47; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compare Genesis 2:10-14 and Ezekiel 47. Wesley also points to Ezekiel 47.
layers.text: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and Ezekiel saw a river flowing from the temple with fruit trees on its banks. John's river of the water of life recalls both. It pictures Eden regained, with the river now flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb.

passages.saying: On either side of the river stood a tree of life
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts and word lists from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), the cross-references from OpenBible.info, and the writers named under each note.

layers.text: John's last vision shows a river of life flowing from God's throne through the new Jerusalem, with the tree of life on both banks and its leaves "for the healing of the nations."

The Bible ends where it began. Eden had a river and the tree of life; after the fall the way to that tree was guarded. Now it stands open: "Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life."
The picture also comes from Ezekiel's vision of water flowing from the temple, with fruit trees on both banks that bear every month and leaves for healing.

"No longer will there be any curse" answers the curse on the ground in Genesis 3 and echoes Zechariah's promise that Jerusalem would never again be under the ban (cherem, which BSB renders "utter destruction").

"They will see His face." Adam and Eve hid from God's presence, and Moses was told no one can see God's face and live. Jesus promised that the pure in heart will see God. At the end, what was lost and forbidden is given.
"The Lord God will shine on them" takes up Isaiah's promise: "the LORD will be your everlasting light."

passages.saying: No longer will there be any curse.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: There will be no more curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and His servants will worship Him there.

layers.evidence: Gill says there will be no curse as there was in Eden; Clarke says our first parents came under the curse in paradise, but neither the saints nor the earth will be cursed again; Barnes says the curse pronounced at the fall, with its thorns and thistles, will be unknown.
layers.text: When Adam sinned, God said, "cursed is the ground because of you," and toil, pain and death followed. In the new city there will no longer be any curse. What was lost in Eden is undone, and God and the Lamb reign there.

layers.evidence: Gill on Zechariah 14:11 says John's words seem to be taken from it, where the Hebrew is cherem; the Companion Bible notes compare Zechariah 14:11 and its Septuagint word anathema; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite it as a foretaste of this promise.
layers.text: Zechariah promised Jerusalem that "never again will there be an utter destruction." His Hebrew word, cherem, means something devoted to destruction, and the old Greek translation renders it anathema. John's Greek here, katathema, is a close relative of that word.

passages.saying: They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads.
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: God's servants will see His face and live in His presence. His name will be on their foreheads, marking them openly as His own.

layers.evidence: Wesley notes that seeing God's face was not granted to Moses, whom God told he could not see His face and live.
layers.text: When Moses asked to see God's glory, God told him, "You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live." Some see a contrast: what was not granted even to Moses is given to all of God's servants in the new city: they will see His face.

layers.evidence: Benson says there seems in this expression to be an allusion to God's name on the golden plate the high priest wore on his forehead. Gill also reports that some see an allusion to the inscription Holiness to the Lord on the high priest's mitre.
layers.text: Some see an echo of the high priest, who wore a gold plate on his forehead engraved HOLY TO THE LORD. Read this way, the name of God that every servant bears on the forehead in the new city marks each one openly as holy and as belonging to Him.

passages.saying: Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain words of the verse; Wesley and Barnes read it as Christ bringing reward and judgment with Him at His coming.
layers.text: Jesus promises that He is coming soon, and that He brings His reward with Him. When He comes He will repay each person according to what he has done.

layers.evidence: Gill says these words are taken out of Isaiah 40:10 and that comparing the two shows Christ is the true Jehovah. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cross-references Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 at this verse, and this verse at Isaiah 40:10.
layers.text: The words "My reward is with Me" seem drawn from Isaiah 40:10, where the Lord GOD comes with might and "His reward is with Him" (see also Isaiah 62:11). If so, Jesus speaks of His own coming in words Isaiah used of the LORD.

passages.saying: Blessed are those who wash their robes
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains washing the robes as washing them in the blood of the Lamb, as in Revelation 7:14.
layers.text: Jesus pronounces a blessing on those who wash their robes, made clean through the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14). They are given the right to the tree of life and may enter the holy city through its gates.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the redeemed would not be forbidden to approach the tree as Adam was; Wesley notes that Adam was driven from the tree of life when he broke God's command.
layers.text: After Adam sinned, he was driven out of Eden and cherubim were set to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). Here the redeemed are given the right to that tree. What was shut off at the fall is opened again.

passages.saying: I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke read the Morning Star as Christ ushering in the everlasting day of glory.
layers.text: Jesus Himself confirms that He sent His angel to give this testimony for the churches. He is the Root and the Offspring of David, the promised King of David's line, and the bright Morning Star whose rising announces the coming day.

layers.evidence: Clarke on Isaiah 11:10 says John took this expression from Isaiah, Christ applying it to Himself in Revelation 5:5 and 22:16. Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 11:10 also link the Root of Jesse to this verse, and Barnes points back to Isaiah 11 here.
layers.text: The title Root of David takes up Isaiah's promise that the Root of Jesse, David's father, would stand as a banner for the peoples, and the nations would seek Him (Isaiah 11:10). Jesus says He is that promised Root.

layers.evidence: Gill says Christ is compared to a star as in Numbers 24:17, and at Numbers 24:17 calls the Messiah the morning star of this verse. Wesley has Christ say, I am the star out of Jacob, citing Numbers 24:17. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes compare Numbers 24:17.
layers.text: The Morning Star recalls Balaam's prophecy: "A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel" (Numbers 24:17). Jesus names Himself as that promised star, whose light ends the night.

passages.saying: let the one who is thirsty come
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's wording; Barnes reads the whole verse as a summary of the gospel's free invitation.
layers.text: The Spirit and the bride, the church, say Come, and everyone who hears is to join the call. Anyone who is thirsty may come, and whoever desires it may take the water of life as a free gift.

layers.evidence: Gill says the freeness here, without money and without price, seems to refer to Isaiah 55:1. Barnes sends readers to his notes on Isaiah 55:1 for the call to the thirsty, and Matthew Henry's Concise ties the living waters of Isaiah 55:1 to this verse.
layers.text: Some hear in this call an echo of Isaiah 55:1: "Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters" and buy "without money and without cost". The Bible closes with this free invitation: the thirsty may come and drink the water of life freely.

passages.saying: If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues
passages.source: Sources: the BSB, the Hebrew and Greek texts from STEPBible (Tyndale House, Cambridge), and the writers named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain words; Barnes says the warning guards the book against any addition or change.
layers.text: A solemn warning closes the book: whoever adds to the words of this prophecy will receive the plagues it describes. The next verse warns that whoever takes words away will lose his share in the tree of life and the holy city.

layers.evidence: Wesley compares this warning to Moses guarding the Law in Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32. Keil and Delitzsch on Deuteronomy 4:2 say that precept is enforced again in Revelation 22:18-19. Bullinger's Companion Bible notes at Deuteronomy 4:2 and Revelation 22:19 compare the two texts.
layers.text: The warning echoes Moses: "You must not add to or subtract from what I command you" (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). The same guard Moses set around God's Law is set around this final book of prophecy.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes on add . . . add that it is just retribution in kind. Wesley says he that adds has the plagues added to him, and he that takes away has the blessings taken from him.
layers.text: In John's Greek the same verb names both the sin and the punishment. If anyone adds (epithe), God will add (epithesei) the plagues to him; if anyone takes away (aphele), God will take away (aphelei) his share. The penalty matches the offense.
